THE EUROPEAN COMMISSION,
Having regard to the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union1,
Having regard to the Agreement on the European Economic Area, and in particular Article 57
thereof,
Having regard  to Council Regulation (EC) No 139/2004 of 20.1.2004 on the  control of
concentrations between undertakings2, and in particular Article 8(2) thereof,
Having regard to the Commission's decision of 17 February 2023 to initiate proceedings in this
case,
Having given the undertakings concerned the opportunity to make known their views on the
objections raised by the Commission,
Having regard to the opinion of the Advisory Committee on Concentrations,
Having regard to the final report of the Hearing Officer in this case,
Whereas:

1.     INTRODUCTION
(1)    On 13  January  2023,  the Commission  received  a  notification  of  a  proposed
        concentration pursuant to Article 4 of Council Regulation (EC) No 139/2004 (the
        ‘Merger Regulation’) by which Korean Air Lines Co. Ltd (‘Korean Air’, Republic of
        Korea, referred to hereinafter as ‘South Korea’), controlled by Hanjin KAL Co., Ltd,
         will acquire within the meaning of Article 3(1)(b) of the Merger Regulation sole
         control  of  the  whole  of  Asiana  Airlines  Inc.  (‘Asiana’,  South  Korea). The
        concentration is to be accomplished by way of purchase of shares.3 Korean Air and
        Asiana are referred to hereinafter as ‘the Parties’.4

2.     THE PARTIES AND THE OPERATION
(2)    Korean Air is a full-service air carrier providing international airline services, mainly
          air passenger and air cargo services. Established in 1962, Korean Air, together with its

         subsidiary Jin Air Co., Ltd, is the largest airline in South Korea. It operates a hub-and-
        spoke flight network with its principal hub at Incheon airport in Seoul, South Korea.
      To a lesser extent, Korean Air has activities in aerospace, maintenance, repair and
        overhaul services, ground handling services, reservation and ticketing information
         services and  freight forwarding among others. Korean Air  is a member of the
      SkyTeam alliance. Korean Air’s largest shareholder Hanjin KAL Co., Ltd is active
      among others in transportation, hotels, tourism and airport businesses. The Korea
       Development Bank (“KDB”) held 3.3% of Korean Air’s shares as of September 2022.
(3)     Asiana is a full-service air carrier providing international airline services, mainly air
        passenger and  air cargo services. Established in 1988, Asiana, together with  its
         subsidiaries Air Busan Co., Ltd and Air Seoul Inc., is the second largest airline in
        South Korea. Through Asiana IDT, Inc. it operates a telecommunications business;
        through Asiana Airport, Inc.  it operates  air transport support services  (air cargo
        loading/unloading and ground operations); and through Kumho T&I, it offers financial
         services. Asiana is a member of the Star Alliance. Asiana’s largest shareholder is
      Kumho Engineering & Construction Co., Ltd (“Kumho E&C”).
(4)     Because of Asiana’s financial situation, the KDB and the Export-Import Bank of
       Korea (“KEXIM”) entered into two agreements with Asiana for the purpose of
        providing  it with financial support, dated 23 April 2019 and 14 September 2020.
       Those agreements confer extensive rights to those two banks over Asiana and its
       management.

3.     THE CONCENTRATION
(5)    On 17 November 2020, Korean Air and Asiana entered into a share subscription
        agreement (‘SSA’) according to which Korean Air will acquire 63.88% of the total
        issued and outstanding stock of Asiana (hereinafter referred to as the ‘Transaction’).
       The remaining shares of Asiana will be retained by Kumho E&C (11.12%), Kumho
        Petrochemical Co. Ltd. (3.98%) and by a large number of smaller shareholders
        holding the remaining 21.03% of the shares. The minority shareholders will not hold
       any veto rights that would allow them to exercise control over Asiana and the
        Transaction would thus result in Korean Air acquiring sole control of Asiana.
(6)        It follows that the proposed transaction is a concentration within the meaning of
         Article 3(1)(b) of the Merger Regulation.

4.     UNION DIMENSION
(7)     The undertakings concerned, Korean Air and Asiana, have a combined aggregate
        world-wide turnover of more than EUR 5 000 million5 (Korean Air: EUR […];
        Asiana: EUR […]). Each of them has an EU-wide turnover in excess of EUR 250
         million (Korean Air: EUR […] million and Asiana: EUR […]), but neither of them
        achieves more than two-thirds of its aggregate EU-wide turnover within one and the
       same Member State.6
(8)     The Parties’ turnover data are based on their audited financial accounts for 2019, for
         the reasons set out in section 4.1, and are calculated according to the "50/50 split"
        methodology, for the reasons set out in section 4.2. Since the date for establishing

4.1.    Relevant date for establishing jurisdiction
(10)    Korean Air and Asiana entered into the SSA on 17 November 2020, but notified the
        Transaction only on 13 January 2023.
(11)    In the present case, the relevant date for establishing jurisdiction would have a direct
        impact on the assessment of jurisdiction. If the triggering event for jurisdiction was the
       SSA, the relevant turnover would concern 2019, the year before the beginning of the
       Covid19 pandemic. If the triggering event was instead the notification on 13 January
        2023, the relevant turnover would concern 2021.10 In the latter case, the relevant
        turnover thresholds would not be met since the Parties’ turnover was affected by the
        Covid19-related travel restrictions.11
4.1.1.   The Commission’s consolidated jurisdictional notice
(12)   As regards the relevant date for establishing  jurisdiction, paragraph 156 of the
        Consolidated Jurisdictional Notice (“CJN”)12 stipulates that the relevant date is (i) the
        conclusion of the binding legal agreement; (ii) the announcement of a public bid; (iii)
         the acquisition of a controlling interest or (iv) the date of the  first notification,
        whichever date is earlier.
4.1.2.   Korean Air’s views
(13)    Korean Air considers that the correct date for establishing jurisdiction should not be
         the SSA but the date of the first notification in January 2023.13 According to Korean
         Air, the Commission’s guidance in the CJN on the relevant date for establishing
         jurisdiction assumes that there is only a limited period between the triggering event for
        a  notification  (for instance the signing of a binding agreement) and the actual
         notification. However, in the present case, three financial years (2020, 2021 and 2022)
       have elapsed between 2019 and the formal notification. Korean Air is therefore of the

        opinion that jurisdiction should not be established based on turnover that is outdated
       and no longer reflects the actual financial position of the Parties.14
(14)    Korean Air claims that this view is confirmed by the ruling of the European Court of
         Justice (‘ECJ’) in case C-202/06 - Cementbouw, in which the ECJ states that the
       competence of the Commission to review a transaction must be established at a fixed
         point in time that “must necessarily be closely related to the notification of the
         concentration”.15 According to Korean Air, the relevant date should therefore be the
        date of the  first notification in January 2023 and the appropriate reference year
        consequently the year before the notification took place.
4.1.3.   Commission assessment
(15)    The Commission considers that no exception should be made in the present case from
         the general rule set out in paragraph 156 CJN, namely that the relevant date for
         establishing jurisdiction should be the SSA of November 2020 as the earlier date and
        not the later date of the first notification in January 2023. This is mainly due to the
        following reasons:
(16)     First, the need for legal certainty as to the determination of the Commission’s
         jurisdiction  under  the Merger  Regulation  requires  a  consistent  application  of
        paragraph 156. In that respect, the ECJ held in the Cementbouw case that “the
         authority having competence to examine a concentration must be able to be identified
         in a way which is foreseeable”16 and that the Commission’s competence “cannot be
        challenged at any time or be in a state of constant flux”.17
(17)    Second, the question which authority examines a transaction should not be in the
        hands of the merging companies. Deviating from paragraph 156 CJN may give the
       merging companies the possibility to influence jurisdiction by delaying or accelerating
          notifications.18
(18)     Third, the close link between the relevant date for establishing jurisdiction and the
         notification  to which the ECJ referred  in the Cementbouw case  relied on “the
        importance of the obligation of notification in the system of control put in place by the
       Community legislature”19 which was  still foreseen in Council Regulation (EEC)
      No 4064/8920, which has since been replaced by the Merger Regulation. The system
        put in place by the Merger Regulation, however, abolished the obligation for the
         parties to a concentration to notify within a certain timeframe from the conclusion of a
          final agreement. Accordingly, under the present system of the Merger Regulation, the
         link between the relevant date for establishing jurisdiction and the notification is not as
           strict as it was at the time of the Cementbouw case and the need for legal certainty, as
        mentioned above and also emphasised by the ECJ, must prevail.

4.2.    Geographic allocation of turnover
4.2.1.   The  Commission’s  jurisdictional  notice and  practice  regarding  air  passenger
         transport services
(19)   As set out by paragraph 196 CJN, the general rule for the geographic allocation of
        turnover is that turnover should be attributed to the place where the customer is
         located. The underlying principle is that turnover should be allocated to the location
       where competition with alternative suppliers takes place. According to paragraph 196
      CJN this location is normally the place where the characteristic action under the
         contract in question is to be performed, that is to say where the service is actually
        provided or the product is actually delivered.
(20)     Specifically for services, paragraph 199 CJN establishes that the place of the provision
        of the service to the customer is relevant. In particular, services containing cross-
        border elements should be considered to fall into three general categories, namely (i)
        cases where the service provider travels; (ii) cases where the customer travels; and (iii)
        cases where a service is provided without either the service provider or the customer
        having to travel. According to paragraph 199 CJN, in categories  (i) and  (ii), the
        turnover generated is to be allocated to the place of destination of the traveller, i.e. the
        place where the service is actually provided to the customer whereas in case (iii) the
        turnover generated is to be allocated to the customer’s location.
(21)    However, as regards air passenger transport services, the Commission is of the view
         that the categories included in paragraph 199 CJN do not properly capture the
          specificities of this type of service. As to the first and second categories, the service
        provider and the customer indeed travel, but not to each other’s location. Instead, they
        both travel between the point of origin and the point of destination of the air passenger
         transport service at stake. The third category does not seem relevant either given that
         the service provider and the customer travel and in any event, competition does not
        take place merely at the location of the customer’s location because the service is not
        provided there.
(22)   To capture the specificities of air passenger transport services the Commission has
        developed  three  methodologies  to  geographically  allocate  the  turnover  of  the
        undertakings concerned, namely the “point of sale”, the “point of departure” and the
        “50/50 split”21 methodology:
       The “point of sale” methodology consists in allocating the turnover to the country
       where the ticket sale occurred.

       The “point of departure” (also referred to as “point of origin”) methodology consists in
         allocating the revenue from an individual route operated by an air carrier to the
        country where the place of departure of the flight is located.

       The “50/50 split” consists in allocating the revenue from an individual route operated
       by an air carrier in a 50% ratio to the country of origin and a 50% ratio to the country
         of final destination of the relevant air transport service.

(23)   As regards air cargo services, para. 201 CJN stipulates that cases concerning the
         transport of goods are different. This is mainly due to the fact the customer, to whom
        those services are provided, does not travel, but the transport service is provided to the

        Airways/ Flybe, footnote 28; M.6447 – IAG/ BMI, footnote 15.

        customer at its location. According to para. 201 CJN, those cases would therefore fall
         into the third category (iii) of para. 199 CJN, according to which the location of the
        customer is the relevant criterion for the allocation of the turnover. The Commission’s
         precedents, however, show that the turnover calculation of air cargo transport services
           is always calculated based on the same three methodologies mentioned above for air
        passenger services without differentiation between turnover related to air passenger or
          air cargo services, whenever the merging parties were active in the provision of both
          air cargo and air passenger transport services.22
(24)    In the case at present, the jurisdictional thresholds are only met under one of the three
        methodologies, notably the “50/50 split” methodology, but not under the “point of
         sale” and the “point of departure” methodology.
4.2.2.   Korean Air’s views
(25)    Korean  Air  claims  that  out  of  the  three  methodologies,  the  “point  of  sale”
       methodology should be relied on as the primary methodology for allocating turnover.23
        This methodology would most accurately reflect the location of the customer, which in
         the Parties’ view is the guiding principle for allocating turnover.24
(26)    Korean Air further points out that in the SAirGroup/SAA case, the Commission
         established jurisdiction solely on the basis of the “point of sale” methodology, without
        mentioning other methodologies.25 According to Korean Air, there do not appear to be
          airline merger cases where jurisdiction was established based solely on any of the two
         other methodologies.26 In Korean Air’s view, the Commission has in contrast only
         relied on the “point of origin” and/or the “50/50 split”  methodology in past airline
       merger cases, where the point of sale methodology could not be applied or where
        turnover already exceeded the thresholds under the “point of sale” methodology.
        According to Korean Air, in such latter cases, the notifying parties have typically
         relied only on the point of sale turnover data where it was available, adding (for the
        sake of completeness) that the applicable concentration would also have a Community
        dimension on the basis of the “50/50 split” and the “point of origin” methodologies.27
        According to Korean Air, this view is supported by the Commission’s decision in the
        Ryanair/Aer Lingus case as this decision seems to acknowledge, in Korean Air’s view,
         that other methodologies should only be applied if the “point of sale” turnover is not
         available.28
(27)    Korean Air further explains that the turnover only meets the Merger Regulation
         thresholds under the “50/50 split” because it includes turnover generated in selling

4.2.3.   Commission assessment
(28)    In the case at present, the jurisdictional thresholds are only met under the “50/50 split”
        methodology. The different turnover results depending on whether the “50/50 split”
        methodology, the “point of sale” or the “point of departure” methodologies are used, is
       due to the fact that the large majority of Korean Air’s and Asiana’s passengers
         originate in Korea32:
        •    For the “point of sale” methodology this has an impact in so far as most of the
               Parties’ tickets are sold in Korea and therefore less turnover is allocated to
             Europe.
        •   As regards the “point of origin” methodology, the Commission has established
                that in cases where roundtrips are sold as a bundle with more advantageous
               prices compared to two one way tickets, the roundtrips are considered as one
               single service with in consequence only one single point of origin in contrast to
            two one-way-tickets which were considered as two services with two points of
               origin (one for each flight).33 As Korean Air and Asiana mostly sell roundtrips
               originating  in  South  Korea,34  also  according  to  the  “point  of  origin”
            methodology most of the turnover would be allocated to Korea.
        •      If the “50/50 split” methodology was followed, half of the turnover would be
               allocated to each end of the routes, that is to say half of the turnover would be
               allocated to Korea and half of the turnover would be allocated to the EU,
              independently from the fact whether tickets have been purchased in Korea or the
         EU and whether the airlines business model consists in selling roundtrips with
             only one point of origin or in rather selling two one-way tickets with one
              separate point of origin for each flight.
(29)    The Commission  is  of  the view  that,  in  this  specific  case,  the Commission’s
         jurisdiction to review the Transaction can be based solely on the “50/50 split” method
         for the following reasons:

(30)     First, the Commission’s decisional practice neither shows that the three methods need
         to be considered cumulatively, nor that at least two out of the three methods need to
        lead to the same results. The Commission’s decisional practice demonstrates that
         allocating  turnover based on one  or even two methodologies  is  sufficient  for
         establishing jurisdiction. This is evidenced by several precedents in the airline sector,
       where the Commission effectively established jurisdiction by either relying in one
         case35 on one methodology and in several cases36 on a combination of two out of the
         three methodologies.
(31)    Second, the Commission’s decisional practice does not show that the “point of sale” or
         the “point or origin” method should be relied on as the primary methodology.37 In
         contrast, the Commission has considered  all three methodologies equally  in  its
         precedents.38 Even though it is indeed correct that in the SAir Group/ SAA case the
       Commission established jurisdiction solely based on the “point of sale” methodology,
         the underlying reasons are not clear from the decision as no mention is made of any of
         the other two methodologies. It is therefore not clear from the decision if reliable data
       was only available for the “point of sale” methodology and not for the other two
        methodologies or if the thresholds were at all only met under this but not under the
         other methodologies.39 In the Commission’s view it can therefore not be deduced from
         that decision  that the Commission in past cases considered the “point of sale”
       methodology as the primary methodology for assessing jurisdiction as claimed by the
          Parties.40 This  is also reflected in the Ryanair/ Aer Lingus decision, where the
       Commission stipulates that the “point of sale” methodology “is also increasingly
          difficult to apply in the air transport sector, given the constantly growing shares of
         direct Internet sales (in particular in case of point-to-point, low-cost airlines such as
        Ryanair and, to a large extent, Aer Lingus with the majority of tickets sold over the
         Internet). The absence of a physical transaction at a brick-and-mortar airline counter
        or travel agent makes  it more difficult to physically locate customers purchasing
          tickets. Further, as the customer could buy the ticket on the Internet from practically
       any place in the world, this information would, even  if available, not necessarily
        support the assumption of the Notice on the calculation of turnover that the location of
        customers when purchasing services will normally reflect where the parties to the
         transaction provide their services and the economic strength of the parties in a

         specific Member State.”41 This reasoning also applies to the Parties’ argument that
         certain services such as ticket booking, ticketing (including cancellation, re-ticketing,
        covenants, refunds, accumulation of mileage, etc.), ancillary procedures for boarding,
          etc. are conducted at the point of sales or at the point of origin and therefore argue in
        favour of the “point of sale” or “point of origin” methodology, as also these services
         are now largely provided online and are therefore accessible from various locations all
        over the world.42
(32)     Third, it appears from past practice that the Commission has not prioritised any of the
         three methods over another because there was no need to do so.43 Indeed, it does not
       seem that the Commission has already analysed a situation where it had sufficient data
         to apply all the three methodologies, but the jurisdictional outcome would depend on
         the choice of the applicable method, as in the present case. In Ryanair/ Aer Lingus, the
         parties relied on the “point of departure” and the “50/50 split” methodologies to
         calculate their respective turnover. To the extent that the jurisdictional thresholds were
       met under these two methodologies, the Commission concluded that it was “therefore
        not necessary in this case to decide which of these two possible methodologies is the
       more appropriate.”44 However, the Commission considers that in such a situation,
       where the available methods lead to conflicting results, a choice must be made and
          that, to this end, it should be established which of the available methods better reflects
         the “underlying principle [...] that turnover should be allocated to the location where
        competition with alternative suppliers takes place”.45 This normally corresponds to
        “the place where the characteristic action under the contract in question is to be
        performed,  i.e. where the service  is actually provided”.46 In order to define the
         “characteristic action under the contract” or the relevant “service”, according to para.
       196 CJN, reference has to be made to the contractual obligations of the service
        provider vis-à-vis the customer. In the case of air passenger transport services that
       would be the air passenger transport service between the point of origin at an airport A
       and the point of destination at an airport B. At present, one of these airports would be
         located in the EU and one in Korea. The relevant service  is therefore provided
       between the EU and Korea and that is where competition takes place. As air passenger
         transport services are provided between two places, i.e. the point of origin and the
         point of destination of the flight at issue – and not at the location of the customer or
         solely at the point of departure – the Commission is of the opinion that the “50/50
          split” method should be considered as the most suitable proxy to allocate the turnover
        of air passenger transport service providers. In the Commission’s view, the “50/50
          split” methodology is the only methodology which takes sufficiently into account this
         particular  geographic and  often  cross-border  nature  of  air  transport  services.47
         Specifically for the present case, customers wishing to travel between South Korea
       and the EU, although they start their trip at one side of the route, purchase a service
       whose characteristic action is transportation from the point of origin in South Korea or
         the EU to the point of destination in South Korea or the EU. The characteristic action

(33)    Fourth, while the Commission has not prioritised any of the three methods, the
       Commission has, however, since the very beginning of its merger control cases always
        applied the “50/50 split” methodology, considering this methodology as being a
         particularly   appropriate  methodology   to   geographically   allocate   turnover.
        Accordingly, the Commission states in one of its first airline merger cases Air France /
       Sabena (M.157):
       “Compte tenu de la difficulté inhérente au choix d'un critère de calcul ainsi que des
         possibles résultats divergents entre eux, la Commission a préféré proposer trois
        méthodes sans se prononcer définitivement sur celle qui s'avèrerait la plus adéquate.
       Ces trois méthodes étaient les suivantes :

           (i)    attribution du chiffre d'affaires résultant de la prestation du service de transport
              aérien au pays de destination. Dans le cas de vols aller-retour ou circulaires, le
             pays de destination est celui qui est différent du pays d'origine (par exemple,
             dans le cas d'une route New York/Paris/New York desservie par une compagnie
              américaine, le chiffre d'affaires correspondant devrait être imputé à la France);
            (ii)   attribution du chiffre d'affaires sur la base d'un ratio 50%-50% respectivement
            au pays d'origine et de destination finale;
            (iii)  attribution du chiffre d'affaires résultant du service de transport aérien à l'État
            où le billet a été vendu.
      Même si le deuxième critère semble être le plus proche de l'esprit de l'article 5
       paragraphe 1 car  il vise les deux endroits entre lesquels le service de transport
        aérien a été effectivement rendu, incorporant ainsi le caractère transfrontalier de
          celui-ci, la Commission a examiné les résultats de l'application de chacun d'entre eux
        dans le cas d'AIR FRANCE et de la SABENA. Selon les trois critères, le chiffre
         d'affaires total réalisé dans la Communauté en 1991 tant par le groupe AIR FRANCE
       que par le groupe SABENA a dépassé le montant de 250 millions d'écus sans que plus
        des deux tiers aient été réalisés à l'intérieur d'un seul et même État membre.”48

(34)     Fifth,  in  the  most  recent  airline  merger  case  which  discusses  the  different
        methodologies, the Ryanair  / Aer Lingus decision, the Commission considered the
        “50/50 split” methodology as being particularly appropriate to geographically allocate
        turnover in airline cases as “it has been accepted as a possible approach in a number
         of past cases and seems, as noted in M.157 – Air France / Sabena, close to the spirit of
         the Merger Regulation since it takes into account the two places between which the
         service is actually provided, reflecting the cross-border character of the service in
         question.49 In that respect, the Parties’ argument that it follows from the Ryanair / Aer
        Lingus decision that the “50/50 split” methodology is not the appropriate methodology
         to use when data under the “point of sale” or the “point of origin” methodologies is
         available, cannot be deduced from the wording of the decision. This is even more
        remarkable against the background that the turnover in that decision was calculated in
        accordance with the predecessor version of today’s Merger Regulation,50 which had

        put an emphasis on the place where the customer is located51 whereas the currently
         applicable rules on the geographic allocation of turnover in the CJN52 (in force since
        2008), puts an emphasis on the “location where competition with alternative suppliers
         takes place”. This location is normally also the place where the characteristic action
        under the contract in question is to be performed, i.e. where the service is actually
        provided and the product is actually delivered”.53
(35)     Sixth,  contrary  to what Korean Air  claims,  the Commission’s  opinion  is  not
         inconsistent with the objective of EU merger control to protect consumer welfare in
         the EU. “Consumer welfare in the EU” as referred to by the Parties does not only
        cover the welfare of EU citizens but the welfare of everybody who is purchasing
        products  or  to whom  services  are provided within  the  territory  of  the EU –
        notwithstanding their origins or nationalities. That also covers citizens from third
         countries (such as e.g. South Korea) who purchase services that are provided within
         the territory of the EU. This principle is also reflected in the CJN, for instance in the
         allocation of turnover to the EU in case of non-EU customers purchasing hotel
       accommodation or other services in the EU (see paras. 199 and 200 CJN). In the case
        of air transport services between an EU Member State and a third country, the air
         transport services are delivered between the point of origin at an airport A and the
         point of destination at an airport B, one of which is located within the territory of the
       EU. In that case, 50 % of the overall air transport services are provided within the
          territory of the EU and therefore to customers in the EU.
(36)    Seventh, in the same vein, the “50/50 split” methodology is reflective of a general
         principle under EU merger control which disregards the nationality or country of
        residence of the customers as well as the location of the purchase but focuses on
         effects in the EU territory. In consequence, the impact on consumption within the EU
        should be assessed  irrespective of the consumers'  nationalities. This  is because
        safeguarding competition for consumption in EU territory yields broader economic
         benefits. This holds true even if the consumers possess non-EU nationalities or if they
        purchase a product or service – which is at least partially provided within the EU –
       from outside the EU. This interpretation is also backed up by the legal framework as
         the Merger Regulation does not refer to EU customers and their nationality. Rather it
         refers to a significant impediment to effective competition (“SIEC”) in the internal
        market, e.g., in Recital 6: “A specific legal instrument is therefore necessary to permit
          effective control of all concentrations in terms of their effect on the structure of
        competition in the [Union]”.54 This would also include follow-on effects, such as more
        general economic effects resulting from a reduction in the number of passengers flying
       between the two territories and affecting the exchange between the two territories.
      Any such effects are  felt  at both ends of the  trip. Therefore, the “50/50  split”
       methodology constitutes a suitable proxy to allocate turnover to where competition
       between alternative suppliers has taken place, that is to say 50% to South Korea and
      50% to the relevant EU country at the other side of the route.
(37)    Eighth, as already mentioned above (see paragraph (34)), the Commission in the
        Ryanair / Aer Lingus decision already considered the “50/50 split” methodology as
        being particularly appropriate to geographically allocate turnover in airline cases as it
         takes into account the two places between which the service is actually provided,

         reflecting the cross-border character of the service in question.55 In addition, the
       Commission considers in that decision that “This method also provides a simple and
         clear criterion, and in this respect appears therefore in line with the very purpose of
         the system of thresholds of the Merger Regulation, that is, to provide a simple and
          efficient method to determine the authority that is competent to review a merger.”56
        This is particularly true as the “50/50 split” methodology avoids arbitrary results
        according to whether air carriers sell roundtrip tickets or one-way tickets. As indicated
       above (see paragraph (28)), the Parties in the case at present sell roundtrips that are
       more advantageous than one-way tickets mainly to South Korean customers.57 In
        consequence, the point of departure of these roundtrips is located in South Korea with
         the turnover of these flights being allocated to South Korea. As a result, the turnover
         thresholds are not met neither under the “point of sale” nor under the “point of origin”
       methodology but only under the “50/50 split” methodology. However, if the Parties
       would rather  sell two one-way  tickets instead of roundtrip  tickets, the turnover
         allocation would be split between Europe and South Korea with most probably the
        turnover thresholds being reached under both the “50/50 split” and the “point of
         origin”  methodology. When  applying  the  “point  of  origin”  methodology,  the
         jurisdiction of the Commission therefore depends on the business model of the
         respective airlines of either selling roundtrips (like Korean Air and Asiana) or rather
       two one-way tickets (like Ryanair and Aer Lingus).58 By opting for the “50/50 split”
       methodology the outcome would in contrast not depend on certain sales methods and
         therefore be more transparent, predictable and in consequence legally secure.

6.     THE COMMISSION’S INVESTIGATION
6.1.     Investigative steps
(53)    The Commission collected evidence from various sources at various stages of the
         investigation.
(54)    In the pre-notification phase, the Commission reviewed the information provided in
         the draft Form CO and its accompanying draft annexes. Furthermore, the Commission
        held meetings and conference calls with the Parties as well as with several customers
       and competitors in air passenger and air cargo services. Towards the end of the pre-
         notification phase, the Commission also sent out advance copies of the Phase  I
         investigation questionnaires to competitors.

7.     RELEVANT MARKETS
(72)    The Transaction mainly affects the supply of passenger and cargo  air transport
         services between the EEA and South Korea. In the following, the Commission will set
        out its findings with respect to market definition in (i) passenger air transport services
         (section 7.1) and (ii) cargo air transport services (section 7.2).
7.1.    Passenger air transport services
7.1.1.   Origin & destination (‘O&D’) approach
7.1.1.1. Commission’s decisional practice
(73)    With regard to scheduled passenger air transport services, the Commission has, in its
         prior decisional practice, defined the relevant markets on the basis of the O&D
        approach, where the target was an active air carrier.71
(74)    In  line with the Commission's notice on market  definition,72 where the merger
        involved airlines actively providing air transport services, the Commission has given
        pre-eminence to demand-side substitution, whereby it considered that customers need
         transportation from one point to another and that competition takes place on an O&D
         city-pair basis.73 Consequently, the Commission has traditionally followed the O&D
        approach. Under the O&D approach, every combination of an airport (or city, where
         relevant) of origin to an airport (or city, where relevant) of destination is defined as a
          distinct market.74 The effects of a transaction on competition are thus assessed for each
     O&D separately.
7.1.1.2. Korean Air’s views
(75)    Korean Air does not object in principle to this approach. However, it submits that the
        market should be defined on a case-by-case basis and that in the context of the
        Transaction two separate markets  for each route can be  potentially considered,
        depending on whether the flight (roundtrip) originates from South Korea or from
         outside South Korea (Point of Origin or ‘POO’ approach).75

(76)    According to Korean Air, this narrower market definition more accurately reflects the
        underlying market characteristics.76 Korean Air argues that customers would prefer to
       book flights with carriers from their region and therefore the Parties’ market shares
      may be different depending on the POO.77 Furthermore, according to Korean Air, the
       demand on certain routes differs substantially depending on the point of origin,
        because there is a much higher demand for airlines to fly South Korean passengers to
         the EEA than for carriers to fly EEA passengers to South Korea.78 Moreover, Korean
        Air submits that there are differences in demand and sales channels for each POO,
       which would affect the competitiveness of airlines for each POO and consequently
          their market shares by PPO∗.79 In addition, while Korean Air explains that its price
         setting decision  is largely based on  its competitors’  prices,80  it explains  that  it
         differentiates its pricing policy based on the POO.81
7.1.1.3. Commission assessment
(77)    The Commission’s investigation has overall confirmed that the Commission’s O&D
        approach should also apply to this case. The investigation does not indicate that the
       Commission should depart from the O&D approach to assess the effects of the merger
       between Korean Air and Asiana, which are both active airlines.
(78)     First, while there is no demand-side substitutability between starting a trip in South
       Korea and starting a trip in the EEA, there is full supply-side substitutability. The
          airlines active on the relevant routes connecting the EEA and South Korea all offer
          flights to/from the EEA and to/from South Korea, meaning that they all offer round-
          trips. When arriving at destination, they all have the capacity to take passengers from
         the destination back to the origin of the route, thus allowing passengers to travel the
         route in both directions starting at either end of the route. This is because if an airline
        has already made investments to transport customers on round trips starting at one end
        of the route (e.g., in terms of putting the flight operations in place and hiring personnel
          at both ends of the  route),  it  is inherent in the business operations  that those
        investments can be used to start transporting customers on round trips starting at the
         other end. This is in fact what all airlines active on the routes have done and there is
       no example of an airline active only from one end of the route. While the results of the
        market investigation were inconclusive as to whether an airline offering round trips on
        a specific O&D originating in the EEA would be able to start providing round trips on
         the same O&D pair originating in South Korea quickly and without significant
         investments,82 this issue seems less relevant because in the present case all carriers
         active on the route have in fact already made those investments, sell seats on the same
          flight simultaneously to customers with different POOs and can therefore react quickly
       and without additional investments to any changes in demand or supply conditions for
         the POOs relevant for the assessment of the Transaction.
(79)    Second,  the competitive  conditions  are comparable  for  the  different POOs.  In
          particular, on the same O&D pair between the EEA and South Korea (regardless of
        whether the passenger starts the round-trip journey from South Korea or from the
       EEA), the air carriers that are present, the available seat capacity and the service levels

(82)     Fifth, the O&D approach is considered to be appropriate by market participants. The
        majority of the respondents to the market investigation expressing views support the
        appropriateness of the O&D approach to assess the effects of the Transaction.91 In

       measure for understanding how many passengers want to  fly between any two
         points.”92 That said, the Commission acknowledges that some market participants
        pointed to some differences in competitive dynamics depending on the POO. For
        example, a competitor noted the differences in the passenger profile depending on
        whether they originate in South Korea or in the EEA.93 In addition, the majority of
        competitors expressing views talked about differences regarding (i) ticket prices; and
            (ii) convenience of the time schedules.94 The Commission will therefore take into
        account the particularities of the competitive dynamics depending on the POO when
         assessing the closeness of competition in the competitive assessment.

(83)     Sixth, the Commission has analysed the differences in market shares between POO
     EEA and POO South Korea.95 For the routes ICN to/from BCN, CDG, FRA and FCO

        approximately [0-5]% up to approximately [10-20]% depending on the IATA season;

        approximately [10-20]% depending on the IATA season. There is a larger difference
       from approximately [20-30]% up to approximately [30-40]% depending on the IATA
        season in terms of market shares between both POOs only in the ICN-FCO route.

        environment as they include Alitalia’s market share. Alitalia ceased its operations on
       15 October 2021.96 When assessing the set of market shares where Alitalia’s market
        shares have been allocated proportionally to  its competitors, as provided by the
          Parties,97 market shares divergences still exist between both POOs on the ICN-FCO
         route, but are less significant and can go up to approximately [20-30]% depending on
         the IATA season. However, these differences do not outweigh the Commission’s other
         findings regarding the O&D approach.
(84)    In light of the above, for the purposes of this Decision, the Commission will apply the
     O&D approach, but will take into account the particularities of competitive dynamics
        depending on the POO when assessing how closely the Parties and their competitors
        compete. Furthermore, the Commission will take account of the fact that both Korean
        Air and Asiana are network carriers that also operate connecting flights – which goes
       beyond the assessment of route-by-route overlaps – and of their strong presence at the
       same airport in its competitive assessment of the effects of the Transaction.
7.1.2.   Distinction between services supplied at wholesale level to tour operators and retail
         level to final customers
(85)     Carriers, both charter and scheduled airlines, may sell seats (or entire flights) to tour
         operators, which resell those seats to end customers or sell package holidays in which
        those seats are integrated.
7.1.2.1. Commission’s decisional practice
(86)    In prior decisions, whenever appropriate, the Commission has regarded the wholesale
        supply of airline seats to tour operators (wholesale market) as a distinct market from
         the supply of scheduled air transport services to end customers (retail market).98 The
       Commission found that from a demand-side perspective, tour operators have different
        requirements from those of individual passengers (for example, purchase of large seat
        packages in advance from the start of the season or negotiation of rebates).99

(87)    In recent  decisions,100 the Commission has considered  that,  for the purpose of
         assessing the horizontal effects of a transaction, the supply of airline seats to tour
         operators only constitutes a meaningful market on routes where both parties are active
         in sales to tour operators to a significant extent. Indeed, in the absence of any
         (material) overlap, a separate assessment of the market for the supply of airline seats
         to tour operators cannot be considered relevant. Conversely, a separate assessment of
         the market for the retail supply of airline seats may be relevant if there is a significant
         difference in competitive position of the air carriers present in the wholesale and retail
        markets.
7.1.2.2. Korean Air’s views
(88)    Korean Air submits that there could be a degree of demand-side substitutability and
        supply-side substitutability between the wholesale supply of seats to tour operators
       and the sales of air transport services to end customers101 and that, in any case, the
         Parties’ sales to European102 tour operators account for only a limited part of their air
        passenger revenues.103
7.1.2.3. Commission assessment
(89)    For the purposes of this Decision, the Commission finds that it is not necessary to
         distinguish between services supplied at wholesale or retail level. While the demand
         characteristics of tour operators, purchasing airline seats at the wholesale market are
         different of those of passengers purchasing tickets at the retail market, on the supply
         side, all airlines are offering services at both segments of the market or could start
        doing so quickly and without incurring significant additional costs.104
7.1.3.   Distinction between passenger groups
7.1.3.1. Commission’s decisional practice
(90)    The Commission has in its decisional practice considered distinguishing, for a given
     O&D route, between (i) time sensitive (“TS” or “premium”) passengers who tend to
         travel for business purposes, require significant flexibility for their tickets and are
         willing to pay higher prices for this flexibility, and (ii) non-time sensitive (“NTS” or
       “non-premium”) passengers who travel predominantly for leisure purposes or to visit
         friends and relatives, do not require flexibility with their booking and are more price-
         sensitive than TS passengers.105
(91)    However, in recent decisions, the Commission has noted that most passengers are
       becoming increasingly price-sensitive and more and more corporate customers apply
        lowest fare policies, at least with respect to short-haul routes.106

(92)    In particular, the Commission has found for short-haul flights107 that the distinction
       between TS and NTS has become somewhat artificial, as the offerings for TS and NTS
        passengers on these routes have become very similar.108 The Commission concluded
         that it was not appropriate on short-haul routes to define separate markets for TS and
      NTS and instead considered a market comprising all passengers.109
(93)    For long-haul flights,110 the Commission has considered that  it may be relevant to
         distinguish between TS and NTS passengers.111 On the one hand, it has concluded that
         services in at least First and Business class, and services in restricted Economy,112
       were in different product markets on transatlantic routes.113 On the other hand, it has
        assessed  the  possible  effects  of  concentrations  on O&D  city-pairs  without
         distinguishing between TS and NTS travellers when the vast majority of the parties’
        passengers were NTS travellers.114
7.1.3.2. Korean Air’s views
(94)    Korean Air does not consider  it meaningful to segment markets between types of
        passengers into TS and NTS. According to Korean Air, the distinction between TS and
      NTS passengers is not appropriate, as (i) business travel is expected to witness a
         structural  decline  in  the post-Covid19  era  as  corporate spending on  travel  is
         reduced;115 (ii) corporate customers are increasingly price sensitive and the offerings
         for TS and NTS passengers are becoming very  similar;116  (iii) the competitive
       dynamics are uniform under this distinction between not only the Parties, but between
           all the market players.117
7.1.3.3. Commission assessment
(95)    For the purposes of this Decision and for the reasons set out below, the Commission
        considers that the question of whether a distinction between TS and NTS passengers is
         relevant can be left open, as this would not change the outcome of the competitive
        assessment. Competition concerns  arise regardless of whether the assessment  is
         carried out on the overall market or on the two potential sub-markets of TS and NTS
        passengers.
(96)    Evidence collected in the course of the investigation is mixed, pointing both towards
       and against distinguishing between TS and NTS passengers.
(97)   On the one hand, first, TS passengers appear to be a noteworthy part of each route. In
          particular, based on information provided by the Parties, the ratio of TS passengers for

       and viability.126
(102)   Third, a market participant estimates  that the  distinction between TS and NTS
        passengers  has become “[…] somewhat  blurred,  as some  business  travellers
         increasingly travel on economy fares, whereas leisure travellers might choose a
       “premium” cabin to secure a seat on a high-demand flight […].”127 This view was
       however not confirmed or expressed equally clear by other market participants.

       and could therefore not be used as  substitutes by customers.140 Given  that the

        assessment concerned primarily short-haul O&Ds.142 This means that the approach for
        long-haul O&Ds would  potentially have  to be  adjusted  accordingly, based on
       consumer preferences and their willingness to travel longer distances.143
(109)   In addition, Korean Air has not conducted an analysis to determine which parameters
       would have to be used for airport substitutability regarding the Transaction and does
        not consider it necessary to conclude on airport substitutability.144
(110)   However, Korean Air also notes the following:
(111)   For Seoul, Korean Air submits that from the demand side, GMP airport is an attractive
         alternative to ICN, as it cuts approximatively 30 minutes of ground transportation.145
       From the supply side, other major airlines fly to GMP, such as Air China.146
(112)   For Barcelona, Korean Air submits that other airline operators such as Ryanair market
          their services to GRO and REU as services to “Barcelona (Girona)” and “Barcelona
        (Reus)” respectively.147
(113)   For Frankfurt, Korean Air states that airline operators such as Ryanair market their
         services to HHN as services to “Frankfurt (Hahn)”, suggesting that HHN airport is
         appropriate for passengers heading for Frankfurt.148 In addition, operators such as
        Ryanair also typically consider carriers serving FRA as competitors for its services to
       HHN.149
(114)   For Paris, Korean Air submits  that, on the demand side, most network carriers
        consider CDG and ORY airports to be substitutable, but that low-cost airlines150
        emphasize the importance of having the choice of airport with a view to minimizing
          their unit costs.151 On the supply side, while both CDG and ORY could be used for
         destinations within the EU and to third countries, in practice, most network carriers
       have focused their activities on CDG while airlines operating at ORY mainly focus on
        domestic traffic.152
(115)   For Rome, Korean Air submits that based on the Commission’s market investigation
         in Case M.4439 – Ryanair  / Aer Lingus, FCO and CIA airports were found to be
         substitutable from the customers’ point of view for a large majority of point-to-point
         passengers.153

7.1.4.3. Commission assessment
(116)   The Commission will assess, for each relevant O&D, whether flights departing from
         airports with overlapping catchment areas belong to the same market.
(117)   Taking into account the relevant routes discussed in this Decision, which are long-haul
         routes, the Commission will analyse in sections 7.1.4.3.1 to 7.1.4.3.5 the question of
         airport substitutability concerning the following cities: (i) outside of the EEA: Seoul;
            (ii) in the EEA: Barcelona, Frankfurt, Paris, and Rome.154 155
7.1.4.3.1.     Seoul
(118)   The city of Seoul  is served by two airports: Incheon airport (ICN), and Gimpo
         International airport (GMP). ICN and GMP are located respectively 68 km and 18 km
       away from Seoul city centre.156
(119)   For the purposes of the O&D assessment, the question of substitutability of ICN and
     GMP is relevant for the long-haul routes between Seoul and the EEA.

(121)   For the purposes of this Decision and for the reasons set out below, the Commission
         will only take into account ICN airport in the competitive assessment, as GMP airport
           is not a close substitutable with ICN on the routes between the EEA and Seoul.
(122)    First, GMP airport is a regional airport, which is currently not used for long-haul direct
        or indirect flights from the EEA to South Korea and vice versa by Korean Air or
        Asiana nor by competing airlines. As a result, customers cannot use this airport to fly
         directly or indirectly, with a single flight ticket, to/from the EEA.157
(123)   Second, GMP airport is focused on domestic and to some extent regional traffic. Only
          five, short-haul international flights are offered from GMP airport, to destinations in
        Japan and China, demonstrating that airlines do not consider it suitable for long-haul
         international flights. Competitors explained that “Korean government never allows
        long-haul routes from GMP”, that “GMP only point-to-point traffic with focus on

        distance from BCN.”170 In addition, the majority of market respondents expressing
        views would not consider operating flights to South Korea from GRO and REU
          airports,171 given that for example “GRO is far away from the primary regional city of
        Barcelona and with significantly less transit options. A majority of passengers would
         prefer to use BCN when traveling to this region for the enhanced amenities and
        convenience”172 and REU is a “Regional European airport and likely challenging for
       widebody operations needing to take long way around Russian airspace.”173

         transportation/accessibility deficits – no primary/hub airport”,193 and that CIA is a
        “low-cost airport with limited infrastructure, services and accessibility”.194
7.1.5.   Distinction between direct and indirect flights
(156)  On a given O&D pair, passengers can travel by way of a direct (or non-stop) flight
       between the point of origin and the point of destination or by way of an “indirect” (or
        one-stop) flight on the same O&D pair via an intermediate destination.195
7.1.5.1. Commission’s decisional practice
(157)   In previous decisions, the Commission has considered that the substitutability between
         direct and indirect  flights on a route-by-route basis depends on various factors,
        including  notably  the  flight  duration,  but  also  price  considerations  or  the
        inconvenience associated with the indirect flight (e.g., obligation to transfer, higher
         vulnerability to disruption).196
(158)   In particular, for short-haul flights, the Commission has considered that indirect flights
       do not generally provide a competitive constraint to direct flights absent exceptional
        circumstances, for example, when the direct connection does not allow for a one-day
         return trip or when the share of indirect flights in the overall market is significant.197
(159)   For long-haul  flights, the Commission has considered that indirect flights could
         constitute a competitive alternative to direct services under certain conditions, in
          particular, if they are marketed as connecting flights on the O&D pair in the computer
         reservation systems, they are operated on a daily basis and cause only a limited
        extension of the trip (maximum 150 minutes connecting time).198
7.1.5.2. Korean Air’s views
(160)   Korean Air submits that indirect one-stop (and not multi-stop)  flights could be
        considered as a close substitute and exert competitive pressure on long-haul direct
          flights.199 Even though indirect flights take longer than non-stop flights, indirect
          flights are offered on more competitive terms (e.g., better price or quality, additional
        options in terms of timing and frequency).200 For example, with relation to the price
         differences between direct and indirect flights, Korean Air submits that “the lowest

7.1.5.3. Commission assessment
(162)   For the purposes of this Decision and for the reasons set out below, the Commission
        considers that the question of whether direct and indirect flights form part of the same
        market for long-haul routes can be left open, as this would not change the outcome of
         the competitive assessment.
(163)    First, the results of the market investigation were mixed:
(164)   The competitors’ views were inconclusive as to whether indirect flights can compete
        with direct flights.202 According to competitors, an indirect flight would need to be
        approx. 19% cheaper than a direct flight for an average TS passenger to prefer it over
        a direct flight and approx. 11% cheaper for an average NTS passenger to prefer it over
        a direct flight.203 Some corporate customers and travel agents and tour operators,
        without making a distinction between TS/NTS passengers, indicated that on average
       an indirect flight would need to be approx. 18% cheaper to be preferred over a direct
          flight.204 Regarding lay over and overall travelling time, market participants had
         different views on how much longer the duration of lay-over time and total travel time
        of an indirect flight could and still compete effectively with a direct flight, however
         the results are not conclusive.205 In any event, the Commission considers that a cut off
        of 150 minutes lay-over time cannot be applied mechanically. In particular, the
        relevance of one-stop flights also depends (among other criteria) of the ticket price, the
        time (during the day) of the stop-over, and of demand composition on the route.
(165)  Some market participants indicated that for TS/business passengers, indirect flights are
        not a close substitute to direct flights, while for NTS/leisure passengers indirect flights
        could be considered a close substitute to direct flights, depending on different factors
        such as price and total duration of the trip.206 For example, a competitor considers
         “that there is a difference between leisure and business travellers with respect to the
        choice of direct versus indirect flights. For leisure passengers, the main choice factor
           is price and they are more willing to put price above the total length of the flight.
        Therefore, compared to business passengers, leisure passengers appear to be more
          likely to consider cheaper indirect flights, depending on how much time this would add
         to their trip […].”207 According to another competitor: “[…] competitors offering
         indirect flights with less than 6 hours of transfer time […] could potentially be
        considered as viable alternatives under certain conditions for non-time sensitive
        passengers and, in some instances, also for time-sensitive passengers.”208

7.2.    Cargo air transport services
7.2.1.   Relevant product market
7.2.1.1. Segmentation between cargo transport services and freight forwarding services
7.2.1.1.1.    Commission’s decisional practice
(170)   In the Commission’s decisional practice,213 the freight market has historically been
        divided into cargo transport services, whereby cargo companies sell space on their
         assets (such as trucks or aircraft), and freight forwarders, which construct a “virtual”
        network consisting of third party assets (transportation capacity) on the basis of
        customers’ requirements. Freight forwarding has been defined as “the organisation of
         transportation of items […]  on behalf of customers according to their needs”.214
        Unlike the providers of cargo transport services, freight forwarders do not generally
      own any part of the network they use and normally hire transportation capacity from
         third parties.
(171)   With regard to intercontinental cargo transportation, the Commission has previously
         indicated that the relevant market is limited to air cargo.215 In the present case, the
          activities of the Parties are limited to air cargo transport.
7.2.1.1.2.    Korean Air’s views
(172)   Korean Air does not object  to the Commission’s  prior decisional  practice and
        considers that the two markets, freight forwarding and air cargo, can be considered as
         vertically related.216
7.2.1.1.3.    Commission assessment
(173)   The market investigation in this case did not provide any reasons to depart from the
       Commission’s prior decisional practice and therefore, for the purposes of the present
        Decision, the Commission will consider a separate product market for  air cargo
         services, where the Parties are active.217
7.2.1.2. Air cargo services; substitutability with other means of transport
(174)   The Parties do not claim that air cargo services are substitutable with cargo services by
         other means of transport.218 They do, however, point to competitive pressure exerted
       by other means of transport.219
(175)   The  market  participants  responding  to  the Commission’s  market  investigation
        confirmed that they do not consider cargo transport by other means of transport to be
         close  substitutes with  air cargo transport between Europe and South Korea,  in
         particular due to the much longer transportation time.220 As an example, one customer
        explained that “transport by sea or ocean does not constitute a viable alternative for

(176)   Customers also do not consider multi-modal transport including a combination of air
       and sea freight to be close substitutes with air cargo transport between Europe and

       most of the respondents to the market investigation as they are usually interested in a
        timely delivery of their shipments for which they accept to pay a higher price but
       which would be slowed down by a combination of air and sea freight.223 Accordingly

         airport and then a transhipment by other modes of transport (i.e. sea freight) to a final

        cargo with delayed delivery times due to the combination of air transport with other
       modes of transport”.224
(177)   In addition, customers fear the risk of complications in the transhipment phase such as
         loss or damage to cargo or additional delays.225 Furthermore, such multi-modal
         transport would need to be organised by the customers themselves as air cargo carriers
       do not offer multi-modal services,226 resulting in further complexity that makes such
         service unattractive.
(178)  On the basis of the above, the Commission agrees with the Parties that air cargo
         services constitute a separate product market from other modes of transport and
        considers that any out-of-market competitive pressure is marginal at best.

(181)   The market investigation in the present case has highlighted that services on dedicated
          aircraft freighters and in the belly-hold of passenger aircraft and in consequence also
         the services of combination airlines offering both, are mainly substitutable. However,
         the results of the market investigation have also highlighted some differences between
        those types of services.
(182)   Most competitors responding to the Commission’s market investigation found that
          their  customers  consider  transport  per  belly-hold  in  passenger  aircraft and  in
        designated freighter aircraft as close substitutes.231 Those holding that view explained
         that the majority of exports from Korea can utilise both passenger and freighter
          aircraft and  that customers desire timely delivery of  their cargo irrespective of
         itinerary or aircraft characteristics. Others disagreed and referred to the fact that this
        question depended on the type of cargo and that larger or heavier shipments always
         require a freighter aircraft.232 In this respect, the majority of competitors responding to
         the Commission’s investigation confirmed that physically or economically particular
       goods (perishables, dangerous goods, large goods, high-tech, high-value goods, etc.)
       would rather be transported by freighters rather than in the belly-hold of passenger
          aircraft.233 As an example, two competitors replied that “Goods with dimensions
       beyond the maximum size of a belly hold aircraft and certain dangerous goods which
        are only permitted on freighter aircraft, would require a freighter aircraft. Otherwise
         either freighters or belly-hold passenger aircraft may be used.”;234 and “Perishables
        require frequency over capacity when it comes to transportation, hence belly-hold is
         opted. Oversized shipments and CAO require freighter capacity.”235
(183)   Several respondents also pointed to differences in service quality between belly-hold
        of passenger aircraft and freighter aircraft offering a superior quality. Two customers

7.2.1.4.3.    Commission assessment
(192)   The Commission’s market investigation has confirmed its previous decisional practice,
        according to which the integrators’ primary focus  lies on the shipment of small
        packages (or else door-to-door business), which is a separate market from air cargo
         services. The latter are only provided by integrators in order to fill any remaining
         available capacity in their aircraft.250
(193)    First, most respondents to the Commission’s market investigation replied that there is
       no demand-side substitutability between the services typically provided by air cargo
         carriers and the services of integrators in the sense that integrators do not compete on
         the same market as the Parties but rather follow a completely different business
        model.251
(194)   In the first place, and contrary to Korean Air’s submission in its Response to the
       Commission’s Statement of Objections,252 integrators themselves explain253 that their
        product offering is totally different to that of air cargo carriers in terms of (i) the type
        of cargo transported,  i.e. mainly small packages and documents,  (ii) the service
         offered, namely a door-to-door service which is inherent to the integrators’ business
       model  in  contrast  to the  airport-to-airport service of  air  carriers,  (iii) the time
       commitment, as the integrators’ services are time definite, and (iv) the customers
         targeted. […] integrators, […] confirmed that their main focus is their door-to-door
         business, while all strategic decisions are being made on this basis and not on the basis
        of the market for general air cargo services.254
(195)   According to [an integrator],255 integrators mainly transport parcels and documents as
       opposed to larger general cargo transported by dedicated freighter services and by
          airlines with belly space capacity in passenger flights. In addition, the integrators’
         pricing for their core door-to-door business is classically higher than air cargo carriers’
         pricing, further suggesting that the two services belong to different markets. To the
         extent there  is some leftover capacity in  its  aircraft, which – according to [an
         integrator] – is “rather the exception than the rule”,256 air cargo services are indeed
        sold on the market for general cargo at lower rates. However, in such cases, [the
         integrator] does not give guaranteed shipment or delivery time in order to be able to
        always  prioritise  the loading  of  its core door-to-door  business. Therefore,  [the
         integrator’s] focus  is on  its core door-to-door  business, which  [the  integrator]

        Objections, Korean Air argues that the Parties and other air cargo carriers contract

       making the two services the same from their point of view. As evidence of this
         statement, Korean Air cites paragraph 27 of the non-confidential Minutes of the
        conference calls with [a competitor] and explains that “[the competitor] and other air
        cargo carriers deliver cargo to freight forwarders, who, in turn, offer door-to-door

         competitor], in that respect. However, in that case, [the competitor] would see itself

(202)   In essence, [the competitor] has explained the exact opposite of what Korean Air
        claimed. In particular, [the competitor] explained that the air carriers’ general air cargo
         services do not form part of the same market with the integrators’ door-to-door
         services,  as  these  are  completely  different  business models  targeting  different
        customers (end customers vs freight forwarders). The integrators can then offer some
        of their capacity for general air cargo services, and therefore compete with the air
          carriers, but “this is not their core business”.
(203)   The differences in terms of customers targeted have also been explained by [an
         integrator]. The core small package delivery service represents a premium service with
        higher pricing due to the door-to-door delivery and the time commitment, addressed to
        “thousands of customers with single (smaller) shipments”.274 By contrast, the ancillary
        general air cargo services are addressed to freight forwarders and typically come at a
        lower quality of that of the Parties and other traditional air cargo carriers, given that
          (a) they will only be an ad hoc product that can only be booked a few weeks in
        advance, and (b) they will be on a deferred stand-by basis with longer lead times, due
         to boarding priority given to the core-door-to-door business.275

(205)   The differences in the two business models between the Parties’ and other general air
        cargo carriers’ airport-to-airport services and the integrators’ door-to-door services
       were  further  substantiated by end  cargo  customers,  i.e.  customers  of  freight

        while  air cargo  carriers mostly compete for larger cargo.293 Another major end

          Parties.294
(206)  On the basis of the above considerations, the Commission considers that there is no
        demand-side substitution between the market for air cargo services, where the Parties
        mainly compete, and the market for small package door-to-door delivery services,
       where integrators mostly compete.
(207)   Second, the Commission’s market investigation has revealed that there is no supply-
         side substitutability between the general air cargo carriers’ airport-to-airport services
       on the one hand, and the integrators’ door-to-door services on the other hand. In
          particular, [integrators], have confirmed that even though they do offer general air
        cargo services to a limited extent, their strategic decisions are not based on those and
        they do not intend to change their focus from their core door-to-door business to the

         capacity. In sum, we are very unlikely to be able to respond to higher prices caused by
         the proposed transaction by opening significant additional capacity”.299

         starting providing comparable services to those provided by integrators would not be
         effective and immediate, given that it would entail significant changes, investment and
         time.300

7.2.1.4.4.     Conclusion
(217)   In light of the above, for the purposes of the present Decision, the Commission
        considers that the Parties’ airport-to-airport air cargo services and the integrators’ core
        door-to-door small package delivery services between Europe and South Korea belong
         to separate product markets. However, the limited extent to which integrators offer
        spare capacity on the market for air cargo services will be taken into consideration in
         the competitive assessment of the present Transaction (see sections 8.11.3.2 and
         8.12.3.2 below).
7.2.1.5. Substitutability between direct and indirect flights with and without transhipment
(218)   Air cargo can be transported in direct flights (which cover non-stop flights and multi-
        stop flights without transhipment, where the cargo stays on the same plane during the
         stop-over) and in indirect flights (or transhipment flights, where the cargo is moved
       from one plane to another during the stop-over).
7.2.1.5.1.    Commission’s decisional practice
(219)   According to the Commission’s precedents, cargo is less time-sensitive than passenger
         transport and thus may be routed with a higher number of stopovers. As a result, the
       Commission considered in previous decisions any indirect route either with or without
        transhipment as generally substitutable to any direct route.311

7.2.1.5.2.    Korean Air’s views
(220)   The Parties agree with that approach and consider that customers’ choice for a specific
          air carrier or connection does mainly rely on price, and that therefore the number of
         stops and/or duration of the flight312 is irrelevant for customers.313
7.2.1.5.3.    Commission assessment
(221)   The Commission’s investigation indicates that non-stop  flights, multi-stop flights
        without transhipment and transhipment flights are substitutable to a certain extent.
      Many respondents found that customers would switch between the services being
        confronted with a permanent price increase of 5-10% while only a minority of
        respondents found that customers would not switch.314 One competitor explained in
          this context: “[t]his is common practice. Customers will consider this option based on
         price, journey time, solution offered and commodity type.”315
(222)   That said, the market is differentiated because non-stop flights, multi-stop flights and
        transhipment flights differ in the quality of service offered to the customer and
         different customers value their service levels in different ways.
(223)   This is reflected in the responses to the Commission’s market investigation where
       most respondents considered that the substitutability ultimately depends on a variety
        of factors, for instance on the nature of the goods transported, the urgency and transit
        time  required, the  rates compared  to the service  level  offered, or  the type of
         customer.316 Against that background, respondents explained that many customers
         prefer direct services (non-stop flights and multi-stop flights without transhipment). In
          particular, direct flights appear to be more suitable in certain cases in which the total
         transport time should be as short as possible such as for very time-sensitive products
        (such as e.g. animals, perishable goods or pharmaceuticals). More generally, however,
      many customers would avoid services with transhipment for risk of delays, damage or
         loss of cargo. The following quotes317 illustrate these considerations:

             According to [customer], even though such transit does not entail customs
             clearance or  significant  formalities, transhipment requires good operation
              control for re-directing the goods as even a two-hour delay might make a
               difference. The risk of delays due to mistakes at the transit hub (e.g. cargo

7.2.1.6. Substitutability between scheduled / regular flights and unscheduled / charter flights
7.2.1.6.1.    Commission’s decisional practice
(226)   In the context of air transport services, the Commission has previously considered324
         that most of the services offered by charter companies are not in the same market as
        scheduled services. Charter  flights, as opposed to scheduled  flights, are usually
        defined  as  taking  place  outside normal  schedules,  normally  through  a  hiring
        arrangement with a particular customer. However, the Commission has  left open
        whether a certain part of charter services should form part of the same market due to
        being available for customers on the open market.
(227)   In the context of air cargo services, the Commission has also assessed overlaps in
         charter services separately.325
7.2.1.6.2.    Korean Air’s views
(228)   In its submissions, Korean Air seems to be including all unscheduled flights, i.e. both
          air cargo carriers’ extra flights and charter flights, in the same product market with
        scheduled cargo operations.326
(229)   In its Responses to the Commission’s Statement of Objections and Letter of Facts,
       Korean Air maintains that unscheduled/charter flights do not have an “exceptional”
