7.2.1.6.3.    Commission assessment
(230)   With regard to charter cargo flights, the Commission considers that they mostly
         represent a  different market segment because  (i) they  are only  offered on an
         opportunistic basis and therefore customers cannot rely on them for their entire
       demand, (ii) they are typically booked through a hiring arrangement with a particular
        customer, thus other customers do not have access to their capacity, and (iii) they have
         different pricing.328
(231)  On the demand side, customers replying to the Commission’s market investigation
        explained that due to their higher pricing, charter cargo flights are mostly used
         exceptionally, either for a specific big project with high volumes where the customer
       would in any event book the entire capacity of the aircraft or during the Covid19
       pandemic due to the irregularities it brought to the market.329 As one freight forwarder,
        customer of the Parties, explained, “[c]harter flights are much more expensive than
       commercial scheduled flights and are therefore not a substitute” for the latter.330 Other
        customers noted that charter cargo flights come at considerably higher rates and
         therefore it only makes sense to book them for large volumes that need to be moved at
       once or for specific large projects. In such case, the customer would then need to book
         the entire aircraft for its own needs.331 Finally, according to one customer, “charter
          flights [are] an entirely different market and business”.332
(232)  On the supply side, air cargo carriers also confirmed that they provide charter cargo
         services only (if at all) in exceptional situations, when there is a specific demand by a
        customer, in which case the customer must book the entirety of the aircraft capacity.333

        should form part of the same market as scheduled services, to the extent that they are
         offered and made accessible to customers on the open market.
7.2.2.   Relevant Geographic Market
7.2.2.1. Commission’s decisional practice
(235)   With  respect  to  the  geographic scope  of  the  air  cargo  transport  market,  the
       Commission previously found  that an O&D approach to the geographic market
         definition  is inappropriate given that cargo  is generally less time sensitive than
        passengers and that cargo is commonly transported by trans-modal methods beyond
       and behind  the  origin and  destination  points.341  Accordingly,  the Commission
        concluded in previous cases that the geographic market in relation to  air cargo
         transport services can be defined as being wider than O&Ds and should rather be
        defined on a country- or continent-wide basis.

         for those continents where local infrastructure  is adequate to allow for onward

7.2.2.2. Korean Air’s views
(238)  As regards the European end of the route, Korean Air agrees with the Commission’s
         practice that the geographic scope of an airport competing against airports in Europe
        should not be limited to the country in which the airport is located but should be
        considered as the entire continent of Europe.346 According to Korean Air this  is
        because Europe has a well-developed land transport network, and it is easy to tranship
       between airports.347
(239)   In contrast, as regards the South Korean end of the route, Korean Air considers that
         the geographic market should not cover Asia as a whole continent, but rather the
        region of East Asia comprising South Korea, China, Japan, Hong Kong and Taiwan.348

       BMI, where the Commission had considered that the geographic scope of the market
        could be wider than national covering Saudi Arabia and neighbouring countries or
       even wide enough to cover the whole Middle Eastern region because of recent
       improvements of the local road networks and free movement agreements entered into
       by some countries of that region.349 Against that background, Korean Air states that
         the geographic scope of the market has to be analysed on a case-by-case basis350 and is
        of the opinion that in the present case a wider catchment area including not only South
       Korea as a country but East Asia as a region should be covered by the geographic
        market, for the following reasons351:

         for a significant portion of Korean Air’s sales.

        Port from different ports in East Asia. Thus, cargo bound for Europe originating all
        over East Asia is shipped via Incheon Port, and subsequently transported by air to
       Europe or elsewhere. According to Korean Air, approximately [10-20]% of the
         transported volumes from South Korea to Europe is originally transported from East
        Asian countries by sea to South Korea.358
(246)   Sixth, according to the Parties the fact that prices in East Asia fluctuate symmetrically

        mainly due to the fact that the air carriers active in the EEA - South Korea trades make
          their capacity available in the entire East Asia region. It is therefore the Parties’ view
         that any price-related strategies need to take into account the entire region and that any
         price change in one trade has a direct impact on the prices on the other trades.

7.2.2.3. Commission assessment of the South Korean end of the routes
(248)   For the geographic market definition, the Commission assesses in which geographic
        area the undertakings concerned are involved in the supply and demand of products or
         services, in which the conditions of competition are sufficiently homogeneous and
       which can be distinguished from neighbouring areas because the conditions of
        competition  are  appreciably  different  in  those  areas.361  In  that  context,  the
       Commission assesses  the  ability on  the supply- and demand-side  to switch  to
        purchasing or selling services in other areas362 as also the Parties seem to suggest.363 In
         the following, the Commission will therefore assess (i) customer’s possibilities to
        switch to air cargo services from or to East Asian countries other than South Korea
       from a demand-side perspective (7.2.2.3.1), (ii) the possibilities of air cargo service
        providers to switch to the offering of air cargo services from or to East Asian countries
         other than South Korea from a supply-side perspective (7.2.2.3.2) as well as additional
        elements which show (iii) that in the case at present the conditions of competition
        cannot be considered as sufficiently homogeneous in East Asian countries to define
         the geographic scope of the air cargo transport market as wide as an East Asian region
         (7.2.2.3.3) and  (iv)  that  the  relevant geographic market (South Korea) can be
         distinguished from  neighbouring  areas  (East  Asia)  because  the  conditions  of
        competition are appreciably different in those areas (7.2.2.3.4).
(249)   Against that background, the Commission is of the view that for the purposes of the
         present decision and in line with  its precedents the continent-to-country approach
        should also be used in the present case for assessing cargo air transport services on the
         routes between Europe and South Korea.
7.2.2.3.1.    No switching to air cargo services to or from outside of South Korea from a
             demand-side perspective
(250)  As regards demand-side factors in respect to the geographic market definition, the
       Commission essentially examines customers' ability to source the relevant product or
         service from a broader geographic area than the one in question. In the case at present,
         the relevant service is the air cargo transport service between Europe and South Korea
        as point of origin and point of destination and vice versa. The Commission therefore
         assesses whether customers could switch to air cargo transport services to or from a
         third country outside South Korea as the relevant point of origin or point of destination
         in response to a hypothetical small and permanent price increase (SSNIP). In other
        words, customers would need to consider air cargo transport services to another
        geographic area than to South Korea as a valid alternative for air cargo transport
         services to or from South Korea. That is not the case.
(251)    First, the Parties claim that for customers, transporting goods between Europe and
        South Korea  is largely substitutable with cargo  air transport services for routes

       between Europe and other East Asian countries. According to the Parties, this claim is
        based on the observation that customers prefer to use transhipment flights through ICN
         instead of direct flights to or from airports in other East Asian countries to where the
        cargo is destined or from where it originates.364 However, this claim disregards the
       Commission’s  product market  definition. As  outlined above  (see  7.2.1.5),  the
       Commission in its precedents has established an approach to assess the effects of the
        Transaction  on  the  overall  market  for  air  cargo  transport  services  without
         distinguishing separate product markets for direct flights (which cover non-stop flights
       and multi-stop flights without transhipment, where the cargo stays on the same plane
        during the stop-over) and indirect flights (or transhipment flights, where the cargo is
      moved from one plane to another during the stop-over). This concerns cargo air
         transport services within a certain O&D route, meaning that the relevant service
         (product) remains the air cargo transport service between a certain point of origin and
        a certain point of destination irrespective of whether the aircraft arrives at its point of
         destination via direct or indirect flight. In consequence, the final destination of such an
         indirect flight would always be South Korea and not another East Asian country,
         limiting the product market definition of air cargo transport services to flights between
        a certain airport in Europe (e.g. Barcelona) and ICN in South Korea. In a second step,
         for the purpose of the delimitation of the geographic scope of that product market, it
        has to be assessed what catchment area around the point of origin and the point of
         destination can be accepted by customers to tranship the cargo from its initial point of
         origin to the airport of departure and/or to its final point of destination from the airport
        of arrival by trans-modal means (that is to say by sea or land transport (road and rail)
        but not by air transport, as transhipment by air would be covered by the same product
         market365). This transhipment would therefore go beyond the airport of departure and
         the airport of destination of the relevant cargo air transport service itself. In the present
         case, the relevant service that needs to be substitutable from a customer’s perspective
           is the cargo air transport service between a point of origin at a specific European
         airport (e.g. Frankfurt, Paris, Barcelona or Rome) and the point of destination at ICN
         airport in South Korea and vice versa. The Parties’ reasoning around the airport at ICN
        being a transhipment hub for cargo destined to points of destination in other East
        Asian countries than South Korea366 is therefore not relevant for the definition of the
        geographic scope of the cargo air transport service market in the present case as this
       would concern other product markets than cargo  air transport services between
         specific airports in Europe (e.g. Frankfurt, Paris, Barcelona or Rome) and ICN in
        South Korea (such as e.g. cargo air transport services from Frankfurt/ Germany to
        Taipei/Taiwan, operated by indirect flights (with transhipment) at ICN airport).367

         countries (which would be covered by another product market as stated above ((251)),
         the Parties do not substantiate how cargo air transport services between specific
       European airports (e.g. Frankfurt, Paris, Barcelona or Rome) and specific airports in
        East Asian countries other than ICN in South Korea as point of origin and point of

7.2.2.3.2.    No switching to offering air cargo services from or to outside of South Korea
            from a supply-side perspective
(254)   Relevant supply side considerations relate to the possibility of other suppliers, located
         outside the geographic area in question, to start supplying that area in the short term
       and without incurring significant additional costs or risks. More precisely, it would
       need to be possible for other air cargo carriers to easily offer air cargo transport
         services between Europe and South Korea when already operating air cargo transport
         services between Europe and another East Asian country. Even though  it might
         theoretically be possible to move the relevant airplanes from one route to another,389
         the Commission has identified a series of barriers to entry (such as necessary traffic
         rights and opportunity costs, see below sections 8.11.4.3 and 8.12.4.3) which would
        hinder an airline from another East Asian country to start offering air cargo transport
         services between Europe and South Korea in the short term and without incurring
         significant additional costs or risks.
7.2.2.3.3.    No sufficiently homogeneous conditions of competition
(255)   Besides the missing demand- and supply-side  substitutability, the conditions of
        competition in providing air cargo services between Europe and South Korea appear to
          differ significantly from providing cargo air transport services between Europe and
        Taiwan/China/Japan.
(256)    First, the market position of the different air carriers, and therefore the identity and
         relative strength of the largest suppliers, differ considerably between those routes, as
          set out in Table 11 and Table 12. While the Parties play a marginal or moderate role
       on the routes between Europe and China and Japan respectively, they are the two
         strongest suppliers on the routes between Europe and South Korea with sizeable
        market shares. This finding is reinforced by the fact that, according to the Parties, the
         Parties’ market shares on the routes between Europe and China and between Europe
       and Japan are in fact overstated.390 These stark differences in market success by the

(259)   Third, the Parties’ claim that price movements between China, Taiwan, Japan and
        South Korea seem to be symmetric does not justify the finding that these countries are
         part  of  the same  geographic market  as  long  as  the  offered  services  are  not
         substitutable. For example, the price for air cargo transport from Europe to Shanghai
        does not impact a customer who needs to transport cargo from Europe to South Korea
            if transporting cargo to Shanghai is not a valid alternative to air cargo transport
       between Europe and South Korea, which is the case here. Furthermore, many different
         factors unrelated  to demand  substitution can cause pre co-movements, such as
      common costs. Therefore, analyses of price co-movements are in principle more
        informative when they indicate that two products or services are not in the same
        market.
7.2.2.3.4.     South Korea as a distinguished market from East Asia

(263)  As regards the European end of the routes, the Commission considers it appropriate to

       Commission recognizes that regional differences within Europe do exist, making  it
        probable for customers to switch air cargo services among some, but not among all,

7.2.2.4.1.     Switching to air cargo services to or from outside of South Korea from a
             demand-side perspective
(264)  As regards the question whether customers could use any airport in Europe for cargo
          air transport services between ICN and Europe or whether the choice would be limited
         to certain inner-European regions, the Commission’s market investigation resulted in
       somewhat mixed results:
(265)  On the one hand the majority of competitors who expressed a view on the issue
        considered that the catchment area by land or sea transportation for European airports
         for air cargo services from/to South Korea is all of Europe.396 As one competitor
        explained: “This is how it’s done, cargo gets consolidated at a central location (Hub)
         to which the material is trucked or flown into.”397 This was confirmed by a customer
      who explained  that: “[customer] transports cargo easily by trucks from various
      Member States to the airport in which the cargo would be then loaded onto the
          aircraft. There is a common concept of “low flying” planes where cargo is loaded on
         trucks and may even be screened and cleared in one airport for it then to be trucked to
       a major airport hub under an Airway bill to be flown out”.398
(266)  On the other hand, the majority of customers considered that the catchment area by
        land or sea transportation for European airports for cargo air transport services from/to
        South Korea  is an inner-European  regional  area,  rather than  all  of  Europe.399
        Accordingly, several customers would not switch to other European airports, or
        explained that such switching decision would depend on various factors, such as the
        type of cargo and the distance to the airport as well as the additional trucking costs and
          transit time.400 As an example, a customer claims that regional differences within the
     EU exist mainly in terms of preferences and convenience:
       “As regards  airports  in Europe,  [a customer] considers  all  airports as being
         substitutable as long as they are in central Europe as this mainly makes a slight
         difference of about 15 minutes flight time. However, as regards e.g. Norway, the 2 – 3
        extra hours flight time would make that option less attractive. The longer flight time
       from Norway is partly due to the restrictions of the Russian airspace following the
        Russian invasion in Ukraine.”401
(267)   In the same vein, other customers claim that they would first look for the nearest
         airport and only under certain circumstances consider using airports that are further
       away:

7.2.2.4.3.    Europe as a distinguished market compared to an inner-European regional
             approach
(273)   Even though the market investigation has mixed results, it also shows that the regional
         differences do in the present case not seem to be significant enough to trigger a
         separation  of geographic markets within Europe.  In  addition,  as every market
         participant seems to have different views and preferences regarding the geographic
        area in which cargo air transport services could be considered as substitutable, the
         identification of appropriate boundaries for regional markets within Europe might be
        problematic. For the purpose of this decision, the Commission will therefore define the
        geographic market as Europe-wide. Potentially diverging competitive conditions in
         different  countries  and  regions  within  Europe  will,  however,  be  taken  into
         consideration in the competitive assessment, in particular when assessing how closely
         the  different  air  cargo  carriers compete  with each  other  (see  sections  8.11.2
       and 8.12.2).


                                     67

[PÁGINA PDF 74]
(274)  As regards the geographical coverage of “Europe”, the Commission has in particular
         investigated whether the relevant geographic market should cover only the European
       Economic Area (“EEA”)406 or in addition also the UK and Switzerland. Even though
         the market investigation showed a tendency among customers to limit the geographic
        market to the EEA407, others were of the view that the geographic market definition
        should cover all of Europe:
       “With respect to geographical markets, [a competitor] considers the whole EEA as
       one geographic market due  to  the available inner-European  infrastructure and
        transport facilities. [The competitor] is of the opinion that Switzerland is certainly part
         of this geographic market on the European side due to the road feeder services and the
       narrow body aircraft with belly hold capacities connecting different destinations
        within the EU. [The competitor] would also consider the UK as part of the same
        geographic market. However, [the competitor] is of the view that due to BREXIT and
         the different regulations that since apply between the EEA and the UK, the use of multi
       modal transport has become less attractive than flying directly to or from an EEA
         destination. According to [the competitor], this is particularly true regarding time
         sensitive cargo (express or temperature controlled).”408
       “As regards Switzerland, it does not make a difference for [a customer] whether an air
         carrier lands there or at another airport in the EEA.”409
(275)   However,  the  difference between  the two approaches seems  to be  of  limited
        importance for the assessment of the present case so that the geographic market
         definition on the European side of the routes can be left open. The Commission will
         therefore carry out  its competitive assessment on the basis of a European-wide
        geographic market including the EEA, the UK and Switzerland.
7.2.2.5. Conclusion on the geographic scope of the market
(276)   In light of the above, for the purposes of the present decision, the Commission will
        follow the continent – to country approach. In this case, the relevant geographic scope
        of the market is air cargo transport services between Europe (i.e. the EEA, the UK and
        Switzerland) and South Korea.
7.2.2.6. Unidirectional nature of the air transport of cargo
(277)   In addition, given the differences in demand on each end of the route, the Commission
        has  in  past  cases  assessed  the  relevant  markets  for  air  cargo  transport  as
         unidirectional.410 Korean Air agrees with this approach due to differences in demand
          at each end of the route, differences in prices and difference in capacity.411 This
        approach is confirmed by Korean Air’s submission that cargo flights from South
       Korea to Europe are more expensive than those from Europe to South Korea because
       demand for consumer goods is higher in Europe than in South Korea. According to
       Korean Air, this is due to the fact that Europe is a consumer destination whereas South
       Korea is a manufacturing area and the South Korea - Europe direction is therefore
         characterized by higher demand for cargo space and, subsequently, by higher prices.412

7.2.3.   Conclusion on market definition for air cargo services
(278)   The Commission concludes that the relevant markets for the purpose of the present
        decision are the markets for air cargo transport on a unidirectional basis from Europe
           (i.e. the EEA, the UK and Switzerland) to South Korea and from South Korea to
        Europe, including  direct and  indirect connections and  all types  of  planes, but
        excluding door-to-door services of integrators. Furthermore, the Commission leaves
       open whether  that market should be sub-segmented  into  scheduled/regular and
        unscheduled/charter flights. The Commission also concludes that these markets are
         differentiated in different ways from both a product and a geographic perspective,
       namely whether the carriers operate freighter aircraft or passenger aircraft, whether
        they offer direct services or services with transhipment and from which airports in
       Europe they offer their services at which frequencies. The Commission will take that
         differentiation into account in the competitive assessment, in particular when assessing
      how closely the different carriers compete.
7.3.    Other activities
7.3.1.   Maintenance, Repair and Overhaul (“MRO”) services
7.3.1.1. Relevant product market
(279)   With regard to MRO services, the Commission has in its past practice distinguished
       between four separate product markets within the MRO  sector, namely  (i)  line
        maintenance, (ii) heavy maintenance, (iii) engine maintenance and (iv) components
        maintenance.413
(280)   The  Parties agree with the Commission's previously established product market
         definition.
(281)  As both Korean Air and Asiana currently only provide line maintenance services to
         third Parties at ICN, the assessment in the present case will be limited to the market
         for line maintenance services.
7.3.1.2. Relevant geographic market
(282)   With regard to the geographic scope of the market for line maintenance services, the
       Commission has in its previous decisions found that the geographic market could be
         regional or even local in scope.414
(283)   For the purposes of this Decision, the assessment will be limited to the narrowest
         possible market for line maintenance services locally at ICN airport, as in the present
        case only MRO services to third parties at ICN airport are of relevance.

8.     COMPETITIVE ASSESSMENT
(289)   Based on the market investigation, the Commission finds:
        •    The Transaction would significantly impede effective competition with respect
               to passenger air services on the routes BCN-ICN, CDG-ICN, FRA-ICN and
          FCO-ICN (“the Overlap Routes”) because the Transaction would create a
             dominant position in the relevant markets.423
        •    The Transaction would significantly impede effective competition in relation to
                 air cargo services on the route Europe-South Korea and the route South Korea-
            Europe because the Transaction would create a dominant position in the relevant
              markets. In any event, the Transaction would also give rise to horizontal non-
              coordinated effects in relation to air cargo services on the route Europe-South
            Korea and the route South Korea-Europe, resulting from the elimination of an
              important competitive constraint.
(290)   This section of the decision details the competitive assessment of the Transaction, and
           is structured as follows: Section 8.1 sets out the legal framework for the competitive
        assessment; Section 8.2 discusses the limited evidentiary value of some of the Parties’
        submissions; Section 8.3 discusses the Parties’ failing firm defence; Section 8.4
         outlines  the  Commission’s  approach  to  the  determination  of  the  relevant
         counterfactual; Section 8.5 sets out general considerations concerning the competitive
         analysis of the Transaction regarding passenger air transport services and Section 8.7
        analyses the impact of the Transaction on passenger air transport services on the
         relevant O&Ds on a route by route basis. Section 8.8 sets out general considerations
        concerning the competitive analysis of the Transaction regarding cargo air transport
         services  Sections  8.11 and  8.12  set  out  the Commission’s  assessment  of  the
        Transaction regarding cargo air transport services markets on the markets Europe-
        South Korea and South Korea-Europe respectively.
8.1.    Legal framework for the assessment
(291)   Under Article 2(2) and (3) of the Merger Regulation, the Commission must assess
        whether a proposed concentration would significantly impede effective competition in
         the internal market or in a substantial part of it, in particular as a result of the creation
        or strengthening of a dominant position.
(292)   The notion of “significant impediment to effective competition” must be interpreted as
        extending, beyond the concept of dominance, to the anti-competitive effects of a
        concentration resulting from the non-coordinated behaviour of undertakings which do
        not have a dominant position on the market concerned. Accordingly, concentrations
        involving the elimination of important competitive constraints that the merging parties
       had exerted upon each other, as well as a reduction of competitive pressure on the
        remaining competitors, may result in a significant impediment of effective competition


423     As explained  in  sections  7.1.4.3.1,  7.1.4.3.4 and  7.1.4.3.5,  for  the purpose of  this decision  the
       Commission leaves open the question whether other airports in the cities of Seoul, Paris and Rome are
         part of the market. As currently no flights to South Korea are operated from other airports besides ICN,
     CDG and FCO, and the market shares remain unchanged under either market definition, in this decision,
         the Commission will refer to the routes using airport names (ICN, CDG, FCO) rather than cities (Seoul,
          Paris, Rome).


                                     71

[PÁGINA PDF 78]
       even if the concentration does not result in the creation or strengthening of a dominant
         position.424
(293)  As concerns the assessment of horizontal overlaps (meaning when the undertakings
        concerned  are  active  in  the same  relevant  markets),  the  Horizontal  Merger
         Guidelines425 distinguish between two main ways in which mergers between actual or
         potential competitors may significantly impede effective competition, namely non-
        coordinated and coordinated effects.426
(294)   Non-coordinated  effects  may  significantly  impede  effective  competition  by
         eliminating  important  competitive  constraints  on  one  or  more  firms,  which
        consequently would have increased market power, without resorting to coordinated
        behaviour. In that regard, the Horizontal Merger Guidelines consider not only the
         direct loss of competition between the merging firms, but also the reduction in
        competitive pressure on non-merging firms in the same market that could be brought
        about by the merger. In particular, a merger giving rise to such non-coordinated effects
       would significantly impede effective competition by creating or strengthening the
       dominant position of a single firm. Furthermore, mergers in oligopolistic markets
        involving the elimination of important competitive constraints that the merging parties
        previously exerted upon each other together with a reduction of competitive pressure
       on the remaining competitors may, even where there is little likelihood of coordination
       between the members of the oligopoly, also result in a significant impediment to
         competition.427
(295)   The Horizontal Merger Guidelines  list a number of factors which may influence
        whether or not non-coordinated effects are likely to result from a merger, such as large
        market shares of the merging firms, the  fact  that the merging firms are close
         competitors, the limited possibilities for customers to switch suppliers, the fact that the
       merger would eliminate an important competitive force, or the existence of barriers to
          entry.428  Furthermore, some  proposed  mergers  would,  if  allowed  to  proceed,
         significantly impede effective competition by leaving the merged firm in a position
       where it would have the ability and incentive to make the expansion of smaller firms
       and potential competitors more difficult or otherwise restrict the ability of rival firms
         to compete. In such a case, competitors may not,  either individually or in the
         aggregate, be in a position to constrain the merged entity to such a degree that it would
        not increase prices or take other actions detrimental to competition. For instance, the
       merged entity may have such a degree of control, or influence over, the supply of
         inputs or distribution possibilities that expansion or entry by rival firms may be more
          costly.429
(296)   Not all of these factors need to be present to make significant non-coordinated effects
         likely and it is not an exhaustive list such that other factors may also be relevant.430
(297)   Based on the Horizontal Merger Guidelines, market shares and concentration levels
        provide  useful  first  indications of the market  structure and of  the competitive


424       Recital 25 of the Merger Regulation.
425      Guidelines on the assessment of horizontal mergers under the Council Regulation on the control of
         concentrations  between  undertakings  (“Horizontal  Merger  Guidelines”),  Official  Journal C  31,
        05.02.2004, p. 5-18.
426     The competitive concerns identified in this case concern non coordinated effects. Coordinated effects will
         therefore not be discussed further in this Decision.
427      Horizontal Merger Guidelines, paragraphs 22 to 25.
428      Horizontal Merger Guidelines, paragraphs 27 et seq.
429      Horizontal Merger Guidelines, paragraph 36.
430      Horizontal Merger Guidelines, paragraph 26.


                                     72

[PÁGINA PDF 79]
        importance of both the merging parties and their competitors.431 The larger the market
         share, the more likely a firm is to possess market power. The larger the addition of
        market share (the increment), the more likely  it is that a merger would lead to a
         significant increase in market power. The larger the increase in the sales base on
       which to enjoy higher margins after a price increase, the more likely  it is that the
       merging firms would find such a price increase profitable despite the accompanying
        reduction in output. Although market shares and additions of market shares only
        provide first indications of market power and increases in market power, they are
        normally important factors in the assessment.432
(298)   The European Courts have consistently held that there is a presumption of dominance
       when an undertaking enjoys a market share of 50% or more.433 Accordingly, the
        Horizontal Merger Guidelines provide that “[a]ccording to well-established case law,
        very large market shares – 50% or more – may in themselves be evidence of the
         existence of a dominant market position”.434
(299)   Indeed, according to the established case law, “although the importance of market
        shares may vary from one market to another, very large shares are in themselves, and
        save  in  exceptional  circumstances,  evidence  of  the  existence  of a  dominant
         position.”435 The General Court has noted that “the Commission could not ignore the
        importance  to be attached  to those  initial  indications, which showed  that  the
        implementation of the notified transaction would have enabled [the acquirer] to
        acquire extremely high market shares.”436 The General Court concluded that “in the
          light of those findings […] the Commission was rightly able to find that the acquisition
         of very high market shares as a result of both the implementation of the concentration
       and the concentration level associated with it were relevant indicators of the market
       power which would have been acquired”.437
(300)   In its prior decisions, the Commission noted that when faced with “a high degree of
        dominance,  the  Commission  must  be  particularly  vigilant,  because  in  such
        circumstances  even  a  very  small  increase  in  market  power  can  have  a
         disproportionately large negative effect on the competitive conditions on the market
         place.”438
(301)   The Horizontal Merger Guidelines clarify that the Commission normally uses current
        market shares in its competitive analysis. However, current market shares may be
        adjusted to reflect reasonably certain future changes, for instance in light of exit, entry
        or expansion. In any event, the Commission interprets market shares in light of likely
        market conditions, for instance if the market is highly dynamic in character and if the
        market structure is unstable due to innovation or growth.439

(302)   While market shares are an important factor, the Commission is also required to
        analyse  the competitive  constraints  the merged  entity  will be  subject  to  post-
         transaction. Specifically in this case, the Commission analyses constraints notably
       from actual competitors and from future competition due to entry or expansion, as well
        as constraints from other one-stop itineraries and from regional/other airports. Further
         details on the framework applied by the Commission with respect to the analysis of
         potential entry and expansion are set out in section 8.6.3.
(303)   Furthermore, concentrations where an undertaking already active on a relevant market
       merges with a potential competitor in this market can have similar anti-competitive
         effects to mergers between two undertakings already active on the same relevant
        market and, thus, significantly impede effective competition, in particular through the
         creation or the strengthening of a dominant position. For a merger with a potential
        competitor  to have  significant  anti-competitive  effects, two conditions must be
          fulfilled. First, the potential competitor must already exert a significant constraining
         influence or there must be a significant likelihood that it would grow into an effective
        competitive force. Second, there must not be a sufficient number of other potential
         competitors, which could maintain sufficient competitive pressure after the merger.440
8.2.    The evidentiary value of the Parties’ submissions
(304)   In its assessment of mergers, the Commission routinely relies on internal documents
         that undertakings prepare in the ordinary course of business. Those documents allow
         the Commission to gain a quicker and better insight into the relevant markets as
       viewed by the market participants themselves.
(305)    Internal documents can prove to be an especially useful source of evidence in relation
         to specific areas of investigation. For example, they often allow the Commission to
         verify factual claims made by the parties and verify data they submit. Internal
       documents are frequently  crucial  to understanding the  factors which  affect  the
         incentives and business strategies of the parties before and after the proposed merger.
(306)   Undertakings are well aware of the importance of internal documents as a source of
        evidence which is likely to be requested by competition authorities during a merger
        review.
(307)   In line with its established practice,441 the Commission considers that in attributing the
        probative value to specific internal documents, the Commission should take into
        account the timing and context in which they were prepared. In particular, internal
       documents prepared in the ordinary course of business (for example, before the
        proposed merger was agreed upon or without the knowledge of the preliminary
        competition concerns), would usually have higher probative value than  internal
       documents that have been prepared for the Commission or that have been or may have
       been influenced by the Commission’s review of the proposed merger. As the former
        type of internal documents usually reflects the information independently of the
       merger control procedure, the evidentiary value of such documents is comparatively
        higher than the evidentiary value of documents prepared for the purpose of or during
       merger proceedings.
(308)  As a  result,  to reach conclusions on  the most  likely developments absent  the
         Transaction, the Commission adopted a holistic approach, interpreting the results of
         the various complementary analyses in light of the overall evidence on the file.

8.3.     Failing Firm Defence
8.3.1.  Framework of assessment
(309)   In line with the case law442 and the Horizontal Mergers Guidelines,443 the Commission
      may decide that an otherwise problematic merger is nevertheless compatible with the
         internal market if one of the merging parties is a failing firm. The basic requirement of
        a failing firm defence is that the deterioration of the competitive structure that follows
         the merger cannot be said to be caused by the merger. This will arise where the
        competitive structure of the market would deteriorate to at least the same extent in the
        absence of the merger.
(310)   This requirement  is consistent with the concept of causal connection set out in
         Article 2(2) of the Merger Regulation, pursuant to which if the significant impediment
         to effective competition is not caused by the concentration, the latter shall be declared
        compatible with the internal market.
(311)   The burden of proof of a failing firm defence  is on the notifying parties. More
         specifically,  it is for the notifying parties to provide in due time all the relevant
        information  necessary  to demonstrate  that  the  deterioration  of  the  competitive
         structure that follows the merger is not caused by the merger.444
(312)   According  to  the Horizontal Merger Guidelines,  the Commission considers  the
        following three criteria to be especially relevant for the application of a “failing firm
         defence”.445
(313)    First, the allegedly failing firm would in the near future be forced out of the market
        because of financial difficulties if not taken over by another undertaking.446 In the
         past, the Commission has concluded that such criterion was met for instance in cases
       where the company had not been profitable for years and was unlikely to become
         profitable in the future,447 and/or was likely to enter into insolvency proceedings in the
        near future.448
(314)   Second, there should be no less anti-competitive alternative purchase than the notified
         merger.449 In the past, the Commission has concluded that such criterion was met for
         instance in cases where  (i) the only potential alternative purchaser that  initially
        manifested an interest, subsequently declined to re-negotiate a possible acquisition;450
            (ii) the only potential alternative purchaser that expressed possible interest was not a
         credible alternative purchaser;451 or  (iii) no alternative buyer had manifested any
        concrete interest.452

        C-30/95, EU:C:1998:148, paragraph 115.

[PÁGINA PDF 82]
(315)   In contrast, the Commission has concluded that such criteria was not met, for instance,
         in cases where  (i) the parties had not actively tried to find less anti-competitive
         solutions than the merger;453 (ii) other potential purchasers expressed an interest in a
         possible acquisition of the company (although this did not materialise into any formal
          offer), and there was no sufficient evidence to exclude that the company may have
       been acquired by another interested purchaser;454 and  (iii) there were competing
        bidders at the time when the transaction was entered into.455
(316)   Furthermore, the Commission has specified that the existence of alternative purchasers
        should include an assessment at the time of the Commission’s decision as well as at
         the time when the choice of the acquirer is made, since the risk taken with the choice
        of a potentially anti-competitive acquisition, instead of other available less anti-
        competitive alternatives, cannot be shifted on the Commission.456 Therefore, the
         parties to a transaction cannot rely on a failing firm defence  if the lack of an
         alternative less anti-competitive purchase is the result of their own choice.
(317)   Third, in the absence of a merger, the assets of the failing firm would inevitably exit
         the market.457 The Horizontal Merger Guidelines also clarify that the inevitability of
         the assets of the failing firm leaving the market may underlie a finding that the market
        share of the failing firm would in any event accrue to the other merging party.458
(318)   In the past, the Commission has considered that such criterion was met, for instance,
       where no party had substantiated an interest in taking over the target’s assets (i.e.
        brand and leased aircraft).459 On the other hand, the Commission considered that such
         criterion was not met when airport slots could be reallocated to other carriers that
        could use them on the problematic routes.460

8.3.3.   Commission assessment
(325)   Even though Korean Air does not raise a full-fledged failing firm defence, the
       Commission has analysed, in any event, whether the conditions for invoking a failing
        firm defence as set out in the Horizontal Merger Guidelines would be fulfilled. On the
         basis of its assessment in this Section, the Commission considers that the conditions
         for invoking a failing firm defence would not be fulfilled.
8.3.3.1. Asiana’s exit from the market absent the Transaction is unlikely
(326)   Based on the information in the Commission’s file, the Commission finds that Asiana
           is in severe financial difficulty,  is controlled by  its creditor KDB following the
         restructuring of its debt in 2019479 and does not have a stable basis to develop its
        business due to its debt structure. […].
(327)   The  Commission  acknowledges   Asiana’s   deteriorating   financial   position.
        Nevertheless, based on the results of the market investigation, the Commission cannot
        conclude that the most likely scenario absent the Transaction would be that Asiana
       would completely and definitively exit the market for air transport services in the near
         future, for the following reasons.
(328)    First, Asiana’s exit from the market is unlikely as even Korean Air does not argue it.
      As explained in section 8.3.2 above, Korean Air does not submit that Asiana would be
        forced out of the market because of financial difficulties completely. Korean Air only
        claims that Asiana would most likely cease its passenger services to the EU (as  it
       would exit those markets).480 Furthermore, Korean Air does not submit that Asiana
       would cease its cargo operations carried out by freighter aircraft between Europe and
        South Korea.

       remedy takers are not willing to commit to purchase any assets of Asiana” and that
        during the remedy discussions with the  potential remedy takers “none  of them
         indicated that they needed to purchase any assets of Asiana” is not substantiated.579
       Korean Air did not provide any evidence to show that potential buyers or potential
       remedy takers were aware that they had a possibility to acquire Asiana’s assets in the
        context of such discussions.
(390)   Second, the results of the market investigation show that in the event that Asiana
       would enter into liquidation, some market participants would be interested in acquiring
        Asiana’s assets such as  slots  at the relevant EEA airports and ICN as well as
          aircraft.580 Korean Air disagrees with this finding and argues that it is unlikely that
          airlines that expressed interest in Asiana’s slots at BCN, FRA, CDG and FCO would
          utilize them on the routes between South Korea and the EEA. In the first place,
       Korean Air did not provide any evidence showing that market participants that showed
          interest in these assets of Asiana would not have intentions to use these assets on the
        Overlap Routes. In the second place, evidence in the Commission’s file shows that
         interested carriers would intend to use such assets on the Overlap Routes. For instance,
      […] and […] indicated that they would be interested in using slots on all four Overlap
         Routes.581 Moreover, as will be discussed in section 8.7.2 8.7.2 below, […], one of the
        market participants that responded to the market investigation, explained that it would
        be interested in acquiring Asiana’s assets and using them on FRA-ICN and CDG-
        ICN,582 was expected to launch its services on the EEA-South Korea routes as of June
        2023, offering 4 weekly services on ICN-FRA. This further shows that if Asiana were
         to enter into liquidation and its assets become available they could be used on the
        Overlap Routes.
(391)   Third, the Commission rejects Korean Air’s argument that the policy goal that KDB
       would be pursuing with the Transaction (i.e. to maintain the South Korean aviation
         industry) will not be served by Asiana’s assets being used on unrelated routes.583 The
       Commission notes that the policy goals of the South Korean government may be well
        reasoned but do not play a role in the Commission’s assessment of whether the
        Transaction would impede effective competition in the internal market.
(392)   The Commission therefore concludes that Korean Air failed to establish that in a
         situation where Asiana would enter into liquidation, its assets would inevitably exit the
        market.
(393)   In conclusion, the Commission considers that the conditions for invoking a failing
        firm defence set out in the Horizontal Merger Guidelines would not be fulfilled.

(395)   In assessing the competitive effects of a concentration, the Commission compares the
        competitive conditions that would result from the Transaction with the conditions that
       would have prevailed absent the Transaction.585
(396)   In most cases the competitive conditions existing at the time of the Transaction
         constitute the relevant comparison  for evaluating  its  effects. However,  in some
        circumstances, the Commission may take into account future changes to the market to
         the extent that they can be “reasonably predicted”.586 A contrario, the Commission
        has no duty to take into account any changes that cannot be reasonably predicted or
         that are uncertain. Indeed, as noted by the General Court, the Commission’s appraisal
        of a concentration within a market cannot be carried out on the basis of “hypothetical
         factors the economic implications of which cannot be assessed at the time when the
        decision is adopted.”587
8.4.2.   Korean Air’s views
(397)   Korean Air submits that absent the Transaction, Asiana will be forced to reduce its
        long-haul operations and most likely exit the EU market with passenger air transport
         services.588 In some parts of the Response to the 6(1)(c) Decision, the Parties argue
         that Asiana will likely exit all of its long haul operations (which could include flights
         to the US, Europe (including the UK and Turkey) and Australia) and become a short-
        haul/medium-haul airline,589 whereas in other parts of the Response to the 6(1)(c)
        Decision, Korean Air claims that Asiana would be restructured by exiting the EU
          routes.590 In certain recent submissions the Parties explain that in the counterfactual,
        Asiana would most likely cease its passenger services to the EU and US.591 Korean
        Air did not provide clarifications in its Response to the Statement of Objections, where
             it submitted that absent the Transaction, “the only possible scenario is a restructuring
         of Asiana into an airline flying short to mid-haul routes in Asia” without clarifying
       which specific routes Asiana would be intending to exit and by when.592 Whereas in
        another place of the Response to the Statement of Objections, Korean Air argued that
       any  restructuring  of Asiana absent  the Transaction   “would  entail  exiting EU
         routes”.593
(398)  As previously explained, Korean Air does not submit that Asiana will exit cargo
         services to/from the EEA with freighter aircraft.

8.4.3.   Commission assessment
8.4.3.1. Asiana’s exit from the EEA-South Korea passenger operations is not sufficiently
         likely
(401)   At the outset of its assessment, the Commission notes that Korean Air has provided a
         variation of claims on Asiana’s future operations absent the Transaction (namely that
        Asiana may exit all EU routes, all EU and US routes or cease all long-haul operations
        with passenger services).598 However, in its reply to the Commission’s request to
         clarify its submission on Asiana’s future operations Korean Air explained that Asiana
         will “at the very least” exit the EU routes.599 Therefore, in the following analysis the
       Commission will concentrate its assessment on whether Asiana’s exit from the EU
         routes is the most likely development.
(402)   The Commission finds that Asiana’s exit from the EEA-South Korea routes with
        passenger air transport services is not sufficiently likely. There are other scenarios that
       would be more likely to materialize.
(403)    First, Asiana has already re-entered the EEA-South Korea routes on which  it had
        suspended its operations due to the Covid19 pandemic, namely on CDG-ICN, FCO-
      ICN and BCN-ICN and at the time of the investigation explained that it expects to
        gradually return to pre-Covid19 flight frequencies on all four Overlap Routes by
         2024.600 Moreover, according to its plans for summer 2023 submitted in the Form CO,
       on CDG-ICN Asiana planned to operate at a higher frequency than before the Covid19
       pandemic (i.e. 6 weekly flights in summer 2023 as compared to 5 weekly flights in
       summer 2019).601 Based on its more recent network planning, Asiana is expected to
        continue  flying on  all  four Overlap Routes  in  winter 2023/2024 with  similar
        frequencies as before the Covid19 pandemic.602 Asiana explained that it does not yet

       companies when taking decisions over allocating planes to routes for a given level of
         fixed assets. This is confirmed by internal documents […].677
(439)   That said, as airlines can adapt their asset base in the long term, the Commission has
         also examined the profit of the individual routes, where aircraft financing costs were
         allocated to the routes. As according to the information provided by Asiana, the level

          profit,678 this is the indicator the Commission has retained to further develop  its
        assessment of route profitability. The Seabury Report submitted by Asiana on 18 April
         2023,679 retains the operating profitability as an indicator, which reflects a certain
       number of fixed costs but does not  reflect the  aircraft specific financing costs
        according to Asiana’s information. For this reason, the operating profit is higher than
         the ordinary route profit and the Commission is taking the most conservative approach
         to appreciate the profitability by referring to the ordinary route profit.

8.4.3.2. Asiana becoming an insignificant competitor is not the most likely development
(461)   The Commission finds that, contrary to Korean Air’s submissions, Asiana becoming
       an insignificant competitor is not sufficiently likely to be taken into account as the
         relevant counterfactual.
(462)    First, as already explained in detail in section 8.3.3 on the failing firm defence (see
        paragraphs (341)-(356) above), the Commission is of the view that Asiana’s main
         creditors, namely KDB and KEXIM, would not let Asiana fail absent the Transaction
        and, for instance, initiate bankruptcy proceedings – which could weaken Asiana’s
        competitiveness temporarily or in the long run. Korean Air’s argument that there is a
         limit to KDB and other state-owned creditors’ willingness and ability to continue
        financing Asiana  is unsubstantiated by evidence (see paragraph (320) above).695
        Indeed, Korean Air simply made statements in this regard, […].
(463)   Second, Korean Air did not provide any evidence in support to its claim that “it would
        be uneconomical and practically impossible for [Asiana] creditors to continue to
        provide  financial support”  to  Asiana.696 Korean  Air’s Response  to  the  6(1)(c)
        Decision, Response to the Statement of Objections and Response to the Letter of facts
         also do not contain any substantiation for this argument.
(464)   […],697 […].
(465)   Fourth, the market investigation did not indicate and Korean Air has not provided
        evidence that Asiana’s debt burden would impact its operational competitiveness in
         the future. In the first place, the Commission’s investigation shows that Asiana has
       been competing head-to-head with Korean Air in both passenger and cargo air services
       between the EEA and South Korea in the last years – despite Asiana’s financial
          difficulties. In the second place, Asiana admitted that […].698 In the third place, as
        already explained in section 8.3.3.1 above, Asiana sold tickets on its long-haul flights
         to Europe for summer 2023 and has been selling them for winter 2023/2024 […]. In
         the fourth place, the results of the market investigation show that passengers do not
          attribute great importance to the financial strength of a carrier when deciding with
       which airline to book a flight on a route between the EEA and South Korea.699 This
        suggests that the financial strength (or weakness for that matter) has limited impact on
        passenger choices between airlines.
(466)   Short of a market or route exit, the Commission therefore does not see reasons to
        conclude that absent the Transaction Asiana would be less competitive going forward.
      As long as Asiana is active on the relevant routes and maintains its quality levels,
       which appears to be the most likely counterfactual, it is likely to remain an important
        competitor to Korean Air.

8.4.3.3. Conditions  prevailing  before  the Covid19  pandemic  constitute  an  appropriate
       benchmark for assessing the effects of the Transaction
(467)   The Commission undertook an  in-depth review  of  various  pieces  of evidence
        submitted by the Parties, stemming from third-party submissions as well as the
         Parties’ internal documents. The results of the market investigation indicate that
          airlines have been restoring their positions on the routes after the effects of the
       Covid19 pandemic, for both cargo and passenger operations, with some limited
         exceptions.
(468)    First, the  results of the market investigation confirm  that the  Parties and  their
        competitors have been in the process of restoring their passenger and cargo  air
         transport positions on the EEA-South Korea routes. Korean Air and Asiana have
        already re-entered all EEA-South Korea passenger Overlap Routes on which their
        operations were suspended during the Covid19 pandemic700 and according to their
        plans submitted in the Form CO, expected to restore their pre-pandemic level of
        frequencies in summer 2023 (for Korean Air)701 and by 2024 (for Asiana).702 Based on
         the Parties’ network planning, both Korean Air and Asiana are expected to operate all
        four Overlap Routes  in […]  with  similar  frequencies  as  before  the Covid19
        pandemic.703 Furthermore, they continued serving the Europe-South Korea-Europe
        cargo routes throughout the pandemic.
(469)   Second, industry experts  project a return  to 2019  levels  for EEA-South Korea
        passenger traffic by around 2024/2025. In contrast, demand for cargo transport has
        remained strong throughout the Covid19 pandemic. Further information on this will be
          set out in sections 8.5.1 and 8.10.1 below.
(470)   Third, Asiana’s external financial analysts also confirm that using 2019 data as a
       benchmark to predict future operating performance in a stabilized post-Covid19
        environment is a standard in the aviation industry.704 In their supplemental submission,
        Asiana’s financial analysts submit that after the extraordinary Covid19 pandemic
         effects dissipate,  it is likely that Asiana’s operational performance will be “more
         similar to its 2019 performance than its 2020-2022 performance”.705 This is further
        supported by the evidence provided in the Parties’ internal documents that have been
        prepared in the regular course of business (see sections 8.5.1 and 8.10.1 below).
(471)   The Commission will take therefore as a starting point the market situation before the
       Covid19  pandemic,  in  particular,  in  air  passenger  services.  Accordingly,  the
       Commission will assess the impact of the Transaction on passenger services taking
         into account data from the last four IATA seasons before the outbreak of the Covid19
       pandemic (IATA seasons Summer 2018, Winter 2018/2019, Summer 2019 and Winter
        2019/2020). By contrast, since it is difficult to interpret market share data in passenger
         services between 2020 and 2022 due to the extremely low passenger numbers and the
         fact that at time the recovery had just started, the Commission will not put much
        weight on the market shares between the IATA Summer season 2020 and Winter
        season 2022/2023. Market shares since the beginning of the Covid19 pandemic are

8.5.    Background to Passenger air transport services
8.5.1.   The impact of the Covid19 pandemic and Russia’s war against Ukraine on passenger
         air transport services
(472)   The Covid19 pandemic had a tremendous impact on the airline industry. In particular,
       due to  travel  restrictions and public health concerns, demand for passenger  air
         transport services significantly decreased. As a result, the aviation industry suffered
        severe losses. All airlines had to temporally suspend and/or significantly reduce
        operations on the vast majority of their routes (sometimes re-focusing on cargo).
(473)   Russia’s war against Ukraine has also had an impact on the European aviation sector
       and especially on the EEA-South Korea routes. Following the start of Russia’s war
         against Ukraine in February 2022, the closure of Russian and Ukrainian airspaces for
       European airlines has shifted traffic south,706 leading to longer flight times between
         the EEA and South Korea, whereas Russian airlines have ceased offering flights to the
     EEA customers.
(474)   That said, the market investigation did not provide evidence that the decline in demand
        caused by the Covid19 pandemic would be structural or permanent. Rather, based on
         industry reports and the  results of the Commission’s investigation, the industry
        consensus seems to be that demand will gradually recover. The following evidence
       shows  that  the  aviation  industry’s  recovery from  the Covid19 pandemic  has
         accelerated in 2022 and the upward recovery trend has continued in 2023.
(475)    First, the general industry projections by Eurocontrol and IATA – of June and
        October 2022, which therefore take account of the start of the Russian war on Ukraine
       – anticipate international travel recovery to at least 90% of pre-pandemic traffic in
        around 2023/2024.707 As noted by Eurocontrol, “[l]ong-haul flows recovering well in
        2022, apart from the China (Asia/Pacific region) and South Atlantic flows. Full
         restoration is expected to occur in 2023.”708 According to IATA, since 2022 the
       number of air passengers continued to grow worldwide and approached pre-pandemic
          levels,  demonstrating  the  eagerness  of  travellers  to  fly  again.709  Indeed,  in
       March 2023, the international traffic recovery reached 81.6% of March 2019 levels.710

(476)   While looking specifically at Asia-Pacific, IATA noted that this region is expected to
        reach  its pre-pandemic  traffic levels by 2024, due to the earlier-than-anticipated
        reopening of China.711
(477)  IATA notes that passenger willingness to travel is demonstrated globally by the rapid
         increase in international revenue per passenger kilometres (“RPKs”). Industry-wide
        revenue per RPKs increased significantly from 41.7% of 2019 RPKs in 2021 to 68.5%
         in 2022.712 Routes between Asia-Pacific and the rest of the world have experienced
         significant growth in international traffic, with RPKs within Asia in Q1 2023 growing
       by 703.8% compared to Q1 2022, and Asia-North America by 251.3%.713 According
         to IATA, in the first quarter of 2023, the available seat capacity, measured in available
         seat-kilometres (“ASKs”), continued to ramp up in line with demand for air traffic,
         rising to 89.5% of 2019 levels in March and 79.8% over the quarter (globally),
        whereas passenger load factors, which indicate the level of demand expressed by
       consumers relative to capacity, were close to the 2019 levels for all regions.714
(478)   Korean Air challenges IATA and Eurocontrol projections and submits that they are
         unreliable and too optimistic.715 More specifically, Korean Air submits that IATA’s

(501)   The data summarized in this section above indicates that the market structure for the
          air  transport  of passengers between  the EEA and South Korea would change
        considerably after the Transaction by combining the leading  air  carriers.  It also
         indicates that there are few competitors with significant passenger volumes between
         the EEA and South Korea.
(502)   Overall,  passenger  traffic between  the EEA and South Korea  appears  to be
         characterized by (i) the presence of two large carriers – the Parties –, the presence of
       two smaller competitors as well as a large number of much smaller air passenger
         carriers and (ii) a market structure where the Parties have been able to gain share over
        time by expanding in a growing market. This shows that the Parties are the strongest
        competitors in passenger traffic between the EEA and South Korea and that there is no
         significant competitor to the Parties, even at that aggregated level. Furthermore, the
        market development over time casts doubt on the likelihood of considerable expansion
       by a competitor in the supply of air passenger services between the EEA and South
       Korea in the future.
8.6.    Passenger air transport services – General considerations relating to the Overlap
       Routes
(503)   This section sets out general considerations concerning the competitive analysis of the
        Transaction regarding passenger air transport services. These general remarks are
         relevant, sometimes to different degrees, for each of the Overlap Routes.
8.6.1.   Closeness of competition on the Overlap Routes
(504)   In light of the results of the market investigation, the Commission considers the Parties
         to be close competitors on the Overlap Routes.
(505)    First, when making commercial decisions, the Parties take into account each other’s
        behavior and react to it to be closer to, match or surpass the other’s offer. In the first
         place, when setting prices, the Parties always benchmark against each other and
       sometimes also against other carriers.765 In the second place, when conducting its

(511)   According to the market feedback set out in paragraphs (509) and (510), Asiana offers
           its high-quality direct air passenger service on each of the four Overlap Routes at
          attractive prices. In the Commission’s view, this makes Asiana a close competitor to
         other high-quality direct air services on the Overlap Routes, including notably those
         offered by Korean Air. The aggressive strategy of Asiana led to particular competitive
        pressure by Asiana on Korean Air, which […] the Overlap Routes, as described in
        paragraph (505).
(512)   In their response to the Statement of Objections, the Parties argued that Asiana’s
         pricing strategy is not aggressive compared to that of its competitors.781 The Parties
        supported this claim with a pricing comparison of the fares charged by Asiana and its
         competitors,782 operating direct flights between ICN and each of BCN, CDG, FRA and
     FCO and stated that the comparison shows that in many cases, it is not Asiana but one
        of its competitors that offers the lowest fares.783The Commission does not consider
         that the Parties’ arguments in this respect change the conclusion that Asiana is price
        aggressive and competes closely with Korean Air. In the first place, the sample used
       by the Parties for the price comparison is not representative and cannot serve to
        demonstrate the general pricing strategy of the airlines: Rather than providing average
         prices, the data provided by the Parties contains prices searched on only two specific
         dates (January 2, 2019 and August 2, 2019) for flights departing in the following
       month (January 2019 and August 2019 respectively).784 In the second place, contrary
         to the Parties’ claims, the information provided by the Parties shows that, according to
         the data set, Asiana did offer the lowest fares on a significant number of occasions.
        For example, Asiana offered the lowest fares for the majority of departures in January
       on the FRA route. In the third place, the Commission considers that in order to
       compete fiercely one does not have to always offer the lowest prices. It is enough that
        a competitor stimulates competition and causes others to reduce their prices as well. In
         the fourth place, overall, the data set provided by the Parties does not invalidate the
         qualitative findings from the market investigation described above.

         competitors.

       between the Parties and the impact this competition has on the profitability of each of

(517)    Fifth, arguments made by the Parties in their response to the 6(1)(c) Decision do not
       change the Commission’s conclusion that the Parties are close competitors.
(518)   In the first place, the fact that market participants identify additional competitors
         active on the Overlap Routes does not mean that these other competitors exert similar
        competitive pressure on the Parties. The example brought by the Parties in their
        response to the 6(1)(c) Decision demonstrate this.791 While [a competitor] considers
           itself as a competitor to the Parties, [the competitor] clearly identifies the Parties as
        each other’s closest competitors.792 When asked to list the three closest competitors to
        each of the Parties, [the competitor]  lists the Parties as each other’s  first closest
        competitor on each of the Overlap Routes. Despite its statement that it competes with
         the Parties, [the competitor] does not list itself as the first, second or third closest
        competitor of any of the Parties on the Overlap Routes.793
(519)   In the second place, the Parties do compete closely also in terms of schedule and
         frequencies. The Parties argue that close competition only exists between airlines
         offering flights on the same day and that airlines not offering flights on the same days
        of the week are not considered as alternatives. These arguments cannot stand with
         respect to long haul flights of over 12 hours. Had this been correct, market shares of
         indirect competitors offering daily (i.e. 7 weekly) services on the BCN-ICN and FCO-
      ICN routes should have been higher than those of Asiana (and Korean Air on BCN),
       which  offers only 3-4 weekly  services on  these  routes. While  the number  of
        frequencies is relevant for passengers’ choice, it is only one of a number of criteria

(521)   Sixth, as described in the following paragraphs, the Commission finds that the Korean
         Air’s econometric model is not reliable. In particular, the model does not fully capture
         the competitive interaction between the Parties or the competitive pressure by Asiana
       on Korean Air.797 To the contrary, if anything, the data seem to indicate that Asiana’s
        presence on routes negatively affect each Korean Air’s prices, and Asiana may even
        be the only pricing constraint to Korean Air, if a minimally modified approach is
        adopted.
(522)   In  particular, Korean  Air  submitted an  econometric  analysis  investigating  the
         relationship between the Parties’ fares and the number of nonstop carriers active on
         the route. According to Korean Air, this analysis does not find systematic evidence of
         fare effects from additional carriers beyond two.798
(523)   Korean Air’s proposed methodology uses pooled data across both Parties, all routes
        worldwide, and all cabin classes together. The methodology attempts to address all
         differences across routes and cabin classes by using (linear) fixed effects.799 This
       means that it is taken as given that the differences between routes cabin classes are
         fixed in magnitude, e.g. a percentage difference that can be estimated and that is fixed
        over time, i.e. never changes during the timeframe of analysis, and are linear, meaning
        equal distanced between categories, e.g. the price difference between business and
       economy class on short-haul routes is equal to the percentage difference on long-haul
         routes. The implication of these assumptions and the critical assessment are laid out in
         the following paragraphs.

(524)   The Commission considers that pooling all data across carriers, routes and cabin
         classes implies a number of very strong assumptions, which may lead to misleading
          results.
(525)    First assumption: Pooling data across the two Parties and using carrier-specific fixed
         effects assumes that differences in pricing between Korean Air and Asiana are linear
       and constant over time for all routes and cabin classes. Carrier-specific (fixed) effects
        describe and measure permanent structural differences in the outcome variable, ticket
         prices in this case, between carriers. In other words, these effects capture if one airline
        consequently/permanently (structurally) offers lower fares that are x% (fixed) lower
        than the fares of another carrier. This assumption and the usage of carrier fixed effects
         largely disregards the possibility of different dynamic pricing strategies that can
       change over time.
(526)   Second assumption: Pooling all routes worldwide may risk not to account adequately
         for opposing seasonality patterns. For example, the effects of seasonality on flights
       from Seoul to Europe can differ from inner-Asian short-haul flights or flights from
        Seoul to the Southern Hemisphere (e.g. Auckland, Brisbane).
(527)   Third assumption: Pooling observations across cabin classes in the proposed model is
        problematic as it implies that the price differences between economy, business and
           first class ticket prices are constant and equal for short-haul and intercontinental long-
        haul routes, and fully disregards any non-linear relationship.
(528)   The Parties’ submission does not provide any complementary analysis supporting
         these assumptions, which appear particularly daring for an econometric analysis. A
       more robust econometric analysis would focus on for example Korean Air or Asiana
          ticket  prices  separately; would  consider  sub-sets  of  routes  that  feature  similar
         characteristics, for example, those of the Northern hemisphere long-haul routes; and
       would focus on economy class travellers only, as it can be assumed that economy class
          travellers are the most price-sensitive group of customers.
(529)   The Korean  Air’s proposed methodology  is  not  in  line with  the econometric
       methodology carried out and employed by the Commission in previous cases in the
         aviation industry.800 In the Commission’s view, the Parties’ proposed methodology in
          this case is unable to identify the competitive constraints that the Parties exert on each
         other.
(530)    If Korean Air were competitively constrained by the presence of Asiana,  it can be
        expected that Korean Air would have to offer lower fares on average when Asiana is
         active on the same  airport or  city  pair. Conversely,  if Korean Air imposes a
        competitive constraint on Asiana one should expect that Asiana fares are negatively
         affected by Korean Air’s continued presence. Korean Air’s proposed methodology
          relies on the number of competitors in its analysis, but this measure does not capture
         the closeness of competition between the Parties and implicitly assumes that all non-
        stop carriers are similarly close competitors.
(531)   In contrast, it is very likely that competitors are different and some are perceived as
         closer than others. Such heterogeneity across competitors, and especially the effect of
         the Parties’ activities on each other’s average fares on given routes, cannot be captured
       by the design of the Parties’ econometric analysis.
(532)   The Commission has therefore tested the Parties’ econometric model by using a
        simple alternative econometric specification. The Commission’s testing methodology
        asks whether the presence of Asiana has an impact on Korean Air’s fares, and attempts

800     M.4439 Ryanair/Aer Lingus; M.6663 Ryanair/Aer Lingus III.
