[PÁGINA PDF 123]
         to quantify the magnitude of such an impact (if any). Specifically, the Commission
          tests the following hypothesis: Is Asiana’s presence associated with a statistically and
        economically significant reduction in Korean Air’s fares on the non-stop long-haul
         routes where the Parties overlap (subject to controlling for demand and supply
         factors)?
(533)   Starting from the Parties’ econometric methodology, the Commission’s  test uses
         variation in Asiana’s or other carriers’ presence on a route to assess whether entry or
         exit and different levels of competition are associated with a change in the Korean
         Air’s fares. The Commission regards this methodology as the most suitable to assess
         the competitive constraint exerted by Asiana.
(534)   The  Commission’s  price  quantitative  analysis  confirms  significant  competitive
         interaction between Korean Air and Asiana and is indicative of close competition
       between  them. Should  this  competitive  pressure  disappear  as  a  result  of  the
         Transaction, the analysis indicates that the Merged Entity would have an incentive to
         increase prices on the routes where they overlap.
(535)   For its econometric analysis, the Commission relied on the same dataset used by
       Korean Air,801 which essentially consists of the Parties’ ticketing data, plus additional
        information on all flights by other airlines, based on the OAG flight data802 for the
       same period, as well as fuel prices.803 The combined dataset is a panel data set with
          airline, month and route identifier for the period January 2013 – December 2019.804
(536)   In order to avoid problems of pooled data, the Commission’s analysis uses a sub-set of
         the data to allow for estimating a more clearly identified potential effect of the
        competitive pressure the Parties exert on each other. That sub-set of data provides for:
           (i) separate estimation for each of the Parties’ fare data;  (ii) only Economy-class
         observations; and (iii) separate estimations for all non-stop routes only as well as sub-
         sets of those routes (that is, non-stop routes connecting South Korea with Europe and
        North America, as well connecting South Korea and the EEA only).
(537)   These reductions of data dimensions allow for better identification of the estimates,
         especially when non-linear effects may influence results, and may help to test the
       above stated hypotheses.

         (b)  The term αi is the route fixed effect, that is, an indicator variable equal to 1 for
              route i and zero otherwise. The αi indicator variable accounts for systematic but
             unobserved or non-measurable differences in supply or demand factors affecting
               prices across routes. Routes are defined as origin and destination pairs, for
             example, FRA-ICN and ICN-FRA constitute a unique fixed effect.
          (c)  The term dPRESENCEit  is a variable indicating the presence of the other
            merging Party on a given route in a given month, that is, it is equal to one if
            Korean Air (Asiana) is operating route i in month t and zero otherwise. This
               variable is the explanatory variable of interest.
         (d)  The term Yt is a monthly indicator variable, that is, a route invariant indicator
               variable equal to 1 for the given month and zero otherwise. The Yi indicator
               variable accounts for systematic but unobserved or non-measurable differences
               in supply or demand factors within a given month.
          (e)   Xit represents time-varying and  partially route-specific supply and demand
               factors that can affect fares, such as whether other competitors are present, the
               Parties’ load factors, and fuel costs.
(539)  A large part of the effects that demand factors may have on fares is captured by the
       month effects (for example, an event that draws a significant number of passengers to
       Europe in a given month), as well as by the route-specific fixed effects (for example,
         the type of destination, different routes having different levels of popularity, route-
         specific fees and others). As airlines are generally interested in ensuring their planes
         are full, they may seek to adapt prices to fluctuations in demand. To control for this
         feature, the load factor806 variable is included as a proxy for demand. It has to be noted
         that  including demand  factors  as  explanatory  variables may cause a  so-called
        endogeneity problem in the regression: It might happen that lower prices increased
       demand which leads to higher load factors, rather than the other way around where
        high load factors lead to high prices. Hence, the Commission tested the estimation
        robustness of the coefficient of interest by excluding the potentially endogenous
         variables in some specifications. The results show that excluding the load factor has no
         significant effect on the estimation of the effect of the other Party’ presence.
(540)   Similarly to the demand factors, a large part of the effects that supply factors may have
       on fares are captured by the month fixed effects (for example, labour or equipment
          costs), as well as by the route-specific fixed effects (for example, airport fees). Fuel
         costs may vary over time and  affect  routes  differently depending on  the  fuel
        consumption for the route in question. Therefore, fuel costs are interacted with the
         fixed distance between the two airports of a route, and included as an additional
         control for supply factors. As fuel may be bought and tickets sold at different points in
         time, a lag in fuel costs of one month is used.807
(541)    It is important to point out that the econometric analysis rests on a limited number of
        “entry or exit events”: There are a number of routes where there is no change in the
        presence  of  air  carriers over  the  entire time  period  and,  therefore, under  the
       Commission’s  modelling  strategy  of  assessing  variation  within  a  route,  these
        observations do not contribute to the estimation of the effect of presence on prices.
      When restricting the analysis to Europe and North America, because there are no

(545)   The Commission is aware of the limited variation in the data that identified the
        negative effects of Asiana’s presence on Korean Air’s price, and acknowledges that
         generalisations of the effects can only cautiously be taken into account, as the
         identification  only  relies on  four  entry/exit  events  in  total.  Nevertheless,  the
       Commission considers that, in principle, the estimated effect is statistically identified
        such that the results hint that prices are more likely to increase post-Transaction than
        being unaffected, although being cautious on any broad generalisation.
(546)  To conclude, the results of the Commission’s analysis show that (i) Korean Air’s
        econometric model does not fully capture the competitive interaction between the
          Parties,  (ii), to the contrary, the data hints that the Parties’ presence on routes
        negatively affect each other’s prices, and Asiana may even be the only pricing
         constraint to Korean Air. Nevertheless, the limited variation identifying the price
         effect has to be taken into account such that the Commission considers the results of
         the quantitative analysis as auxiliary secondary evidence.
8.6.2.   Limited constraints from indirect flights on the Overlap Routes
(547)   Generally, there is no strict measure or threshold that could predict whether an indirect
          flight competes  with a  direct  flight on  the Overlap  Routes. As  explained  in
         section 7.1.5, the Commission considers that a cut-off of 150-minute lay-over time
        cannot be applied mechanically. In particular, the relevance of one-stop flights also
        depends on other criteria such as the time during the day of the stop-over, of the ticket
         price and of demand composition on the route. However, together with other factors
        such as the market shares and availability of one-stop and non-stop flights, the added
         travel time of one-stop flights still provides a useful indication as to the competitive
         constraint they exercise.
(548)   Based on its market investigation, the Commission considers that competitors offering
        one-stop  flights exert only limited competitive constraints on the Parties’ direct
        operations on the Overlap Routes.
(549)    First, as explained in section 8.6.3.1, most of the competitors offering indirect services
       on the Overlap Routes are in any event unable to expand their services on these routes
       due to the exhaustion of traffic rights between their hubs and Seoul. As explained in
         section 8.7, the presence of any remaining competitors offering indirect services is
         insignificant and unlikely to be able to restrain the merged entity.
(a)     Second, Korean Air generally benchmarks its prices against airlines operating direct
          flights.810
(550)   Third,  the  Parties’  internal documents show  that  the  Parties  consider  indirect
        competitors as a weaker competitive constraint.
(551)   For example, in a request for amendment to Korean Air’s Benchmarking Scheme for
        Routes from Europe of April 2018,811 […],812,813In this document, Korean’s pricing
        revenue management department asks to “[…],814 […].

(557)   Fourth, the view that one-stop flights are less preferred by customers and exert lower
        competitive pressure on the Parties’ direct services is shared by market participants.
(558)   In the first place, the majority of competitors expressing a view consider that indirect
         services exert a lower level of competitive pressure on the Parties’ services compared
         to direct services.825
(559)   In the second place, whether a flight is direct or indirect was rated as one of the three
       most important criteria when choosing with which airline to book a flight on routes
       between the EEA and South Korea by market participants replying to the Commission
        phase I questionnaires. On average, the importance of this criteria was rated (on a
         scale from 1 to 5) 4.35 by customers,826 4.24 by travel agents and tour operators827 and
        4.33 by competitors.828 Market participants considered price of the flight as the most
        important  criteria. Customers rated the  total  flight duration as the second most
        important criteria (rated 4.39 on average, on a scale from 1 to 5),829 which is affected
       by whether a flight is direct or includes a stop.
(560)   In the third place, market participants explain that direct flights are generally preferred
       by passengers, that, where available, business passengers would almost always choose
         direct flights over indirect flights and that while leisure passengers might opt for
         indirect flights, they would do so only if the indirect flight is offered at a considerably
        lower price and the total flight time is not significantly longer.830 While competitors
        operating indirect flights consider themselves to some extent part of the competition,
          this is conditional on their ability to offer prices at lower prices, short connecting time
       and overall travel time, and limited capacity of direct services.831
(561)    Fifth, the very limited market share  that each of the competitors with  indirect
        connections have been able to achieve demonstrate that one-stop flights represent a
         different value proposition and would only be an alternative to a subset of passengers.
       The market shares of competitors offering indirect flights on the Overlap Routes are
         significantly lower than those of the competitors offering direct services on the same
         route. Pre-Covid19 market shares of individual competitors offering indirect services
       on the Overlap Routes were generally lower than [5-10]% for the routes FRA-ICN,
      CDG-ICN and FCO-ICN and lower than [10-20]% for BCN-ICN (where only the
         Parties offered direct services).

(562)   Sixth, contrary to the Parties’ claim that indirect flights are generally less expensive
       and therefore more attractive for passengers,832 the Commission market investigation
       shows that the relevance of one-stop flights and their ability to exert competitive
         constraints on direct services depends on various criteria.
(563)   In the first place, the ticket price affects the customer’s choice. Market participants
       have rated the ticket price as the most important criteria (on average) when choosing
       an  airline for a  flight between the EEA and South Korea.833 However, market
         participants note that the ticket price has to be considerably lower to be attractive, and
         that business passengers are generally more likely to opt for a direct flight (even if the
         indirect alternative is significantly cheaper).834 In the second place, the total elapsed
        time of the trip, as well as the length and time of day of a stop-over affect the
         attractiveness of indirect flights and are likely to make them less attractive and
         therefore less competitive compared to direct flights. Both criteria were rated highly
        (above 3.5 on average, on a scale from 1 to 5) by market participants replying to the
       Commission questionnaires.835 Market participants explained that considerably longer
         travel time or transit time, as well as stop-over during the night would make indirect
          flights less attractive.836 Other criteria considered as important by market participants
         are the time of departure/arrival and distance to the starting point and final destination
        of the trip, overall passenger experience and frequency offered per week.837
(564)   The competitive pressure exerted by indirect competitors will be further assessed, inter
          alia based on these criteria on a route by route basis in sections 8.7.1 to 8.7.4.
8.6.3.   Entry and expansion on the Overlap Routes
(565)   This section contains some general remarks with respect to the likelihood of new entry
        or expansion by existing carriers and the conditions for it to be considered sufficient to
         constrain the Merged Entity, which to varying degrees are relevant for all routes
        covered by this Decision. In addition, this section describes barriers to entry and
        expansion on each of the Overlap Routes.
(566)   According to the Horizontal Merger Guidelines, the entry or expansion of a competitor
         in a relevant market may provide a sufficient competitive constraint on the merging
          parties. Therefore, entry and expansion analysis constitutes an important element of
         the Commission’s competitive assessment. For entry to be considered a sufficient
        competitive constraint on the merging parties, it must be shown to be likely, timely
       and sufficient to deter or defeat any potential anti-competitive effects of the merger.838
(567)   The General Court has noted that “the starting point for the issue of the entrance of
       new competitors onto the relevant markets is a situation where the new entrant is

        seeking to access the market on which the Merged Entity would be present, and where
         that  entity […] would eliminate current competition between the parties to the
        concentration to the detriment of customers.”839 Consequently, the Court has held that
        “the mere ‘threat’ of an entry, on which the applicant relies, is not sufficient. […]
       What counts is the prospect of an entrant which offsets the anti-competitive effects
         specifically established in the contested decision at that stage of the assessment.”840
(568)  To determine the likelihood of new entry, one consideration is that entry must be
         sufficiently profitable, taking into account the price effects of that entry and possible
        responses of the incumbents.841 The attractiveness of the route in terms of size and
        geography is another relevant factor to assess the new entrant’s incentives. Finally, the
         existence of barriers to entry is also relevant to assess the likelihood of new entry
        through their impact on the profitability of entry. Barriers to entry are specific features
        of the market, which give incumbent firms advantages over potential competitors.
      When entry barriers are low, the merging parties are more likely to be constrained by
         entry. Conversely, when entry barriers are high, price increases by the merging firms
       would not be significantly constrained by entry. Historical examples of entry and exit
         in the industry may provide useful indications about the size of entry barriers. Barriers
         to entry can take various forms. For instance, barriers to entry may exist because of the
         established position of the incumbent firms on the market.842
(569)   The expected evolution of the market should be taken into account when assessing
        whether or not entry would be profitable. Entry is more likely to be profitable in a
        market that is expected to experience high growth in the future than in a market that is
        mature or expected to decline. Scale economies or network effects may make entry
         unprofitable unless the entrant can obtain a sufficiently large market share.843
(570)   Based on the framework for the assessment of entry and expansion described above,
         the Commission’s assessment of entry and expansion in the current case is presented
         in the following paragraphs.
(571)   Based on the Commission’s market investigation, the most important criteria for an
          airline to decide to enter or expand operations on any of the Overlap Routes are the
         overall level of profitability of the route, slot availability and traffic size/demand.844
       The number of competitors on the route is rated on average as the eighth criterion in
        order of importance.845 As such, the number of competitors on the route does not
        appear as the primary criterion to decide on entry or expansion on a route. This implies
         that a reduction in the number of competitors is unlikely on its own to trigger market
         entry. Market entry will rather be determined by the attractiveness of the route and the
         existence of barriers to entry.
(572)   The market investigation did not identify new entry or expansion on any of the
        Overlap Routes by existing carriers that could be considered as likely, timely and

8.6.3.1. Availability of traffic rights
(575)   In order for an airline to operate flights outside its home jurisdiction and enter another
        country’s airspace, an air-services agreement (‘ASA’) needs to be in place for traffic
         rights between the two countries and the airline would have to obtain the rights to
        operate services between the two countries. ASAs can grant different degrees of
        freedoms/rights to airlines and can limit the number of services operated between the
         countries, the type of services these carriers can provide and the number of carriers
        allowed to operate these services.
(576)   The market investigation shows that the exhaustion of traffic rights granted to carriers
        according to existing ASAs may constitute a barrier to entry and expansion on the
        Overlap Routes.
(577)    First, air carriers consider that the availability of traffic rights is an important factor in
         the decision whether to enter or expand on a new route.846 In a similar way, air carriers
        consider the lack of availability of traffic rights to be a barrier to entry and expansion
       on routes between the EEA and South Korea.847
(578)   Second, as explained in the route by route assessment in sections 8.7.1 and 8.7.4
        below, the limited availability of traffic rights according to the ASAs between South
       Korea and each of Germany, France and Italy may limit the ability of Korean (and to
       some extent EU) carriers from entering or expanding passenger air services on routes
       between these countries.
(579)   Third, the market investigation shows  that the exhaustion of  traffic  rights also
         constitutes a barrier to expansion for carriers providing indirect flights and wishing to
       expand their services on the Overlap Routes. In several cases, competitors offering
         indirect services on the Overlap Routes cannot increase the frequencies operated
       between their hubs and South Korea, as all the traffic rights provided for in the ASA
       between their countries and South Korea are used and no additional traffic rights are
         available.
(580)   There are currently no available traffic rights allowing for entry or expansion on routes
       between Seoul and the following countries: Qatar, United Arab Emirates, Turkey and
        Poland, as well as on the route Helsinki-Seoul.848 Competitors offering indirect
         services between the EEA and South Korea through hubs in these countries explained
         that the lack of traffic rights on routes between their hubs and Seoul does not allow
       them to expand on the routes.849

8.6.3.2. Availability of slots
(587)   The market investigation shows that slot constraints at relevant airports constitute a
         barrier to entry and expansion on the Overlap Routes.
(588)    First, air carriers consider that the availability of slots for take-off and landing is one
        of the most important criteria when deciding to enter a new long-haul route between
         the EEA and South Korea.856
(589)   Second, all the airports on the Overlap Routes (ICN, BCN, CDG, FCO and FRA) are
        categorized by IATA as “level 3 airports”.857 Typically, level 3 airports are considered
        as  airports with congested  slots. The IATA Worldwide Airport Slot Guidelines
      (WASG) defines a level 3 airport as one where demand for airport infrastructure
         significantly  exceeds  the  airport’s  capacity  during  the  relevant  period.   The
         categorization of these airports as “level 3 airports” indicates therefore that they might
        be slot congested, at least during some hour bands.858
(590)   Third, the market investigation shows that ICN airport is highly congested. In the first
         place, ICN slot coordinator confirms that every day of the week,“[t]he whole day time
        periods (0505-2400 Local […]) are highly congested”; that “[t]he whole day time
        periods are considered as peak times” and that “[d]uring peak times, the amount of
          slots requested in the initial coordination always exceed the capacity […]”.859 ICN
          slot coordinator therefore considers  that  “[i]t  is not easy  for any  airline (both

        of the Overlap Routes.
8.6.3.3. The strong position of the Merged Entity
(598)   The market investigation shows that the strong competitive position of the Merged
         Entity post-Transaction constitutes a barrier to entry.
(599)    First, this view is shared by several competitors and potential entrants. When asked to
         rate to what extent different elements constitute a barrier to entry for air passenger
         services (from 1: does not constitute a barrier at all to 5: constitutes an important
          barrier), potential entrants rated the strong position of competitors on the route
       between 4 and 5 on all Overlap Routes.873 When asked what impact,  if any, the
        Transaction will have on barriers to entry and expansion, competitors and potential
         entrants refer to the advantage the Merged Entity will have in terms of slots and
         frequencies.874 Some carriers explained that the Merged Entity could deter entry or
        expansion on the routes by engaging in a ‘price war’.875
(600)   Second, as is evident from its internal documents, Korean Air considers that post-
        Transaction the Merged Entity would hold [40-50]% of the slots at ICN (taking into
        account affiliate companies) and states an aim to obtain more than [50-60]% of the
          slots at ICN, as this would strengthen its position.876 Korean Air considers that the
         Parties’ combined slot holdings at ICN airport, as well as their combined traffic rights,
        could strengthen and promote the Merged Entity’s competitiveness and the use of slots
          at ICN airport and of traffic rights should therefore be maximised.877 As both slots and
          traffic rights are constrained resources, maximization of their usage by the Merged
         Entity would strengthen its position, allow it to respond easily to competition from
      new entrants and limit the ability of competitors to use such resources, which are

8.6.3.4. Other barriers to entry and expansion
(601)    First, the market investigation shows that the profitability of the route is an important
         factor when deciding to enter a new route878 and therefore limited profitability can be
        as a barrier to entry. Profitability of the route is affected by various factors, such as the
         level of demand on the route, the passenger mix on the route and the share of business
       demand, the air carrier’s ability to attract connecting passengers and more. Each of
         these elements could serve as a barrier to entry on its own due to its effect on the
          profitability of the route.
(602)   In the first place, the market investigation shows that the level of demand and the
        passenger mix on the route can be a barrier to entry to the Overlap Routes.879 The
        passenger mix may include visiting friends and family, tourists and business and
       premium travellers. The mix and share of each group would affect the ability of air
         carriers to operate the route profitably. For example, business passengers provide
        higher revenue to air carriers (if the air carrier is able to offer premium services).880 In
          this respect, the share of TS/premium passengers on some of the Overlap Routes is
         significant: during IATA seasons Winter 2018/2019, Summer 2019 and Winter
        2019/2020, the share of TS passengers was around [5-10]% on the ICN-BCN route,
        [10-20]%-[10-20]% on the ICN-FRA route, [5-10]%-[10-20]% on the ICN-CDG route
       and [5-10]%-[5-10]% on the ICN-FCO route.881 A market participant explained that
      “FRA and CDG are considered as the largest O&D market with MICE (Meetings,
         Incentives, Conferences & Exhibitions) infrastructure and events, FCO and BCN are
        recognized as highly leisure-driven destinations with cultural heritage and sight-
        seeing spots”.882
(603)   In the second place, the market investigation shows that economies of scale and scope
         are important to operate the routes profitably and can be a barrier to entry on routes
       between the EEA and South Korea. Competitors consider that economies of scale and
        scope at origin and/or destination airport constitute a barrier to entry and expansion on
           all Overlap Routes (rated, on average, above 3 on a scale from 1 to 5 on all Overlap

        South Korea and the EEA, and therefore for shorter travel time and lower costs. Trans-

         travel in its airspace. Market participants note that, should Russian air space re-open,
         the availability of such overflight rights is crucial for their ability to enter or expand on
         the route.

8.6.4.   Limited competitive constraints from other one-stop itineraries from other airports
(611)   According to the Notifying Party, it is necessary to look at indirect flights from other
         airports and the possibility of self-connecting passengers to appropriately take into
        account the competitive constraint faced by the Parties. The Notifying Party argues
         that (i) a substantial portion of passengers on Overlap Routes do not have the O&D
         airports as origin or final destination; and (ii) market shares without due recognition of
         self-connecting behind  or beyond  the O&D  pair would  assess  the competitive
         constraints on a given route incompletely.905
(612)   More specifically, Korean Air claims that the large proportion of passengers who may
          fly alternatively from regional airports on one-stop itineraries after a price increase for
         the Parties’ services, prevents the Parties to independently increase prices at hub
          airports.
(613)   Korean Air argues  that country-wide market shares would  better  represent  the
        competitive situation than market shares based on O&D pairs.906
(614)   Korean Air based its analysis on redirect data from Skyscanner,907 instead of billing
        address data on the Parties’ customers as the Parties do not retain credit card billing
        information for booking via their website or sales offices, nor do they receive such
        information from travel agents. Korean Air argues that looking at the Parties’ data
        only would reduce the sample size and would not allow for a complete picture of the
        market. Korean Air also argues that information on the other airlines is an integral part
        of  the  analysis  as Skyscanner  data  also  reveals information about  the options
        passengers weigh.908
(615)   Korean Air argues that the redirect data show that a significant proportion of travellers
         living closer to an airport (e.g. a regional airport in Germany) self-connect to a farther
       away hub airport (e.g. the hub airport in Frankfurt) because they prefer to fly directly
       from the hub airport rather than to fly indirectly from their local airport. Korean Air
        argues  that these  self-transferring passengers would  constraint  the  Parties from
         increasing prices or worsening any parameter of competitor post Transaction because,
        should prices at the hub airport increase post-merger, passengers would no longer self-

        placed on them as evidence.916 The Commission disagrees with this argument as the
       wording used in the phase 1 questionnaires to competitors, corporate customers, and
         tour operators and travel agents provides sufficiently detailed instructions with respect
         to the definition of leakage used. Moreover, these respondents are experts in their
         respective fields that would very unlikely misinterpret these two distinct meanings.
        Furthermore, if respondents had actually misinterpreted these terms, this would imply
         that the market investigation would have likely overestimated the extent of customer
         leakage, thus implying the Commission’s conclusions were even conservative. Lastly,
       Korean Air argues that, failing to ask passengers directly via a survey, the market
         investigation was further limited in its ability to gather meaningful information. The
       Commission notes that corporate customers, competitors and travel agents and tour
         operators are all market experts with direct access to end customers. If customer
        leakage were such a strong and important driver of competitive interactions as
        portrayed by the Notifying Party, these market participants would have surely flagged
           its relevance during the phase 1 investigation, and the subsequent interactions.

          result of a given flight on Skyscanner to a merchant’s website, by selecting to inspect
         the offer of a specific merchant on its website, are not equivalent to actual bookings.
       The majority of redirections does not result in a purchase of a ticket.917 Results based
       on  redirection  data  are  not  necessarily  representative  for  the  actual  purchase
        behaviour. Moreover, compared to actual bookings, Skyscanner redirect data may not
        adequately reflect passengers’ location, and thus provides a biased picture of initial

(623)   Third, considering that the large majority of passengers originate in South Korea, it is
        questionable whether the extent of passengers self-connecting in Europe is sufficiently
         large to generate critical loss and constrain a price increase.919
(624)   Fourth, the analysis submitted by the Notifying Party does not provide evidence for
         the reasons that drive the passengers’ choice of airport. The Notifying Party suggests
         that lower prices at the hub airport would spur self-connecting passengers. However,
         the analysis does not demonstrate that price is a decisive factor in the choice of airport
        as the study itself does not use pricing data but merely the geo-location of internet
         users. Any other factor can equally or even more likely induce self-connection, such as
        a strong preference for non-stop flight itineraries. The study fails to demonstrate that
         the elasticity of substitution between non-stop and one-stop itineraries is price driven,
        nor demonstrates how many passengers would potentially not self-connect in case of a
         likely price increase. Hence, the existence of some self-connecting passengers in
         redirection data does not allow to conclude that a price increase at the hub airport will
        lead self-connecting passengers to divert to one-stop flights. It might well be that a
        majority of self-connecting passengers strongly prefer direct flights from a hub airport
        over indirect flights from a closer airport.
(625)    Fifth, even if the Parties’ arguments related to passengers leakage were fully accepted,
         the Parties’ country-wide market shares remain high nonetheless (ranging between
       [50-60]% and [60-70]%) for each of South Korea-Germany, South Korea-France,
        South Korea-Italy and South Korea-Spain.920
(626)   Korean Air argues that the interpretation based on results of the leakage analysis
        should allow valid conclusions, as long as Skyscanner data is representative of total
        customer bookings as regards the geographic  distribution and  airport choice of
        passengers flying to Seoul.
(627)   The Commission agrees in  principle,  if and only  if Skyscanner data would be
         representative. As explained in the above, the Commission doubts that Skyscanner
        data can probably be considered as representative given the discrepancies between
        market shares based on Skyscanner data, representing website redirection or at best
         intentions to buy, and market shares based on DDS data, that represents actual
        purchase behaviour. Hence, the discrepancies suggest that Skyscanner is precisely not
         representative  of  total customer bookings  of  passengers  flying  to  Seoul. The
       Commission contemplates that representativeness of any data set is essential for the
          reliability of any quantitative analysis and consequently for its interpretation. Given
         that in the case of Skyscanner data there are several reasonable concerns regarding
         representativeness, the Commission concludes that the analysis based on Skyscanner
        data is insufficient to eliminate its concerns.

8.6.5.  MOLIT price regulation will not constrain the merged entity
(628)   The Commission does not consider that the price regulation applied by the South
       Korea Ministry of Land Infrastructure and Transport (‘MOLIT’) will exert sufficient
         constrains on the Merged Entity prices post-Transaction.
(629)   Korean Air argues that the Parties are currently not able to freely increase prices on at
          least one leg of the overlapping routes, as prices charged for flights originating in
       Korea are strictly controlled by the South Korean government.921 The Commission
        considers that these claims cannot be accepted for several reasons.
(630)    First, MOLIT’s control over prices only concerns outbound flights from Korea, which
           is only one part of the price passengers on the Overlap Routes are required to pay.
      MOLIT’s price ceiling does not concern inbound flights.922
(631)   Second, MOLIT’s price ceiling is significantly higher than the Parties’ average prices,
         especially with respect to economy and business class where the gaps between
      MOLIT’s price ceiling and each of the Parties’ average prices are as high as […]%,
        implying that the Parties could […] increase their prices before being constrained by
      MOLIT’s price ceiling.923
(632)   Third, the Parties internal documents confirm that MOLIT’s price regulation does not
         constrain their ability to increase prices. An internal document of […].
Figure 39: [Figure redacted]


Source: reply to RFI11, Annex RFI11 – Q1.1.d, pages 3,4.
(633)   Fourth, the Commission considers that a regulatory price ceiling, which requires that
         “fares must be reasonable in light of expenses and profits”924 is unlikely to constrain
         the Merged Entity prices to a level that is similar to the pressure exerted by the
        competitive process. Korean Air confirms that “MOLIT’s control over prices is not
       however  the main  driver  of Korean  Air’s  pricing  policy”.925 As  explained  in
        Section 8.6.1, closeness of competition, the main driver of the Parties’ pricing is the
         other party’s prices.
(634)    Fifth, Korean Air’s claim that the behavioural remedies accepted by the KFTC
         regulating the price the merged entity will be able to charge on the Overlap Routes
        cannot change the Commission’s assessment. The remedies accepted by the KFTC are
        not enforceable by the Commission and could be waived or left unenforced.
8.6.6.   Effect of the Transaction
(635)   The Commission’s market investigation shows that the Transaction is likely to have a
        negative impact on competition in passenger air services on the Overlap Routes.
(636)    First, the Parties’ internal documents show that they consider the Transaction is meant
         to eliminate price competition between them, would allow them to increase prices and
         to reduce the number of services on the Overlap Routes, and would lead to consumer
        harm.

         Parties are the only competitors offering direct services on the route. In the second
         place, as described in section 8.6.2, the Parties face limited constraints from indirect
          flights on the Overlap Routes: the Parties’ internal documents show that the Parties
        consider indirect competitors as a weaker competitive constraint; market participants
        share the view that one-stop flights are less preferred by customers and exert lower
        competitive pressure on the Parties’ direct services; the limited market share that each
        competitor with indirect connections has been able to achieve demonstrates that one-
        stop flights represent a different value proposition and would only be an alternative to
        a subset of passengers, and; the fact that the relevance of one-stop flights and their
          ability to exert competitive constraints on direct services depends on various criteria,
       and not only price. In the third place, as described in section 8.6.3, barriers to entry
       and expansion such as availability of slots, availability of traffic rights, the strong
         position of the Merged Entity on the route, the profitability of the route, availability of
          aircrafts and crews and the closure of Russian airspace, are high, also when focusing
         the assessment on EU based passengers, and no sufficient entry is expected on the
        Overlap Routes.
8.6.7.   The Parties’ high market shares on each of the Overlap Routes indicate that the
       Merged Entity would hold a dominant position after the Transaction on each of the
        routes
(653)  As explained in section 8.7, the Transaction would lead to the Merged Entity holding a
        very strong market position on each of the Overlap Routes. The Commission considers
         that the Parties’ combined markets shares on the Overlap Routes indicate that the
       Merged Entity would hold a dominant position after the Transaction.
(654)   In their Response to the Statement of Objections, the Parties argue that high market
        shares in the airline industry are not indicative of market power.959 The Commission
         disagrees with that reasoning and instead finds that market shares are a useful first
         indicator for the existence of market power on each of the routes, for the following
         reasons.
(655)   In the first place, as explained in section 8.1 (paragraph (298)), the European courts
       have confirmed that high market shares are indicative of market power in the aviation
         industry.
(656)   In the second place, the markets for air passenger services on different O&Ds are not
         characterised by lumpy consumption or infrequent purchases but rather by daily
        purchases by hundreds,  if not thousands  of customers.  In such  circumstances,
        customer constantly reveal their purchasing preferences in each of their purchasing
         decisions, which reflect the competitive strength of the offers available on the market.
        Therefore, there is no reason to assume that market shares are not representative of
        market power.
(657)   In the third place, contrary to the Parties’ claim that market shares are volatile,
         significant variations in market shares are limited to the period of the Covid19
       pandemic due to the pandemic’s specific effects on supply and demand. By contrast,
         prior to the Covid19 pandemic, the market shares of the Parties and their competitors
       were relatively stable over time.960
(658)   In the fourth place, the Parties themselves use market shares as an indicator of market
        power. In an internal document related to the […],961 Korean Air decides […].

(661)   In the fifth place, as evident from Sections 8.6 and 8.7, the Commission’s assessment
        does not rely solely on market shares and the mere fact of the reduction of the number
         of players on a given market. The Commission has notably carefully considered the
        closeness of competition between the Parties, the competitive constraint exerted by
         existing competitors, as well as the probability of additional competitive constraint
        exerted by  likely, timely and  sufficient entry or expansion and the  likely and
         significant impact  of  the  Transaction on competition  in each  relevant market.
        Furthermore, as explained in more detail in section 8.5.1, the Commission has taken
         into account changes that have occurred since the start of the Covid19 pandemic, as
        well as future changes to the markets that can be reasonably predicted, to the extent
        they will likely continue to be relevant also after demand will have recovered from the
        temporary Covid19 shock. These changes for instance cover duly documented entry or
         exit plans or changes in competitiveness that will have lasting and structural effects.
       At the same time, the Commission has also given due importance – both in the
         description of the framework of its assessment and in each route-by-route assessment
        taking into account the facts of this case – to the often very high combined market
        shares of the Parties over several IATA seasons, in line with established case law and
       Commission practice.

(663)   For the reasons set out below, the Commission concludes that the Transaction would
        lead to a significant impediment to effective competition on the route ICN-BCN.
(664)    First, the Transaction would lead to the Merged Entity holding a very strong market
         position on  the  route. Asiana  entered  this  route  in 2018 and has  acquired a
        considerable share of that market. As set out in Table 22, the Parties combined have
        held market shares between [40-50]% and [60-70]% on the route between Winter 2018
         (the year Asiana started offering direct flights on the route) and 2019, which indicates
         that the Merged Entity would hold a dominant position after the Transaction.987 When
         redistributing the market shares of competitors who have since then exited the market,
         the Parties combined market shares are even higher (up to [60-70]%).988 The Parties
       have also been the only two carriers with direct flights between 2018 and 2019, giving
       them a share of weekly frequencies for direct flights of [90-100]% for the entire
         period.
(665)   In their Response to the Statement of Objections, the Parties argue that high market
        shares in the airline industry are not indicative of market power.989 The Commission
         disagrees and considers that the Parties’ high market shares are indicative of market
        power, for the reasons listed in section 8.6.7. Namely, the European courts have
        confirmed that high market shares are indicative of market power in the aviation
         industry; the markets are characterised by daily purchases, constantly revealing
        customers’ purchasing preferences and reflecting the competitive strength of the offers
         available on the market; following the entry of Asiana on the route in Summer 2018
       and prior to the Covid19 pandemic, market shares of the Parties and their competitors
       were stable over time, apart for the variation related to Asiana’s entry on the route (as
        evident in Table 22), and the Parties themselves use market shares as an indicator of
        market power.
(666)   Second, the increment brought about by the Transaction would be particularly large
        based on figures for the years 2018 (the year Asiana started offering direct flights on
         the route) to 2019:  at [10-20]%  (in Summer 2018) [20-30]%-points  (in Winter
        2018/2019) to [30-40]%-points due to Asiana. This results in a high increase in the
      HHI of more than […]. The large level and increment in the Parties’ joint market
         position is a clear indicator that the Transaction would create a dominant position.
(667)   Third, while the Covid19 pandemic has had a temporary significant impact on demand
       and supply, the Commission does not expect the competitive dynamics on the route to
       change significantly in the long-term.

(670)   Fourth, the remaining competitors would likely be insufficient to constrain the Merged
         Entity on the route.
(671)   In the first place, the market shares of the remaining competitors pre-Covid19 are
        smaller by a large margin than those of each of the Parties and of the Merged Entity
            (i.e., following Asiana’s entry on the route in Summer 2018, market shares of all other
         carriers on the route did not exceed [10-20]% each and many of them remained well
       below [5-10]%, see Table 22).
(672)   In the second place, all other competitors apart from the Parties offer only one-stop
          flights between ICN and BCN. While one-stop flights may compete with non-stop
          flights for long-haul travel, they represent a different value proposition, and would
        only be an alternative to a subset of passengers, for the reasons set out in section 8.6.2.
       Namely, as explained in section 8.6.2, the Parties’ internal documents show that the
         Parties […]; market participants […] that one-stop  flights are less preferred by
        customers and exert lower competitive pressure on the Parties’ direct services; the
         limited market share that each competitor with indirect connections has been able to
        achieve demonstrate that one-stop flights represent a different value proposition and
       would only be an alternative to a subset of passengers, and; the fact that the relevance
        of one-stop flights and their ability to exert competitive constraints on direct services
        depends on various criteria, and not only price.
(673)   In the third place, Asiana has entered the route during IATA season Summer 2018,
       and within the following IATA season Winter 2018/2019, the first season in which it
        completed ramping up its frequencies, Asiana already achieved a market share of [20-
       30]%, which is larger than the market share of any other competitor offering indirect
         services on the route (see Table 22). This shows the superior value proposition of
         direct flights and customer preference for them, if offered at competitive conditions.
(674)   In  the  fourth  place,  the  majority  of  one-stop  flights on  the ICN-BCN  route
         significantly extend travel time and reduce travel convenience as compared to direct
          flights and  therefore  exert only  limited  competitive  constraint on  the  Parties’
        operations on the route ICN-BCN. During IATA season Summer 2023, the vast
        majority of one-stop flights on the ICN-BCN route are at least 3 and up to 6 hours (i.e.
      22% to 43%) longer than the Parties’ direct services on the route, with flights offered
       by Cathay Pacific, Emirates, Qatar and Turkish Airlines having a stop-over during

         disagrees and considers that the Parties’ high market shares are indicative of market
        power, for the reasons listed in section For the reasons listed in section 8.6.7. Namely,
         the European courts have confirmed that high market shares are indicative of market
       power in the aviation industry; prior to the Covid19 pandemic, market shares of the
         Parties and their competitors were stable over time (as evident in Table 27, and the
         Parties themselves use market shares as an indicator of market power.

(704)   In  their Response  to  the Statement  of  Objections,  the  Parties claim  that  [the
         competitor’s] market presence on the ICN – FRA route could substantially increase
        should it become more profitable to use its existing capacity on the route for non-stop
          itineraries, instead of one-stop itineraries as it currently does.1048 However, this claim
        ignores the opportunity costs [the competitor] would face should  it pursue such a
         strategy. These costs concerns giving up capacity on another route, which it currently
          prioritizes over the ICN-FRA route. Market participants confirmed the importance of
        opportunity costs to their network planning.1049 One competitor explained: “If there
         aren't any aircraft available in your fleet,  it is highly unlikely you would consider
        entering a new market. Unless, of course, the new market provided [profitability]
       above and beyond other opportunities and current routes in your network. In which
         case, you would cancel a route in order to enter a new one”.1050 Another competitor
        explained that “Internally crew and aircraft [resources] are typically [allocated] to
        most profitable routes”.1051 In  this respect, the Horizontal Merger Guidelines1052
         clarify that an output expansion by competitors is unlikely when competitors face
        binding capacity constraints and the expansion of capacity is costly or  if existing
        excess capacity is significantly more costly to operate than capacity currently in use.

(724)    Finally, as explained below (paragraphs (725) to (733)), the market investigation does
        not enable the Commission to conclude that passengers’ leakage to/from FRA airport
       would be sufficient to constrain the Parties post-Transaction nor that Germany-wide
        market shares would provide a more accurate representation of the competitive
         constraints faced by the Parties than standard market shares based on FRA-ICN O&D
          city-pair.
(725)   Korean Air argues that self-connecting passengers who could travel via one-stop
          itineraries from/to regional airports across Germany constrain the Parties’ prices on
         direct flights from FRA.1093
(726)   Korean Air argues that  (i) The results of the closer-airport analysis indicate that
        around half of the users choosing direct flights from Frankfurt to Seoul were located
         closer to another major German airport than to FRA;1094 (ii) The review of available
          flight options from other German airports compared to the travel time by train or car to
        Frankfurt paired with a direct flight to Seoul shows similar total travel time between
         the two itineraries and thus supports the view that passengers from these regions can
         substitute between direct flights from FRA and an indirect flights from their respective
         local airport;1095 and (iii) the catchment-area analysis does not suggest that a specific
        catchment area can be defined for Frankfurt airport but that all areas of Germany
         contribute  significant numbers  of marginal passengers  flying on  the FRA-ICN
          route.1096
(727)   Korean Air argues that the Parties will be constrained from increasing prices, or
        worsening any other parameter of competition post-merger because around half of the
        passengers choosing flights from Frankfurt to Seoul were located closer to another
        major German airport than to Frankfurt. These passengers contribute significantly to
         the total number of direct flight passengers from Frankfurt and, in the Notifying
         Party’s view, should be considered as “marginal” passengers to the FRA-ICN route,
         that  is, in a position to switch to other airports which are closer to them. In the
       Commission’s view, this argument implies that  all passengers not located nearby
        Frankfurt who choose a direct flight from/to Frankfurt would likely choose an indirect
          flight from a regional airport over a direct flight from Frankfurt in case of an increase
         in prices. The Commission acknowledges that some passengers located in proximity of
         regional  airports may change  their  preferred  itinerary from  direct  flights from
        Frankfurt to indirect flights from regional airports, but it is unlikely that all passengers
       would deviate from Frankfurt. The Notifying Party  fails to demonstrate that the
         diversion may reach a critical level such that unilateral increases in prices or reduction
        of  service  quality  in  Frankfurt  post-transaction would make  a  price  increase
         unprofitable.
(728)   Additionally, the mere existence of a group of passengers who pre-Transaction
        decided to self-connect to fly directly from Frankfurt rather than flying indirectly from
         other airports located nearby does not imply that post-Transaction these passengers
       would  all switch away from  Frankfurt,  if  prices charged by  the  Parties  post-
        Transaction were to increase. Even though in theory passengers may self-connect less
        should prices at FRA be higher, the extent to which passengers would actually switch

         into account as shown by the Commission’s market investigation.1097 The review of
         available travel itineraries submitted by the Notifying Party does not provide any
         indication  that  passengers  consider  these  different  travel  itineraries  as  actual
         alternatives to direct connections on FRA-ICN, nor that the additional travel costs
         associated  with  the  transfer would  generally make  these  itineraries  attractive
         alternatives.
(731)   Based on the available evidence, the Commission considers that the large majority of
        passengers that pre-Transaction self-connect to FRA would likely continue using FRA
         in in case prices would increase.
(732)   Furthermore, contrary Korean Air’s claim,1098 as described in paragraph (622) above,
         the Skyscanner  data does not prove  to be an adequate proxy  for competitive
         interactions in the market. This can be seen in Table 31, which compares market
        shares for FRA-ICN calculated following the appropriate methodology using booking
         sales data against (redirection) shares for FRA-ICN implied by the Skyscanner data.
         Significant discrepancies can be observed, in particular with respect to the Parties’
        shares and the share of other  airlines, which disproves the  Parties’ claim  that
         redirection data is necessarily representative of the actual purchase behaviour.

(735)   For the reasons set out below, the Commission concludes that the Transaction would
        lead to a significant impediment to effective competition on the route ICN-CDG.
(736)    First, the Transaction would lead to the Merged Entity holding a very strong market
         position on the route. As set out in Table 32, the Parties combined have held market
        shares between [50-60]% and [60-70]% on the route between 2017 and 2019, which
         indicates  that  the  merged  entity  would  hold  a  dominant  position  after  the
         Transaction.1121 When redistributing the market shares of competitors who have since
        then exited the market, the Parties combined market shares are even higher (ranging
       between [50-60]% and [60-70]%).1122 The Parties, as well as Air France-KLM, have
         also been the only carriers with direct flights between 2017 and 2019, giving them a
        share of weekly frequencies of more than [50-60]% for the entire period.
(737)   In their Response to the Statement of Objections, the Parties argue that high market
        shares in the airline industry are not indicative of market power.1123 The Commission
         disagrees and considers that the Parties’ high market shares are indicative of market

(738)   Second, the increment brought about by the Transaction would be particularly large
        based on figures for the years 2017 to 2019 at [20-30]%-points to [20-30]%-points due
         to Asiana. This results in a high increase in the HHI of more than […]. The large level

(740)   In the first place, the identity of the competitors active on the route has not changed
         materially. Asiana had ceased operations from March 2020 until June 2022.1124 To the
         extent any indirect competitors suspended their operations on the route and did not
       resume them, such competitors had very small market shares on the route in the first
         place. As explained in paragraph (695), redistributing the market shares of these
        competitors has led only to a small increase in the Parties’ combined market shares.
(741)   In the second place, Korean Air and Asiana plan to continue operating on the route.

        frequencies of […] and […] for the same seasons.1127
(742)   Fourth, remaining competitors would likely be insufficient to constrain the Merged
         Entity on the route.
(743)   In the first place, the market shares of the remaining competitors pre-Covid19 are
        smaller than those of the Merged Entity by a large margin (i.e., between Summer 2017
       and Winter 2019/2020 Air France KLM had a market share of up to [20-30]% while
           all other carriers offering indirect services on the route had a market share lower than
       [0-5]% each and up to [20-30]% when combined together, see Table 32).
(744)   In the second place, apart from the Parties and Air France, all other competitors offer
        only one-stop flights between ICN and CDG. While one-stop flights generally do
       compete with non-stop flights for long-haul travel, they represent a different value
         proposition, and would only be an alternative to a subset of passengers, for the reasons
          set out in section 8.6.2. Namely, as explained in section 8.6.2, the Parties’ internal
       documents show that the Parties […]; market participants […] that one-stop flights are
         less preferred by customers and exert lower competitive pressure on the Parties’ direct
         services; the limited market share that each competitor with indirect connections has
       been able to achieve demonstrate that one-stop flights represent a different value

         Parties’ direct services.

         route. In addition, the following competitors offering indirect services on the route
        cannot expand on the route due to exhaustion of traffic rights between their hubs and
        Seoul: [a competitor],1142 [a competitor],1143 [a competitor],1144 [a competitor],1145 [a
         competitor]1146 and [a competitor].1147 All other carriers offering indirect services on
         the route had market shares lower than [0-5]% each between Summer 2017 and
        Winter 2019/2020, showing they are of marginal significance on the route and would
       need  to  increase  their  activities  tremendously  to  have  an  impact on  market
         conditions.1148
(754)   In their Response to the Statement of Objections the Parties  list […] carriers as
         additional  airlines with available  traffic rights on the route ICN-CDG, however
         [competitors] are not operating any services on the route and do not have concrete
        plans to operate such services in the next three years.1149
(755)   The Parties claim that [a competitor] considers that traffic rights do not hinder its
          ability to enter or expand capacity on the ICN-CDG route.1150 In support of this claim,
         the Parties bring a partial quote of [the competitor], without indicating that the quote is
          partial and skips a few words in the middle of the quote.1151 The part of the quote that
       was removed by the Parties reads “For South Korea and […] capacity there are
          limitations.”,1152 thus, confirming that traffic rights limit [the competitor’s] ability to
       expand on the route. The fact that [the competitor] could expand its services on the leg
       between […] and the EEA does not allow an increase of [the competitor’s] capacity on
         the ICN-CDG route.
(756)   In the third place, as regards the availability of slots, the market investigation shows
       some indications that CDG airport is slot constrained, at least at peak hours and that
     ORY airport  is highly slot congested.1153 As explained in section 8.6.3.2 above,
       Korean confirms that all the airports on the Overlap Routes are slot congested and that
          slots’ availability constitutes a barrier to entry on all the Overlap Routes.1154

       and competitors who express a view, consider the Transaction will have negative
        impact on air passenger services on the ICN-CDG route, or at least do not exclude
        negative impact. Out of 19 customers who provided a non-confidential reply to the
        question on the likely impact of the Transaction on air passenger services, majority of
        customers (11 customers, 58%) say they do not know, demonstrating that customers
         generally do not feel informed about the likely impact of the Transaction. Out of the
         eight customers who express a view, three customers (37%) expect positive or no
        impact, three customers (37%) expect negative impact and two customers (25%) think
           “it depends”, which means negative impact is not excluded. Therefore, the majority
       (62%) of customers expressing a view expect or do not exclude negative impact.1161
       Out of 16 travel agents and tour operators who provided a non-confidential reply to the

(760)    Finally, as explained (paragraphs (617) to (627) above and (763) to (766) below), the
        market investigation does not enable the Commission to conclude that passengers’
        leakage to/from CDG airport would be sufficient to constraint the Parties post-
        Transaction nor that France-wide market shares would provide a more accurate
         representation of the competitive constraints faced by the Parties than standard market
        shares based on CDG-ICN O&D city-pair.
(761)   Korean Air argues that self-connecting passengers who could travel via one-stop
          itineraries from/to regional airports across France constrain the Parties’ prices on
         direct flights from CDG.
(762)   Korean Air argues that:  (i) The results of the closer-airport analysis indicate that
        around a third of users choosing direct flights from Paris to Seoul were located closer
         to another major French airport than to CDG;1164 (ii) The review of available flight
        options from other French airports compared to the travel time by train or car to Paris
        paired with a direct flight to Seoul shows similar total travel time between the two
          itineraries and thus supports the view that passengers from these regions can substitute
       between direct flights from CDG and an indirect flights from their respective local
          airport;1165 and  (iii) The catchment-area analysis does not suggest that a specific
        catchment area can be defined for Paris CDG airport but that all areas in France
         contribute  significant numbers  of marginal passengers  flying on  the CDG-ICN
         route. 1166
(763)   In line with the discussion related to passengers leakage in Germany (paragraphs (725)
         to (733) above), it is unlikely that all passengers not located nearby Paris who choose a
         direct flight from/to Paris would likely choose an indirect flight from a regional airport
        over a direct flight from Paris in case of an increase in prices. Korean Air fails to
        demonstrate that the diversion may reach a critical level such that unilateral increases
         in prices or reduction of service quality on CDG-ICN post-transaction would make a
         price increase unprofitable. Even though in theory passengers may self-connect less
        should prices at CDG be higher, the extent to which passengers would actually switch
       away from CDG in response to higher prices is not known, and not demonstrated by
       Korean Air to be sufficient to constrain the Parties from increasing prices post-
         Transaction.
(764)  As explained in section 7.1.4 the evidence does not support the Notifying Party’s
        claim that all self-connecting passengers would switch away from CDG. Similarly,
       even though alternative travel itineraries may display similar total travel time as shown
       by the Notifying Party, total travel time is not the only factor passengers take into
         account.1167
(765)   Based on the available evidence, the Commission considers that the large majority of
        passengers that pre-Transaction self-connect to CDG would likely continue using
     CDG in case prices would increase.

         for passengers travelling on this route.

(769)   For the reasons set out below, the Commission concludes that the Transaction would
        lead to a significant impediment to effective competition on the route ICN-FCO.
(770)    First, the Transaction would lead to the Merged Entity holding a very strong market
         position on the route.
(771)   In the first place, as set out in Table 37, the Parties combined have held market shares
       between [60-70]% and [70-80]% on the route between 2017 and 2019, which indicates
         that Korean Air would hold a dominant position after the Transaction.1205 The Parties
         (as well as Alitalia) have also been the only two carriers with direct flights between
       2017 and 2019, giving them a share of weekly frequencies of more than [60-70]% for
         the entire period.
(772)   In the second place, as set out in Table 41, when adjusting the market shares to take
        account of the exit of Alitalia and additional indirect competitors such as Aeroflot
       from the market, the Parties’ combined market shares are even higher and range
       between [70-80]% and [80-90]%. When taking into account the exit of Alitalia from
         the market, the Parties are the only two carriers still operating direct flights on the
         route, giving them a share of weekly frequencies of [90-100]%.
(773)   In their Response to the Statement of Objections, the Parties argue that high market
        shares in the airline industry are not indicative of market power.1206 For the reasons
          listed  in  section  8.6.7, the Commission cannot accept  this claim. Namely,  the
       European courts have confirmed that high market shares are indicative of market
       power in the aviation industry; prior to the Covid19 pandemic, market shares of the
         Parties and their competitors were relatively stable over time (as evident in Table 37
        above), and the Parties themselves use market shares as an indicator of market power.
(774)   Second, the increment brought about by the Transaction would be particularly large
        based on figures for the years 2017 to 2019 at [30-40]%-points to [30-40]%-points due
         to Asiana ([30-40]%-[40-50]% adjusted to take account of Alitalia’s exit). This results
         in a high increase in the HHI of more than […] ([…] when adjusted to take account of
          Alitalia’s exit). The large level and increment in the Parties’ joint market position is a
         clear indicator that the Transaction would create a dominant position.
(775)   Third, the Covid19 pandemic has deteriorated the competitive dynamics on the route
         in the long-term.
(776)   In the  first place, Alitalia, the only other competitor on the route offering direct
         services pre-Covid19 has exited the route since October 2021.1207 Several carriers
        providing indirect services on the route such Aeroflot have suspended their operations
       on the route and did not resume them.
(777)   In the second place, Korean Air and Asiana plan to continue operating on the route
       and have expanded flight frequencies recently. In Summer 2023 Korean Air has
       expanded its services to […] on the route and Asiana has expanded from […] to […]
       weekly  services  in Summer  2023.1208  Pre-Covid19,  Korean  Air  had  weekly
        frequencies of […] and […] in IATA Winter 2018/2019 and Summer 2019 seasons
         respectively, while Asiana had weekly frequencies of […] and […] for the same
         seasons.1209

(778)   Fourth, the constraint from the remaining competitors would likely be insufficient to
         constrain the Merged Entity on the route.
(779)   In the first place, the market shares of the remaining competitors pre-Covid19 are
      much smaller than those of the Parties by a large margin (i.e., between Summer 2017
       and Winter 2019/2020, Alitalia’s market share per season did not exceed [10-20]%
       and the market share of all other carriers offering indirect services on the route were
        lower than [0-5]% each and up to [20-30]% when combined together (per season), see
        Table 37).
(780)   In the second place, all other competitors apart from the Parties offer only one-stop
          flights between ICN and FCO. While one-stop flights generally do compete with non-
        stop flights for long-haul travel, they represent a different value proposition, and
       would only be an alternative to a subset of passengers, for the reasons set out in
         section 8.6.2. Namely, as explained in section 8.6.2, the Parties’ internal documents
       show that […]; market participants […] that one-stop flights are less preferred by
        customers and exert lower competitive pressure on the Parties’ direct services; the
         limited market share that each competitor with indirect connections has been able to
        achieve demonstrate that one-stop flights represent a different value proposition and
       would only be an alternative to a subset of passengers, and; the fact that the relevance
        of one-stop flights and their ability to exert competitive constraints on direct services
        depends on various criteria, and not only price.
(781)   In the third place, during IATA season Summer 2023, all of the one-stop flights on the
      ICN-FCO route are at least 3 and up to 8 hours (26%-73%) longer than the Parties’
         direct services on the route, with the flights offered by Emirates and Etihad having a
        stop-over during night time at least on one way of the route.1210  Similarly, during
      IATA season Winter 2023/2024, the vast majority of one-stop flights on the ICN-FCO
         route are at least 3.5 and up to 10 hours (26%-74%) longer than the Parties’ direct
         services on the route, with the flights offered by Emirates, Qatar Airways, Turkish
         Airlines, AF-KLM and Singapore Airlines having a stop-over during night time at
          least on one way of the route. 1211 These indirect competitors will exert at most a very
         limited competitive constraint on the Parties’ operations on the route ICN-FCO.
(782)   In the fourth place, majority of passengers on the ICN-FCO route have demonstrated
          their strong preference for non-stop over one-stop flights, allowing the Parties to exert
        market power on the route. In 2019, above [70-80]% of the passengers preferred the
         Parties’ direct services on the route over all indirect flights available on the route, (see
        Table 37 above) despite the fact that, according to Korean Air, the price of these direct
         services was [10-20]%-[30-40]% higher than the price of indirect services on the
         route. 1212 This shows the inability of indirect flights to restrain the Parties’ direct
         services.
(783)   In the fifth place, and as explained further below (paragraph (786)), the majority of
        competitors offering one-stop services on the ICN-FCO route cannot expand their
         services on the route due to exhaustion of traffic rights.
(784)    Fifth, for the reasons set out in section 8.6.1, the Parties are close competitors on the
         route. In the first place, as explained in section 8.6.1, […]. In the second place, the
        majority of market participants expressing a view consider that the Parties are each

(792)    Finally, as explained below, the market investigation does not enable the Commission
         to conclude  that passenger leakage to/from FCO  airport would be  sufficient to
         constraint  the  Parties post-Transaction nor  that Italy-wide market shares would
        provide a more accurate representation of the competitive constraints faced by the
         Parties than standard market shares based on FCO-ICN O&D city-pair.
(793)   The Notifying Party argues that self-connecting passengers who could travel via one-
        stop itineraries from/to regional airports across Italy constrain the Parties’ prices on
         direct flights from FCO.
(794)   The Notifying Party argues that (i) The results of the closer-airport analysis indicate
         that around half of users choosing direct flights from Rome to Seoul were located
         closer to another major Italian airport than to Rome;1235 (ii) The review of available
          flight options from other Italian airports compared to the travel time by train or car to
      Rome paired with a direct flight to Seoul shows similar total travel time between the
       two itineraries and thus supports the view that passengers from these regions can
         substitute between direct flights from FCO and an indirect flight from their respective
         local airport;1236 and (iii) the catchment-area analysis does not suggest that a specific
        catchment area can be defined for FCO but that all areas in Central and Southern Italy
         contribute significant numbers of passengers flying on the FCO-ICN route. 1237
(795)   In line with the discussion related to passengers leakage in Germany and France
        (paragraphs (725) to (733) and (763) to (767)), it is unlikely that all passengers not
         located nearby Rome who choose a direct flight from/to Rome who would likely
        choose an indirect flight from a regional airport over a direct flight from Rome in case
        of an increase in prices on FCO-ICN. The Notifying Party fails to demonstrate that the
         diversion may reach a critical level such that unilateral increases in prices or reduction
        of  service  quality on FCO-ICN  post-transaction would make a  price  increase
         unprofitable. Even though in theory passengers may self-connect less should prices at
     FCO be higher, the extent to which passengers would actually switch away from FCO
         in response to higher prices is not known, and no not demonstrated by the Notifying
        Party to be sufficient to constrain the Parties from increasing prices post-transaction.

(799)   In view of the above, the Commission concludes that the Transaction would lead to a
         significant impediment to effective competition on the route ICN-FCO due to the

        This is likely to lead to increased prices, a lower level of service and reduced choice
         for passengers travelling on this route.
