8.9.    Passenger air transport services – potential competition
(806)  As  mentioned  in  section 5  above,  in  the  6(1)(c)  Decision  the Commission
         preliminarily concluded that Transaction could eliminate potential competition in
        passenger air transport services between the EEA and South Korea, because (i) Korean
        Air holds a strong position on a number of EEA-South Korea passenger routes on
       which Asiana is currently not active;1245  (ii) the preliminary market investigation
         indicated that Asiana might be likely to add additional EEA destinations to its long-
        haul network in the short term and (iii) there are unlikely to be a sufficient number of
         other actual or potential competitors, which could maintain sufficient competitive
        pressure after the Transaction.
(807)   During its in-depth market investigation, the Commission assessed whether Asiana
       would likely enter new routes between South Korea and the EEA, on which Korean
        Air  is already active with direct services. Based on Korean Air’s replies to the
       Commission’s request for information and the Commission’s assessment of Asiana’s
         internal documents containing its plans for future operations,1246 […].
(808)  As a  result, the Commission concludes that the Transaction does not lead to a
         significant impediment to effective competition by eliminating a potential competitor
       on any of the EEA-South Korea routes.
8.10.   Cargo air transport services – general considerations
8.10.1.  The impact of the Covid19 pandemic and the Russian war against Ukraine on cargo
         air transport services
(809)   The Covid19 pandemic has had a severe impact on the cargo air transport services
        across the globe. Due to travel restrictions and public health concerns, the demand for
        passenger air transport services had significantly decreased since the beginning of the
       pandemic in 2020. Airlines reacted to this dramatic decrease in demand by reducing or
       even suspending part of their services. Therefore, without the belly-hold capacity of

        passenger air transport aircrafts available on the market, the overall supply of cargo air
         transport services declined significantly. At the same time, the increased consumer
       demand for certain goods caused a significant imbalance between demand and supply
         (of cargo services), with demand significantly exceeding supply. Therefore, rates for
          air cargo services soared, bringing more profitability to cargo carriers and helping
        combination carriers to offset the losses incurred by their passenger air transport
          activities.1247
(810)   Similarly, the Russian war against Ukraine has also had an impact on the European
         aviation sector and in particular on the routes between Europe and South Korea. Since
         the beginning of the war in February 2022, European and other carriers which operate
          flights between Europe and South Korea have been facing longer flight times due to
         the closure of the Russian airspace. Furthermore, the capacity of Russian carriers on
         the routes between Europe and South Korea is no longer available.1248 […].1249
(811)   In the Commission’s view, the uncertainties brought about by the Covid19 pandemic
       and the Russian war against Ukraine war require the Commission to look beyond any
        temporary effects of these developments. As a result, in line with the provisions of the
        Horizontal Merger Guidelines, the Commission will not take into account the short-
        term effects of these developments in making its assessment, and will only take into
        account any structural changes that have occurred in the market or that can reasonably
        be expected, such as the lasting entry or exit of competitors or structural shifts in
        competitiveness.
(812)  As explained below, the investigation has not provided sufficient evidence that the
        extreme fluctuations in demand and supply and the effects on the prices in air cargo
         services between Europe and South Korea caused by the Covid19 pandemic and in
         particular the lack of available belly-hold capacity on the  routes,  constitutes a
         structural change. Indeed, as the emergency of the Covid19 pandemic seems to have
         abated, its effects on the air cargo transport sector do not seem to be lasting – although
         price levels have not yet come down and may  still need time to reach levels
        comparable to the situation before the Covid19 pandemic. However, the Commission
        considers that for the assessment of the Transaction, the effects of the Russian war
         against Ukraine on the cargo routes between Europe and South Korea, namely the exit
        of Russian carriers from the routes as well as the increase of flight times between
       Europe and South Korea for many carriers (and the effects that this has on capacity
       and prices), should be treated as structural changes as those effects are not likely to
        disappear in the foreseeable future.
(813)  On the one hand, the market  investigation has not provided evidence  that the
        imbalance between demand and supply caused by the Covid19 pandemic has been
         structural  or  permanent.  Rather,  based  on  the  results  of  the  Commission’s
         investigation, the industry consensus seems to be that this imbalance is normalising,
          albeit with still higher cargo rates.1250
(814)    First, as the Covid19 restrictions have started to ease, a significant part of the
        suspended passenger air transport services has been resumed. Therefore, even though

        southern route, resulting in longer flight times. The additional distance generates
         additional costs (mainly for fuel), impacting, in turn, the flight payload and leading to
       an increase in costs and rates. According to one competitor, capacity on each flight has
       been also reduced due to longer flight times.1256

(822)   The Parties are the number 1 and number 2 carriers offering cargo air transport from
       and to South Korea. Together, Korean Air and Asiana accounted for around [40-50]%-
       [50-60]% of all cargo traffic coming in and out of South Korea. While Asiana is
        smaller than Korean Air, the Transaction would lead to a sizable increment of around
        [10-20]%-[20-30]%. That indicates that the market structure for the global air cargo
         transport in and out of Korea would change considerably after the Transaction by
       combining the leading air carriers. It also indicates that there are few competitors
         globally with significant traffic volumes in and out of South Korea. Indeed, the second
         player, DHL, only has a share of [10-20]% and, as an integrator, operates a different
        business model.
(823)   The market structure was relatively stable until 2019, as illustrated in Table 46. As of
        2020, the beginning of the Covid19 pandemic, the Parties’ market position further
        increased due to the continued use of their freighter capacity throughout the pandemic,
        while competitors relying on passenger planes to transport cargo in and out of South
       Korea reduced or suspended their operations. The overall size of the market has
         fluctuated but overall remained roughly stable as well. Overall, air cargo traffic in and
        out of South Korea appears to be characterized by (i) the presence of two large carriers
       – the Parties – as well as a large number of much smaller air cargo carriers and (ii) a
        very stable market environment in terms of market sizes and relative size of the
        competitors without significant shifts in competitive strength over time. This shows
         that the Parties are by far the strongest competitors in cargo traffic in and out of South
       Korea globally and that there is no significant competitor to the Parties. Furthermore,
         the market structure has remained remarkably stable over time, casting doubt on the
         likelihood of considerable entry or expansion in the supply of air cargo services in and
        out of South Korea in the near future.

8.10.3.3. Integrators
(851)   In its decisional practice,1304 the Commission has defined integrators’ door-to-door
         offering by  reference  to  five  basic  characteristics:  first, ownership  of  or  full
         operational control over  all transportation  assets, including an  air network with
        scheduled flights, through which a large proportion of the volumes handled by the
       company is carried; second, a sufficient geographic coverage on a global level; third, a
       hub and spoke operating model; fourth, a proprietary IT network, such that all relevant
        data runs across one network;  fifth,  integrators have the reputation of  reliably
         delivering parcels on time (so-called ‘end-to-end’ credibility). In this regard, there are
         three integrators in the world, all of whom also operate within the EEA: DHL, FedEx
       and UPS.
(852)   The main differentiating factor of an integrator is that it has operational control over
         the logistical chain of cargo (mainly small package) delivery from origin to destination
         (including air transport) so that  it can ensure delivery in accordance with a time
        commitment.1305
(853)   The interplay between freight forwarders that use airport-to-airport air cargo services
        as an input on the one hand, and the vertically integrated offering of the integrators on
         the other, is presented in the figure below. As analysed in section 7.2.1.4 above, the
         Parties’ airport-to-airport air cargo services and the integrators’ core door-to-door
        small package delivery services belong to separate product markets. The limited extent
         to which the integrators’ spare capacity offered for airport-to-airport air cargo services
        poses a competitive constraint to the Parties will be assessed in sections 8.11.3.2
       and 8.12.3.2 below. In addition, any indirect out-of-market constraint to the Parties
        posed by the integrators’ door-to-door services, to the extent these compete for end
        cargo customers / shippers, will be assessed in sections 8.11.5 and 8.12.5 below.

8.11.   Cargo air transport services – assessment of the route Europe to South Korea
(855)   Based on its investigation and all the evidence available to it, the Commission finds
          that:
          (a)  The Transaction would change the market structure significantly and lead to
             high combined market  shares with a high increment  in a  stable market
             environment which has shown little variation over time (section 8.11.1).
         (b)  The Parties are close – if not the closest – competitors as well as the most
              competitive suppliers in the market (section 8.11.2).
          (c)  The competing  air cargo  carriers and  integrators  provide only a  limited
              competitive constraint in the air cargo market (section 8.11.3).
         (d)  The Parties’ competitors face barriers to expand their services in reaction to
               potential negative effects of the Transaction (section 8.11.4).
          (e)   There is no or at best a limited indirect constraint on the Parties’ activities from
              the integrators’ sales to shippers (section 8.11.5).
           (f)   The customers are unlikely to have sufficient buyer power to off-set the negative
               effects of the Transaction (section 8.11.6).

1306     Reply of [an integrator] to question B.1 of Questionnaire Q2 to cargo competitors (ID 8457); Response of
        [an integrator] to RFI 2 – Non-confidential minutes of the conference call with [an integrator]; Non-

                                    191

[PÁGINA PDF 198]
         (g)   There is insufficient evidence of timely, likely and sufficient market entry to off-
                set the effects of the Transaction (section 8.11.7).
         (h)   Several market participants have expressed concerns about the strong market
               position of the Merged Entity and the potential negative effects on competition
              as a result of the Transaction (section 8.11.8).
(856)   The Horizontal Merger Guidelines state that according to well-established case-law,
        very large market shares – 50% or more – may in themselves be evidence of the
         existence of a dominant position. A merger involving a firm whose market share will
        remain below 50% after the merger may also raise competition concerns, due to the
         creation of a dominant position, in view of other factors such as the strength and
       number of competitors and the presence of capacity constraints.1308 As set out in
         section 8.11.1, the merged entity would have a high share in terms of sales (around
        [50-60]%) and capacity (around [40-50]%) in the relevant market. Moreover, as
        discussed in sections 8.11.3 to 8.11.7, the relevant market is characterised by limited
        competitive pressure exerted by competitors, substantial barriers to expansion as well
        as a lack of likely, timely and sufficient market entry or countervailing buyer power.
        Therefore, the Commission considers that the Transaction would create a dominant
         position in relation to air cargo services on the route Europe-South Korea.
(857)   In any event, paragraphs 26 to 38 of the Horizontal Merger Guidelines list factors
       which may influence whether significant non-coordinated effects are likely to result
       from a merger. “Paragraph 26 of those guidelines states in that regard, correctly, that
        those factors, taken separately, are not necessarily decisive. In addition, not all of
        those factors need to be present for significant non-coordinated effects to be likely. In
         that context, it must be found that those factors may, in principle, constitute evidence
         that a concentration would give rise to significant non-coordinated effects, which must
       be the subject of an overall assessment.”1309
(858)   Considering the overall assessment of the findings in sections 8.11.1 to 8.11.8 and in
          light of the merged entity’s high share in air cargo services on the route Europe-South
        Korea, the Commission concludes that the Transaction would, in any event, give rise
         to horizontal non-coordinated  effects on the relevant market as a  result of the
         elimination of an important competitive constraint.

(861)   In order for market shares and additions of market share to provide first indications of
        market power and increases in market power, market shares ought to reflect the entry
        of competitors expected to exert significant competitive pressure in the future on the
         other firms in the market and the exit of competitors no longer expected to exert any
        competitive pressure. This approach is aligned with the Horizontal Merger Guidelines,
        paragraph 15, which provide that “current market shares may be adjusted to reflect
        reasonably  certain  future changes,  for  instance  in  the  light  of  exit,  entry or
         expansion”1310. The following paragraphs and tables thus show how market shares
       would look like once the exit of both competitors like the Russian-based carriers

8.11.1.2. The Commission’s assessment of the market structure
(869)   The Transaction would change the market structure on the route Europe to South
       Korea significantly and lead to high combined market shares with a high increment in
        a stable market environment which has shown little variation over time.
(870)    First, the Transaction would lead to the Merged Entity holding a very strong position
       on the route between Europe to South Korea. As set out in Table 47, the Parties
       combined have held market shares of [40-50]% in 2018, [40-50]% in 2019, [50-60]%
         in 2020, [40-50]% in 2021, and [50-60]% in 2022, with increments of [10-20]-
        [20-30]%. The Parties’ market shares in 2020 and 2021 and to a certain extent also
       2022 appear to have been influenced by potentially temporary effects of the Covid19
        pandemic.
(871)   Should Russian carriers, Alitalia and Czech Airlines be excluded and their volumes re-
         allocated across all other carriers proportionally, the Parties would remain the two
         largest providers with combined market shares of [40-50]-[50-60]%, with increments
        of [10-20]-[20-30]%. Should the entry of MSC Air Cargo and Air Premia be reflected,
         the Parties would remain the two largest providers with combined market shares of
        [40-50]-[50-60]%,  with  increments  of  [10-20]-[20-30]%.  Under  any  of  those
        methodologies, the Parties are the  first and second largest providers of cargo air
         services on the route Europe to South Korea and would be the undisputed market
         leader after the Transaction, reinforcing Korean Air’s already strong position.
(872)   Second, as illustrated already above, the Transaction entails a significant increment in
       volume market shares of [10-20]-[20-30]%, which  is indicative of a  significant
         increase in market power due to the Transaction.
(873)   Third, the merged entity’s market position would be significantly larger than that of its
        next largest competitors: Qatar Airways and DHL would follow with significantly
        smaller shares with respectively around [5-10]% and between [5-10]% and [5-10]%
       from 2018 to 2021. All other competitors, including Lufthansa, Cargolux, Air France-
      KLM, Turkish Airlines and Finnair each have market shares below [5-10]% in each
         year.
(874)   Fourth, with the exception of the impact of the Covid19 pandemic and of the Russian
       war against Ukraine (see section  8.10.1), the market  structure has shown  little
         variation  over  time  which  indicates  that  this  concentrated  market  structure
         characterised by the Parties and a long fringe of smaller competitors is likely to persist
         in the future. Market shares between 2018 and 2021 have varied little: Korean Air’s
        market share (excluding Russian  carriers,  Alitalia and Czech Airlines) has […]

8.11.2.  Closeness of Competition between the Parties
(875)   The market investigation has shown that the most important factors for customers’
        choice for the purchase of air cargo transport services on the route between Europe
       and South Korea are offered frequencies (4.76)1315, the reliability (4.64) and quality
         (4.43) of the offered services, the price (4.29) and main deck space availability on
         freighter aircraft (4.11). In particular for these factors of choice, Korean Air and
        Asiana are largely perceived as each other’s closest competitor by market participants.
        Against that background and in light of the results of the market investigation, the
       Commission considers the Parties to be close competitors on the air cargo routes
       between Europe and South Korea for the following reasons:
(876)    First, the Commission’s market investigation also shows that market participants
        consider the Parties to be the two most competitive air cargo carriers on the routes
       between Europe and South Korea.1316 The Parties are ranked as the number 1 and
       number 2 most  competitive  carriers on  the  routes by  both  competitors  and
         customers.1317 As regards the competitiveness of the Parties, both Asiana and Korean
        Air received the highest rates respectively for  their overall competitiveness, the
        frequencies offered per week, the overall duration of the flights, the reliability in terms
        of flight times, the quality of the service in terms of cargo handling and the capacity
         offered on the route.1318
(877)   Second, the Commission’s market  investigation shows  that both customers and
        competitors overwhelmingly recognize the Parties as each other’s closest competitor:
       The  vast  majority  of  competitors who  replied  to  the  Commission’s  market
         investigation questionnaire consider Asiana as Korean Air’s closest competitor1319 and
       Korean Air as Asiana’s closest competitor.1320 As regards customers, the majority of
        customers who have expressed their views in response to the Commission’s market
         investigation questionnaire consider Asiana as Korean Air’s closest competitor1321 and
       Korean Air as Asiana’s closest competitor.1322 The results of the Commission’s market
         investigation questionnaire also show that no other carrier is perceived as competing
         closely with either of the Parties.1323 The air cargo customers the Commission spoke to
        as part of its market investigation widely confirmed that the Parties are each other’s
         closest competitors.1324 As an example, [a customer] explained that they currently still

(879)   More precisely, market participants view the Parties as closest competitors and as the
       two most competitive air cargo carriers on the route Europe-South Korea for the
        following reasons:
(880)   In the first place, the Parties’ offer is very similar, in contrast to the Parties’ claim that
         the majority of air cargo service providers offer services which do not significantly
          differ from the Parties’ offer.1329 Both offer scheduled, high-frequency, high-capacity
          air cargo flights in both freighter and passenger aircraft between Incheon and several
       European airports. Considering the airports they serve, the Parties closely compete
       from a geographic perspective. Asiana serves Brussels, Frankfurt, Milan, London and
       Vienna  with  regular  scheduled  dedicated  cargo  flights  (in  addition  to  cargo
         transportation in the belly-hold of its passenger flights from Frankfurt, Paris, Rome
       and Barcelona). Korean Air also serves Frankfurt, Milan, London and Vienna with
        dedicated cargo flights, among other European destinations, (in addition to cargo
         transportation in the belly-hold of its passenger flights from Frankfurt, Paris, Rome
       and Barcelona) and serves Amsterdam in the vicinity of Brussels. Accordingly the
         Parties state that “Korean Air operates a long-haul network to Europe which covers
         several  destinations throughout Europe.  It covers Northern, Western, Southern,
       Middle and Eastern Europe. Neither Korean Air nor Asiana focuses on one specific
        region within Europe”.1330 Which makes their offer similarly interesting for the same
        scope of customers in all European regions, in particular when considering that the
         vast majority of respondents to the market investigation indicated that they see some
         regional differences in the competitive conditions at the European end of the routes
         (see above, section 7.2.2).1331
(881)  Due to the Parties’ focus on similar airports and regions in Europe, their share of sales
         are very high when looking at specific countries in Europe. As set out in Table 52 by
      way of example for the year 2019, the Parties achieved a high combined share of the
         sales in certain geographic segments of the relevant market, namely in […].

(882)   In the second place, the Parties each offer direct (non-stop) services between Europe
       and South Korea whereas most competitors offer only indirect flights which are a less
         preferred option for customers.1332 As an example, the market investigation reveals
         that “[i]t depends on the specific customer needs, flying direct is the fastest option and
        most preferable option for time critical shipments”.1333 The Parties both offer direct
         freighter services between Europe and South Korea and are besides Lufthansa the only
          air cargo carriers who offer at the same time direct belly hold capacities and direct
         freighter capacities on the routes between Europe and South Korea. The Parties can
         therefore both offer to ship high volumes without transhipment at once and thus
       compete closely with each other compared to other carriers for direct  air cargo
         transport services between Europe and South Korea. This is also reflected in very high
        shares in the market segment for direct air cargo transport volumes only, due to
         limited alternative offerings.

(887)   Accordingly, a customer stated that the Parties are the preferred option on the routes
       between Europe and South Korea as they have the most frequencies.1345 Another
        customer explained that they have a long-lasting relationship with both Korean Air
        (35 years) and Asiana (20 years) and that in the past, Korean Air was more often used,
        while more recently he has more often relied on Asiana’s services: “Whether one or
         the other is chosen mostly depends on their frequency: Korean Air operates […]
         freighter services weekly compared to […] freighters of Asiana.”1346
(888)   In the fifth place, the market perceives the Parties as each other’s closest competitors
       due to the high quality of their respective services.1347 The market investigation
         reveals that the market’s understanding of the concept “quality” mainly concerns the
         timeliness and  reliability of the  air cargo  transport services which seem  to be
        comparable between the Parties.1348 Accordingly, a customer explained that “they
        possess superior service and quality. The customs clearance  is done before the
        shipment arrives – it allows for the cargo to be picked up very quickly. There are no
        delays with pick-ups as well. The Parties dominate in terms of quality of service.”1349
        Another customer noted that “when purchasing air cargo services from cargo carriers
       on the routes between Europe and South Korea, [a customer] prefers to purchase from
       Korean Air and Asiana, as they provide better services on the route than any other
         carrier”.1350 According to this customer, the Parties have in particular an advantage
        with regard to their cargo terminal at ICN airport, which allows them to handle
         arriving cargo considerably faster and more efficient than any competitor.1351 In
         addition, a market participant stated in relation to competitors who are offering
         indirect services that “not all of them are of the same level of quality as Korean Air
       and Asiana as they offer longer connection times due to transshipment and some of
       them are considered as  less  reliable  (e.g. cargo  is not flown due  to canceled
          flights)”.1352 Moreover, the Parties’ internal documents emphasize […], page 56). In
         contrast to the Parties’ claim in their Response to the Letter of Facts1353, both Korean
        Air and Asiana, as South Korean flag carriers, have a particular position in customers’
        perception and provide a similar level of quality that customers seem to value. Even
        though the Parties in their Response to the Letter of Facts uphold that as regards air
        cargo transport services brand loyalty is not a decisive factor,1354 a customer is of the

        customer describes these similarities between Korean Air and Asiana as follows:
       “Korean Air and Asiana are very similar in that they offer direct and first in class
         services between Europe and Korea. Their “flown as booked” rating is very high,

        2023, Korean Air and Asiana have only reduced their prices […] so far. The trade

        accept that.”1359 “[...] Other airlines, such as […] and […], immediately pass on fuel
         price increases or decreases to their customers. […]. They have loyal customers so
        they do not need to be flexible.”1360
(890)   Based on the above, the Commission considers the rivalry between the Parties as an
        important source of competition on the market and therefore concludes that the Parties
         are close – if not the closest – competitors on the market for air cargo services on the
         route from Europe to South Korea.1361
8.11.3.  Competitive Constraints from competitors and ability of customers to switch suppliers
8.11.3.1. Competitive constraints from air cargo competitors
(891)   Post-Transaction, customers of the Parties would have difficulties switching suppliers,
        as there are insufficient alternatives and the existing competitors’ cargo operations
        only provide a limited competitive constraint on the Parties on the route from Europe
         to South Korea.
(892)    First, as shown in section 8.11.1, the Parties are the first and second largest providers
        of air cargo transportation services on the route from Europe to South Korea. Besides
         the Parties, the market is highly fragmented, with no other carrier having market
        shares of 10% or above and only Qatar Airways and DHL consistently having market

(893)   Contrary to what Korean Air argues in its Responses to the Commission’s Statement
        of Objections and Letter of Facts,1362 the Commission notes that its Phase I market
         investigation has only generated mixed results with regard to the customers’ switching
         options. For example, among the eight customers replying that they would be able to
         easily switch to other air cargo carriers on the relevant routes, (i) there is one customer
        explaining that they do not in any event have influence on the choice of the air cargo
         carrier (which is rather decided by the freight forwarder),1363 (ii) there is one customer
        expressing a wish to switch but nevertheless expecting the Transaction to have a
        negative impact on prices, capacity, quality of service and level of competition, and
        considering that post-Transaction  “it will be only one carrier (direct service) to
         ICN”,1364 (iii) there is [a customer] which is in any event the biggest customer of [a
        competitor] and therefore does have a preferred alternative,1365 (iv) there are two
        shippers of […] and […] who are both nevertheless excluding transhipment as a
        choice and considering the market being under-supplied,1366 and finally (v) there is
       one customer with “extremely high volumes” who considers the Parties expensive,
         especially Korean Air that “does not really move” in pricing, but is nevertheless using
       them as “the preferred option”.1367
(894)   In view of the above mixed results, during Phase II, the Commission contacted and
        held conference calls with 10 of the Parties’ largest customers, nine of whom have
         indicated that they use dual sourcing, i.e. sourcing between the two Parties either
         exclusively or for the far largest part of their volumes in order to obtain competitive
          prices:1368
          (a)  The first customer believes it has some bargaining power only because it can
              switch between Korean Air and Asiana as needed, while post-Transaction it will
             be impossible for  freight forwarders to negotiate  prices. According to the
              customer, the two Parties are the dominant providers on the Europe-South Korea
              route and  the  closest competitors with  superior  service and  quality. The
             customer’s major concern is that the Parties effectively own the market. If the
               Parties raise their prices, customers will still have to choose them because of
                their quality and their Korean brand. Therefore, freight forwarders will have to
              pass-on the price increase or absorb  it internally. The customer considers to
             absorb a price increase until it reaches a painful level and then pass on the price
               difference to its customers. At the same time, the customer is concerned that
              post-Transaction the Parties might decrease capacity and lower their quality,
             something that freight forwarders will have to accept.1369

          flights and flights with transhipment, are substitutable. The Commission notes that
        indeed transhipment carriers compete on the same market with direct-service carriers,
        such as the Parties. This is also reflected in the market definition, section 7.2.1.5,
        above. However, they are not as close competitors as the Parties are to each other,
        given that direct and transhipment services typically cater for different customers’
        needs. [A customer’s]  full quote gives a more clear picture: “According to [the
        customer], when it comes to transport of goods between Europe and South Korea,
         direct flights, indirect flights and also transhipment flights are all valid options. It,
        however, hugely depends on clients’ preferences and pricing which of all available
        options is in the end the most suitable. [The customer] therefore makes its choice on a
        case-by-case basis according to its customers’ needs. Given that airfreight is quite
         expensive, it is mostly used for time-sensitive goods and for high-value cargo (e.g.
        server racks). Pharmaceuticals are a characteristic example in this regard, because
         clients look for short transit time, leaving direct flights (without stopover or with
        stopover but without transhipment) as the only realistic option. Also for high value
        products or sensitive cargo customers prefer to avoid transhipment. In contrast,
        customers will opt for (usually cheaper) indirect connections with transhipment when
         the cargo consists of low-value and no time-sensitive goods”.1406 In paragraph 145 of
           its Response to the Commission’s Letter of Facts, Korean Air  insists  that [the
        customer’s] quote confirms Korean Air’s view that direct and transhipment flights
       compete as closely because all options are viable alternatives and ultimately a choice
           is made on a case-by-case basis. The Commission notes that indeed all such options
       compete on  the same  market,  albeit many times  catering  for  different  needs.
        Therefore, transhipment carriers are of a somewhat different nature of that of the
          Parties.
(911)   Last but not least, the Commission’s market investigation clearly contradicts Korean
         Air’s submission in its Responses to the Commission’s Statement of Objections and
         Letter of Facts that price – and not the number of stops – is the key driver for
        customers when choosing an air cargo carrier.1407 The Commission notes in this
         respect that price was actually ranked fourth (4.29) by customers, after the frequencies
         (4.76), the reliability in terms of flight times (4.64) and the quality of cargo handling
          (4.43).1408

        cannot be transported in the belly-hold of a passenger aircraft, such as dangerous or

        oversized goods.1412 In addition, the belly-hold of a passenger  aircraft offers a
         significantly lower capacity (maximum load: 25 tons) than freighter (maximum load:
       100 tons).1413 This makes belly-hold air cargo transport services less attractive in
         particular for larger customers (such as major freight forwarders), which often need to
         transport  significant volumes  at a  time.1414 Furthermore,  if necessary, passenger
          airlines will prioritize passenger baggage over air cargo, which means that capacity
         available on passenger aircraft  is not always predictable and will depend on the
       amount of passenger baggage on the respective aircraft. This may also mean that
        passenger airlines leave behind cargo in order to transport passenger baggage. As [a
        competitor] states, “[f]or passenger aircraft, passenger baggage takes priority over
       any belly cargo.”1415 This is confirmed by [a competitor] with regard to  its own
        passenger flights between South Korea and […], by which all cargo between Europe
       and South Korea is being transported, stating that “[a competitor] cargo needs to share
         available capacity with passengers’ baggage. Subject to space availability wherein the
        passengers’ baggage takes precedence, cargo is uplifted only on an ad-hoc basis and
         there  is no specific or fixed cargo allocation. Accordingly, [they] are unable to
        determine the cargo capacity due to the fact that [their] passenger flights could be full
        because of belly-hold space constraints rather than weight”.1416
(914)   In the same vein, [a competitor] considers that “the operation of freighters has an
        advantage as it is less limited than belly hold“ and “Flight Flight times for passenger
         services are optimized to fit passenger demand/requirements, the transport of cargo
       on such services is a resulting by-product”,1417 which confirms how operators only
         relying on belly-hold capacity tend to be less competitive than operators that can also
         rely on freighters and that cargo-related considerations are generally subordinated to
         passengers-related considerations for passenger carriers.
(915)   [A competitor] confirmed that only being able to transport belly-hold constitutes a
        competitive disadvantage on the route, due the difference in payload of a dedicated
         freighter and the inability to transport certain larger goods on passenger aircraft.1418
       [The competitor] actually considers freighter capacity and belly-hold capacity as
         “different sectors of the air freight market. It is caused by different aircraft capacity,
        payload vs. operating costs. We have less ability to transport huge parcels  if they
        require all-cargo aircraft. […] Usually all cargo transportation is more expensive
        than belly cargo due to cost & revenue structure”.1419
(916)   [A competitor] further submits that being able to offer both belly space and freighter
        capacity makes them more competitive because they are able to offer cost-efficient
       and tailor-made solutions to customers as long as there is no restriction on capacity
        being  offered.1420 Therefore, being able  to  offer both  freighter and belly space
         capacity, like the Parties do,  is a significant competitive advantage over carriers
         offering just the belly.

        appears that virtually no other competitor can imitate the Parties’ competitive offering,

        mostly used exceptionally, either for a specific big project with high volumes where
         the customer would in any event book the entire capacity of the aircraft or during the

        considerable number of unscheduled flights.1453 For example, in 2018 and 2019,1454
       Korean Air offered […] unscheduled cargo flight frequencies between the EEA and

(928)   Therefore, the Commission cannot consider unscheduled  flights as a  significant
        competitive constraint to the Parties, given that these are only offered – if at all – on a
         clearly opportunistic basis. As put by [a competitor], “depending on the market
       demand for charter-flights and lead-times we do not see charter-/non scheduled flights
        as an appropriate counterweight to any potential market power”.1455
(929)   In the fifth place, and contrary to Korean Air’s submission in paragraphs 711-714 of
           its Response to the Commission’s Statement of Objections, the Parties’ competitors
         for direct air cargo flights are each providing air cargo services to ICN from a
         significantly smaller number of European airports and have a significantly smaller
        geographical coverage of Europe than the Parties do. The fact that the Parties serve
       more European airports than any competitor for direct air cargo flights on the Europe
         to South Korea route gives them a competitive advantage that further limits the
        competitive constraint that these competitors can impose on the Parties.
(930)  As indicated in section 7.2.2, and despite the Commission’s conclusion to assess the
         effects of the Transaction on a European-wide market, the majority of customers
        considered that the catchment area by land or sea transportation for European airports
         for air cargo services from/to South Korea is an inner-European regional area, rather
        than all of Europe.1456 Accordingly, several customers claim that they would not
        switch to other European airports, or explained that such a switching decision would
       depend on various factors, such as the type of cargo and the distance to the airport as
        well as the additional trucking costs and transit time.1457 Similarly, according to [a
         competitor], the primary catchment area for their cargo flights to South Korea from
      […] and […] is at most one day of trucking away from these airports. This statement
           is confirmed by the fact that according to [the competitor], 95% of the cargo on [the
         competitor’s]  flights from […]  to ICN  in 2022  originated from  [the  airport’s
         country].1458

       where the air cargo carrier can land/the proximity to the origin or final destination of
         the cargo in Europe with an importance of 3.75/5, with 1 being “not important” and 5

(932)  As shown in section 8.10.3 the Parties are providing non-stop air cargo transport

        operates services from […] different European Airports. By comparison, no other
        competitor operates direct flights between more than two European airports and South
        Korea. While competitors which offer indirect flights involving transhipment, such as
        Qatar Airways, Turkish Airlines, Emirates, Etihad and Silk Way West are able to

         that of the Parties for the reasons stated above.
(933)   In the sixth place, and contrary to Korean Air’s submission in paragraphs 715-716 of
           its Response to the Commission’s Statement of Objections, competitors are unable to
         offer the same high level of quality of service as the Parties do and are therefore more
         distant competitors and only exert a limited competitive constraint on the Parties.
(934)   Competitors responding to the phase I market investigation confirmed that quality and
          reliability are very important, rating quality of the service as the most important
          criterion, while rating reliability of the air carrier in terms of flight times as the fifth
       most important criterion when choosing an air cargo carrier on the route (out of
          14).1461 Furthermore, customers rated quality of the service as the third and reliability
        of the air carrier in terms of flight times as the second most important criterion for
        customers when choosing an air cargo carrier on the route (out of 14).1462
(935)   Competitors and customers responding to the market investigation have furthermore
        both ranked Korean Air and Asiana as the most and second most competitive air
         carriers on the route in terms of reliability of flight times, as well as quality of service
         in terms of cargo handling.1463 Customers which were contacted as part of the Phase II
        market investigation have furthermore confirmed that the Parties both have a very high
         quality of services1464 and one has indicated that competitors such as Qatar Airways,
        Emirates, Singapore Airlines, China Eastern Airlines, Air China and Silk Way West
         are more likely to experience delays, lose cargo or damage cargo.1465
(936)   In summary, as shown above, all competitors have one, or in most cases several,
        shortcomings compared to the Parties, namely that they offer less frequencies, only
         offer transhipment  flights, do not offer  freighter  flights, do not have the same
        geographic coverage of European airports, have a lower quality of service.
(937)  On the basis of the above, the Commission concludes that the existing competitors’
        cargo operations only provide a limited competitive constraint on the Parties on the
         route from Europe to South Korea

8.11.3.2. Competitive constraints from integrators in their airport-to-airport offering
(938)   The  Commission  concludes  that,  contrary  to  Korean  Air’s  submissions  in
        paragraphs 722-725 of its Response to the Commission’s Statement of Objections and
        paragraphs 147-153 of its Response to the Commission’s Letter of Facts, integrators
        only exert a limited competitive constraint on the Parties in general air cargo services
       on the route from Europe to South Korea, as (i) they mostly compete on a different
        market, that of door-to-door delivery services,1466 and therefore offer spare capacity on
         the air cargo market on an exceptional basis, (ii) air cargo carriers do not consider
       them as their competitors or only consider them to a limited extent, (iii) customers of
         the Parties do not see them as close alternatives but rather as limited available options
         for only parts of their volumes, and (iv) end cargo customers1467 of freight forwarders
       do not consider their services comparable due to the risk of delay entailed in the
         integrators’ airport-to-airport cargo offering.
(939)    First, integrators submit that they only offer extremely limited spare capacity on the
        general air cargo market and therefore compete with the Parties to a limited extent,
        including a different quality of service, lower capacity, different pricing considerations
       and different targeted customers. [An integrator] noted1468 that its general air cargo
         offering is very different to the one provided by the Parties, as it is less certain and
        only open to the market after filling-up the aircraft with all door-to-door business. As
       demand for integrators in their core door-to-door business can be extremely volatile,
          their filler air cargo product is only offered on a deferred stand-by basis, with a
        3-to-5-day transit time in case of South Korea. This is because [the integrator’s] core
        door-to-door business is always prioritised over the general cargo, which will be left
        behind until there is some capacity left after all door-to-door demand has been loaded
         to the aircraft. Therefore, the space made available in [the integrator’s] aircraft for
         freight forwarders typically comes at lower rates because of the lower quality of the
         service deriving from the fact that customers are not given guaranteed shipment  /
         delivery time. Therefore, [the integrator] expects to compete with the Parties in
        general airport-to-airport air cargo services only for a marginal part of the market, for
        customers, i.e. freight forwarders (i) that are not as time-sensitive, (ii) that do not need
         to book their air cargo services well in advance or plan ahead the entire season, and

1466      In paragraphs 118 et seqq. of its Response to the Commission’s Statement of Objections, Korean Air
         allegedly provides some “concrete examples of integrators and air cargo carriers competing”. The
       Commission notes that those examples do not in fact show strong competitive constraints exerted by
         integrators on the Parties: (i) In its reply to question 45, in conjunction with the introduction of RFI 2 (ID
        11459), [an integrator] confirmed that shipping Covid19 vaccines was part of their small package
        business and therefore not part of its “[limited] air cargo services to third parties on a space available
         basis”. Therefore, this is rather an example of the limited indirect out-of-market constraint posed to the
         Parties by the integrators, which has been acknowledged by the Commission and will be further analysed
         in section 8.11.5 below. This example does not in any event mean that  all general cargo can be
         transported by the integrators’ door-to-door delivery of small parcels and packages, but it rather confirms
          that integrators compete with freight forwarders for only a marginal part of end customers. (ii) The fact
          that Korean Air aspires to enter the market of door-to-door services as provided by integrators does not
       mean that the Parties’ airport-to-airport services compete with the integrators’ (different in nature) door-
         to-door services. To the contrary, as indicated by Korean Air’s internal documents, e.g. Response of
       Korean Air to RFI 14, “M.10149 - KE - OZ - Annex RFI14.Q5a.3”; “M.10149 - KE - OZ - Annex
        RFI14.Q5a.6”, Korean Air can only compete for customers like […] by integrating in  its offering
        Hanjin’s door-to-door services. It is Hanjin bidding for […] volumes on the routes between Europe and
        South Korea and not Korean Air with its airport-to-airport cargo services.

(942)   All three main integrators responding to the Commission’s market investigation
        confirmed that they do not consider the Parties as their competitors but rather only the
         other integrators.1475 On the contrary, integrators can rather be considered customers
        of the Parties – not competitors – as they integrate the Parties’ air cargo services in
          their door-to-door offer.1476
(943)   Therefore, the Commission considers that the integrators’ airport-to-airport product is
      much less reliable than that of the Parties and can satisfy only a limited part of the
        customers’ demand. As a consequence, the integrators can only represent a weak
        competitive constraint to the merged entity post-Transaction.

        providers of air cargo services on the route Europe to South Korea by the majority of
          air cargo  carriers responding  to the Commission’s market  investigation.1477 The
        majority of air cargo carriers responding to the Commission’s market investigation has
         also indicated that they only compete to a limited extent (if at all) to integrators.1478

8.11.4.  Expansion – Competitors are unlikely to increase supply if prices increase
(950)   Market conditions in the market for air cargo transport services between Europe and
        South Korea are such that the Merged Entity is likely to have an incentive to reduce its
        capacity below the combined pre-Transaction level, thereby increasing prices within
         the meaning of paragraph 32 of the Horizontal Merger Guidelines. Competitors are
         unlikely to increase supply in response. This is mainly because of the following
         reasons:
          (a)  The Parties have higher capacity shares than what they have estimated and have
            by far the highest individual and combined capacity shares on the market. High
            combined capacity shares indicate that the merged entity may have post-merger
             a greater incentive to increase prices.
         (b)  The spare capacity of competitors is too limited to be used to offset the effects of
              the Transaction: the Commission was not able to confirm Korean Air’s claim of
               existing significant excess capacity in the market.1493 The capacity available in
              the market as a whole is limited in the sense that all competitors’ excess capacity
              taken together would only be a fraction of the Parties’ combined supply.

             Furthermore, capacity has to be assessed in the light of the findings on closeness
              of  competition analyzed above  in  section  8.11.2. Air cargo  services  are
               differentiated on  the  basis  of  different  factors from both a  product and
             geographic perspective, expressed, among other  factors,  in delivery times,
              frequencies and reliability. Therefore, the excess capacity provided by numerous
              competitors would in any event be inferior in many instances to the services
              offered by the Parties.
          (c)   Essentially  all competitors face  barriers  to expand  their supply  either by
              increasing aircraft utilization or increasing frequencies post-Transaction. These
               barriers can be due to unavailability of traffic rights, network considerations (in
               particular in the case of passenger carriers), or access to aircraft and personnel.
         (d)   Competitors have limited or no incentives to shift available capacity to the route
            between Europe and South Korea by diverting it from other uses between East
             Asia and Europe.

        Objections – the capacity shares provided by the Parties are likely erroneous. This is
        because of the following reasons.
(953)    First, the Parties’ estimates of available capacity appear to be inflated, not reflecting
         actual capacities. The Parties included in their capacity calculations flights that did not
         carry cargo between Europe and South Korea, but rather simply touched down at
        Incheon airport to avoid Covid19 restrictions in China. Both [an integrator] (through
           its operating airline […]) and [a competitor] used such flights with technical stops
        over the last years. As [an integrator] explained, it would be erroneous to include such
          flights with technical stops in any capacity calculations.1494
(954)   In paragraphs 730-732 of its Response to the Commission’s Statement of Objections,
       and in paragraph 170 of its Response to the Commission’s Letter of Facts, Korean Air
        argues that technical stops should actually be taken into account because competitors
        can easily turn technical stops into proper stops for cargo. The Commission considers
         that  this has not been confirmed by the market  investigation. For example, as
         explicitly put by [a competitor]: “Scheduled technical stops mean that the crew is
       changed and/or refueling takes place. Therefore, scheduled technical stops do not
       change the capacity of the respective market”.1495
(955)   Second, according  to the  Parties’ capacity estimates reported  in Table 57, the
         integrators DHL, UPS, and FedEx represent around [40-50]% of the available capacity
       on the two routes, but this estimate fails to recognize that integrators’ capacity is for
         the  most  part  reserved  for  the  integrators’ own  door-to-door  business  (see
         section 8.11.3.2 above for additional details on the role played by integrators in the
        general air cargo market). Therefore, if the capacity share estimates took into account
         that most of the integrators’ capacity is used captively for their door-to-door business
       and is not available to the general market, the extent of excess capacity available to the
        general cargo market would be significantly reduced. Furthermore, integrators also
         rely on the Parties’ aircrafts for their own express cargo business,1496 which would
        question how much spare capacity they have and how strong a competitive constraint
        they would exert on the merged entity post-Transaction. For instance, [an integrator]
         consistently appears as one of the largest customers of both Parties.1497
(956)   Third, the 2020 and 2021 capacity data appears to reflect temporary effects of the
       Covid19 pandemic. [A competitor] was granted an exceptional additional weekly
        frequency for the route […]-South Korea during the Covid19 pandemic by MOLIT,
       which was then discontinued in 2022 without immediate prospects of being granted
         again.1498
(957)   Fourth, capacity utilization does not appear to be uniform throughout the year. The
        market investigation indicates – and the Parties have confirmed – that there are
       demand peaks before Christmas, before the Lunar New Year and in early summer.1499
       Data at the annual level might suggest that the available capacity is evenly spread
        throughout the year, while instead capacity may be more restricted at certain times of

(958)    Fifth, the capacity estimates provided by the Parties represent the overall theoretical
      maximum amount of cargo that can be transported on the routes, not the capacity
         actually available. In  its responses,1501 Korean Air defines the difference between
        capacity and volume  estimates  as excess  capacity and argue  that  the sum  of
         Lufthansa’s, DHL’s and Turkish Airlines’ excess capacity is greater than the total
       volume carried by Asiana from the EEA to South Korea in 2021. Further, the Parties
        claim that these excess capacity estimates suggest that customers would be able to
        switch to competitors in the event of a price increase by the Parties, and that the
       Merged Entity would be severely constrained in its ability to increase prices post-
         Transaction. This reasoning is flawed. The difference between capacity and volume
         estimates cannot be defined as excess capacity because it is actually composed of two
          distinct elements: (i) excess capacity in the sense of unused space on the aircraft; and
            (ii) capacity already used to transport cargo on the same aircraft on other routes. For
        example, carriers fly the same aircraft out of Europe with cargo bound for South
       Korea as well as cargo bound for other destinations, like Japan or China, where they
      may stop in on their way to/from South Korea. The Parties’ analysis does not take
        account of the fact that capacity already used for other destinations is not available,
       and thus substantially overestimates the amount of excess capacity in the market.
(959)   Given those deficiencies, the Commission has endeavoured to collect more accurate
        data on capacities from market participants through the market reconstruction exercise
        described in Annex  I.  Table 58 below shows the result of those calculations for
       Europe to South Korea between 2019 and 2021 based on data provided by the main
        market participants. It is worth noting that, in order to show that, contrary to Korean
         Air’s claim,1502 the Commission’s conclusions do not depend on the methodology
        followed, the Commission assessed whether capacity shares would differ if market
         sizes and competitors’ capacity estimates were calculated as suggested by Korean Air.
        Table 58 thus shows capacity shares and market sizes both adjusted according to the
       Commission’s methodology and according to Korean Air’s methodology. Differences
         are very negligible.
(960)   The Commission’s analysis shows that the Parties significantly underestimated their
      own capacity shares, while overestimating their competitors’ capacity shares.
(961)   For the reasons discussed in sections 7.2.1.4 and 8.11.3.2, integrators’ capacities play
        a role only to the extent they serve the general cargo market, and not their entire door-
        to-door  business.  Therefore,  the  Parties  have  significantly  overestimated  the
         integrators’ capacities.1503
(962)   Both because of the Parties’ handling of technical stop-over and because of general
        data limitations of the sources available on carriers’ capacity on the route between
       Europe and South Korea, the Parties tended to overestimate the capacities of a number
        of their competitors.

8.11.4.2. No  significant spare capacity for competitors on the route, taking into account
        closeness of competition
(965)   The Phase II investigation focused on investigating further the Parties’ claim that the
         current market situation  is characterized by overcapacity due to available excess
        capacity on existing flights. The results of the Phase II investigation indicate that –
         also contrary to Korean Air’s submission in paragraphs 742-770 of its Response to the
       Commission’s Statement of Objections – competitors already active on these routes do
        not appear  to have enough capacity or incentive  to be able  to expand supply
         sufficiently to counteract an increase in prices post-merger, nor to deter it in the first
         place.
(966)    First, the market investigation did not confirm Korean Air’s claim that there  is
         structural excess capacity1505 on the route Europe-South Korea. Only a small minority
        of respondents having expressed a view stated that the air cargo markets between
       Europe and South Korea  are  characterized by overcapacity (defined as supply
        exceeding demand).1506 In fact, the Commission’s market investigation has indicated
         neither over-capacity nor under-capacity on the routes between Europe and South
        Korea. The majority of respondents has  replied  that “demand and supply are



1504    Annex  I provides additional  details about the comparison between the Notifying Party’s and the

         or not has only a very marginal impact on market shares.

         balanced”.1507 Therefore, there is no structural excess capacity on the route, contrary
         to what Korean Air argues in paragraphs 744-748 of its Response to the Commission’s
        Statement of Objections, and in paragraphs 154 and 172 of  its Response to the
       Commission’s Letter of Facts.
(967)    Interestingly, Korean Air’s arguments on the availability of excess capacity on the
        market are not confirmed by  its own internal business documents. For example,
       Korean Air considers that flights from Europe to Asia are generally characterized by
         limited supply.1508 In addition, Korean Air confirms in its documents that the Russian
       war against Ukraine has further decreased the available capacity on the market.1509
(968)   Second, the likely absence of overcapacity is demonstrated by the fact that the Parties’
      own capacity utilization, as indicated by their load factor, has been constantly at least
        or above [80-90]% between 2018 and 2021 in both trade directions of the Europe-
        South Korea routes.1510 Thus, even pre-Covid19, the Parties did not have much excess
        capacity on the routes between Europe and South Korea, which are thus characterized
       by high capacity utilization. By comparison, the global load factor for cargo transport
        of all suppliers was [40-50]% in 2019 and [60-70]% in 2021 and thus much lower than
         the load factor of the Parties.1511 In addition, the Parties’ overall load factor for all
       worldwide cargo trade between 2018-2021 was also consistently lower each year than
         that on the routes between the EEA and South Korea. This further indicates that by
        comparison, the routes between Europe and South Korea rather have a higher capacity
          utilization and lower excess capacity than average air cargo transport routes.
(969)   In its responses,1512 Korean Air argues that the load factor cannot be used as a reliable
         indicator to determine if there is excess capacity in the market because, among other
         reasons, the load factor is manipulated by carriers in order to achieve as high load
         factors as possible. Feedback from competitors, however, suggests that carriers do rely
       on the load factor as a proxy for their utilization rate.1513 Moreover, most competitors
       have stated that they do not cancel flights to maximize their load factor on the route,
        thus the load factor does not appear to be generally manipulated to achieve as high
        load factors as possible.1514 Furthermore, even if carriers were indeed systematically
        manipulating the load factor by cancelling flights to maximise the load factor, the load
         factor would still provide a reasonable approximation of the aircrafts’ utilization rate.
        For example, this issue might be relevant on routes where adding more flights to cater
         for the additional demand  is not possible, for example, because of traffic rights
         limitations (this is explained further in the below). Furthermore, the Parties themselves
         relied on the load factor to quantify the amount of additional capacity currently unused
       by other trades that they could add to the route between Europe and South Korea.1515

       The Commission therefore deems the load factor as a relevant and reliable indicator to
        determine  if there  is excess capacity in the market, also taking into account the
        following considerations:
(970)    If anything, the load factor as used by the Commission can indicate a higher level of
        excess capacity in the market than is in fact available and is therefore in any event
         likely to overestimate the spare capacity that is available on the market. A competitor
        has explained in this respect: “Many flights on this route tend to be volume-restricted,
       meaning the volumetric space runs out before the weight capacity of the aircraft. As
        such the numbers are highly dependent on the density of the cargo carried. Many
          flights on this route tend to be volume-restricted, meaning the volumetric space runs
        out before the weight capacity of the aircraft. As such the numbers are highly
        dependent on the density of the cargo carried”.1516 Another competitor has further
        noted the following: “A load factor of 100 % is only a theoretical limit, in reality we
        see a maximum at approx. 90 % as other factors like volume consumption, product
         characteristics or handling restrictions limit the way pallets or containers can be build
         up”.1517 In the same vein, [an integrator] has explained that a weight load factor might
          reflect available space but in reality, all positions in any given flight will be utilised
       when the percentage is above [80-90]%.1518
(971)   With regard to Korean Air’s argument that the load factor is manipulated by carriers in
        order to achieve as high load factors as possible, a competitor has explained that at
          least when it comes to belly-hold carriers, this is not possible: “As passengers are
        carried on the same flights individual flights are seldomly cancelled purely due to a
        lack of cargo demand on that flight. In general the optimization is done for the
          profitability, rather than load factor. […] The passenger / belly-hold cargo service is
        operated regularly to protect valuable slot positions in ICN. Cancellations may only
         result due to exceptional operative circumstances”.1519 This was also substantiated by
        another competitor.1520 Therefore, for at least the belly-hold carriers, load factor
        cannot be manipulated even if they wanted to.
(972)   In its internal business documents, Korean Air puts […]. In fact, it considers [80-90]%
        as the relevant threshold for a “good” load factor.1521
(973)   Third, data gathered from third parties during the Phase II investigation allowed the
       Commission to estimate the amount of excess capacity available on the route and
       compare it against the Parties’ combined volumes. Excess capacity in this regard is
        defined as the additional volumes a carrier could transport by filling up the unused
        capacity on aircraft (equal to the difference between overall capacity and volume
         transported). The underlying assumption of that analysis is that post-merger, if all the
         Parties’ customers find an alternative to the Parties, then it is unlikely that the Parties
       would be able to increase prices. If, however, only a fraction of the Parties’ customers
        could find an alternative supplier, the Parties are expected to have at least some
         incentive to increase prices.1522 This is because, if capacity is scarce, competitors can
        enjoy some degree of market power, and could be thus able to increase prices to
        customers. Moreover, competitors could in turn also find profitable to follow price
         increases. If competitors are not able to cover the entirety of market demand, the

       merger would enable the merged entity to enjoy an increased degree of market power,
       and be thus capable of increasing prices to customers. This market power-increasing
         effect of a post-merger increase of the merged entity’s excess capacity (relative to the
          rivals, who are capacity-constrained) would arise even if the rivals’ capacity would be
         perfect substitutes of the merged entity’s capacity. As will be further evidenced below,
         the rivals’ capacity is not of the same quality as that of the Parties, who are each
         other’s close – even the closest – competitors. This quality differential reinforces the
        capacity-based effect.
(974)   This approach is aligned with the Horizontal Merger Guidelines, paragraphs 32 to 34,
       which provide that “(32) When market conditions are such that the competitors of the
       merging parties are unlikely to increase their supply substantially if prices increase,
         the merging firms may have an incentive to reduce output below the combined pre-
       merger levels, thereby raising market prices. The merger increases the incentive to
        reduce output by giving the merged firm a larger base of sales on which to enjoy the
        higher margins resulting from an increase in prices induced by the output reduction.
        (33) Conversely, when market conditions are such that rival firms have enough
        capacity and find it profitable to expand output sufficiently, the Commission is unlikely
         to find that the merger will create or strengthen a dominant position or otherwise
         significantly  impede  effective  competition.  (34)  Such  output  expansion  is,  in
         particular, unlikely when competitors face binding capacity constraints.”1523 Also,
        paragraph 24 of the Horizontal Merger Guidelines provides that “Non-merging firms
         in the same market can also benefit from the reduction of competitive pressure that
         results from the merger, since the merging firms' price increase may switch some
       demand to the rival firms, which, in turn, may find  it profitable to increase their
         prices. The reduction in these competitive constraints could lead to significant price
        increases in the relevant market.”1524
(975)  Annex I provides a description of the methodology followed and the data used for this
         analysis.  Table 59  provides  the  Commission’s  estimates  for  the sum  of  all
        competitors’ excess capacities. The detailed estimates for each individual competitor’s
        excess capacity were only available to Korean Air’s external advisors in the context of
        a data room procedure. The figures relied upon by the Commission in this Decision
         are based on the figures included in the RBB Economics Second Data Room Report.
(976)   The sum of all competitors’ excess capacities is around [30-40]% of the Parties’
       combined volumes on the route Europe to South Korea. This implies that less than half
        of the Parties’ customers could find an alternative supplier other than the Parties.
        Competitors face severely binding capacity constraints and are therefore unlikely to be
        able to increase their supply sufficiently if prices increase, which implies that the
       merging firms may have an incentive to increase prices.
(977)   Table 59 also contains two sensitivities where excess capacity is calculated based on
         the load factor, and falls in the range [40 - 50]% and [60 - 70]%, respectively. As
        explained further in Annex I and above in paragraph (970), the load factor as used by
         the Commission can indicate a higher level of excess capacity in the market than is in
         fact available and is therefore in any event likely to overestimate spare capacity that is
         available on the market.

        capacity constraints. The capacity constraints explained above and the closeness based
        arguments are then reinforcing each other.

(982)   In response to this analysis, Korean Air argued that on the route from Europe to South
        Korea, prices would have to increase by approximately 20-30% before rivals’ excess
        capacity  is exhausted.1526 This statement  is flawed for several reasons, these are
        explained in the below.
(983)    First, of  all, the Commission notes that paragraph 24 of the Horizontal Merger
        Guidelines unambiguously provides that “Non-merging firms in the same market can
        also benefit from the reduction of competitive pressure that results from the merger,
         since the merging firms' price increase may switch some demand to the rival firms,
        which, in turn, may find it profitable to increase their prices.”1527 This follows from
        standard economic theories of non-coordinated horizontal competition: The merging
          parties' competitors, faced with an increase in demand following a price increase by
         the merged entity, will in general respond by both increasing their price and by
        expanding their output. In a differentiated product setting, such reactions by rivals can
         generally not be expected to make a price increase unprofitable for the merged entity.
        In fact, both the merged entity and its rivals might enjoy some price increase with the
        former increasing its price more than the latter. Such price changes may also involve
         relative output changes with the merged entity’s volume decreasing relative to its
          rivals’.1528 The exact amounts that prices could increase or relative outputs change
         ultimately depend on the characteristics of the market, and in particular on (i) the
         strength of differentiation between the merged entity and its rivals, and (ii) the rivals’
         available spare capacity.
(984)    It is only in the extreme case, referred to as “pure” or “standard” Bertrand competition,
       where there  is no product  differentiation (each firm’s capacity being a  perfect
         substitute of all others’), and there are no capacity constraints (each individual firm’s
       volume can be covered by the rivals’ combined spare capacity), that the merged entity
        cannot profitably raise its price as the rivals’ reactions would defeat any price increase
         attempt: In this case, the post-merger price equilibrium is the same as that in the
        absence of the merger.1529 None of the conditions necessary for this extreme case to
         prevail are met: (i) capacity is differentiated, and (ii) the rivals’ spare capacity is not
       unambiguously sufficient to cover the merged entity’s combined volume, with the
        spare capacity clearly being insufficient on the Europe to South Korea route.
(985)   Furthermore, while individually the volumes of each Korean Air and Asiana can easily
        be covered by the rivals’ spare capacity, the impact of the Transaction is such that this
       would no longer hold post-merger for the merged entity. Moreover, excess capacity is
         also very strongly fragmented, which means that essentially all competitors would be
       needed to replace the Parties, even if the differentiation issue is put aside. Hence, such
        fragmentation might adversely affect customers with large shipments.1530 However,
       Korean Air’s claims on rivals defeating any price increase of the merged entity heavily
       depend  on  the   implicit  assumption  of  capacity  being  homogenous  and

1526     Response of Korean Air to the Commission’s Statement of Objections, Annex 5, page 6. Response of
       Korean Air to the Commission’s Letter of Facts, paragraphs 174-181, 191.
1527     Horizontal Merger Guidelines, paragraph 24.
1528     All these changes are meant relative to the counterfactual, that is, the market situation in absence of the
        merger.
1529     This extreme case is referred to as pure Bertrand competition. In addition to the conditions listed, the
        following should also hold: customers have no switching costs, firms have no fixed costs, there are at
          least two firms (post-merger). The first two of the additional conditions does not hold in the current case,
         neither are the two conditions mentioned in the main text. It is also important that these conditions are
        cumulative for pure Bertrand competition to emerge. If, for example, products are differentiated a merger
        might lead to price increases. If, in addition, rivals face some capacity constraints competition is further
       dampened that in turn further supports the merger price effects.
1530     See sections 8.11.3.1 and 8.12.3.1.
