         undifferentiated, and the rivals having ample spare capacity. As these assumptions are
        not supported by the evidence, the setting in the relevant cargo markets in this case is
         better characterised as differentiated markets with capacity constraints as opposed to
        standard Bertrand competition. Hence,  it is incorrect to apply the insights of the
        standard Bertrand competition framework without capacity constraints as done by
       Korean Air.
(986)    Fifth, as discussed in paragraph (978) above, the amount of excess capacity faced by
         the merged entity is also substantially smaller than what each of the Parties faced pre-
        merger. As discussed in section 8.11.2, rivalry between the parties has been an
        important source of competition on the market, and the merged entity will face
         significantly less rival excess capacity post-merger than each of the merging firms is
        facing pre-merger. This reduction in the countervailing spare capacity held by rivals
        thus indicates that the competitive pressure on the merged entity is lower relative to
         the competitive pressure faced by each of the merging firms pre-merger. As a result,
          this merger-induced consolidation of levels of capacities a will, in general, increase the
        market power of the merged entity.
(987)   Sixth, Korean Air notes that previous cases such as Outokumpu / INOXUM and INEOS
             / Solvay1531 do not serve as appropriate guides in the case at hand because capacity is
      much more fixed in industrial markets such as steel and chemical products than in
          airline cargo.1532 The Commission agrees with Korean Air that capacity in airline
        cargo is possibly significantly more flexible than in steel and chemical industries,
        however, as explained in the following sections, expansion is not likely: competitors
        face  significant  barriers  to expansion and are unlikely  to expand  their  activity
         sufficiently to prevent any potential anti-competitive effects of the Transaction.
(988)   Lastly, Korean Air argues that the Commission should have also considered excess
        capacity stemming from swing capacity, from increased utilisation rates, and from
        deploying additional  aircraft. Korean Air claims  that, had the Commission also
        considered these other sources of excess capacity, the rivals’ excess capacity as a
        proportion of the Parties’ sales would be materially greater than indicated in Table
          59.1533 A more detailed discussion on competitors shifting capacity across routes
        follows in section 8.11.4.4. The Commission notes, however, that, in the case when
       swing capacity would come from capacity already on the market but committed to
         other trades (for example, capacity on Europe-South Korea currently allocated to
         transport goods from Europe to Japan on a multi-stop route without transhipment), this
       swing capacity would imply two inter-related effects: (i) on the routes of concern,
        post-merger prices increased enough to prompt some competitors to consider re-
         allocating capacity away from their most profitable trade pre-merger; and (ii) Post-
       merger prices on the other trades would also increase as supply becomes smaller and
       demand has not changed (competitors would not have the incentive to offer customers
        a lower price if other competitors put less capacity on the trade).1534
(989)   Korean Air  states1535 on the one hand that  it does not believe  it  is likely that
        competitors would respond to price rises by the Merged Entity by increasing their own

        constrained  time.1592 This may  further complicate the operation of the  existing
        frequencies on the route, let alone any further expansion.

        can carry. However, Korean Air contests that the closure of the Russian airspace has
       added a barrier to entry and expansion on either of the routes due to the fact that there
        has been no example of discontinuation of operations of air cargo carriers who need to
        bypass the Russian airspace.

(1020)  In the first place, as stated above and as acknowledged by the Parties, [a competitor] is
         currently  restricted by  existing  traffic  rights and  has  confirmed  traffic  rights
         constituting a barrier to entry on the route.1613 Expansion by [the competitor] can
         therefore not be considered timely or likely. In the second place, while [a competitor]
           is expecting the delivery of additional Boeing 777F aircraft between 2023 and 2027
        (and further  aircraft post 2027), the carrier has confirmed that “[d]etails of the
         potential expansion are not concrete and are being evaluated”.1614 In addition, [the
        competitor] has not added any frequencies/flights on the route from/to South Korea in
         the last five years.1615 This does not, fulfil the criteria of timely, likely and sufficient
         entry. In the third place, [a competitor] has stated that “[s]ince we are planning to

        frequency and we can serve it with the additional supply of capacity”.1616 Similarly,
          this statement also does not fulfil the criterion of timely, likely and sufficient entry.
(1021)  Lastly, given that integrators have an entirely different business model and focus, as
        described in detail in section 7.2.1.4 above, it is unlikely that they would respond to a
         hypothetical price increase post-Transaction by adding more capacity to their airport-
         to-airport general cargo services, which is only considered a filler product for leftover
         capacities. Boeing’s World Air Cargo Forecast 2022-20411617 projects that the e-
       commerce / express market will significantly expand (even double) in the near future.
        Therefore, contrary to what Korean Air argues in paragraph 168 of its Response to the
       Commission’s Letter of Facts, integrators – whose main focus and business model is
         the e-commerce / express delivery market, as opposed to airport-to-airport transport of
        general cargo – will be having less and less capacity available for their filler product
        of airport-to-airport transport. This is in line with [an integrator]’s submission: “its
        core door-to-door business has always been the basis of its network planning and [...]
         contribution on [our] flights is expected to be less and less over time, assuming
        underlying growth of its door-to-door business”.1618
(1022) On the basis of the above considerations, the table below provides an illustration of the
         Parties’ competitors’ ability and/or incentive to expand. Contrary to Korean Air’s
        submission in paragraph 169 of its Response to the Commission’s Letter of Facts, it
        appears that […] competitors could practically expand their service on the route,
       namely [competitors]. However, no concrete plans have been confirmed during the
       Commission’s market investigation, whereas their incentive can only be seen as highly
         speculative.

8.11.4.4. Competitors are unlikely to shift available capacity within the routes between East
        Asia and Europe
(1024)  The Commission’s market investigation has not confirmed the  Parties’ claim –
         reiterated by Korean Air in paragraphs 804-823 of its Response to the Commission’s
        Statement of Objections, and in paragraph 167 of its Response to the Commission’s
         Letter of Facts – that competitors are able and likely to increase sales volumes on the
         route from Europe to South Korea by shifting available capacity within the routes
       between East Asia and Europe. According to the Parties, all the capacity that is used
       between East Asia and Europe can and would at any point in time become available
         for the routes between the EEA and South Korea.1631 Competitors responding to the
       Commission’s market investigation have for the most part not confirmed this claim.
(1025)   First, this strategy could not be pursued by carriers which only transport point-to-point
          air cargo on direct non-stop flights from Europe to South Korea, with the exception of
         potential behind and beyond routes. The reason for this is that these carriers carry
        cargo from Europe to South Korea or the other way around, without having the ability
         to offload or on-board other cargo on the way. The only way these carriers could
        pursue such a shifting strategy would be, if they had a hub at the East Asian end of the
         route, or if they had interlining agreements in place, between this end of the route and
        South Korea. This was confirmed by [a competitor], when stating that the only way
        they could shift their capacity would be by using interline-partners in ICN, which
       would connect their flights to other East Asian directions.1632 Neither the Parties, nor
         the market investigation has presented sufficient evidence for the Commission to
       assume that these carriers would adopt such an approach.
(1026)  Second, any competitor that would pursue such a strategy would face the opportunity
         costs of giving up capacity on another route, which it currently prioritizes over the
         route from Europe to South Korea.1633 Concretely, [a competitor] currently operates all
      […] flights between Europe and ICN […]. [The competitor] would therefore have to
        forego transporting cargo between Europe and […] in order to increase capacity on the
        Europe-South Korea routes by way of replacement. To the degree that such a strategy
       would be profitable, this capacity shifting is already conducted by [the competitor] on
          this route. However, according to [the competitor], “[b]usiness to […] is historically
       more  important  for  [our company]  than  business  to South Korea”.  1634 [The
        competitor] therefore stated that “a further increase is not possible”. 1635 It is therefore
         unlikely that [a competitor] would pursue such a strategy.
(1027)  Similarly, according to [a competitor], “there are opportunity costs of giving up cargo
        trade on other routes. We also have commitments to existing customers. These will
        prevent us from re-allocating more freighter capacity to the Europe-South Korea
         route.”1636
(1028)  Furthermore, [a competitor] is also unlikely to shift capacity in this way. According to
         [the competitor], the South Korean market  is not important for  its business and
         therefore not a focus. This is exemplified by the fact that they do not operate freighter
          aircraft on the route between […] and South Korea.1637 Consequently, despite stating
         that  it  expects  the  Transaction  to  increase  barriers  to  entry on  the  route  for

         increase prices as well.

         reflected in the internal business documents of either of Korean Air and/or Asiana.
       The Parties rather only refer to a vague monitoring of capacity on a worldwide basis,
       which is of limited evidentiary value for the purpose of evaluating the availability of
        spare capacity on the routes between Europe and South Korea.1651
(1038)  In light of the above and because, as shown in sections 8.11.2 and 8.11.3, many
        customers have a preference for direct, freighter flights at high frequencies and also
        perceive a quality difference between the Parties and many of their competitors, even
            if competitors would pursue a strategy of shifting available capacity towards the
       Europe to South Korea route in response to a capacity decrease by the Merged Entity
         post-Transaction, that would not constitute an adequate alternative to the Parties’
         services for customers.
8.11.5.  Indirect out-of-market constraint from integrators
(1039)  Korean Air submits that there are further indirect constraints that integrators pose on
         the Parties’ airline cargo pricing. End customers/shippers can obtain door-to-door
         delivery services from freight forwarders and integrators. Air cargo services can be
        considered as an upstream input into the service provided by freight forwarders.
         Integrators, on the other hand, are vertically integrated and rely on in-house airline
        cargo services. If prices of general air cargo services as an upstream input increase,
          this increases the cost for freight forwarders. According to Korean Air, this is likely to
        cause freight forwarding customers to switch to integrators. These customers would no
        longer use air cargo services as provided by the Parties, but instead use those provided
        in-house by integrators – resulting in a disincentive for the Parties to increase
          prices.1652
(1040)  In paragraphs 825-838 of its Response to the Commission’s Statement of Objections,
       Korean Air reiterates that integrators actually pose significant indirect competitive
         constraints on the Parties’ business as they offer similar services as the Parties offer in

(1041)  The Commission considers that to a certain extent the integrators’ core door-to-door
         services as analysed in section 7.2.1.4 above, may be in competition with freight
        forwarders’ services (using air cargo services as an input). However, such competition
           is only limited and can only pose a limited indirect constraint – at best – to the
        upstream market for airport-to-airport air cargo services, where the Parties are active.
(1042)   First, the Commission notes that the integrators’ core business consists in the door-to-
        door delivery of mainly small packages and parcels, as opposed to larger general
         cargo,  i.e. freight, which  is the core focus of freight forwarders. As integrators
         explain,1653 their product offering is different to that of freight forwarders using air
        cargo services as an input, in terms of the type of cargo mainly transported and the
         service offered, namely a door-to-door service which is inherent to the integrators’
        business model and not always a given for the freight forwarders’ business model. [...]
         integrators, […] confirmed that their main focus is their door-to-door business, for
       which they make all their strategic decisions.1654
(1043)  Therefore, from the outset, the overlap of activities between integrators and freight
        forwarders is only limited; integrators mainly deliver small packages requiring little to
       no special handling,1655 whereas freight forwarders focus on heavy consignments and
         typically outsource small package delivery services to third parties.1656 This is also
        probably the reason why the integrators are mostly seen as customers of the Parties in
          their internal business documents1657 –  if not as third-tier competitors, as further
        explained in paragraph (948) above. The two are not contradictory as Korean Air
        argues in paragraph 192 of its Response to the Commission’s Letter of Facts, but
         rather complementary. As analysed in section 7.2.1.4 above, the Parties’ airport-to-
         airport air cargo services and the integrators’ core door-to-door small package delivery
         services belong  to  separate product  markets. The  limited  extent  to which  the
         integrators’ spare capacity offered for airport-to-airport air cargo services poses a
        competitive constraint to the Parties is assessed in section 8.11.3.2 above. There,
         integrators are evaluated in  their capacity as  airport-to-airport general  air cargo
          carriers, and they are considered rather distant competitors to the Parties. On the
         contrary, in this section the Commission assesses any indirect out-of-market constraint
         to the Parties posed by the integrators’ door-to-door services, and therefore takes into
        account that, exactly because of the difference in their activities, integrators are rather
        seen as customers of the Parties.
(1044)  The different focus between integrators and freight forwarders has been investigated
       and confirmed in the Commission’s prior decisional practice.1658 Freight and small
        packages are usually transported via different infrastructures which are designed in a

[PÁGINA PDF 257]
         different way. The handling of freight necessitates special equipment that  is not
       needed for small package delivery, such as forklifts; whereas the sorting of palletised
       goods is done manually. Freight forwarders usually deliver palletised goods to a more
         limited number of clients arranging the transport of their goods on a more point-to-
         point basis. As the number of items is significantly smaller and the items are much
         heavier, the freight forwarding model does not involve a hub-and-spoke system such
        as the one used by integrators. Small package networks are characterised by a
         significantly higher level of automation than freight networks, notably at the level of
         sorting centres, which are based on conveyor belts and scanners. Every day, the (local)
         sorting centres accumulate a high number of packages which are usually channelled
         via hubs and again sorted and dispatched to the delivery hubs and sorting centres.
        Furthermore, in order to deliver small packages efficiently, operators need a dense
        network. These features allow companies operating small package networks to ship
        high numbers of units between points of origin and points of destinations spread over
       wide geographic areas and within relatively limited timeframes compared to those
         prevailing in the freight forwarding sector. Due to the different characteristics of
         freight and small package networks,  it is commonly agreed that there is a weight
         threshold below which small package delivery companies like the integrators are more
        competitive than freight forwarders and above which freight should be considered as a
         cost effective alternative.
(1045)  The above considerations from the Commission’s prior decisional practice have been
        confirmed by the Commission’s market investigation in the present case. According to
        [an integrator], the business model of integrators is different to the one of freight
        forwarders in four core elements:1659 (i) the speed of delivery and time commitment
         that comes at a higher price. In other words, according to [the integrator], at least non-
         time-sensitive customers would never switch from a freight forwarder to an integrator
        because the integrator would charge them with the premium door-to-door pricing that
        they would not need;  (ii) the door-to-door service, which  is not inherent in the
        business model of freight forwarders. As [an integrator] explained, what is inherent in
         the integrators’ business model is the pick-up and delivery which will happen at the
         specific address the customer will indicate. Freight forwarders do not have such a
         capillary distribution network and therefore they do not typically sell a door-to-door
        element, at least not within their standard product offering; (iii) the different customers
         targeted. As [an integrator] explained, integrators would typically target thousands of
        customers with single (smaller) shipments, whereas freight forwarders would typically
         target a few customers with high volumes/quantities, e.g. heavy car parts; (iv) the
         different nature of the service. If for example [an integrator’s] aircraft has a capacity
        of 100 tons and a customer wishes to transport 120 tons, [the integrator] would not
         turn away the customer. On the contrary, freight forwarders sell out their capacity
         against  their inventory and do not accept any more shipments  after  that point.
        According to [the integrator], the difference lies on the fact that integrators’ customers
        order pick-ups, whereas customers of freight forwarders (using air cargo carriers as an
         input) book capacity.
(1046)  In addition, [an integrator] explained that “the unique selling point of integrators is
         [the] one-stop-shop with end-to-end tracking capabilities. This is something that a
         freight forwarder cannot offer. Freight forwarders typically offer lower rates but there

(1049)  In the same vein, [a customer] explained that the integrators have an entirely different

8.11.6.  Countervailing buyer power
(1058)  Customers are unlikely to have sufficient buyer power to off-set the negative effects of
         the Transaction on the route Europe to South Korea.
(1059)   First, the customers are unlikely to have bargaining strength due to their size or
       commercial significance for the Parties on the route Europe to South Korea.
(1060)  In the first place, the customer base on the route Europe-South Korea is fragmented.
       The largest customer of Korean Air – […]– accounted for only about [5-10]-[10-20]%
        of Korean Air’s volumes on the route Europe-South Korea in 2018-2022. The second
       and third largest customers – whose identity varied in 2018-2022 – each accounted for
        only about [5-10]-[5-10]% and [5-10]-[5-10]% in 2018-2022 respectively. Similarly,
        Asiana’s largest customer – […] – accounted for only about [5-10]-[10-20]% of
        Asiana’s volumes on the route Europe-South Korea in 2018-2022 while the second
       and third largest customers – whose identity varied in 2018-2022 – accounted for only
        about [5-10]% and [0-5]-[5-10]% of Asiana’s volumes respectively. Already among
         the ten largest customers of each of the Parties, there are several customers that

         prices over the last four years is related to the circumstances brought about by the

(1064)  Fourth, the results of the Commission’s market investigation did not confirm that
        customers exert sufficient buyer power in the air cargo transport market from Europe
         to South Korea to prevent any negative effects of the Transaction.
(1065)  In the first place, only a minority of customers responding to the relevant question of
         the Commission’s phase I questionnaire considered that customers exert significant
        buyer power. The clear majority of customers considered that there is no buyer power,
         that customers do not exert much buyer power or that they exert only a small degree of
        buyer power. Others considered that it depends, for instance on the specific market
         conditions, including the season.1681 A customers explained its views on this also in a
       phone call with the Commission.1682
(1066)  In the second place, the competitors responding to the relevant question of the
       Commission’s phase I questionnaire did not provide a clear view and therefore did not
        confirm that there is sufficient buyer power on the route Europe to South Korea. While
        a limited number (3) of competitors considered that customers exert significant buyer
        power, a slightly larger number of competitors (4) considered that there is no buyer
        power, that customers do not exert much buyer power or that they exert only a small
        degree of buyer power.1683 Others considered that  it depends, for instance on the
       supply-demand balance in the different seasons or on the volume purchased. This was
        confirmed during the Commission’s phase II investigation where an integrator (and
        former customer) explained that “currently, neither the air carriers nor the customers
        (be it freight forwarders, integrators or other customers) have any particularly strong
        bargaining power over the other side”.1684 This notion was further confirmed by
         competitors. Some (2) competitors consider that there are no customers present at the
      moment who have the ability to exercise their buyer power to a significant degree.
        Other competitors (2) stated that customers’ buyer power is contingent on the actual
        supply/demand situation on a particular route.1685 It is notably explained that it is only
         the  “large and  global market  players  with  significant and  consistent volumes
        throughout the year” that indeed do possess buyer power.1686
(1067)  Fifth, several customers of air cargo services indicated in their responses to the market
         investigation that they would likely pass on price increases for air cargo services to
          their end-customers.1687 This ability would further limit the incentive of customers to
          resist industry-wide price increases by air cargo carriers on the route from Europe to
        South Korea.
(1068)  Sixth, independently of how strong the bargaining power  is that customers may
         currently enjoy, the Transaction not only reduces the number of providers active on

         the route from Europe to South Korea but it eliminates the second best alternative
        customers have (as explained in section 8.11.2). Furthermore, other competitors exert
        a more limited constraint (as explained in section 8.11.3). This means that customers’
        choice of alternative suppliers on the route Europe to South Korea would be limited
          after the Transaction and that they would not be able to switch easily to alternative
          suppliers.1688 This implies that post-Transaction customers’ bargaining power will be
         inevitably reduced by removing a credible alternative, thus making more likely a price
         increase, or another type of worsening of parameters of competition.
(1069)  Seventh, there is no evidence to suggest that customers could credibly threaten to
         vertically integrate into supplying air cargo services, in particular in the light of the
         barriers to entry as set out in section 8.11.4. There is no example of such entry of the
          last five years. In particular, and contrary to Korean Air’s claims regarding [names of
        customer], both freight forwarders replied to the Commission’s market investigation
         that they have not vertically integrated into providing general air cargo services on the
         route Europe to South Korea.1689 The Parties appear to refer to instances where those
         freight forwarders cooperate with cargo airlines to offer charter flights1690 or block
        space agreements1691 to end customers. In addition to the fact that charter flights exert
        only a remote  constraint on the  Parties’ operations  for the reasons  set out  in
         section 7.2.1.6, this does not constitute vertical integration by freight forwarders as
        they do not invest in flight capacity but cooperate with existing airlines – precisely by
        purchasing capacity from cargo airlines as described in this Decision as the relevant
        market on which the Transaction is likely to have negative effects, based on the
       outcome of the investigation.
(1070)  Eighth, (as explained in section 8.11.4) the Parties have achieved high load factors in
         recent years on the route Europe to South Korea: Korean Air’s load factor varied
       from[80-90]% in 2018 to [90-100]% in 2022, while Asiana’s varied from [80-90]% in
       2018 to [90-100]% in 2022.1692 Therefore, the Parties’ arguments according to which
         the customers hold buyer power because the Parties need business with all of them to
        achieve a sufficiently high load factor1693 is unfounded.
(1071)  Ninth, buyer power cannot be found to sufficiently off-set potential adverse effects of
         the Transaction if it only ensures that a particular segment of customers with particular
        bargaining  strength  is  shielded from  significantly  higher  prices  or  deteriorated
         considerations after the Transaction.1694 Therefore, the Parties’ argument that several
        of the customers are global companies with a strong presence in the European cargo
        market, such as […], […] or […],1695 is in any event irrelevant because there are many
         other customers that are smaller and do not share those characteristics.
(1072)  For all these reasons, the Commission, therefore, deems that customers are unlikely to
       have sufficient buyer power to off-set the negative effects of the Transaction on the
         route Europe to South Korea.

8.11.7.  Market entry
(1073)  The Commission’s market investigation did not identify any potential entry by a
         carrier not currently active on the Europe – South Korea route that could be considered
        as likely, timely and sufficient to prevent any potential anti-competitive effects of the
         Transaction.1696
(1074)  The Commission has contacted the potential entrants identified by the Parties, namely
       [names of potential entrants], as well as […], who was identified as a new entrant.
       [Names of potential entrants] replied to the Commission’s market investigation by
        confirming that they do not have any concrete plans to start offering air cargo services
       on the route between Europe and South Korea in the next three years.1697 No concrete
        plans of entry on the relevant routes have been confirmed by [names of potential
         entrants], either.1698
(1075)  Concretely, only [a potential entrant] has indicated that it would be willing to enter the
          air cargo transport service routes between Europe and South Korea independently of
         the Transaction, by offering direct passenger flights on the route ICN-FRA and
        providing belly-hold air cargo services on this route.1699 However, in addition to the
         considerations made with regard  to  the  entry of  [a  potential  entrant] […]  the
       Commission considers that an entry by […] on this route with […] or […] weekly
         frequencies1700 would not be sufficient to prevent any anti-competitive effects of the
        Transaction in air cargo transport, given the significantly higher volume and frequency
         offered by the Parties and the increment brought about by Asiana on this route. […], [a
         potential entrant] is planning […]. [A potential entrant] has already […]. Should [a
         potential entrant] reach its target […] tons of cargo per flight, its entry would initially
        correspond to [0-5]% on Europe – South Korea. While timely and likely, this entry
       would not by itself alter the competitive landscape sufficiently in order to prevent a
         significant  impediment  to  effective  competition,  also  taking  into  account  the
         considerations made under section 8.11.4 above with regard to competitors being
         unlikely to increase supply if prices increase.
(1076)  The Commission also notes that even Korean Air in paragraph 867 of its Response to
         the Commission’s Statement of Objections agrees that the entry of [a potential entrant]
      […] not lead to [a potential entrant] gaining significant market presence on the EEA-
       Korea trade routes.

(1077)  Finally, as a new entrant, […] replied to the Commission’s market investigation that

(1079)  Therefore, the market investigation did not reveal timely, likely and sufficient entry on

         anti-competitive effects of the Transaction. The Commission notes that this is also due
         to the barriers to entry and expansion that were identified and described in detail in
         section 8.11.4.3 above.
8.11.8.  Effect of the Transaction
(1080)  Although the results of the Commission’s market investigations were mixed overall,
         several market participants have expressed concerns about  (i) the strong market
         position of the Merged Entity, (ii) potential negative effects of the Transaction on
        competition and  (iii) potential negative effects of the Transaction on  their own
        business model.
(1081)   First, the market investigation has shown that several market participants fear the
        strengthening of the Parties’ already strong market position following the Transaction.
      As an example, one customer’s major concern is that post-Transaction the Parties
         “effectively own the market”.1704 One competitor explained that “the merger would
       weaken [competitor’s] position on the market – basically due to the important
         capacities the Partis have following extensive traffic rights. Korean Air and Asiana
         will have more than 200 aircrafts and a large fleet of freighters enabling them to
        dominate the market even more than they currently do. When the Parties dominate the
        market from a market share perspective, it is in [competitor’s] view possible that they
        also use their dominant position in terms of pricing.”1705Another competitor explained
         that “it seemed highly likely that the Parties would be in a position to control a large
        part of the market post-Transaction”.1706 Another competitor concurred by stating “As
         for air cargo services, [competitor] noted that the merged entity will become by far
         the  largest player between Europe and Korea which  will lead  to a dominant

         suppliers and it is presumed that this could mean lower capacities and higher rates. In
         that case, that customer is of the opinion that the merged entity could be able to have
         greater influence on the market due to the limited remaining competition.1715

        market itself is significant and as “second-tier-choice carriers” together would not
       have  the  necessary  scale  in  case […]  will  be  discontinued  following  the
         Transaction.1717
(1084)  Fourth, […].1718 […].”1719
8.12.   Cargo air transport services – assessment of the route South Korea to Europe
(1085)  Based on its investigation and all the evidence available to it, the Commission finds
          that:
          (a)  The Transaction would change the market structure significantly and lead to
             high combined market  shares with a high increment  in a  stable market
             environment which has shown little variation over time (section 8.12.1).
         (b)  The Parties are close – if not the closest – competitors as well as the most
              competitive suppliers in the market (section 8.12.2).
          (c)  The competing  air cargo  carriers and  integrators  provide only a  limited
              competitive constraint in the air cargo market (section 8.12.3).
         (d)  The Parties’ competitors face barriers to expand their services in reaction to
               potential negative effects of the Transaction (section 8.12.4).
          (e)   There is no or at best a limited indirect constraint on the Parties’ activities from
              the integrators’ sales to shippers (section 8.12.5)
           (f)   The customers are unlikely to have sufficient buyer power to off-set the negative
               effects of the Transaction (section 8.12.6).
         (g)   There is insufficient evidence of timely, likely and sufficient market entry to off-
                set the effects of the Transaction (section 8.12.7).
         (h)   Several market participants have expressed concerns about the strong market
               position of the Merged Entity and the potential negative effects on competition
              as a result of the Transaction (section 8.12.8).
(1086)  As set out in paragraph (856)(856) above, the Horizontal Merger Guidelines state that
        according to well-established case-law, very large market shares – 50% or more – may
         in themselves be evidence of the existence of a dominant position. A merger involving
        a firm whose market share will remain below 50% after the merger may also raise
        competition concerns, due to the creation of a dominant position, in view of other
         factors such as the strength and number of competitors and the presence of capacity
          constraints.1720 As set out in section 8.12.1, the merged entity would have a high share

1716     Non-confidential minutes of the conference call with [a customer].
1717     Non-confidential minutes of a call with [a customer].
1718     […].
1719     […].
1720     Horizontal Merger Guidelines, paragraph 17.


                                    262

[PÁGINA PDF 269]
         in terms of sales (around [40-50]%) and capacity (around [40-50]%) in the relevant
        market. Moreover, as discussed in sections 8.12.3 to 8.12.7, the relevant market is
         characterised by limited competitive pressure exerted by competitors, substantial
         barriers to expansion as well as a lack of likely, timely and sufficient market entry or
         countervailing buyer power. Therefore, the Commission considers that the Transaction
       would create a dominant position in relation to air cargo services on the route South
        Korea-Europe.
(1087)  In any event, paragraphs 26 to 38 of the Horizontal Merger Guidelines list factors
       which may influence whether significant non-coordinated effects are likely to result
       from a merger. “Paragraph 26 of those guidelines states in that regard, correctly, that
        those factors, taken separately, are not necessarily decisive. In addition, not all of
        those factors need to be present for significant non-coordinated effects to be likely. In
         that context, it must be found that those factors may, in principle, constitute evidence
         that a concentration would give rise to significant non-coordinated effects, which must
       be the subject of an overall assessment.”1721
(1088)  Considering the overall assessment of the findings in sections 8.12.1 to 8.12.8 and in
          light of the merged entity’s high share in air cargo services on the route South Korea-
        Europe, the Commission concludes that the Transaction would, in any event, give rise
         to horizontal non-coordinated  effects on the relevant market as a  result of the
         elimination of an important competitive constraint.

(1091)  In order for market shares and additions of market share to provide first indications of
        market power and increases in market power, market shares ought to reflect the entry
        of competitors expected to exert significant competitive pressure in the future on the
         other firms in the market and the exit of competitors no longer expected to exert any
        competitive pressure. This approach is aligned with the Horizontal Merger Guidelines,
        paragraph 15, which provide that “current market shares may be adjusted to reflect
        reasonably  certain  future changes,  for  instance  in  the  light  of  exit,  entry or
         expansion”1722. The following paragraphs and tables thus show how market shares
       would look like once the exit of both competitors like the Russian-based carriers

       which stopped operating cargo air services between South Korea and Europe in 2022
       and operators like Alitalia and Czech Airlines which ceased their operations, as well as
         the entry of competitors expected to exert significant competitive pressure in the future
           is accounted for. In the absence of more accurate information as to which competitors
       would win and lose the most from the exit and entry of these operators, sales volumes
       have been allocated to all other carriers in proportion to their market shares.

(1099) A comparison of the Parties’ combined market shares according to the Commission’s
        market reconstruction and the Parties’ submissions, as also set out in
(1100)  Table 70 shows that any deviations in market shares are very limited at [0-5]-[0-5]
        percentage points. Furthermore, the Commission’s analysis shows that, although some
        competitors’ shares were overestimated and some others were underestimated, these
         discrepancies were not substantial and mostly tended to cancel each other  out,
         therefore  not  affecting  the  Parties’ combined market  shares  significantly. This
       complementing methodology is conservative because it starts from the Parties’ own
         estimates, and updates them with more reliable information whenever available. The
       Commission’s analysis also confirms the significantly fragmented structure of the
        market, with very few competitors with a market shares between 5-10%, and long tail
        of smaller competitors. Therefore, the Commission will base its assessment on the
        market shares estimates provided by the Parties.

8.12.1.2. The Commission’s assessment of the market structure
(1101)  The Transaction would change the market structure on the route South Korea to
       Europe significantly and lead to high combined market shares with a high increment in
        a stable market environment which has shown little variation over time.
(1102)   First, the Transaction would lead to the Merged Entity holding a very strong position
       on the route between South Korea and Europe. As set out in Table 66, the Parties
       combined have held market shares of [30-40]% in 2018, [30-40]% in 2019, [40-50]%
         in 2020, [40-50]% in 2021, and [40-50]% in 2022, with increments of [10-20]-
        [10-20]%. The Parties’ market shares in 2020 and 2021 and to a certain extent also
       2022 appear to have been influenced by potentially temporary effects of the Covid19
        pandemic.
(1103)  Should Russian carriers, Alitalia and Czech Airlines be excluded and their volumes re-
         allocated across all other carriers proportionally, the Parties would remain the two
         largest providers with combined market shares of [30-40]-[40-50]%, with increments
        of [10-20]-[10-20]%. Should the entry of Air Premia be reflected, the Parties would
        remain the two largest providers with combined market shares of [30-40]-[40-50]%,
        with increments of [10-20]-[10-20]%. Under any of those methodologies, the Parties
         are the first and second largest providers of cargo air services on the route Europe to
        South Korea and would be the undisputed market leader after the Transaction.
(1104)  Second, as illustrated already above, the Transaction entails a significant increment in
       volume market shares of [10-20]-[10-20]%, which  is indicative of a  significant
         increase in market power due to the Transaction.
(1105)  Third, the Merged Entity’s market position would be significantly larger than that of
           its next largest competitors: Qatar Airways and Cargolux would hold market shares of
        around [10-20]% and [5-10]-[5-10]% respectively. Lufthansa Group, Silk Way Group
       and Air France KLM would hold  [5-10]-[10-20]%,  [0-5]-[5-10]% and  [5-10]-
       [10-20]% respectively.
(1106)  Fourth, with the exception of the impact of the Covid19 pandemic and of the Russian
       war against Ukraine (see section  8.10.1), the market  structure has shown  little
         variation  over  time  which  indicates  that  this  concentrated  market  structure
         characterised by the Parties and a long fringe of smaller competitors is likely to persist
         in the future. Market shares between 2018 and 2021 have varied little: Korean Air’s
        market share (excluding Russian  carriers,  Alitalia and Czech Airlines) has […]
       between 2018 and 2021, while Asiana’s market share has […] within the same
        timeframe. At the same time, Qatar Airways’ market share (the Parties’ largest
        competitor on the route), has […].

8.12.2.  Closeness of Competition between the Parties
(1107)  The market investigation has shown that the most important factors for customers’
        choice for the purchase of air cargo transport services on the route between South
       Korea and Europe are offered frequencies (4.76)1725, the reliability (4.64) and quality
         (4.43) of the offered services, the price (4.29) and main deck space availability on
         freighter aircraft (4.11). In particular for these factors of choice, Korean Air and
        Asiana are largely perceived as each other’s closest competitor by market participants.
        Against that background and in light of the results of the market investigation, the
       Commission considers the Parties to be close competitors on the air cargo routes
       between South Korea and Europe for the following reasons:
(1108)   First,  the Commission’s  market  investigation shows  that  both  customers  and
        competitors overwhelmingly recognize the Parties as each other’s closest competitor:
       The  vast  majority  of  competitors who  replied  to  the  Commission’s  market
         investigation questionnaire consider Asiana as Korean Air’s closest competitor1726 and
       Korean Air as Asiana’s closest competitor.1727 As regards customers, the majority of
        customers who have expressed their views in response to the Commission’s market
         investigation questionnaire consider Asiana as Korean Air’s closest competitor1728 and
       Korean Air as Asiana’s closest competitor.1729 The results of the Commission’s market
         investigation questionnaire also show that no other carrier is perceived as competing
         closely with either of the Parties.1730
(1109)  Second, the Commission’s market investigation also shows that market participants
        consider the Parties to be the two most competitive air cargo carriers on the routes
       between South Korea and Europe.1731 The Parties are ranked as the number 1 and
       number 2 most  competitive  carriers on  the  routes by  both  competitors  and
         customers.1732 As regards the competitiveness of the Parties, both Asiana and Korean
        Air received the highest rates respectively for  their overall competitiveness, the
        frequencies offered per week, the overall duration of the flights, the reliability in terms
        of flight times, the quality of the service in terms of cargo handling and the capacity
         offered on the route.1733 The air cargo customers the Commission spoke to as part of
           its market investigation widely confirmed that the Parties are each other’s closest
         competitors.1734 As an example, [a customer] explained that they currently still have a
         certain degree of bargaining power because they can switch between Korean Air and
        Asiana as needed, fearing that this will not be the case anymore post-Transaction when
        both Korean Air and Asiana – as the dominant providers on the South Korea-Europe
         route and each  other’s  closest competitors – become  one.1735  […].1736 Another

(1111)  More precisely, market participants view the Parties as closest competitors and as the
       two most competitive air cargo carriers on the route South Korea-Europe for the
        following reasons:
(1112)  In the first place, the Parties’ offer is very similar, in contrast to the Parties’ claim that
         the majority of air cargo service providers offer services which do not significantly
          differ from the Parties’ offer. 1739 Both offer scheduled, high-frequency, high-capacity
          air cargo flights in both freighter and passenger aircraft between Incheon and several
       European airports. Considering the airports they serve, the Parties closely compete
       from a geographic perspective. Asiana serves Brussels, Frankfurt, Milan, London and
       Vienna  with  regular  scheduled  dedicated  cargo  flights  (in  addition  to  cargo
         transportation in the belly-hold of its passenger flights from Frankfurt, Paris, Rome
       and Barcelona). Korean Air also serves Frankfurt, Milan, London and Vienna with
        dedicated cargo flights, among other European destinations, (in addition to cargo
         transportation in the belly-hold of its passenger flights from Frankfurt, Paris, Rome
       and Barcelona) and serves Amsterdam in the vicinity of Brussels. Accordingly the
         Parties state that “Korean Air operates a long-haul network to Europe which covers
         several  destinations throughout Europe.  It covers Northern, Western, Southern,
       Middle and Eastern Europe. Neither Korean Air nor Asiana focuses on one specific
        region within Europe”.1740 Which makes their offer similarly interesting for the same
        scope of customers in all European regions, in particular when considering that the
         vast majority of respondents to the market investigation indicated that they see some
         regional differences in the competitive conditions at the European end of the routes
         (see above, section 7.2.2).1741
(1113)  Due to the Parties’ focus on similar airports and regions in Europe, their share of sales
         are very high when looking at specific countries in Europe. As set out in Table 71 by
      way of example for the year 2019, the Parties achieved a high combined share of the
         sales in certain geographic segments of the relevant market, namely in […].

(1114)  In the second place, the Parties each offer direct (non-stop) services between South

         reveals that “[i]t depends on the specific customer needs, flying direct is the fastest

        important source of competition on the market and therefore concludes that the Parties

(1127)  Second, the Commission’s market investigation shows that most other  air cargo
         carriers are perceived as rather distant competitors to the Parties. Only a small share of
        respondents named any other carrier as Korean Air’s closest competitors on the route,
        with Asiana receiving the overwhelming majority of mentions. Amongst the Parties’
         competitors, only Emirates was one time individually named as Korean Air’s closest
        competitor on the route, apart from that, only Asiana received mentions.1785 Similarly,
         the overwhelming majority of respondents named Korean Air as Asiana’s closest
        competitor. Amongst competitors, Emirates being the only other competitor named
       even once as Asiana’s top competitor. Amongst customers, Lufthansa was the only
         other carrier named more than once.1786
(1128)  Third, the Parties’ competitors are not able to provide a similar service of non-stop,
        high-frequency and high capacity air cargo transport on dedicated freighters and
        passenger carriers to a significant number of European destinations at a reliable quality
       from ICN airport, that would be similar to the service both Asiana and Korean Air are
         currently providing.
(1129)  In the first place, and contrary to Korean Air’s submission in its Response to the
       Commission’s Statement of Objections,1787 all other competitors compete with much
        fewer frequencies than the Parties combined and/or to fewer airports in Europe and
        accordingly offer significantly less capacity and less choice of airports. Table 74
       above shows the flight frequencies in a representative week in summer 2019 (week of
        5th August) and winter 2019/2020 (week of 2nd December). The considerable
         difference between the Parties’ high-frequency and high-capacity proposition and that
        of their competitors can be observed for both the carriers that most closely resemble
         the Parties’ offer, like Cargolux and Lufthansa, as well as passenger belly-hold carriers
       and transhipment carriers. Moreover, the carriers with the most frequencies are those
        with a proposition somewhat inferior to that of the Parties, like Cathay Pacific
        Airways, Thai Airways, and Singapore  Airlines. The  closest  competitors have
         significantly fewer frequencies than the Parties.

          carriers, which are unable to offer direct flights on the route, can provide alternative

(1136)  As shown in sections 7.2.1.5 and 8.12.2, respondents to the market investigation
        explained that many customers prefer direct services or multi-stop services without
        transhipment. In particular, given the delay involved with transhipment, direct flights
        appear to be more suitable in certain cases in which the total transport time should be
        as short as possible such as for very time-sensitive products (e.g. animals, perishable
       goods or pharmaceuticals). Many customers would avoid services with transhipment
         in general, in view of risks of delays, damage or loss of cargo.
(1137)  Consequently, except for Qatar Airways, transhipment carriers have been rated as

        having responded to the market investigation, the Parties’ overall competitiveness was

         Airlines (2.8/5) and China Airlines (2.8/5).1797 Similarly, customers having responded

        above. However, they are not as close competitors as the Parties are to each other,

         Letter of Facts that price – and not the number of stops – is the key driver for
        customers when choosing an air cargo carrier.1813 The Commission notes in this
         respect that price was actually ranked fourth (4.29) by customers, after the frequencies
         (4.76), the reliability in terms of flight times (4.64) and the quality of cargo handling
          (4.43).1814
(1143)  In the third place, and contrary to what Korean Air argues in its Responses to the
       Commission’s Statement of Objections and Letter of Facts,1815 passenger carriers
       which transport air cargo only in the belly-hold of the passenger aircraft are more
         distant competitors and only exert a limited competitive constraint on the Parties
         (offering both freighter and belly space capacity). On the route from South Korea to
        Europe, carriers which only transport belly-hold cargo are […], […], […], […],
         […],1816 […],1817 and […].
(1144)  As indicated in section 8.12.2, there are significant downsides of carriers carrying only
         belly-hold cargo, compared to those offering dedicated freighter flights. Some goods
        cannot be transported in the belly-hold of a passenger aircraft, such as dangerous or
        oversized goods.1818 In addition, the belly-hold of a passenger  aircraft offers a
         significantly lower capacity (maximum load: 25 tons) than freighter (maximum load:
       100 tons).1819 This makes belly-hold air cargo transport services less attractive in
         particular for larger customers (such as major freight forwarders), which often need to

         available on passenger aircraft  is not always predictable and will depend on the
       amount of passenger baggage on the respective aircraft. This may also mean that

        advantage as it is less limited than belly hold“ and “Flight Flight times for passenger
         services are optimized to fit passenger demand/requirements, the transport of cargo
       on such services is a resulting by-product”,1823 which confirms how operators only
         relying on belly-hold capacity tend to be less competitive than operators that can also
         rely on freighters and that cargo-related considerations are generally subordinated to
         passengers-related considerations for passenger carriers.
(1146)  [A competitor] confirmed that only being able to transport belly-hold constitutes a
        competitive disadvantage on the route, due the difference in payload of a dedicated
         freighter and the inability to transport certain larger goods on passenger aircraft.1824

         “different sectors of the air freight market. It is caused by different aircraft capacity,
        payload vs. operating costs. We have less ability to transport huge parcels  if they
        require all-cargo aircraft. […] Usually all cargo transportation is more expensive
        than belly cargo due to cost & revenue structure”.1825
(1147)  Furthermore, [a competitor] states that “Operating only passenger aircraft, where
        cargo is transported in the belly of the aircraft, will limit the flexibility in where to
        deploy the aircraft. The booking window for passengers is longer than for cargo. As
        such the flight schedules for the passenger aircraft are already set up well before the
        cargo booking window opens. The limited flexibility will limit the competitiveness.
        Furthermore the destinations within the network will depend both on the passenger
       demand and the cargo demand. As such operating passenger flights only will in
         practice limit the ability to deploy these aircraft into cargo hubs where there is limited
        passenger demand. Additionally different cargo may be able to be carried on the
        upper deck, further limiting the competitiveness of carriers operating only passenger
          aircraft.”1826 And again, “[d]ifferent cargo may be carried on the upper deck or in
         freighters than purely in the belly hold of passenger aircraft, possibly impacting the
          price”.1827

         (3.07/5), and China Airlines (2.46/5).1831

(1154)  With regard to charter cargo flights, the Commission considers that they only pose a
       weak competitive constraint on the Parties, given that (i) they are only offered on an
         opportunistic basis and therefore customers cannot rely on them for their entire
       demand, (ii) they are typically booked through a hiring arrangement with a particular
        customer, thus other customers do not have access to their capacity, and (iii) they have
         different pricing.1844 On the demand side, customers replying to the Commission’s
        market investigation explained that due to their higher pricing, charter cargo flights are
        mostly used exceptionally, either for a specific big project with high volumes where
         the customer would in any event book the entire capacity of the aircraft or during the
       Covid19 pandemic due to the irregularities it brought to the market.1845 On the supply
         side, air cargo carriers also confirmed that they provide charter cargo services only (if
          at all) in exceptional situations, when there is a specific demand by a customer, in
       which case the customer must book the entirety of the aircraft capacity.1846

8.12.3.2. Competitive constraints from integrators in their airport-to-airport offering
(1168)  The Commission concludes that, contrary to Korean Air’s submissions in paragraphs
       722-725 of its Response to the Commission’s Statement of Objections and paragraphs
       147-153 of its Response to the Commission’s Letter of Facts, integrators only exert a
         limited competitive constraint on the Parties in general air cargo services on the route
       from South Korea to Europe, as (i) they mostly compete on a different market, that of
        door-to-door delivery services,1869 and therefore offer spare capacity on the air cargo
        market on an exceptional basis, (ii) air cargo carriers do not consider them as their
        competitors or only consider them to a limited extent, (iii) customers of the Parties do
        not see them as close alternatives but rather as limited available options for only parts
        of their volumes, and (iv) end cargo customers1870 of freight forwarders do not

1869      In paragraphs 118 et seqq. of its Response to the Commission’s Statement of Objections, Korean Air
         allegedly provides some “concrete examples of integrators and air cargo carriers competing”. The
       Commission notes that those examples do not in fact show strong competitive constraints exerted by
         integrators on the Parties: (i) In its reply to question 45, in conjunction with the introduction of RFI 2 (ID
        11459), [an integrator] confirmed that shipping Covid19 vaccines was part of their small package
        business and therefore not part of its “[limited] air cargo services to third parties on a space available
         basis”. Therefore, this is rather an example of the limited indirect out-of-market constraint posed to the
         Parties by the integrators, which has been acknowledged by the Commission and will be further analysed
         in section 8.12.5 below. This example does not in any event mean that  all general cargo can be
         transported by the integrators’ door-to-door delivery of small parcels and packages, but it rather confirms

         reasons:
          (a)  The Parties have higher capacity shares than they have estimated and have by far
              the highest individual and combined capacity shares on the market. High
            combined capacity shares indicate that the merged entity may have post-merger
             a greater incentive to increase prices.
         (b)  The spare capacity of competitors is too limited to be used to offset the effects of
              the Transaction: the Commission was not able to confirm Korean Air’s claim of
               existing significant excess capacity in the market.1885 The capacity available in
              the market as a whole is limited in the sense that all competitors’ excess capacity
              taken together would only marginally equal the Parties’ combined supply.
             Furthermore, capacity has to be assessed in the light of the findings on closeness
              of competition summarized above in section 8.12.2. Air cargo services are
               differentiated according to different factors from both a product and geographic
               perspective, expressed, among other factors, in delivery times, frequencies and
                 reliability. Therefore, the excess capacity provided by numerous competitors
            would in any event be inferior in many instances to the services offered by the
                Parties.
          (c)   Essentially  all competitors face  barriers  to expand  their supply  either by
              increasing aircraft utilization or increasing frequencies post-Transaction. These
               barriers can be due to unavailability of traffic rights, network considerations (in
               particular in the case of passenger carriers), or access to aircraft and personnel.
         (d)   Competitors have limited or no incentives to shift available capacity to the route
            between South Korea and Europe by diverting it from other uses between East
             Asia and Europe.
8.12.4.1. The Parties hold high capacity shares
(1178)  Capacity is the same on both the route from Europe to South Korea and the route from
        South Korea to Europe, therefore the arguments presented in section 8.11.4.1 with
         respect to Europe-South Korea also fully apply to the route South Korea – Europe.1886
8.12.4.2. No  significant spare capacity for competitors on the route, taking into account
        closeness of competition
(1179)  The Phase II investigation focussed on investigating further the Parties’ claim that the
         current market situation  is characterized by overcapacity due to available excess
        capacity on existing flights. The results of the Phase II investigation indicate that
        competitors already active on these routes do not appear to have enough capacity or
         incentive to be able to expand supply sufficiently to counteract an increase in prices
        post-merger, nor to deter it in the first place.
(1180)   First, the market investigation did not confirm Korean Air’s claim that there  is
         structural excess capacity1887 on the route South Korea-Europe. Only a small minority

(1181)  Second, the likely absence of overcapacity is demonstrated by the fact that the Parties’
      own capacity utilization, as indicated by their load factor, has been constantly at least

(1182)  In its responses,1891 Korean Air argues that the load factor cannot be used as a reliable
         indicator to determine if there is excess capacity in the market because, among other
         reasons, the load factor is manipulated by carriers in order to achieve as high load
         factors as possible. Feedback from competitors, however, suggests that carriers do rely
       on the load factor as a proxy for their utilization rate.1892 Moreover, most competitors
       have stated that they do not cancel flights to maximize their load factor on the route,
        thus the load factor does not appear to be generally manipulated to achieve as high
        load factors as possible.1893 Furthermore, even if carriers were indeed systematically
        manipulating the load factor by cancelling flights to maximise the load factor, the load
         factor would still provide a reasonable approximation of the aircrafts’ utilization rate.
        Furthermore, the Parties themselves relied on the load factor to quantify the amount of
         additional capacity currently unused by other trades that they could add to the route
       between  Europe  and  South   Korea.1894  The   considerations  made  under
        paragraphs (969)–(972) above also apply here, therefore, the Commission deems the
        load factor as a relevant indicator to determine  if there is excess capacity in the
        market.
(1183)  Third, data gathered from third parties during the Phase II investigation allowed the
       Commission to estimate the amount of excess capacity available on the route and
       compare it against the Parties’ combined volumes. Excess capacity in this regard is
        defined as the additional volumes a carrier could transport by filling up the unused
        capacity on aircraft (equal to the difference between overall capacity and volume
         transported). The underlying assumption of that analysis is that post-merger, if all the
         Parties’ customers find an alternative to the Parties, then it is unlikely that the Parties

       would be able to increase prices. If, however, only a fraction of the Parties’ customers
        could find an alternative supplier, the Parties are expected to have at least some
         incentive to increase prices.1895 This is because, if capacity is scarce, competitors can
        enjoy some degree of market power, and could be thus able to increase prices to
        customers. Moreover, competitors could in turn also find profitable to follow price
         increases, If competitors are not able to cover the entirety of market demand, the
       merger would enable the merged entity to enjoy an increased degree of market power,
       and be thus capable of increasing prices to customers. This market power-increasing
         effect of a post-merger increase of the merged entity’s excess capacity (relative to the
          rivals, who are capacity-constrained) would arise even if the rivals’ capacity would be
         perfect substitute of the merged entity’s capacity. As will be further evidenced below,
         the rivals’ capacity is not of the same quality as that of the Parties, who are each
         other’s close competitors. This quality differential reinforces the capacity-based effect.
(1184)  This approach is aligned with the Horizontal Merger Guidelines, paragraphs 32 to 34
        provide that “(32) When market conditions are such that the competitors of the
       merging parties are unlikely to increase their supply substantially if prices increase,
         the merging firms may have an incentive to reduce output below the combined pre-
       merger levels, thereby raising market prices. The merger increases the incentive to
        reduce output by giving the merged firm a larger base of sales on which to enjoy the
        higher margins resulting from an increase in prices induced by the output reduction.
        (33) Conversely, when market conditions are such that rival firms have enough
        capacity and find it profitable to expand output sufficiently, the Commission is unlikely
         to find that the merger will create or strengthen a dominant position or otherwise
         significantly  impede  effective  competition.  (34)  Such  output  expansion  is,  in
         particular, unlikely when competitors face binding capacity constraints.”1896 Also,
        paragraph 24 of the Horizontal Merger Guidelines provides that “Non-merging firms
         in the same market can also benefit from the reduction of competitive pressure that
         results from the merger, since the merging firms' price increase may switch some
       demand to the rival firms, which, in turn, may find  it profitable to increase their
         prices. The reduction in these competitive constraints could lead to significant price
        increases in the relevant market.”1897

         analysis.  Table 76  provides  the  Commission’s  estimates  for  the sum  of  all
        competitors’ excess capacities, while the estimates for each individual competitor’s
        excess capacity are instead only available to Korean Air’s external advisors in the data
       room procedure. The figures relied upon by the Commission in this Decision are based
       on the figures included in the RBB Economics Second Data Room Report.

        South Korea, competitors’ excess capacity is limited nonetheless, as shown further
        below. And, as also discussed more in detail in section 8.11.4, competitors face
        binding capacity constraints and are therefore unlikely able to increase their supply
         sufficiently  if prices increase, which implies that the merging firms may have an

        already indicated in section 8.11.4.2, however, the Commission notes that these two
          sensitivities based on the load factor indicate a significantly higher level of excess
        capacity in the market than is in fact available and likely overestimate spare capacity
         that is available on the market. First, excess capacity measured as capacity multiplied
       by the difference between 100% and the load factor implies  that 100%  is the
       benchmark for cargo airlines to be considered fully utilized. However, this is not the
         case. As discussed in section 8.11.4, cargo airlines are deemed already fully utilized

        100%,1898 then excess capacity would be substantially lower: [90-100]% on the route

        Appendix, some carriers measured the load factor using actual weights, which can be
       even up to 10 percentage points lower than load factors measured using chargeable
        weights. This  implies  that  these  carriers’  excess  capacity  is  also  significantly
        overestimated.

(1189)  Fourth, furthermore, the Phase II investigation confirms that customers regard capacity
         in cargo as differentiated (see also sections 8.12.2 and 8.12.3). For example, non-stop
        connections with air cargo carriers like the Parties’, [names of competitors] generally
         represent  a  higher  value  proposition  […].  Should  therefore  only  [names  of
        competitors] excess capacity be considered, […], then the available excess capacities
       would be much lower: about [10-20]% on South Korea to Europe.1899 On the route
       from South Korea to Europe, six competitors have excess capacity exceeding [5-10]%
        of the Parties’ combined volumes, and a long tail of competitors has excess capacity
       below [0-5]%. In fact, as explained in section 8.12.2 above, the Parties are close
        competitors of each other. This means that, in the event of a price increase post-
        merger, a large share of the  Parties’ customers would  likely not switch  to an
         alternative supplier capable of offering an inferior type of capacity (as compared to
         that offered by the Parties) at the same pre-merger prices. These customers will then
        be worse-off because they will either endure the increased prices or switched to a less
         favorite types of connection (for example, with transhipment or via integrators).
        Moreover, customers switching away from the Parties would present a windfall
       demand for the Parties’ competitors, who themselves will also have then an incentive
         to raise their prices. These post-merger pricing incentives of the Parties and their rivals
       stemming from the close competition between the Parties could be present even in
        absence of the rival capacity constraints. The capacity constraints explained above and
         the closeness based arguments are then reinforcing each other.

         route between South Korea and Europe, this competitor had market shares between

         in 2021: It is highly unlikely this competitor could suddenly decide to dedicate their
        excess  capacity  to  the  affected markets  considering how  limited  their  current
        involvement is.

8.12.4.3. Competitors are unable and/or unlikely to expand
(1193)  The market investigation has revealed that, contrary to the Parties’ claims1901 and
       Korean Air’s submission in paragraphs 771-803 of its Response to the Commission’s
        Statement of Objections, current competitors face significant barriers to expansion and
         are unlikely  to expand  their  activity  sufficiently  to prevent any  potential  anti-
        competitive effects of the Transaction, either by increasing the amount or capacity of
          aircraft on the route or increasing frequencies post-Transaction.
(1194)   First, many competitors are unable to increase their frequencies or add additional
          aircraft to the route, because they have maximized the traffic rights available under the
         respective air service agreement (ASA) concluded between their home country and
        South  Korea.1902 According  to information provided by  the  Parties, [names  of

(1223)  Based on  the above,  the Commission concludes  that  current  competitors  face

8.12.4.4. Competitors are unlikely to shift available capacity within the routes between East
        Asia and Europe
(1224)  The market investigation has not confirmed the Parties’ claim that competitors are able
       and likely to increase sales volumes on the route from South Korea to Europe by
         shifting available capacity within the routes between East Asia and Europe. According
         to the Parties, all the capacity that is used between East Asia and Europe can and
       would  at any point in time become available for the Korea – EEA  routes.1989
        Competitors responding to the Commission’s market investigation have for the most
         part not confirmed this claim.
(1225)   First, this strategy could not be pursued by carriers which only transport point-to-point
          air cargo on direct flights from Europe to South Korea, with the exception of potential
        behind and beyond routes. The reason for this is that these carriers carry cargo from
       Europe to South Korea or the other way around, without having the ability to offload
        or on-board other cargo on the way. The only way these carriers could pursue such a
         shifting strategy would be, if they have a hub at the East Asian end of the route, or if
        they have interlining agreements in place, between this end of the route and South
        Korea. This was confirmed by [a competitor], when stating that the only way they
        could shift their capacity would be by using interline-partners in ICN, which would
        connect their flights to other East Asian directions.1990 Neither the Parties, nor the
        market investigation has presented sufficient evidence for the Commission, to assume
         that these carriers would adopt such an approach.
(1226)  Second, any competitor that would pursue such a strategy would face the opportunity
         costs of giving up capacity on another route, which it currently prioritizes over the
         route from South Korea to Europe.1991 Concretely, [a competitor] currently operates
      […] freighter flights between ICN and Europe […]. [The competitor] would therefore
       have to forego transporting cargo between Europe and […] in order to increase
        capacity on the South Korea-Europe route by way of replacement. To the degree that
        such a strategy would be profitable, this capacity shifting is already conducted by [the
        competitor] on this route. However, according to [the competitor], “[b]usiness to […]
           is historically more important for [the competitor] than business to South Korea”. 1992

(1234)  Fourth, some competitors have confirmed that they have not employed such a strategy

(1235)  Fifth, as shown in sections 8.12.2 and 8.12.3, customers regard capacity in air cargo
         services on the route from South Korea to Europe as a differentiated product. For
        example, non-stop connections generally represent a higher value proposition than
        connections with transhipment. In markets with differentiated products, it is especially
         likely that competitors may respond to a price rise by the merged entity by increasing
          their own prices.2006 Paragraph 24 of the Horizontal Merger Guidelines provides that
       “Non-merging firms in the same market can also benefit from the reduction of
        competitive pressure that results from the merger, since the merging firms' price
        increase may switch some demand to the rival firms, which, in turn, may find  it
         profitable to increase their prices. The reduction in these competitive constraints
        could lead to significant price increases in the relevant market.”2007
(1236)  In addition, several customers have indicated that the quality and type of service of the
         carrier is more important than rates or that such alternatives would only be considered
         for  less important  cargo.2008 Therefore, should the Parties reduce supply and/or
         increase prices on the routes post-merger, we would rather expect competitors to
         increase prices as well.
(1237)  In light of the above and as shown in sections 8.12.2 and 8.12.3 many customers have
        a preference for direct, freighter flights at high frequencies and also perceive a quality
         difference between the Parties and many of their competitors. For this reason, even if
        competitors would pursue a strategy of shifting available capacity towards the South
       Korea to Europe route in response to a capacity decrease by the Merged Entity post-
         Transaction, that would not constitute an adequate alternative to the Parties’ services
         for customers.

(1239)  In paragraphs 825-838 of its Response to the Commission’s Statement of Objections,

(1240)  The Commission considers that to a certain extent the integrators’ core door-to-door
         services as analysed in section 7.2.1.4 above, may be in competition with freight
        forwarders’ services (using air cargo services as an input). However, such competition
