         for airport-to-airport air cargo services, where the Parties are active.
(1241)   First, the Commission notes that the integrators’ core business consists in the door-to-
        door delivery of mainly small packages and parcels, as opposed to larger general
         cargo,  i.e. freight, which  is the core focus of freight forwarders. As integrators
         explain,2010 their product offering is different to that of freight forwarders using air

         service offered, namely a door-to-door service which is inherent to the integrators’

       which they make all their strategic decisions.2011
(1242)  Therefore, from the outset, the overlap of activities between integrators and freight
        forwarders is only limited; integrators mainly deliver small packages requiring little to
       no special handling,2012 whereas freight forwarders focus on heavy consignments and
         typically outsource small package delivery services to third parties.2013 This is also
        probably the reason why the integrators are mostly seen as customers of the Parties in
          their internal business documents2014 –  if not as third-tier competitors, as further
        explained in paragraph (1175) above. The two are not contradictory as Korean Air
        argues in paragraph 192 of its Response to the Commission’s Letter of Facts, but
         rather complementary. As analysed in section 7.2.1.4 above, the Parties’ airport-to-
         airport air cargo services and the integrators’ core door-to-door small package delivery

         to the Parties posed by the integrators’ door-to-door services, and therefore takes into

        seen as customers of the Parties.
(1243)  The different focus between integrators and freight forwarders has been investigated
       and confirmed in the Commission’s prior decisional practice.2015 Freight and small
        packages are usually transported via different infrastructures which are designed in a
         different way. The handling of freight necessitates special equipment that  is not
       needed for small package delivery, such as forklifts; whereas the sorting of palletised
       goods is done manually. Freight forwarders usually deliver palletised goods to a more
         limited number of clients arranging the transport of their goods on a more point-to-
         point basis. As the number of items is significantly smaller and the items are much
         heavier, the freight forwarding model does not involve a hub-and-spoke system such
        as the one used by integrators. Small package networks are characterised by a
         significantly higher level of automation than freight networks, notably at the level of
         sorting centres, which are based on conveyor belts and scanners. Every day, the (local)
         sorting centres accumulate a high number of packages which are usually channelled
         via hubs and again sorted and dispatched to the delivery hubs and sorting centres.
        Furthermore, in order to deliver small packages efficiently, operators need a dense
        network. These features allow companies operating small package networks to ship
        high numbers of units between points of origin and points of destinations spread over
       wide geographic areas and within relatively limited timeframes compared to those
         prevailing in the freight forwarding sector. Due to the different characteristics of
         freight and small package networks,  it is commonly agreed that there is a weight
         threshold below which small package delivery companies like the integrators are more
        competitive than freight forwarders and above which freight should be considered as a
         cost effective alternative.
(1244)  The above considerations from the Commission’s prior decisional practice have also
       been confirmed by the Commission’s market  investigation  in the present  case.
        According to [an integrator], the business model of integrators is different to the one
        of freight forwarders in four core elements:2016 (i) the speed of delivery and time
       commitment that comes at a higher price. In other words, according to [the integrator],
          at least non-time-sensitive customers would never switch from a freight forwarder to
       an integrator because the integrator would charge them with the premium door-to-door
         pricing that they would not need; (ii) the door-to-door service, which is not inherent in
         the business model of freight forwarders. As [an integrator] explained, what is inherent
         in the integrators’ business model is the pick-up and delivery which will happen at the
         specific address the customer will indicate. Freight forwarders do not have such a
         capillary distribution network and therefore they do not typically sell a door-to-door
        element, at least not within their standard product offering; (iii) the different customers
         targeted. As [an integrator] explained, integrators would typically target thousands of
        customers with single (smaller) shipments, whereas freight forwarders would typically
         target a few customers with high volumes/quantities, e.g. heavy car parts; (iv) the
         different nature of the service. If for example [an integrator’s] aircraft has a capacity
        of 100 tons and a customer wishes to transport 120 tons, [the integrator] would not
         turn away the customer. On the contrary, freight forwarders sell out their capacity
         against  their inventory and do not accept any more shipments  after  that point.
        According to [the integrator], the difference lies on the fact that integrators’ customers

         [the  customer’s]  point  of  view,  “there  is no  significant  competition  between
         integrators and freight forwarders […] integrators are useful for smaller cargo, and
        they provide door-to-door services”.2029 Another major end customer also submitted
         that it applies different considerations between the airline service (of integrators) and
         the capabilities of freight forwarders.2030
(1254)  Fourth, the Parties also did not provide internal documents that would show that they
        take into account the indirect constraints imposed by integrators in sales to end
        customers/shippers in their internal business decisions. The evidence provided by the
         Parties does not cover such indirect constraint but rather shows that integrators, in
         particular DHL, offer some air cargo services on the market, as acknowledged in this
        Decision, and that integrators are customers of the Parties.2031
(1255)  In paragraph 837 of Korean Air’s Response to the Commission’s Statement of
        Objections, Korean Air reiterates that the Parties have provided several documents
       showing how Korean Air and the freight forwarding arm of Korean Air’s parent
       company offer services to cargo end customers which ship small packages and/or
         express. The Commission notes that the mere fact that Korean Air aspires to enter the
        market of door-to-door services as provided by integrators does not mean that the
         indirect competitive pressure exerted by the integrators’ vertically integrated offering
         to the Parties’ airport-to-airport services is getting higher. To the contrary, as indicated
       by Korean Air’s internal documents, […].2032 In other words, […].
(1256) On the basis of the above considerations, the Commission considers that integrators
       compete with freight forwarders for only a marginal part of end customers / shippers.
        Therefore, the Commission acknowledges that integrators might pose an indirect out-
        of-market competitive constraint to the Parties, but this is only to a very limited extent
       and cannot in any event substantially constrain the merged entity post-Transaction.
8.12.6.  Countervailing buyer power
(1257)  Customers are unlikely to have sufficient buyer power to off-set the negative effects of
         the Transaction on the route South Korea to Europe.
(1258)   First, the customers are unlikely to have bargaining strength due to their size or
       commercial significance for the Parties on the route South Korea to Europe.
(1259)  In the first place, the customer base on the route South Korea-Europe is fragmented.
        Already among the ten largest customers of each of the Parties, there are several
        customers that represent only about [0-5]% or [0-5]% of each of the Parties’ sales
       volumes on the route South Korea to Europe. As a consequence, the bottom [20-30]-
       [30-40]% of the Parties’ sales volumes  is characterized by customers that each
         represent less than [0-5]% of each of the Parties’ sales volumes on the route. The same
       would therefore hold true for the merged entity. The purchase ratios of each of the

(1263)  Fourth, the results of the Commission’s market investigation did not confirm that

       Korea to Europe to prevent any negative effects of the Transaction.
(1264)  In the first place, only a minority of customers responding to the relevant question of
         the Commission’s phase I questionnaire considered that customers exert significant
        buyer power on the route South Korea to Europe. The clear majority of customers
        considered that there is no buyer power, that customers do not exert much buyer
       power or that they exert only a small degree of buyer power. Others considered that it
        depends, for instance on the specific market conditions, including the season.2038 Two
        customers, namely the purchasing arms of integrators, explained their views on this
         also in phone calls with the Commission.2039
(1265)  In the second place, the competitors responding to the relevant question of the
       Commission’s phase I questionnaire did not provide a clear view and therefore did not
        confirm that there is sufficient buyer power on the route South Korea to Europe. While
        a limited number (3) of competitors considered that customers exert significant buyer
        power, a slightly larger number of competitors (4) considered that there is no buyer
        power, that customers do not exert much buyer power or that they exert only a small
        degree of buyer power.2040 Others considered that  it depends, for instance on the
        supply/demand balance in the different seasons or on the volume purchased. This was
        confirmed by competitors during the Commission’s phase  II investigation. Some
        competitors (2) consider that there are no customers present at the moment who have
         the ability to exercise their buyer power to a significant degree. Other competitors (2)
         stated that customers’ buyer power is contingent on the actual supply/demand situation
       on a particular route.2041 It is notably explained that it is only the “large and global
        market players with significant and consistent volumes throughout the year” that
        indeed do possess buyer power.2042

         investigation that they would likely pass on price increases for air cargo services to
          their end-customers.2043 This ability would further limit the incentive of customers to

(1267)  Sixth, independently of how strong the bargaining power  is that customers may
         currently enjoy, the Transaction does not only reduce the number of providers active
       on the route from South Korea to Europe but it eliminates the second best alternative
        customers have (as explained in section 8.12.2). Furthermore, other competitors exert
        a more limited constraint (as explained in section 8.12.3). This means that customers’
        choice of alternative suppliers on the route South Korea to Europe would be limited
          after the Transaction and that they would not be able to switch easily to alternative
          suppliers.2044 This implies that post-Transaction customers’ bargaining power will be
         inevitably reduced by removing a credible alternative, thus making more likely a price
         increase, or another type of worsening of parameters of competition.
(1268)  Seventh, there is no evidence to suggest that customers could credibly threaten to
         vertically integrate into supplying air cargo services, in particular in the light of the
         barriers to entry as set out in section 8.12.4.3. There is no example of such entry of the
          last five years. In particular, and contrary to Korean Air’s claims regarding […] and
       […], both freight forwarders replied to the Commission’s market investigation that
        they have not vertically integrated into providing general air cargo services on the
         route Europe to South Korea.2045 The Parties appear to refer to instances where those
         freight forwarders cooperate with cargo airlines to offer charter flights2046 or block
        space agreements2047 to end customers. In addition to the fact that charter flights exert
        only a remote  constraint on the  Parties’ operations  for the reasons  set out  in
         section 7.2.1.6, this does not constitute vertical integration by freight forwarders as
        they do not invest in flight capacity but cooperate with existing airlines – precisely by
        purchasing capacity from cargo airlines as described in this Decision as the relevant
        market on which the Transaction is likely to have negative effects, based on the
       outcome of the investigation.
(1269)  Eighth (as explained in section 8.12.4), the Parties have achieved high load factors in
         recent years on the route South Korea to Europe: Korean Air’s load factor varied from
       [80-90]% in 2018 to [80-90]% in 2022, while Asiana’s varied from [90-100]% in 2018
         to [90-100]% in 2022.2048 Therefore, the Parties’ arguments according to which the
        customers hold buyer power because the Parties need business with all of them to
        achieve a sufficiently high load factor2049 is unfounded.
(1270)  Ninth, buyer power cannot be found to sufficiently off-set potential adverse effects of
         the Transaction it if only ensures that a particular segment of customers with particular
        bargaining  strength  is  shielded from  significantly  higher  prices  or  deteriorated
         considerations after the Transaction.2050 Therefore, the Parties’ argument that several
         of the customers are global companies with a strong presence in the European cargo
        market, such as […], […] or […],2051 is in any event irrelevant because there are many
         other customers that are smaller and do not share those characteristics.

8.12.8.  Effect of the Transaction
(1278)  Although the results of the Commission’s market investigations were mixed overall,
         several market participants have expressed concerns about  (i) the strong market
         position of the Merged Entity, (ii) potential negative effects of the Transaction on
        competition and  (iii) potential negative effects of the Transaction on  their own
        business model.
(1279)   First, the market investigation has shown that several market participants fear the
        strengthening of the Parties’ already strong market position following the Transaction.
      As an example, one customer’s major concern is that post-Transaction the Parties
         “effectively own the market”.2058 One competitor explained that “the merger would
       weaken [competitor’s] position on the market – basically due to the important
         capacities the Partis have following extensive traffic rights. Korean Air and Asiana
         will have more than 200 aircrafts and a large fleet of freighters enabling them to
        dominate the market even more than they currently do. When the Parties dominate the
        market from a market share perspective, it is in [competitor’s] view possible that they
        also use their dominant position in terms of pricing.”2059Another competitor explained
         that “it seemed highly likely that the Parties would be in a position to control a large
        part of the market post-Transaction”.2060 Another competitor concurred by stating “As
         for air cargo services, [competitor] noted that the merged entity will become by far
         the  largest player between Europe and Korea which  will lead  to a dominant
         position.”2061 Furthermore, a competitor stated that “[t]he Transaction will make  it
        even more difficult to compete given the combined size of the merged entity from a
        cargo perspective” and  that “we are  of the opinion that  it  will be even more
        complicated for smaller competitors to enter the market or maintain their current
         position”.2062 One of the integrators, which is also a significant customer of the Parties,
        explained “the Transaction might have a negative impact on competition as the
       number of the main air cargo priders will be reduced from 3 to 2. […] it would be
         anticipated the mered entity to reduce services between Europe and Korea and
        increase capacity on transpacific routes where the yields are better. This in turn would
       have a negative effect on prices between Europe and Korea as the remaining players

8.13.1.3.2.   From a vertical perspective
(1293)  In addition to the arguments stated under Section 8.13.1.3.1, even in the hypothetical
        scenario where Korean Air increases its prices post-Transaction, the impact on Air
        Passenger service providers would likely be limited. This is due to the fact that
        Maintenance, Repair, and Overhaul (MRO) services for passenger aircraft constitute
        only a small fraction—approximately 2.5%—of the total global costs associated with
          air passenger transport services. Therefore, any price changes in  this sector are
        expected to have a relatively small effect on the overall expenses of these service
         providers.

         services account for a small proportion of the overall costs for Air Passenger Services

9.      EFFICIENCIES
(1307)  Korean Air submits that the Transaction will bring efficiencies to the market. Such
         efficiencies are based on three main claims: (1) increased connectivity and frequencies
         for air passengers with better customer experience on Overlap Routes as well as on
         other routes from/to Europe, (2) cost efficiencies in the form of savings resulting from
        increased seat capacity, improved aircraft utilization, reduction of purchase unit cost,
        reduced  training  costs, more optimal  fleet  structure and more  efficient  aircraft
         configuration, and (3) a more efficient operation of the cargo aircraft fleet.


2087     Market shares of the Parties in MRO for all air carriers at ICN airport (excl. Korean Air  / Asiana)
        according to Korean Air’s estimate: [20-30]% in 2023, [20-30] in 2022, [30-40] in 2021, see Response to
        Question 5 of the RFI on turnover and market share data of 22 December 2023. The Parties claim that
        they do not have access to MRO services of competitors nor are they aware of any industry report
         including such information and can therefore not provide any market share data for competitors.

9.1.    Korean Air’s view
(1308)   First, Korean Air submitted an analysis of supply synergies describing how the
         transaction would allow for a joint schedule planning with departure times more
        evenly  spread  throughout  the  day.  Scheduling  improvements,  including  a
         diversification of overlapping flight schedules and expansion of the number of routes
         operated, would create a more convenient and better quality services for customers in
       Korean Air’s view. Scheduling efficiencies created by the optimized flight planning
       and expansion of operated routes are considered by Korean Air to spill-over to
        passengers flying on other routes from/to the EU and would equally apply to several
         other destinations in East Asia and Oceania. A better customer experience would
         consist  of  streamlined  check-in  and  baggage  handling  and  merged  rewards
        programmes.(2088)
(1309)  Second, Korean Air submits that the Transaction would generate significant annual
         cost savings and annual cost efficiencies through an improved aircraft utilization,
        increased operational efficiency of the cockpit crew and ground handling services,
        reduction of purchase unit cost, reduction of overlapping functions and reduced
         training costs through sharing the aviation training resources, as well increased seating
        capacity that allows to actively respond to the fluctuating demand by operating various
         configurations of the same aircraft. Economies of scale realized would lead to a
         decline  in production costs according  to Korean  Air. Korean Air provided the
       Commission with an analysis prepared by Compass Lexecon which quantifies –
         allegedly on a conservative basis – the total merger specific consumer benefits on all
         routes between Korea and the EU and UK at more than USD […] per year.(2089)
(1310)  Third, Korean Air argues that the Transaction would lead to significant efficiencies in
         relation to air cargo through reduced fixed costs (financial costs), synergies derived
       from an integrated cargo fleet thereby reducing transportation, repair and staffing costs
        as well as increasing the operational efficiency of cockpit crew and ground handling
         services. Rationalization of routes (including overlapping routes) would free capacity
         to pioneer new routes.(2090)
9.2.    The Commission’s assessment
(1311) On the basis of the documents submitted, the Commission sought to assess (1) whether
         the efficiencies described are specific to the proposed transaction, (2) whether these
         efficiency gains would be passed-on to the end customers, and (3) whether the
         efficiency claims are verifiable.
(1312)  Paragraph 78 of the Horizontal Merger Guidelines provides that “For the Commission
         to take account of efficiency claims in its assessment of the merger and be in a position
         to reach the conclusion that as a consequence of efficiencies, there are no grounds for
        declaring the merger to be incompatible with the common market, the efficiencies
        have to benefit consumers, be merger-specific and be verifiable. These conditions are
         cumulative.”2091 The Commission will then in principle only take account of those
         efficiencies that offset the harm suffered by the consumer groups that are adversely



2088    Form CO, Annex QP6.Q23 – “[…]” and Response of Korean Air to the Commission’s Statement of
         Objections, paragraphs 887-902.
2089    Form CO, Annex QP6.Q23 – “[…]” and Response of Korean Air to the Commission’s Statement of
         Objections, paragraphs 887-902.
2090    Form CO, Annex QP6.Q23 – “[…]” and Response of Korean Air to the Commission’s Statement of
         Objections, paragraphs 887-902.
2091     Horizontal Merger Guidelines, paragraph 78.


                                    328

[PÁGINA PDF 335]
         affected by the merger. This implies only efficiencies generated in the market in which
         the competitive harm occurs and that can be relied upon to offset that harm.
(1313)  The Commission’s assessment finds that the efficiencies claimed do not fulfil the
        aforementioned criteria in this case for several reasons.
(1314)   First, with respect to the non-price parameters such as better customer experience and
        prospective more efficient operations, Korean Air does not sufficiently explain why
         these efficiencies are  (i) a direct consequence of the merger and  (ii) cannot be
        achieved by  less  anti-competitive means  than  the merger,  e.g.  interlining and
        codeshare agreements. Effects from network combinations, which are the majority of
         the quantified efficiencies in form of consumer benefits, can in principle be achieved
       by interlining and code-sharing agreements between the two airlines. Hence, effects
       from  network  combination  are  not  necessarily  merger-specific  such  that  the
       Commission cannot consider them as offsetting potential consumer harm.
(1315)  Second, the submission quantifies consumer benefits using results from a “Quality of
        Service Index” model, which estimates the improvement in quality of the network by
        adding additional potential route-combinations and predicts the additional passengers
         in the network and on given routes when holding prices fixed.  The Commission
        acknowledges  that  increased  connectivity  is  to  the  benefit  of  the  consumer.
         Nevertheless,  as  described, only  efficiencies  that  offset  the harm  to consumer
        adversely  affected by  the merger can be  accepted.  Increased  connectivity by
       combining networks generally benefits consumers that use the increased network
        reach but not passengers that fly the affected O&D pairs between Seoul and the four
       European destinations. Korean Air claims to quantify the consumer benefits by
         estimating the price reduction necessary to attract the equal number of passengers
        while maintaining the same network of routes. This implies that the efficiencies
         benefitting consumers are due to an expansion of the network and the resulting
         increase in passenger numbers. However, this also implies that these efficiencies are
         neither equivalent nor connected to ticket fares or other parameters of competition on
         affected and existing routes. These efficiencies would, therefore, more likely be ‘out
         of market’ efficiencies as they would not provide benefits to the same category of
       consumers  that would be  negatively  affected by  the  Transaction.  Benefits  to
       consumers using an increased network cannot be allocated as monetary equivalent to
         existing routes and can therefore not offset adverse effects caused by the Transaction
       on the Overlap Routes.
(1316)  Third, as table 3 of the analysis prepared by Compass Lexecon shows, almost all
         benefits from the network combination are associated with benefits and positive
        changes in passenger numbers in the high yield segment, i.e. business and first class
         passengers. Hence, even if network connectivity benefits could be taken into account
       by the Commission, the submission itself explains that low yield (economy class)
        passengers would minimally or not benefit at all from them on the Overlap Routes.
        Hence, the efficiencies also cannot offset any detrimental effect to those passengers.
        Table 3 actually even shows that combining the Parties’ networks would lead to a
        decrease in the number of passengers flying over the routes CDG-ICN, FCO-ICN and
       BCN-ICN.
(1317)  Fourth, and as acknowledged by the  Parties, many of the claimed  efficiencies
         primarily relate to routes in East Asia and Oceania. Freed air cargo capacity would
         also mainly be employed on new routes in East Asia and Oceania. However, as set out
         in paragraph (1315), only efficiencies that offset the harm to the consumers adversely
         affected by the merger can be accepted.



                                    329

[PÁGINA PDF 336]
(1318)  Fifth, as to cost savings, most of the savings related to cargo are on fixed costs for
       which there is a reduced likelihood of these being passed on to consumers rather than
        simply boosting the profits of the merged entity. Cost savings that lead to a reduction
         of variable or marginal costs are more likely to be passed on to consumers. Whilst a
       number of the alleged cost savings for air passengers – and to a lesser degree air cargo
         services – could be qualified as variable, Korean Air has also submitted that these
        savings will only materialize in the medium to long term. In addition, Korean Air has
        submitted that  it considers operating Asiana independently from Korean Air for a
        period of time. Without integration, the alleged cost savings and efficiencies cannot
         materialize. The longer the time needed for the variable cost savings to materialize, the
         greater must be the efficiencies to compensate also for the loss to consumers during
         the period preceding their generation.
(1319)  Sixth, even if the Commission would take all cost savings as efficiencies into account
      (EUR […] per year allocated to routes between Seoul and Europe, including UK
         routes), which it cannot for the reasons outlined in paragraph (1318), this amounts to
        only EUR […] up to […] EUR per passenger, based on approximately […] million
        passengers on the four overlapping routes in 2019 which is unlikely to be (i) fully
        passed on to consumers, in particular in the light of the limited competitive constraint
         the merged entity would face as explained in section 8, and (ii) sufficient to offset
        adverse price effects as it amounts to only approximately [0-5]-[0-5]% of the average
          ticket  fare  in economy  class. Korean Air did not provide a  similar quantified
        assessment of the expected cost savings as efficiencies for cargo. In any case, the fact
        remains that most of the savings related to cargo are on fixed costs and are therefore
         less likely to be passed on to consumers rather than simply boosting the profits of the
       merged entity.
(1320)  Finally, as to the verifiability of the efficiency claims, whilst the Parties have provided
         quantified cost savings and efficiencies for air passengers, these are aggregated either
       on a worldwide basis or for all Overlap Routes between Korea and the EU as well as
         the UK. No quantification is provided solely for the EU air passenger routes of
        concern. As to cargo services, no quantification is provided at all.
9.3.    Conclusion on efficiencies
(1321)  The Commission concludes that consumer benefits related to network combinations
         are neither merger-specific, as they are likely to be at least widely achievable by less
         anti-competitive alternatives, nor offset the adverse effects on passengers on the
        Overlap Routes.
(1322)  With  respect  to  the  cost  savings  indicated by Korean  Air,  the Commission
        acknowledges that some cost savings may be merger-specific and could benefit
         affected consumers, to the extent these would be passed-on. However, these cost
        savings are likely to only materialize in the medium to long run, which makes them
         inherently less likely to be passed on to affected consumers.2092 In any event, these
         cost savings are unlikely to be sufficient to offset the harm caused by the Transaction.
(1323)  With respect to the efficiencies related to air cargo, the Commission acknowledges
         that some of these efficiencies can be in principle merger-specific, but concludes that
         these efficiencies are unlikely to benefit the affected consumers, as they mostly relate
         to fixed costs that are less likely to be passed on, and are not verifiable, as the
       Commission cannot be  reasonably  certain  that  these  efficiencies  are  likely  to

2092     Horizontal Merger Guidelines, paragraph 86: ‘In general, the longer the start of the efficiencies is
         projected into the future, the less probability the Commission may be able to assign to the efficiencies
         actually being brought about.’


                                    330

[PÁGINA PDF 337]
         materialise and be substantial enough to offset the adverse effects of the Transaction
       on the affected markets.
(1324)  In sum, the Commission concludes that the efficiencies claimed do not sufficiently
           fulfil  all  criteria of merger-specificity, to the benefit of affected consumers and
          verifiability, as well as are not sufficient, such that these efficiencies can be considered
         as offsetting the adverse effects of the Transaction.

10.    OTHER ASPECTS
10.1.   Delayed integration of the Parties’ businesses
(1325)  Korean Air has explained that it will take approximately two years to fully integrate
         the Parties’ operations. In addition, Korean Air would avoid a substantial corporate
       income tax burden if closing is delayed. Accordingly, Korean Air intends to operate
        Asiana as a separate subsidiary for two years. According to Korean Air, unless Korean
        Air and Asiana are regarded as a single business unit under the Korean laws, Korean
        Air and Asiana will be prohibited from anti-competitively coordinating their fare, seat
         capacity, transaction terms vis-à-vis consumers and business partners even after the
         closing of the Transaction until the two entities are fully integrated.2093 Korean Air
        implies that there cannot be anti-competitive effects for two years because the Korean
        competition authority could intervene against collusive behaviour between Korean Air
       and Asiana during that period, leading to “significant legal risk including potential
        criminal penalties”.2094
(1326)  The Commission considers that any delayed integration of the Parties’ business
         operations has no bearing on its findings of competition concerns in this case. Upon
         closing of the Transaction, Korean Air will hold sole control over Asiana. Moreover, it
         will take part in the profits of Asiana in proportion with its shareholding and therefore
         benefit also from profit achieved with customers that switch away from Korean Air to
        Asiana. This would align their commercial incentives and lead to a dampening of
        competition between them, irrespective of any collusive acts. In addition, Korean Air
        has not substantiated further how high the likelihood is of the Korean competition
         authority initiating antitrust proceedings against the two parties of a merger that it has
          just approved – which prima facie appears to be low. Korean Air has not been able to
         identify a precedent case by the Korean competition authority in this respect.2095
        Furthermore,  the Korean competition  authority  itself has  identified competition
        concerns in this case, indicating that the Korean competition authority itself does not
        consider any antitrust powers it may have over the Parties before full integration of
          their business activities to be sufficient to eliminate all competitive harm from the
         Transaction.
(1327)  Furthermore, even if there was delay in bringing about the full negative effects of the
         Transaction,  which  is  unlikely  to  be  the  case  for  the  reasons  set  out  in
        paragraph (1326), the Transaction would nonetheless impede effective competition at
         that delayed time and accordingly be incompatible with the internal market and the
        functioning of the EEA Agreement.
10.2.   Comity considerations
(1328)  The principle of comity is part of the agreement between the European Community
       and the Government of Korea concerning cooperation on anti-competitive activities


2093    Form CO, paragraph 2.
2094    Form CO, footnote 3.
2095     Reply to RFI9, question 1.


                                    331

[PÁGINA PDF 338]
       (EC-Korean Agreement (ECKA))2096. It reflects the broad concept of mutual respect
       among equal sovereign entities2097 and enshrines the principle that the competition
         authority of each Party shall give careful consideration to the important interests of the
         other Party throughout all phases of its enforcement activities.2098
(1329)  In that respect, Article 5(2) ECKA foresees that if a specific enforcement activity
        envisaged by a competition authority of one Party may affect the important interests of
         the other Party, the former, without prejudice to its full discretion, shall use its best
        endeavours: (a) to provide to the other Party timely notice of significant developments
         relating to the interests of the latter; (b) to give the other Party an opportunity to
        provide comments; and (c) to take into consideration the comments of the other Party,
        while fully respecting the independence of each Party to make its own decision. The
       Commission in line with these procedural obligations has (i) given the Government of
       Korea the opportunity to provide comments in meetings before the issuing of this
        Decision; has  (ii) taken note of a briefing paper submitted by Korean Air which
        “explains the Korean public interests which are driving the proposed acquisition by
       Korean Air Lines Co., Ltd (Korean Air) of sole control of Asiana Airlines Incas”2099
       and has (iii) taken note of “KDB’s Opinion on Korean Air’s Acquisition of Asiana
         Airlines” which has also been submitted by Korean Air.2100
(1330)  According to Article 5(3) ECKA, where either Party considers that enforcement
          activities by its competition authority may adversely affect the important interests of
         the other Party, the Parties should consider the relative significance of the effects of
         the anti-competitive activities on the enforcing Party’s important interests as compared
         to the effects on the other Party’s important interests in addition to any other factor
         that may be relevant in the circumstances in seeking an appropriate accommodation of
         the competing  interests. The Commission confirms  that the  effects of  possible
        enforcement measures on  the  interests  of  the Korean Government have been
        considered as part of the competitive assessment of the Transaction, in particular with
         respect to  (i) the counterfactual2101, and  (ii) the efficiencies stemming from the
         Transaction2102.

11.    CONCLUSION
(1331)  For the reasons set out above, the Commission concludes that the Transaction would
         significantly impede effective competition with respect to passenger air services on the
         routes BCN-ICN, CDG-ICN, FRA-ICN and FCO-ICN because the Transaction would
         create a dominant position in the relevant markets.
(1332)  Furthermore, the Commission concludes that the Transaction would significantly
       impede effective competition in relation to air cargo services on the route Europe-
        South Korea and the route South Korea-Europe because the Transaction would create
        a dominant position in the relevant markets. In any event, the Transaction would also
        give rise to horizontal non-coordinated effects in relation to air cargo services on the

12.    COMMITMENTS
(1333)  In order to render the Transaction compatible with the internal market in relation to
        both (i) the markets for passenger air services on the routes BCN-ICN, CDG-ICN,
      FRA-ICN and FCO-ICN, and (ii) the markets for air cargo services on the routes
        Europe-South Korea and South Korea-Europe, Korean Air submitted commitments
        pursuant to Article 8(2) of the Merger Regulation.
(1334)  In order to address the concerns related to the markets as indicated above, those
       commitments  are  divided  into  the  “Passenger Commitments” and  the “Cargo
       Commitments”. The two different sets of commitments will be assessed separately in
         sections 12.2 and 12.2.5 below.
12.1.    Analytical framework
12.1.1.  Overview
(1335) When a concentration raises competition concerns because  it would significantly
       impede effective competition, in particular as a result of the creation or strengthening
        of a dominant position, the parties may seek to modify the concentration in order to
         resolve the competition concerns and thereby gain clearance of their merger. The
       commitments have to eliminate the competition concerns entirely and have to be
        comprehensive  and  effective  in  all  respects.  In  assessing  whether  proposed
       commitments  are  likely  to  eliminate  the  competition  concerns  identified,  the
       Commission considers all relevant factors including inter alia the type, scale and scope
        of the proposed commitments, judged by reference to the structure and particular
         characteristics of the markets in which the competition concerns arise, including the
         position of the parties and other participants on the markets.2103
12.1.2.  Elimination of all identified competition concerns
(1336)  The Commitments have to eliminate the competition concerns entirely and have to be
        comprehensive and effective from all points of view.
(1337)  Regarding the exact form of the commitments, the General Court has pointed out that,
        while the Merger Regulation lays down the principle whereby the Commission may
         authorise a merger only  if  the proposed commitments address  the competition
        concerns  identified,  it  “leaves  it a wide  discretion as  to  the form which  the
       commitments in question may take.”2104 Commitments may be structural in nature,
        such as the commitment to divest a certain business unit. It may also be however, that
         other types of commitments are capable of preventing the significant impediment to
         effective competition.2105 In particular, other types of structural commitments may be




2103     See Commission notice on remedies acceptable under Council Regulation (EC) No 139/2004 and under
       Commission Regulation (EC) No 802/2004 ("the Remedies Notice"), paragraphs 5, 9, and 12 (OJ 2008/C
         267/01).
2104     Case T-177/04 easyJet v Commission [2006] ECR II-1913, paragraph 197: "Article 6(2) of Regulation
      No 4064/89 provides that the Commission may authorise a merger if the commitments proposed by the
         parties dispel the serious doubts as to the compatibility of the merger with the common market.
        Regulation No 4064/89 thus lays down the objective to be achieved by the Commission, but leaves it a
       wide discretion as to the form which the commitments in question may take."
2105     Remedies Notice, paragraph 15.


                                    333

[PÁGINA PDF 340]
         suitable to resolve all types of concerns if they are equivalent to divestitures in their
          effects.2106
(1338)  As regards divestitures, the Remedies Notice sets out that the divested activities must
         consist of a viable business that, if operated by a suitable purchaser, can compete
         effectively with the Merged Entity on a lasting basis and that is divested as a going
        concern. For the business to be viable, it may also be necessary to include activities
       which are related to markets where the Commission did not identify competition
        concerns if this is required to create an effective competitor in the affected markets.2107
       The business has to include all the assets which contribute to its current operation or
       which are necessary to ensure  its viability and competitiveness and all personnel
       which is currently employed or which is necessary to ensure the business’ viability
       and competitiveness.2108 In the description of the business, the Parties also have to set
        out the arrangements for the supply of products and services by them to the divested
        business or by the divested business to them. Such on-going relationships of the
        divested business may be necessary to maintain the  full economic viability and
        competitiveness of the divested business on a transitional basis.2109 The business to be
        divested has to be viable as such. Therefore, the resources of a possible or even
       presumed future purchaser are not taken into account, in principle, by the Commission
          at the stage of assessing the remedy. The situation is different if already during the
        procedure a sale and purchase agreement with a specific purchaser is concluded whose
        resources  can  be  taken  into  account  at  the  time  of  the  assessment  of  the
        commitments.2110 A divestiture consisting of a combination of certain assets which did
        not form a uniform and viable business in the past creates risks as to the viability and
        competitiveness of the resulting business. Such an approach may be accepted by the
       Commission only if the viability of the business is ensured notwithstanding the fact
         that the assets did not form a uniform business in the past.2111
(1339)  The intended effect of the divestiture will only be achieved if and once the business is
         transferred to a suitable purchaser in whose hands it will become an active competitive
         force in the market.2112 In general, there are three ways to ensure that the business is
         transferred to a suitable purchaser. First, the business is transferred within a fixed
         time-limit after adoption of the decision to a purchaser which is approved by the
       Commission on the basis of purchaser requirements set out in the commitments.
        Second, in addition to the conditions set out for the first category, the commitments
      may foresee that the parties cannot complete the notified operation before having
        entered into a binding agreement with a purchaser for the business, approved by the
       Commission (so-called ‘upfront buyer’). Third, the parties identify a purchaser for the
        business and  enter  into a binding agreement  already during  the Commission's
        procedure (so-called ‘fix-it-first’ remedy).2113 The Commission welcomes fix-it-first
        remedies in particular in cases where the identity of the purchaser is crucial for the
         effectiveness  of  the  proposed  remedy.  This  concerns  cases  where,  given  the
        circumstances, only very few potential purchasers can be considered suitable, in
         particular as the divested business is not a viable business in itself, but its viability will

        1931, paragraph 183, the Court held that with regard to the divestiture of slots, Commitments offered by
         the parties “may be regarded as structural”.

[PÁGINA PDF 341]
        only be ensured by specific assets of the purchaser, or where the purchaser needs to
       have  specific  characteristics  in order  for  the remedy  to solve  the competition
         concerns.2114
(1340)  For mergers in the air transport sector, the Commission has previously clarified that
         “in air transport mergers, a mere reduction of barriers to entry by a commitment of
         the parties to offer slots on specific airports may not always be sufficient to ensure the
         entry of new competitors on those routes where competition problems arise and to
        render  the remedy  equivalent  in  its  effects  to a  divestiture”.2115  Rather,  the
       Commission has found in previous assessments of airline mergers that: “In airline
         cases, commitments are acceptable to the Commission where it is sufficiently likely
         that actual entry by new competitors will occur and where such entry would eliminate
       any serious doubts as to the compatibility of the concentration with the internal
        market.” This principle corresponds to the assessment of entry as a competitive
         constraint on the merging parties. As stated in paragraph 68 of the Horizontal Merger
        Guidelines, "for entry to be considered a sufficient competitive constraint on the
       merging parties, it must be shown to be likely, timely and sufficient to deter or defeat
       any potential anti-competitive effects of the merger."2116
(1341)  Concerning the sufficient likelihood of entry, in the case of air transport mergers, the
        Court previously held that “the mere threat of an entry […] is not sufficient. […] What
        counts  is  the prospect  of an  entrant which  offsets  the  anti-competitive  effects
         specifically established in the contested decision […].”2117 As to a timely entry, what
         constitutes an appropriate time period may depend on the characteristics and dynamics
        of the market, as well as specific capabilities of potential entrants.2118 While in its past
          airline cases, the Commission held that an entry occurring within the next two years
      may be considered as timely,2119 what constitutes a “timely entry” has to be assessed
         for each case individually.
12.1.3.  Capable of being implemented effectively within short period of time
(1342)  Commitments must be capable of being implemented effectively within a short period
        of time as the conditions of competition on the market will not be maintained until the
       commitments have been fulfilled.2120 The Commission has to be able to conclude with
         the requisite degree of certainty that it will be possible to implement the commitments
       and that it is likely that the new commercial structures resulting from them will be
         sufficiently workable and lasting to ensure that the significant impediment to effective
        competition will not materialise.2121
(1343)  The requisite degree of certainty concerning the implementation of the proposed
       commitments may in particular be affected by risks in relation to the transfer of a
        business to be divested, such as conditions attached by the parties to the divestiture,
         third party rights in relation to the business or the risks of finding a suitable purchaser,
        as well as risks in relation to the degradation of the assets in the time before the
         divestiture has taken place.2122

12.2.   Passenger Commitments
12.2.1.  Description of the Commitments
(1344)  In order to render the Transaction compatible with the internal market in relation to the
        markets for air passenger services on the routes BCN-ICN, CDG-ICN, FRA-ICN and
       FCO-ICN, Korean Air submitted first passenger commitments pursuant to Article 8(2)
        of the Merger Regulation on 3 November 2023, while the time limit for a decision set
         in Article 10(3) of the Merger Regulation was suspended. The Commission did not
        market  test  those commitments  during  the  period when  the time  limits were
        suspended.
(1345) On 5 December 2023, the day on which the deadline suspension expired, Korean Air
        submitted  second  passenger commitments  (“the  Passenger Commitments  of 5
       December  2023”). The Commission  proceeded  to  market  test  the  Passenger
       Commitments  of  5  December  2023  on  6  December  2023.  The  Passenger
       Commitments of 5 December 2023 contained the following provisions:
(1346)  With regards to air passenger transport services, Korean Air committed to make
         available several assets necessary to procure the entry by a passenger remedy taker on
         the four Passenger Overlap Routes (‘Passenger Remedy Routes’). These assets include
           (i) slots for take-off and landing at Incheon airport and at BCN, FRA, CDG and FCO
          airports; (ii) traffic rights required to operate the Passenger Remedy Routes, and (iii)
        Trans-Siberian (‘TSR’) overflight rights. The number of slots, traffic rights and TSR
         rights Korean Air committed to make available would allow the remedy taker to
        operate the same level of services as Asiana’s level of services pre-Covid19  (i.e.
       20 weekly frequencies in the IATA Winter seasons and 23 weekly frequencies in the
      IATA Summer seasons on all Overlap Routes together).
(1347)  In addition, Korean Air committed to conclude with the remedy taker agreements for
           (i) […] (‘Remedy Aircraft’) for a transitional period of […] years with a possibility to
        extend the lease for another […] years, and sublease to the passenger remedy taker up
         to […] (‘Sublease Aircraft’) for a period that would be discussed and agreed between
         the Remedy Taker and Korean Air, provided that the passenger remedy taker fails to
        procure such aircraft independently; (ii) the temporary secondment of trained flight
       crew with a licence to operate the Remedy Aircraft for a transitional period of […]
        (and a possible extension for […]) as well as access to […] model aircraft flight
        simulators for training, (iii) maintenance, repair and overhaul (‘MRO’) support for the
      Remedy Aircraft during the leasing period of such aircraft.
(1348)  Korean Air proposed the South Korean low-cost carrier T’way Air Co., Ltd (‘T’way’)
        as the passenger remedy taker. T’way has a primary hub at ICN and operational hubs
          at Gimpo International Airport and Daegu International Airport. It was founded in
        2010, acquiring the assets of the bankrupt Hansung Airlines (which operated between
       2005 and 2008).2123 T’way’s fleet comprises of more than 30 aircraft. Currently T’way
        operates approximately 60 short- and mid-haul routes to a number of countries that
        include Japan, China, Hong-Kong, Taiwan, Thailand, Philippines, Vietnam, Laos,
      Guam (USA), Saipan (USA), Mongolia, and Singapore. In 2022, T’way also started
        long-haul  operations,  its  first  destination  being Sydney  (Australia), and  since
        June 2023 it started operations to Bishkek (Kyrgyzstan). T’way is willing to enter all
        Passenger Remedy Routes with direct air passenger services as part of its strategy to
       become a global network carrier that operates multiple aircraft models.

(1365)  Third, the Passenger Commitments set Passenger Remedy Taker criteria which add
         additional requirements compared  to the standard purchaser requirements  set  in
        paragraph 48 of the Remedies Notice. In addition to the three standard requirements,
        clause 47(c) of the Passenger Commitments adds that in order to be approved by the
       Commission, the Passenger Remedy Taker “shall be an existing airline with the ability
         to operate a hub and spoke network from ICN”. This  additional requirement
         strengthens the Passenger Commitments by ensuring that the remedy taker will have a
         suitable profile, allowing  it to compete effectively with the merged entity on the
      Remedy Routes.
(1366)  Fourth, the Ministry of Land Infrastructure and Transport (‘MOLIT’) of the Republic
        of Korea has affirmed  to  the Commission  its  position  to  actively support  the
        implementation of the Passenger Commitments. While the EU Slot Regulation allows
         for a transfer or exchange of slots between airlines under certain conditions, including
          at the request of public authorities pursuant to the Merger Regulation,2146 the Republic
        of Korea’s rules on allocation of slots currently do not allow for a transfer of slots
       from the Parties to the Passenger Remedy Taker as envisaged in the Passenger
       Commitments. Similarly, procedures must be established to allow for the transfer of
          traffic rights and TSR overflight rights from the Parties to the Passenger Remedy
        Taker pursuant to the Passenger Commitments. MOLIT’s affirmation of its position is
         therefore  important  to  allow  the  effective  implementation  of  the  Passenger
       Commitments. In any event, as explained above, the closing of the Transaction is
         subject to the Passenger Remedy Taker operating a certain level of services on the
         route, meaning that the Transaction would not close until the slots and traffic rights are
         transferred to the Passenger Remedy Taker. Therefore, it is Korean Air who will bear
         the risk in case the required changes are not implemented by MOLIT.
(1367)  Fifth, the Commission confirmed with the Korean Fair Trade Commission (‘KFTC’)
         the compatibility of the Commitments with the remedies imposed by the KFTC.
12.2.3.  Assessment of the suitability of the Passenger Remedy Taker
(1368)  In clause 47 of the Passenger Commitments Korean Air names T’way as the proposed
        Passenger Remedy Taker and requests the Commission to approve T’way as the
        Passenger Remedy  Taker  and  to  approve  the  Entry Commitment Agreement
        concluded between Korean Air and T’way in the Decision.
(1369)  For the reasons set out below, the Commission considers that T’way is a suitable
       remedy taker, in line with the provisions of clause 48 of the Passenger Commitments
        of 9 January 2024. The Commission therefore approves T’way as the remedy taker for
         the Passenger Commitments of 9 January 2024.
12.2.3.1. Framework of the Commission’s assessment of the Remedy Taker
(1370)  Paragraph 56 of the Remedies Notice provides for situations when Parties identify and
         enter into an agreement with a buyer outlining the essentials of the purchase during the
       Commission procedure (fix-it-first remedy). In this case, the Commission will be able

2145     Independent Advisor’s report, paragraphs 535-538.
2146   EU Regulation 95/93 on common rules for the allocation of slots at Community, (‘EU Slot Regulation’),
         Article 8b.


                                    341

[PÁGINA PDF 348]
         to decide in the final decision whether the transfer of the divested business to the
         identified purchaser will remove the competition concerns. Under the  fix-it-first
        assessment,  if the Commission authorises the notified concentration, no additional
       Commission decision for the purchaser approval will be needed and the closing of the
         sale of the divested business may take place shortly afterwards.
(1371)  The standard purchaser requirements are set in paragraph 48 of the Remedies Notice:
           (i) the purchaser is required to be independent of and unconnected to the parties, (ii)
         the purchaser must possess the financial resources, proven relevant expertise and have
         the incentive and ability to maintain and develop the divested business as a viable and
         active competitive force in competition with the parties and other competitors, and (iii)
         the acquisition of the business by a proposed purchaser must neither be likely to create
      new competition problems nor give rise to a risk that the implementation of the
       commitments will be delayed. Therefore, the proposed purchaser must reasonably be
        expected to obtain all necessary approvals from the relevant regulatory authorities for
         the acquisition of the business to be divested. According to paragraph 49 of the
       Remedies Notice, these standard requirements may have to be supplemented on a
        case-by-case basis.
(1372)  Clause 47 of the Passenger Commitments sets the following  criteria, which the
        Passenger Remedy taker must fulfil in order to be approved by the Commission: “(a)
       The Passenger Remedy Taker shall be independent of and unconnected to Korean Air
       and its Affiliated Undertakings (this being assessed having regard to the situation
        following the implementation of these Passenger Commitments). (b) The Passenger
       Remedy Taker shall have the financial resources, proven expertise, incentive and
          ability to operate a Competitive Air Service as a viable and active competitive force on
         the Remedy Routes; (c) The Passenger Remedy Taker shall be an existing airline with
         the ability to operate a hub and spoke network from ICN; and (d) The operations on
         the Remedy Routes by the Passenger Remedy Taker must neither be likely to create, in
          light  of  the information  available  to  the Commission, prima  facie competition
        concerns nor give rise to a risk that the implementation of the Commitments will be
        delayed. In particular, the Passenger Remedy Taker must reasonably be expected to
        obtain  all necessary approvals from the relevant regulatory  authorities  for the
        operations on the Remedy Routes”.
(1373)  Against this background, the Commission has assessed the suitability of T’way as the
        Passenger Remedy Taker and has come to the conclusion that T’way is independent of
       and unconnected to the Parties (section 12.2.3.2), T’way has the financial resources,
        proven expertise, incentive and ability to operate a Competitive Air Service as a viable
       and active competitive force on the Remedy Routes (section 12.2.3.3), T’way is an
         existing  airline with the  ability to operate a hub and spoke network from ICN
         (section 12.2.3.4), the operations on the Remedy Routes by T’way do not create prima
         facie competition concerns nor give rise to risks of delays (section 12.2.3.5).

12.2.3.3. T’way has the financial resources, proven expertise, incentive and ability to operate a
        Competitive Air Service as a viable and active competitive force on the Remedy
        Routes
(1378)  Korean Air submits that T’way has the profile, financial resources, proven expertise
       and capabilities and incentive to maintain and develop the Passenger Remedy Routes
        as a viable and active competitive force in competition with the Parties and other
          airlines.2153
(1379)  In its briefing paper concerning its suitability to be a remedy taker, T’way explained
         that it initially mainly operated short-haul routes covering Japan, China, and various
         countries in Southeast Asia. Prior to the Covid19 pandemic, T’way started to plan and
        execute a more diversified business plan, moving away from the traditional LCC
        model, to become an airline with a global network operating multiple types of aircraft.
       T’way went from short to medium haul and finally, starting in December 2022, to
        long-haul routes, after adding new types of aircrafts to its fleet.2154 T’way explained
         that  it has been developing a more nuanced approach that puts the airline into the
        “hybrid” business model – moving from purely “low cost” to “affordable premium”
         for those increasing numbers of customers with a premium demand but who are cost
        conscious. According  to T’way,  this makes the  airline  attractive  for customers
        searching for a Business Class-product but unwilling to pay traditional Business Class
          fares.2155 T’way explained that it has the incentive to enter the Remedy Routes, as it
        has been planning to expand into Europe since early 2019, and has secured traffic
         rights to Croatia. According to T’way, the Passenger Commitments offer T’way with a
        valuable opportunity to enter routes for which the required traffic rights and slots were
        not available to it.2156 As explained in section 8.6.3, the lack of slots and traffic rights
         constitute barriers to entry on the Remedy Routes. These barriers were a major

(1382)  The  Independent Advisor  notes  that T’way  has  recovered  well  post Covid19

         financial resources to implement and sustain the Remedy Routes and has not identified
       any particular concerns regarding the viability and suitability of T’way as a Remedy
        Taker. […]. However, the Independent Advisor considers that the four Remedy Routes
        support T’way  in becoming more  diversified and  potentially becoming more

(1383)  The Independent Advisor further reviewed T’way’s proven expertise, experience and
          activities. In  particular, the Independent Advisor assessed T’way’s strategy and
        experience to operate long haul flights. The Independent Advisor also assessed the
         incentives of T’way to maintain and develop operations on the four Remedy Routes as
        a viable and competitive force in competition with the Parties and other competitors.
(1384)  With respect to T’way’s experience in operating long haul routes, the Independent

       Sydney in December 2022, which was well received by the market. Given the success

12.2.4.  Assessment of the proposed Entry Commitment Agreement
(1392)  As explained in paragraphs (1349) (1349)and (1352)(1352) above, Korean Air and
       T’way concluded a legally binding Entry Commitment Agreement which sets out the
        terms and conditions implementing the Passenger Commitments (a so called “fix-it-
          first” solution as described in the Remedies Notice, paragraphs 56-57).
(1393)  In the view of the Commission, the Entry Commitment Agreement is compliant with
         the obligations that Korean Air undertook under the Passenger Commitments and is
        capable of facilitating the effective implementation of the Passenger Commitments for
         the reasons set out below.
(1394)   First, the contractual object of the Entry Commitment Agreement corresponds to the
         object of the Passenger Commitments. In particular, Korean Air has committed in the
        Entry Commitment Agreement to transfer or provide to T’way the assets necessary to
        operate on  the Passenger Remedy  Routes,  including  slots,  traffic  rights, TSR
         overflight rights, aircraft, crew and MRO support.2166
(1395)  Second, under the Entry Commitment Agreement, T’way has contractually committed
         to start operations on the Passenger Remedy Routes according to the agreed entry
        schedule  for 23 weekly frequencies  in IATA Summer seasons and 20 weekly
        frequencies  in IATA Winter  seasons.2167 This  contractual  obligation  of T’way
        corresponds to Korean Air’s commitments under the Passenger Commitments. The
        timeframe of T’way’s commitment to  start operations on the Passenger Remedy
        Routes  within  the IATA Summer season 2024  and,  following  entry,  continue
        operations on all four Passenger Remedy Routes for a minimum period of at least 4
      IATA seasons (i.e. from the start of the IATA Winter season 2024/2025 until the last
       day  of  the IATA Summer  season  2026)  also  corresponds  to  Korean  Air’s
       commitments under the Passenger Commitments.
(1396)  Third, the contractual obligations arising under the Entry Commitment Agreement are
        robust  and  sufficiently  binding  upon T’way  and  Korean  Air,  because  their
        implementation will be enforced by fast-track arbitration,2168 in combination with an
        indemnity clause.2169 Therefore, the Commission considers that the binding nature of
         the Entry Commitment Agreement mitigates the risk that the Passenger Remedy Taker
        does not comply with the entry schedule provided in the Passenger Commitments.


2165    As explained in section 12.2.3.2 above, the agreement between Asiana and T’way is immaterial. As
        explained in section 12.2.4 below, the support Korean Air will provide to T’way pursuant to the
        Passenger Commitments is temporary in nature and will not create dependency of T’way on Korean Air.

(1397)  Fourth, the Entry Commitment Agreement contains two types of provisions, i.e. (i)
        those that are fully binding and cannot be amended, namely the terms and conditions
         relating to the transfer of slots, traffic rights and TSR overflight rights, and  (ii)
        provisions which relate to the key terms of transitional agreements that will be
        concluded at a later stage (subject to the approval of the Monitoring Trustee in
         consultation with the Commission),2170 namely:
         •  A dry lease agreement for the Remedy Aircraft;
         •  A sublease agreement for the Sublease Aircraft (if required);
         •  A flight crew support agreement, which would include a crew secondment
             agreement and a simulator access agreement;
         •  An MRO support agreement.
(1398)  The key terms of the transitional agreements as provided in the Entry Commitment
       Agreement and its Schedules are binding upon Korean Air and T’way. However,
       Korean Air and T’way are able to amend the key terms of the transitional agreements
        with a prior approval of the Monitoring Trustee in consultation with the Commission.
        Moreover, certain non-key provisions of the transitional agreements will be negotiated
       and agreed between Korean Air and T’way after the adoption of this Decision.
(1399)  In the Commission’s view, the dual nature of the provisions contained in the Entry
       Commitment Agreement (i.e. the legally binding provisions which cannot be amended
       and those that can be amended subject to the Monitoring Trustee’s approval) ensures
         the necessary level of flexibility with regard to T’way’s operations on the Passenger
      Remedy Routes. The fact that T’way will have the ability to propose or request
        changes to the transitional agreements in the course of negotiations with Korean Air
         will allow  it to achieve the optimal conditions necessary for the effective start of
        operation on the Passenger Remedy Routes. At the same time, the fact that any
        changes to the key terms of the transitional agreements will have to be approved by
         the Monitoring Trustee will ensure that T’way is not put at an undue disadvantage.
(1400)  Fifth,  the  Commission  considers  that  the  individual  elements  of  the  Entry
       Commitment Agreement are sufficiently clear and comprehensive in order to ensure
       an effective implementation of the Passenger Commitments.
(1401)  In  the  first  place,  in  order  to  ensure  the  implementation  of  the  Passenger
       Commitments, the Entry Commitment Agreement foresees the procedures under
       which T’way should obtain slots, traffic rights and TSR overflight rights. Different
          slot transfer procedures exist on the EU and South Korea ends of the routes.2171 The
     EU Slot Regulation allows for a transfer or exchange of slots between airlines under
         certain conditions, including at the request of public authorities pursuant to the Merger
         Regulation,2172 therefore the Commission considers that the process for slot transfers
          at the EU airports foreseen in the Entry Commitment Agreement will allow for an
         effective implementation of the Passenger Commitments. As regards slot, traffic right
       and TSR overflight right transfer in South Korea, the Commision considers that
      MOLIT’s affirmation to the Commission (see paragraph (1366) above) will allow to
         effectively implement the provisions of the Entry Commitment Agreement.

         request for such an agreement.

(1402)  In the second place, the Entry Commitment Agreement foresees the key terms and

         Decision.2173 The Commission considers that the key terms and conditions of the
      Remedy Aircraft lease agreement as contained in the Entry Commitment Agreement
        correspond to the provisions of the Passenger Commitments and will allow for an
         effective implementation of the Passenger Commitments.
(1403)  More specifically, under the Entry Commitment Agreement, Korean Air is obliged to
        reconfigure the Remedy Aircraft prior to its delivery to T’way to ensure that the
        Passenger Remedy Taker is able to use the Remedy Aircraft to offer a competitive

        conduct an  inspection of each  aircraft’s condition and documents between  the
        conclusion of the Remedy  Aircraft  lease and the delivery of the  aircraft. The
        Independent Advisor did not identify any concerns in relation to the Remedy Aircraft
         reconfiguration conditions or the delivery schedule.2174
(1404)  The Entry Commitment Agreement includes agreed lease  rates for the Remedy
         Aircraft which T’way will be required to pay Korean Air […].2175 In order to assess
        whether the proposed […] lease rates are in line with Korean Air’s commitment to
         lease the Remedy Aircraft to T’way […],2176 the Independent Advisor analysed the
       manner in which Korean Air’s calculation of […] lease rates […] aligns with market
          aircraft lease rates. While on the basis of the available market data for similarly aged
          aircraft, the Independent Advisor acknowledged that the […] lease rates for the
      Remedy Aircraft lease extension ([…]) are […] the market suggests, on balance the
        Independent Advisor is of the view that the proposed […] lease rates are reasonable,
         especially considering (i) the time it would take T’way to source an aircraft lease from
         the market for operations starting in June 2024 and (ii) the uncertainty of being able to
        procure suitable aircraft.2177 Furthermore, in the view of the Independent Advisor, the

12.3.   Cargo Commitments
(1420)  In order to render the Transaction compatible with the internal market in relation to the
        markets for air cargo services on the routes Europe to South Korea and South Korea to
        Europe, Korean Air submitted first cargo commitments pursuant to Article 8(2) of the
       Merger Regulation on 3 November 2023 (the “First Cargo Commitments”), while the
        time limit for a decision set in Article 10(3) of the Merger Regulation was suspended.
       The Commission did not market test the First Cargo Commitments during the period
       when the time limits were suspended.
(1421) On 5 December 2023, the day on which the deadline suspension expired, Korean Air
        submitted second cargo commitments  (the “Second Cargo Commitments”). The
       Commission  proceeded  to  market  test  the  Second  Cargo  Commitments  on
       6 December 2023.
(1422)  In order to address the issues raised in the market test and the Independent Advisor’s
         report, Korean Air submitted a final set of cargo commitments on 9 January 2024 (the
        “Final Cargo Commitments”).
(1423)  All three cargo commitments submitted by Korean Air – the First, Second and Final
       Cargo Commitments – essentially consist in the divestment of the air cargo assets and
        personnel currently owned and employed by Asiana in the operation of its global
        cargo freighter activities (the “Divestment Business”), including  (i) […],  (ii) the
         relevant slots, traffic rights and TSR overflight rights as currently used by Asiana for
           its global cargo freighter activities,  (iii) some licences and permits related to the


2189     Independent Advisor’s report, paragraphs 676-678.


                                    351

[PÁGINA PDF 358]
          aircraft, (iv) some of the main supplier contracts and lease agreements for office space
       and cargo terminals, (v) all Asiana’s air cargo customer contracts and all historic
        customer data, full customer lists and records of customers that can practically be
        served by the Divestment Business, (vi) approximately […] employees and some Key
        Personnel, and (vii) the arrangement for the continued supply by the Parties with IT
         support, ground-handling at ICN airport, access to simulators and hangars, for a
         transitional period of […] years.
(1424)  The Divestment Business  is not an existing stand-alone business but rather one
         integrated with the business which is to be retained by Korean Air post-Transaction.
        Therefore, the abovementioned air cargo assets and personnel would need to be
         ‘carved-out’ and the Divestment Business would not include any assets solely related
         to Asiana’s passenger and/or belly space cargo operations. This is because, on the one
        hand, any competition concerns arisen on the markets for passenger air services on the
         routes BCN-ICN, CDG-ICN, FRA-ICN and FCO-ICN are addressed through the
        Passenger Commitments as described in section 12.2 above, and on the other hand,
         belly space cargo operations cannot be disentangled from the  rest of Asiana’s
        passenger activities.
(1425)  All three cargo commitments submitted by Korean Air have an upfront buyer structure
         since the implementation of the Transaction can only take place  after the  final
        approval by the Commission of the purchaser and the purchase agreements.
