12.3.1.2. Assessment of the First Cargo Commitments
(1441)  The Commission considered that the First Cargo Commitments appeared to concern
         the divestment of a sufficiently large part of Asiana’s cargo operations, to address the
        competition concerns raised by the Transaction. The divestment of the global cargo
         freighter business of Asiana geographically extended beyond the overlap on which the
       Commission had identified competitive concerns. Although it did not entirely replicate
         the competitive constraint exerted by Asiana on Korean Air pre-Transaction, as it did
        not include the belly space capacity of Asiana’s passenger flights to Europe, it would
       have provided the remedy taker with sizeable capacity to exert competitive pressure on
         the merged entity.
(1442)  The Commission considered, however, that the First Cargo Commitments presented
         several  risks, mainly stemming from the carve-out  structure of the Divestment
        Business.
(1443)   First, the Commission considered that Korean Air’s caveat in the purchaser criteria of
         the First Cargo Commitments that “proven expertise’ does not necessarily require that


                                    355

[PÁGINA PDF 362]
         the Purchaser  is an existing airline” would not be appropriate in view of the
        complexity of the carve-out structure of the proposed divestment and the number of
        outstanding items that would need to be addressed by the Purchaser at a later stage,
          e.g. securing licences and permits, putting in place supply contracts, as well as
        obtaining third party consent for some of the aircraft, the lease agreements and all
         other supply agreements, including for ground handling services, MRO services and
         fuel services.
(1444)  As designed, the Divestment Business would lack an air operator certificate and other
         licences, and would exclude several central assets and capabilities, as well as any
         assets solely related to passenger and/or passenger belly space cargo operations.
        Therefore, the Commission considered that the purchaser criteria entailed large risks
       by not ensuring that the purchaser should only be a sizeable airline with an existing air
        operator certificate and a hub at ICN airport in order to replicate sufficiently the
        network and size of pre-Transaction Asiana.
(1445)  Second, the Commission noted that the Divestment Business was based on Asiana’s
         freighter fleet, part of which is considerably aged. Out of the […] to be divested in
          total, the […] of Asiana are gradually moving towards the end of their lifecycle, with
      […] of them requiring imminent replacement. In addition, the remaining […], which
        exposes the Divestment Business to the risk of not securing the consent of each lessor.
        In light of this issue, the considerations about the identity of the Purchaser set out in
        paragraph (1443) became even more relevant.
(1446)  Third, the Commission could only accept any cargo commitments, which require the
        carve-out of Asiana’s global cargo freighter business, if it can be certain that, at least
          at the time when the business is transferred to the purchaser, a viable business on a
        stand-alone basis will be divested and the risks for the viability and competitiveness
        caused by the carve-out will thereby be reduced to a minimum.2191
(1447)  In the Commission’s view, the interim period between the Commission’s adopted
        Decision pursuant  to Article 8(2) of the Merger Regulation and the Purchaser
        approval, which would bring about the closing of the Transaction, would create a gap
       where the Divestment Business would remain integrated in Asiana’s overall network,
        including passenger and cargo (both belly space and freighter) operations. During this
         period, no step would be taken under the First Cargo Commitments in relation to the
        implementation of the carve-out, whereas the Asiana Designated Representative’s role
        as a point of contact assisting the Monitoring Trustee in collecting and providing
        information for the planning of the carve-out of the Divestment Business would not be
         sufficient to ensure that a viable business on a stand-alone basis would be divested at
         the time of the Divestment Closing.
(1448)  Fourth, the Commission noted  that the Divestment Business would not entirely
         replicate the competitive constraint exerted by Asiana on Korean Air pre-Transaction,
        given the loss of the belly space capacity in Asiana’s passenger flights to Europe.
(1449)  The Commission did not market test the First Cargo Commitments during the period
       when the time  limits referred to in Article 10 of the Merger Regulation were
        suspended. However, the Commission informed Korean Air about the concerns
         identified above.





2191     Remedies Notice, paragraph 36.


                                    356

[PÁGINA PDF 363]

              Transaction. At the same time, Korean Air also clarified that post-closing of the

            Korean Air as the Hold Separate Manager, responsible for managing the day-to-

       were still not addressed, and in particular those related to the identity of the Purchaser
        of the Divestment Business and the Divestment Business’ ageing  aircraft  fleet.
       However, the Commission decided to subject the Second Cargo Commitments to a
        market test, which was launched on 6 December 2023.
12.3.2.2. Results of the market test
(1453)  The market test mainly aimed at assessing: (i) the suitability of the Purchaser criteria;
            (ii)  whether  the  transfer  of  Asiana’s  cargo  freighter  fleet  would  affect  the
        competitiveness and viability of the Divestment Business; (iii) the sufficiency of the
        scope of assets to be transferred to the Divestment Business in view of creating a
         viable and competitive air cargo carrier on the market; (iv) whether the divestment of
        only the freighter capacity (as opposed to the combined freighter and belly space cargo
         capacity) of Asiana would  replicate  sufficiently the pre-Transaction competitive
         constraint exerted on Korean Air; and (v) the overall suitability of the Second Cargo
       Commitments to effectively remove the competitive concerns identified in air cargo
         services on the routes Europe to South Korea and South Korea to Europe.
(1454)  The market test showed that the Second Cargo Commitments could be suitable to
         effectively remove the competitive concerns identified2192 but there were doubts about
         the effectiveness of the Purchaser  criteria, the sufficiency of the divested cargo
         freighter fleet, the scope of the assets to be transferred to the Divestment Business, and
         the loss of the belly space capacity.2193

12.3.2.2.1.    Suitability of the Purchaser criteria
(1455)  The vast majority of respondents replying to the Commission’s market test indicated
         that the Purchaser could only be an existing airline.2194
(1456)  Especially the competitors responding to the Commission’s market test were vocal
        about the benefits that an existing airline would bring to the Divestment Business in
       view of (i) the complexity of the carve-out structure of the cargo remedy and (ii) the
        age of the cargo freighter fleet being divested:

              the necessary licences and permits for the Divestment Business to become
              operational may take 12-24 months but only if the Purchaser is an airline;2195
         b.   [A competitor/potential  entrant/potential purchaser] noted  that the  potential
             Purchaser must have great records on successfully running a cargo business,
             while also highlighting that, given the age of the freighter fleet to be divested,
              the Purchaser might have difficulties if they are not a well-established player in
              the sector. In addition, [a competitor/potential entrant/potential purchaser] added
                that the Purchaser should also have experience in operating long-haul air cargo
              routes in order to have better chances on successfully operating the Divestment
               Business;2196
          c.    According to [a competitor/potential entrant/potential purchaser], “considering
              the non transferred  [air operator  certificate] and other associated permits,
                licenses, there is inherent risk in the divestment business as well as anticipated

               entrant/potential purchaser] believes that a Korean airline is the most suitable
             candidate for takeover due to these factors”;2197
         d.   [A competitor/potential entrant/potential purchaser] explained that the suitability
              of the Cargo Commitments would depend – among others – on who the

12.3.2.2.3.   The sufficiency of the Divestment Business’ assets
(1466)  The Commission’s  market  test  of  the Second Cargo Commitments aimed  at
        understanding whether the series of assets intended to be transferred to the Divestment
        Business would be sufficient to create an effective competitor in the market of air
        cargo services on a lasting basis. The results suggest that – subject to certain changes –
         the scope of the assets is sufficient – without prejudice to the issue of the aged aircraft
          fleet discussed in section 12.3.2.2.2.
(1467)  In  particular,  the  majority  of  competitors  and  customers  responding  to  the
       Commission’s market test considers the scope of intangible assets, i.e. slots, traffic
         rights and TSR overflight rights, to be sufficient for the Divestment Business to
       become a viable and competitive air cargo transport operator in the hands of a suitable
         Purchaser.2232 The majority of slot coordinators and airport managers also believes that
         the scope of slots, traffic rights and TSR overflight rights includes all rights necessary,
        while also considering that the slot transfer of Asiana’s global cargo freighter business
           is compatible with the slot regime that applies to the airport under their management
        and/or slot coordination.2233
(1468)  In addition, the majority of respondents indicated that the scope of the main licences,
         permits, contracts, agreements, leases, commitments and understandings, as well as
         the scope of the Key Personnel and the transitional services arrangements are all
         sufficient for the Divestment Business.2234 At the same time, the respondents to the
       Commission’s market test did not identify any major issues stemming from the non-

(1469)  However, the results of the Commission’s market test were mixed for competitors as

        operations and the effective transfer of personnel.2239
(1470)  In addition, other feedback from the market test with the purpose of mitigating the

          a.    Licences and permits: the Commission’s market test indicated that not only the
                 air operator  certificate, which  is necessary for the Divestment Business to
           become operational, but also all other licences and permits, which would need to

                practically) be transferrable, would require considerable time and effort in case

               entrant/potential  purchaser]  explained  the  following:  “[o]n one  hand,  the

12.3.2.2.4.   The loss of belly space capacity
(1471)  Several competitors and customers responding to the Commission’s market  test
         indicated that the loss of belly space cargo capacity may affect the viability and
        competitiveness of the Divestment Business.2247
(1472)  In particular, competitors suggested that belly space cargo capacity be leased to the
        Purchaser of the Divestment Business for a transitional period of time in order to
        ensure effective competition on the routes between Europe and South Korea from the
         beginning.2248 Alternatively, competitors also mentioned that this would depend on the
         identity of the Purchaser and their ability to deploy their own belly space capacity
        through their own network.2249
(1473) On the side of customers, one explained that in air cargo services the most important
        aspect is capacity and there is also demand for low deck space coming from the belly
         hold.2250 Another customer added that the risk is “essentially made up of the difficulty
         to maintain a large cargo only operation operating in healthy financial conditions
        overtime without benefiting from the broader base of a cargo + passenger type
         operation”.2251
12.3.2.2.5.    Suitability of the Second Cargo Commitments
(1474)  The risks and issues identified above notwithstanding, the Commission’s market test
        otherwise showed that the Second Cargo Commitments could be suitable to effectively
       remove the competitive concerns identified on both routes between Europe and South
         Korea.2252
(1475)  In particular, competitors considered a suitable Purchaser to be able to run a viable and
        competitive air cargo business that can exert a sufficient competitive constraint on the
       merged  entity post  Transaction.2253 In  addition, competitors considered  that the
        Divestment Business as envisaged is likely to attract a suitable Purchaser.2254 In fact,
         there were several competitors indicating their interest to acquire the Divestment

12.3.2.3. The Independent Advisor’s report
(1477)  In  its  report,  the Independent Advisor, appointed by Korean Air  to  assist  the
       Commission in the assessment of the Cargo Commitments, also assessed the Second
       Cargo Commitments with particular attention to the following areas: (i) the viability of
         the Divestment Business as a freighter-only business; (ii) the proposed perimeter of
         the Divestment Business following the carve-out to confirm the extent to which the
        Divestment Business can be considered stand-alone;  (iii) the extent to which the
        Divestment Business is transferred with certainty; and (iv) whether the carve-out can
       be implemented within the proposed timeline.
(1478)  The Independent Advisor concluded that the proposed carve-out broadly provides the
        Divestment Business with the elements required to compete in the market. However,
         the transfer of licences, customer contracts and service agreements would need to be
        monitored carefully to ensure that the transfer is timely and that any delay or required
         renegotiation does not result in a disruption to operations which could harm the
        Divestment Business, through a reduction of customers or an increase in costs.2261
(1479)  In this respect, the Independent Advisor identified similar risks and challenges as the
        ones emerged through the Commission’s market test, such as (i) the Purchaser criteria
       and the identity of the buyer of the Divestment Business, (ii) the Purchaser’s position
         to decide on, manage and finance a fleet replacement programme,  (iii) the timely
         transfer of all necessary assets to the Divestment Business, and (iv) the potential need
         for belly space cargo capacity to ensure the Divestment Business’ profitability.2262 In
         addition,  the  Independent  Advisor  also  identified  a  few  additional  areas  of
        improvement, namely (v) making sure that MOLIT has implemented the necessary
         legislative amendments and procedures in order to facilitate the transfer of the required
          slots, traffic rights and TSR overflight rights; (vi) Korean Air committing to use “best
         efforts” instead of “reasonable endeavours” in all cases where  it commits to help
        ensure that the Divestment Business has all the necessary assets in place, e.g. in case
        of licences and permits; (vii) making sure that any required consent from any third

12.3.2.4. Assessment of the Second Cargo Commitments
(1482)  The Commission found that the results of the market test and the report of the
        Independent Advisor highlighted a variety of risks associated with the Second Cargo
       Commitments.
(1483)  The Commission considered that both the responses to the market  test and the
        Independent Advisor’s report suggested that the Divestment Business would be a
         suitable remedy to address the competitive concerns identified in relation to the cargo
          air transport services on the routes between Europe and South Korea, subject to, inter
          alia, (i) the identity of the Purchaser being restricted to an existing airline only, (ii) the
        replacement of the […] oldest aircraft reaching […] years of age before Divestment
        Closing, while at the same time making sure that the […] youngest aircraft that are
         currently leased by Asiana will also be transferred to the Divestment Business without
       any issues arising from third party consent requirements,  (iii) taking on board all
         mitigating factors available for dealing with the complexities of the carve-out structure
        of the Divestment Business, and  (iv) addressing the need for belly space cargo
        capacity for at least a transitional period of time post Divestment Closing.2266
(1484)  The Commission further considered that the reservations of the respondents to the
        market test were mostly related to the identity of the potential Purchaser, i.e. the need
         to be an existing airline, rather than the suitability of the Divestment Business to
       become a sufficient competitive constraint to the merged entity post Transaction in the
        hands of the  right Purchaser. In addition,  all the remaining concerns and  risks
         identified could also be mitigated by the relevant existing operations, expertise and

12.3.3.  Final Cargo Commitments
12.3.3.1. Description of the Final Cargo Commitments
(1486)  In light of the issues described in section 12.3.2 above, Korean Air submitted the Final
       Cargo Commitments on 9 January 2024, improving the Second Cargo Commitments
         in order to address the Commission’s concerns that remained in the light of  its
        evaluation of the market test and the report of the Independent Advisor.

        with the Commission.
12.3.3.2. Assessment of the Final Cargo Commitments
(1496)  The Commission considers that the Final Cargo Commitments, once implemented,
         fully and unambiguously address the competition concerns raised and are adequate
       and sufficient to eliminate the significant impediment to effective competition in the
        markets for air cargo transportation services on the routes between Europe and South
        Korea.
(1497)   First, the Purchaser in the Final Cargo Commitments addresses the concerns raised
       and the criteria appear suitable to identify a suitable buyer of the Divestment Business.
       The Commission considers that the reservations of the respondents to the market test

                                    370

[PÁGINA PDF 377]
        of the Second Cargo Commitments, as expressed in section 12.3.2.2 above, were
        mostly related to the identity of the potential Purchaser, i.e. the need to be an existing
          airline, rather than the suitability of the Divestment Business to become a sufficient
        competitive constraint to the merged entity post Transaction in the hands of the right
        Purchaser. Similarly, the Independent Advisor’s report was rather positive as to the
        proposed cargo commitments, with the only caveat that a non-airline company could
        not feasibly be considered as a suitable Purchaser due to the time it would take for
        obtaining the air operator certificate. Therefore, the Purchaser criteria in the Final
       Cargo Commitments have fully addressed the concerns raised.
(1498)  Second, the scope of the Divestment Business appears suitable to effectively compete
       on the market for air cargo services. In the first place, the inclusion of […] newer
          aircraft to replace the [...] aircraft that is already exceeding / approaching the age of
      […] years before divestment closing addresses the issue of the ageing aircraft fleet in
         the near future in order to ensure that the Purchaser of the Divestment Business has
         sufficient time to plan its network and fleet. This is in line with considerations made
       by  both  competitors  in  the  Commission’s  market  test  of  the Second Cargo
       Commitments, as analysed in section 12.3.2.2.2 above, and by the Independent
        Advisor, who did not consider the age of the aircraft itself as a problem as long as the
        purchaser  is in a position to decide on, manage and finance a fleet replacement
        programme.2267 The Commission further notes that the other considerations made
        during the market test with regard to the expertise and know-how of the Purchaser, as
        well as  its own capabilities and network, have also been addressed through the
       amendment of the Purchaser criteria.
(1499)  In the second place, all other assets and personnel included in the perimeter of the
        Divestment Business appear sufficient to create a stand-alone freighter cargo carrier.
      As analysed in section 12.3.2.2.3 above, the respondents to the Commission’s market
          test overall found the scope of assets to be sufficient for the Divestment Business to
       become a viable and competitive air cargo transport operator in the hands of a suitable
        Purchaser. To the extent the results were mixed as to the carve-out structure of the
        Divestment Business, respondents seemed to imply that their concerns would be
        mitigated in case (i) the Purchaser was an existing airline with the expertise and know-
      how to deal with those open points in a relatively short time, and (ii) the loss of belly
        space cargo capacity was mitigated. The Commission notes that both of these issues
       have been addressed in the Final Cargo Commitments. In addition, the Commission
        notes that all other feedback from the market test with regard to (a) licences and
         permits, (b) Key Personnel, (c) personnel, and (d) the duration of the Transitional
        Services Agreements,  as  described  in  section  12.3.2.2.3  above, has  also been
        addressed in the Final Cargo Commitments.
(1500)  In any event, according to Clause 4 of the Schedule of the Final Cargo Commitments,
            if there is any other asset or personnel which is not covered by the scope of the
        Divestment Business but is used for Asiana’s global cargo business and is necessary
         for the continued operation, viability and competitiveness of the Divestment Business
        as a provider of air cargo services, that asset/personnel or an adequate substitute will
       be offered to the Purchaser of the Divestment Business.
(1501)  In the  third place, the Commission considers  that the  transitional Block Space
       Agreement  in passenger  flights operated by Korean Air and/or Asiana on  the
        Passenger Remedy Route(s) for a maximum of […]% of the belly space capacity of
        each such flight, for a transitional period of up to […] post divestment closing,

12.3.4.  Conclusion on the Cargo Commitments
(1506)  Based on the assessment set out in sections 12.3.1, 12.3.2 and 12.3.3, including the
         identity of the Purchaser and the scope of the Divestment Business, the Commission
        concludes that the Final Cargo Commitments of 9 January 2024 are likely to create a
         viable business capable of competing effectively on a lasting basis in the relevant
        markets. Therefore, the Final Cargo Commitments are suitable to eliminate entirely
         the competition concerns identified in relation to the cargo air transport services on the
         routes between Europe and South Korea.

[PÁGINA PDF 380]
12.4.   Conclusion on the Proposed Commitments
(1507)  In the light of the assessment set out in sections 12.2 and 12.3, the Commission
        concludes that the Final Commitments of 9 January 2024 are adequate and sufficient
         to entirely eliminate the significant impediment to effective competition in the markets
         for air transport and air cargo transportation services. Therefore, the Commission
        considers  the Final Commitments of 9 January 2024 capable of rendering  the
        Transaction compatible with the internal market and the EEA Agreement.

13. CONDITIONS AND OBLIGATIONS
(1508)  Pursuant to the second subparagraph of Article 8(2) of the Merger Regulation, the
       Commission may attach to its decision conditions and obligations intended to ensure
         that the undertakings concerned comply with the commitments they have entered into
         vis-à-vis the Commission with a view to rendering the concentration compatible with
         the internal market.
(1509)  The fulfilment of the measure that gives rise to the structural change of the market is a
         condition, whereas the implementing steps which are necessary to achieve this result
         are generally obligations on the  parties. Where a condition  is not  fulfilled, the
       Commission’s decision declaring the concentration compatible with the  internal
        market is no longer applicable. Where the undertakings concerned commit a breach of
       an obligation, the Commission may revoke the clearance decision in accordance with
         Article 8(6) of the Merger Regulation. The undertakings concerned may also be
         subject to fines and periodic penalty payments under Articles 14(2) and 15(1) of the
       Merger Regulation.
(1510)  In accordance with the basic distinction described in paragraph (1509) as regards
        conditions and obligations, this Decision should be made conditional on the full
        compliance by the notifying party with Section B, paragraphs 2-33, of the Passenger
       Commitments of 9 January 2024 and Section B and the Schedule of the Cargo
       Commitments of 9 January 2024. All other relevant sections should be obligations
        within the meaning of Article 8(2) of the Merger Regulation. The full texts of the final
       commitments are attached as Annexes 2 and 3 to this Decision and form an integral
         part thereof.

              Case M.10149 – KOREAN AIR / ASIANA
                     Annex I to the Decision

1.     INTRODUCTION
(1)     This Annex describes the Notifying Party’s and the Commission’s air cargo market
        share calculation methodologies, measured in sales, capacity and frequencies (Section
          2), the Commission’s analysis of excess capacity in the air cargo markets (Section 3)
         as presented in Sections 8.11 and 8.12 of the Decision.

2.    MARKET SHARE CALCULATIONS
(2)     This section describes the Notifying Party’s and the Commission’s market share
         calculation methodology for the routes between Europe (i.e. the EEA plus UK and
        Switzerland) and South Korea.1 This section also describes the revisions to the
       Commission’s market shares  reflecting the  criticism and remarks  raised by the
        Notifying Party in its Response to the Statement of Objections and in its response to
         the Letter of Facts (hereinafter, together ‘the Notifying Party’s remarks’).
2.1.    The Notifying Party’s initial market shares calculation methodology
2.1.1.   Introduction
(3)     This section describes the Notifying Party’s market share methodology, which relies
       on the Notifying Party’s internal data as well as data from external data providers. The
        following  sub-sections  describe how  the  different  data sources were combined
         together to obtain, respectively, (i) the Parties’ sales volumes, (ii) market sizes, and
            (iii) the competitors’ estimates.
(4)     Table 2 below illustrates step-by-step the methodology of volume-based market shares
       on the route Europe to South Korea in 2019. The steps of the methodology are the
         following.
          (a)   Step  1:  Original volume and  value  data from IATA’s Cargo Accounts
              Settlement Systems (“CASS”)2 provide the starting point. These sales data are
             only available for the Parties and for market sizes.
         (b)   Step 2: The relative proportion of competitors’ sales are estimated based on
             Trade Statistics Services (TRASS)3 and Flight Operation Information System
             (FOIS)4 data.


1       For details on the Parties’ market share calculations related to other geographic segmentation, see Annex
       QP10.Q28.3 - Methodology Note on Cargo Market Share Calculations.
2     CASS data is provided to each Party from IATA and include both the total volumes and total value
          settled through CASS on an O&D basis  (i.e., including transhipments between origin airport and
         destination airport). Auxiliary volumes not settled through CASS (e.g. postal mail, internal cargo and
       volume settled directly with General Sales Agents) are excluded as are airlines that do not settle through
       CASS. No information on individual competitors is provided to the Parties. The volume unit used is
        chargeable weight.
3     TRASS data is based on customs information and include volumes originating and loaded in Korea
       showing the airport at which they are first unloaded and the final destination country of the cargo, as well
         as the same information in the other direction, i.e., volumes unloaded in and destined for Korea by
         original origin country of the cargo as well as the airport where the cargo was last loaded. All information
           is provided for the market total only, i.e., not by airline. The volume unit used is customs weight, i.e.,
        weight excluding packaging and ancillary items.

[PÁGINA PDF 383]
          (c)   Step  3: The  difference between market  sizes and  the  Parties’  sales  data
              according to CASS is split according to the proportions from Step 2.
         (d)   Step 4: The Parties’ estimates according to CASS are replaced with their
               internal data, and competitors’ estimates are scaled up by the same proportion.
             This scaling is carried out (i) on the basis of the Parties’ combined data, and (ii)
               separately for each route and year.
          (e)   Step 5: The sales data by carriers not included in CASS are estimated. This
               applies primarily to integrators, but also to some other airlines which appeared in
           FOIS but not in CASS.
           (f)   Final sales data: Estimates from Step 4 and Step 5 are added together to arrive
                at total market sizes.
(5)     The Notifying Party’s methodology for capacity and frequency shares partially differs
       from that for volume and value-based market shares. These differences are explained
        below.
2.1.2.   The Parties’ data
(6)     Data for the Parties are based on their internal data. This applies to both volume and
        value market shares, as well as to capacity and frequency shares.
2.1.3.   Market sizes
(7)     Data from CASS provides the basis for both value and volume market sizes.
(8)    CASS data does not appear to cover the Parties’ whole business. Table 1 provides for
        a comparison between the Parties’ internal volumes data and CASS estimates for the
          Parties. To account for these discrepancies, market sizes are scaled up in proportion to
         the difference between the Parties’ volume and value data as reported in CASS and
          their own internal volume and value data.

2.1.4.   Competitors’ estimates
2.1.4.1. Volume and value-based estimates
(11)    Competitors’ estimates are based on allocating the difference between market sizes
       and the Parties’ sales data using a combination of FOIS, TRASS and Seabury.6
(12)     First, the amounts are allocated among loading/unloading airports on the basis of
      TRASS data. For loading/unloading airports outside Europe, their volume/value are
        assigned to competitors based on the Notifying Party’s best understanding of which
          airlines use those airports as transhipment hubs. For loading/unloading airports within
        Europe, their volume/value are assigned to competitors based on FOIS data.
(13)    Seabury data is used to identify whether any carriers fly on behalf of integrators. If so,
       volume and value data are assigned partly to the airline and partly to an integrator in
        proportion to capacity.
(14)    The split between belly and freighter aircraft is determined for each competitor based
       on FOIS data (where available) or Seabury capacity data. Where neither FOIS data nor
        Seabury capacity data  is available for an  airline, the proportional  split between
         freighter and belly is assumed to be the same as the rest of the market.
(15)      If any airline is encountered in the FOIS or TRASS data which is known not to be
        covered by CASS,  the  Parties have added  their volume/value  to market  sizes

2.1.4.2. Capacity and frequency-based estimates
(18)    The capacities and frequencies provided by Seabury serve as the starting point for
        estimating competitors’ capacities and frequencies.
(19)    The Parties indicate that each row of data extracted from Seabury data is based on the
          flight number and then aggregated weekly or monthly by the routing. A new row is
        used when the flight number changes. For multi-stop flights, one direction may not be
        included in the data if the flight number changes at Asian airports other than ICN. The
         Parties argue that the frequency for the outbound is by definition the same as for the
        inbound as all aircrafts return to their home-base after flying a rotation, thus they use
         the higher value between the outbound and the inbound routes. This maximum is taken
       by year, week/month, carrier code, aircraft, aircraft size, belly/freighter  split, and
         charter/regular  split. The same approach of using the higher of the inbound and
       outbound capacities and frequencies that is used for competitors is used on the Parties'
         internal data.
(20)    The Parties account for technical stops made in Korea owing to the COVID-19
          restrictions in China by cross-checking the list of competitors seen in the Seabury data
         in 2020 and 2021 with those that appear in the FOIS data in the same years, and, if any
          airlines are included in Seabury that do not have any volume in FOIS, they assume
         that these airlines made a technical stop only, and exclude them from the sample. As


                                              5

[PÁGINA PDF 387]
        discussed in Sections 8.11 and 8.12 of the Decision, however, this approach results in
        a significant overestimation of capacity for competitors who relied on technical stops.
(21)    The Parties estimate capacity and frequency for transhipment carriers based on the
        lower between the capacities  (i) to or from Korea, and  (ii) to or from Europe.
        Combinations of airlines and hubs with overall market shares smaller than 0.2% are
        excluded.
(22)     Integrators are separately recorded in Seabury. Where the data indicates that another
          carrier's cargo space was on behalf of an integrator, these frequencies and capacities
         are reallocated to the relevant integrator.
2.1.5.   Market share estimates for 2022
(23)    Market shares for 2022 are only available to a limited extent: except for CASS, all
         data sources relied upon by the Parties for the period 2018-2021 are no longer
         available. This implies that (i) Market sizes for 2022 are not fully comparable to
        market sizes for 2018-2021 because integrators’ data are not included; (ii) No estimate
         for competitors could be provided; (iii) No subdivision into belly/freighter or non-
         stop/multi-stop/transhipment  is available. Similar issues would also affect market
         shares for 2023.
2.2.    The Commission’s market share calculation methodology
(24)    This section describes the Commission’s market share methodology, which relies on
         the Notifying Party’s own methodology and combines it with data and feedback from
         competitors.
2.2.1.   The data
(25)    The Commission requested competitors to provide their own internal data on volume
       and value sales, as well as on capacity and spare capacity for the routes between
       Europe and South Korea for the years 2019, 2020, and 2021.
(26)    The Commission initially reached out to 24 competitors, where 19 replied to the data
         request.7 Table 4 provides an overview of the competitors contacted, and whether their
         data is available in the data room. The data gathered by the Commission represents
         close to [70-80]% of  all volumes on the route Europe to South Korea in 2019
        according to the Notifying Party’s sales volumes and about [70-80]% on the route
        South Korea to Europe.





7      The Commission interacted with a number of market participants via follow-up phone calls and via e-
        mails to explain the instructions for filling in the data templates, as well as to clarify any questions that
        market participants might have had.

                                              6

[PÁGINA PDF 388]
Table 4 – Overview market reconstruction exercise

2.2.1.1. On the measurement units used to gather data on volumes (actual weight volumes
        versus chargeable weight volumes) and on the load factor
(29)    The  Notifying  Party  argues  that  the  Commission’s  questions  in  the  market
         investigation questionnaires as well as the Phase II questionnaires were not precise
       enough to identify the measurement unit of volumes and capacity, and that the failure
         to specify such measurement unit could easily lead different respondents to provide
         data on different bases. In particular, the Commission did not specify that data should
        have been provided as chargeable weight for  it to be consistent with the Parties'
        market shares methodology.8
(30)   To address the Notifying Party’s criticism, the Commission contacted all third party
         data providers to clarify the measurement unit used, and, in case a unit other than
        chargeable weight was used, asked them to submit data based on chargeable weight or
         alternatively to provide a ‘rule of thumb’ to convert the submitted data into chargeable
        weight. Where no information on chargeable weight could be retrieved, a rule of
       thumb based or the Parties’ own data were used.

        weight and  actual weight  for Korean Air and  for Asiana. The competitor-by-

        discussed further below, and will be made available to the Notifying Party’s external
         advisors via the Data Room procedure.

         data provided by the Parties, (iii) the load factor could be measured in weight (tonnes),

       number of positions used; (iv) it is unclear how to provide a load factor across multi-
        stop routes and for transhipment carriers, arguing that the relevant load factor when
        estimating spare capacity is the maximum across all legs of a route that could carry
        cargo between Korea and Europe.9
(33)    The Commission  disagrees with  the Notifying  Party’s remarks  for  the reasons
        explained in Section 8.11.4 and 8.12.4 of the Decision, and notes that respondents’
        load factors provide helpful evidence on competitors’ excess capacity even if they are
       measured with a certain degree of uncertainty. The load factor is widely regarded in
         the industry as a reliable measure for capacity utilisation.10
(34)    Moreover, as the following tables show, load factor estimates based on alternative
         specifications and alternative levels of aggregation11 do not differ to an extent that
        render them an invalid measure for capacity utilisation. The tables below also show
         that load factors measured on the basis of actual weight are generally lower than load
         factors measured on the basis of chargeable weight or tonne-kilometres. This means
         that measures of rivals’ excess capacity based on ‘actual weight’ load factors tend to
        overestimate the amount of excess capacity actually available that is faced by the
          Parties. For Korean Air, the ‘actual weight’ load factor is about [10-15] percentage
         points lower than the ‘chargeable weight’ load factor for both directions, similarly for
        Asiana on the route from Europe to South Korea while it is about [0-5] percentage
         points lower on the route from South Korea to Europe. This most likely indicates that
         the ‘actual weight’ load factor  is generally lower than the ‘chargeable weight’.
        Accordingly, the Commission’s  analysis of excess capacity tends  to be  in the
        Notifying Party’s favour (indicating there is more excess capacity than actually exists)
         the higher the number of competitors who relied on actual weight.

2.2.1.2. On the respondent’s interpretation of the Commission’s requests for information
(35)    The  Notifying  Party  alleges  that  respondents may  have  misinterpreted  the
       Commission’s questions, and, instead of providing information on cargo transported
       between Europe and Korea, provided information on cargo transhipped behind or
       beyond Europe and South Korea, cargo transhipped at hubs outside Europe or South
        Korea, or cargo for O&Ds on multi-stop freighter flights.12
(36)    The Commission notes that the information requested is ordinarily gathered by cargo
         carriers as part of their business, and the Notifying Party did not provide any evidence
         in  support  of  such  alleged  extraordinary  level  of  misinterpretation  of  the
       Commission’s questions. Moreover, the data provided by respondents is generally
         close to the Parties’ competitor estimates, which provides further reassurance that such
          startling misinterpretation has not taken place.
2.2.1.3. On the approach followed to compile market shares and to define total market sizes
(37)    The Notifying Party argues that the Commission’s methodology combines a top-down
       and bottom-up approach in way that is flawed and likely to lead to less accurate
         estimates for the Parties’ market shares than the top-down approach originally taken
       by the Parties.13
(38)     In this regard, the Notifying Party claims that the Commission’s approach is incorrect
        because  (i) the Parties based the volume and value market totals on a top-down
        approach using a reliable and consistent data source;  (ii) differences between the
         Parties’ potentially imprecise estimates about the distribution of the volumes between
        various competitors combined with their own data from competitors randomly biased
         the market total, and (iii) even though the Commission’s approach with respect to
         integrators makes sense in principle, in practice the data provided by integrators are
         also incomplete and inconsistent, which means the market investigation failed to
         represent the shares of integrators accurately.14
(39)    The Notifying Party argues that the Commission’s approach would have been sensible
            if it had been able to collect consistent and reliable data from practically all of the
         market.15 Furthermore, the Notifying Party argues that, because of the above, the
         Parties’ market size estimates should not be adjusted to reflect the more accurate data
        provided by competitors.16

(40)    The  Notifying  Party  misrepresents   its own  market  shares  methodology. As
       summarised  in  Section 2  of Annex  I  to  the SO and  in Annex QP10.Q28.3
       Methodology Note on Cargo Market Share Calculations, Korean Air only partially
        follows a top-down approach:
          (a)  CASS volumes data are in themselves based on aggregating information and
              data from cargo intermediaries, agents and airlines participating in CASS, and
             can thus not be regarded as a “top-down” data source.
         (b)  Korean Air itself recognizes that CASS does not fully reflect the Parties’ own
               data, and thus CASS market totals need to be revised, see for example paragraph
              (446) of the Form CO and paragraphs (4) and (5) in Annex QP10.Q28.3: “CASS
             does not cover the Parties’ or competitors’ whole business. To compensate for
                 this, the market total  is scaled up according to the proportional difference
             between   the   Parties’  CASS   volumes/revenues   and   their   internal
              volumes/revenues”.
(41)    The Notifying Party misrepresents the accuracy of its own methodology for taking into
        account integrators in the market size calculations. In  fact, the Notifying Party
         estimates integrators’ volumes (which are then added on top of the CASS-based
        market totals) based on combining together multiple different sources. For example, as
       Annex RFI5.Q10 shows, DHL’s estimate is based on:
          (a)   Identifying in the FOIS data airlines that could be transporting cargo on behalf
              of integrators;
         (b)   Identifying in the TRASS data, volumes bound or originating from Korea loaded
              or unloaded in hubs where DHL is based (that is, Anchorage, Hong Kong, and
             Tokyo);
          (c)   Scaling the abovementioned estimates based on the relative difference between
              the Parties’ internal data and the Parties’ data in CASS; and
         (d)  Summing up the estimates obtained in the previous point.
(42)    Because the Parties’ methodology to estimate competitors’ market shares rests on a
       number of assumptions and approximations, it is highly questionable that third party
         actual data gathered by the Commission should be deemed by the Notifying Party of
        lower order of consistency and accuracy.
(43)    The Notifying Party misrepresents the market coverage of the Commission’s exercise.
        For both  routes between Europe and Korea,  third-party  data  gathered by  the
       Commission represents about [70-80]% of the volume market totals, and effectively
          reflects the entirety of integrators’ general cargo business. Although a coverage of
      100% would have clearly been a hypothetically better outcome, because of the
         relatively high market fragmentation, this threshold is only a theoretical possibility,
       and reaching a coverage of around [70-80]% means that a substantial share of the
        market responded to the Commission’s market investigation, with almost all important
        market players, thus ensuring a wide coverage.
(44)     Lastly, because of the aforementioned, it is reasonable to correct market sizes to take
         into  account  discrepancies  between  the  Parties’  estimates  of  competitors  and
        competitors’ actual data (and not just those of the integrators). For those competitors
      who did provide actual data, these actual sales figures on average were lower on the
         route from Europe to South Korea and higher on the route from South Korea to
       Europe than the estimates provided by the Parties. This implies that not using the
         correction would very likely overestimate the Europe to South Korea market size
        underestimate the market size on South Korea to Europe. This is especially striking in
         the latter case as the methodology proposed by the Notifying Party is inherently
         inconsistent insofar as the sum of the Parties’ and their competitors’ volumes is larger

                                             11

[PÁGINA PDF 393]
        than  the market  itself. To address  this  issue,  the Notifying  Party  suggests  to
        compensate for a discrepancy in one competitor’s volumes by adjusting the volumes
         for  all the  airlines where there were no volumes submitted in response to the
         questionnaire and the volumes still rely on the Parties’ estimates, including those that
         are named and those that are only identified as “Others”.17
(45)   As shown further below, the Commission assessed whether market shares would differ
            if market sizes and competitors’ estimates were adjusted as suggested by the Notifying
         Party. This is not the case. Nonetheless, in order to show that the Commission’s
        conclusions do not depend on the methodology followed, the Commission relies on
         the methodology proposed by the Notifying Party in its analysis.

        according to the Notifying Party’s submissions shows that any deviations in market
         shares are very limited at less than [0-5][0-5] percentage points.

         shares were overestimated and some others were underestimated, these discrepancies
       were not substantial and mostly tended to cancel each other out, therefore not affecting
         the Notifying Party’s combined market shares significantly.

2.2.3.   Conclusion
(50)   As indicated in Section 8.11 and 8.12, the Commission based its assessment on the
        Notifying  Party’s  data on  sales  volumes  where  these  sales  volumes do  not
         substantially differ from the outcome of the market reconstruction exercise, namely for
       what concerns volume and value-based market shares. Where instead the Notifying
         Party’s  sales volumes  differed  substantially from  the outcome  of  the  market
         reconstruction, namely for what concerns capacity shares, the Commission primarily
         relied on its own market reconstruction exercise taking into account feedback received
       from the Notifying Party during the Phase 2 Investigation.

3.     EXCESS CAPACITY ANALYSIS
(51)    This section describes the Commission’s analysis of excess capacity in the air cargo
        markets presented in Sections 8.11 and 8.12 of the Decision.
3.1.    Data
(52)    The Commission relied on the Notifying Party’s sales volumes as well as on data
         collected from competitors.
3.1.1.   Data from the Parties
(53)    The market reconstruction exercise described in Section 2 is the starting point of the
       Commission’s analysis.





                                             13

[PÁGINA PDF 395]
3.1.2.   Data from Competitors
(54)    The Commission issued RFIs to  all the major competitors (see Table 4 for an
        overview) to gather three types of information for each route between Europe and
        South Korea:
          (a)   Data and information on how much more cargo competitors could have
              transported on their aircrafts simply by filling up unused space on the aircraft
              (without changing flight schedules). This information was asked for 2019, 2022,
            and 2023.
         (b)   Data and information on how much more cargo competitors could have
              transported (i) by increasing the utilization rate of the aircraft already active on
              the route beyond the usual schedule, (ii) by flying additional aircraft on the
               route; or  (iii) by re-allocating volumes from other destinations on the same
                flights (e.g. substituting 1,000 tons of cargo bound for China or Japan with 1,000
              of cargo bound for Europe). This information was asked for 2019, 2022, and
             2023.
          (c)   Data and information on competitors’ load factor. This information was asked
               for the period between 2018 and 2023.
(55)   As discussed above, to address the Notifying Party’s criticisms, the Commission
        undertook to collect additional data and clarifications from third parties. Further
        information on the data and clarifications provided by each third party is included in
       Appendix I and is made available to the Notifying Party’s external advisors via the
        Data Room Procedure.
(56)    The Commission combined these data sources with the market reconstruction data
        described in Section 2.
3.2.    Methodology
(57)    Excess capacity is defined as the additional volumes a carrier could transport by filling
       up the unused capacity on aircraft entirely (equal to the difference between overall
         capacity and volume transported). This is equal to the difference between overall
         capacity  and  volume  transported  –  also  taking  into  account  cargo  destined
         to/originating from other destinations. For example, carriers flying from a European
        country to South Korea via Japan may load both cargo destined to South Korea and to
        Japan. Not accounting  for  this Japan-destined cargo  will  result  in  substantially
        overestimating the capacity available.
(58)    The data described under paragraph (54)(a) is the primary source of information to
       measure each competitor’s excess capacity.
(59)      If such data is not available, data on the load factor is used instead. Excess capacity is
        thus calculated as capacity multiplied by 100% minus the load factor. For example, if
        competitor A on the route Europe to South Korea has capacity of 10 000 tons and a
        load  factor  of 60%,  then  its  approximate  excess  capacity  will  be  equal  to
        (10 000) * (100% – 60%) = 4 000 tons. As discussed in Section 8.11 and 8.12 of the
        Decision, cargo load factors only rarely approach 100%, therefore this approach would
        tend to overestimate excess capacity.
(60)    Where data on the load factor is not available either, excess capacity is calculated
        based on the weighted average load factor of all other competitors active on the route
         in the year excluding the Parties.





                                             14

[PÁGINA PDF 396]
(61)   To verify the robustness of its results to alternative measurements of excess capacity,
         the Commission’s analysis entails two sensitivities:
          (a)   Sensitivity 1: Where data on excess capacity is not available, excess capacity is
               calculated as capacity multiplied by 100% minus the minimum load factor
           among all competitors active on the route in the year.
         (b)   Sensitivity 2: Excess capacity is calculated as capacity multiplied by 100%
            minus the load factor.
(62)    The Commission’s analysis also relies on the following assumptions:
          (a)   In line with Section 8.4, 2019 data is the starting point for the analysis.18 Data
               for 2019 data is then revised to take into the latest changes to the market
                situation. This implies that:
               (1)   Carriers who entered the routes after 2019 are included, namely MSC Air
                 Cargo and Air Premia.
               (2)  Volumes transported by carriers no longer active (e.g. Russian carriers,
                       Alitalia, Czech  Airlines)  are  reallocated  proportionally  to  the  other
                    competitors.
               (3)  The volumes of operators no longer active are reallocated proportionally
               among other operators already active, while the capacities of operators no
                   longer active are instead excluded from the markets entirely rather than
                   being re-allocated to other competitors.19
         (b)   Excess capacity estimates cannot be greater than the available capacity. If this
             happens, excess capacity estimates are revised to be consistent with capacity and
            volume estimates.
3.3.     Results
3.3.1.   Overall
(63)    Table 12 and Table 13 show the Commission’s estimates for competitors’ excess
         capacity for the route Europe to South Korea and South Korea to Europe, respectively,
        according to the main method and according to two sensitivities where excess capacity
           is  calculated based on  the  load  factor. These  results  are  further  discussed  in
        Section 8.11.4.2 and 8.12.4.2 respectively for the route Europe to South Korea and
        South Korea to Europe. The un-redacted tables are only provided to the Parties
         external advisors in the data room. The figures relied upon by the Commission in this
        Decision are based on the figures included in the RBB Economics Second Data Room
        Report.
(64)    The amount of excess capacity available on the route is benchmarked against the
         Parties’ combined volumes: the Parties would unlikely be able to increase prices post-
       merger if all the Parties’ customers could find an alternative to them (putting aside the
         issue of differentiated capacities). The Parties are expected to have at least some
         incentive to increase prices, however, if only a fraction of the Parties’ customers could



18     One competitor could only provide data for 2022, this was used instead of 2019.
19       This different treatment is motivated by both qualitative and quantitative reasons: (i) it is reasonable to
        expect that the demand served by these carriers did not automatically disappear when these carriers could
       no longer serve it. It is therefore reasonable to reallocate volumes across competitors because most likely
        customers of operators no longer active started looking for other alternative carriers; and (ii) capacity
         calculations are ultimately based on frequency calculations: the disappearance of any of these operators
        did not automatically translate into a proportional increase in the number of frequencies competitors
        could operate on these routes.

                                             15

[PÁGINA PDF 397]
         find an alternative supplier.20 This is because, if capacity is scarce, competitors can
        enjoy some degree of market power, and could be thus able to increase prices to
        customers. Moreover, competitors could in turn also find profitable to follow price
         increases. If competitors are not able to cover the entirety of market demand, the
        merger would enable the merged entity to enjoy an increased degree of market power,
       and be thus capable of increasing prices to customers.21
(65)    This market power-increasing effect of a post-merger increase of the merged entity’s
        excess capacity (relative to the rivals, who are capacity-constrained) would arise even
            if the rivals’ capacity would be perfect substitute of the merged entity’s capacity. Also,
         the rivals’ capacity is not of the same quality as that of the Parties, who are each
         other’s particularly close competitors. This quality differential reinforces the capacity-
        based effect.
(66)    This approach is aligned with the Horizontal Merger Guidelines, paragraphs 32 to 34
        provide that “(32) When market conditions are such that the competitors of the
       merging parties are unlikely to increase their supply substantially if prices increase,
         the merging firms may have an incentive to reduce output below the combined pre-
       merger levels, thereby raising market prices. The merger increases the incentive to
        reduce output by giving the merged firm a larger base of sales on which to enjoy the
        higher margins resulting from an increase in prices induced by the output reduction.
         (33) Conversely, when market conditions are such that rival firms have enough
        capacity and find it profitable to expand output sufficiently, the Commission is unlikely
         to find that the merger will create or strengthen a dominant position or otherwise
         significantly  impede  effective  competition.  (34)  Such  output  expansion  is,  in
         particular, unlikely when competitors face binding capacity constraints.”22 Also,
        paragraph 24 of the Horizontal Merger Guidelines provides that “Non-merging firms
         in the same market can also benefit from the reduction of competitive pressure that
         results from the merger, since the merging firms' price increase may switch some
       demand to the rival firms, which, in turn, may find  it profitable to increase their
         prices. The reduction in these competitive constraints could lead to significant price
        increases in the relevant market.”23
(67)    The sum of all competitors’ excess capacities is around [30-40]% of the Notifying
         Party’s combined volumes on the route Europe to South Korea. This implies that less
        than half of the Notifying Party’s customers could find an alternative supplier other
        than the Parties. Competitors face severely binding capacity constraints and are
         therefore unlikely able to increase their supply sufficiently if prices increase, which
        implies that the merging firms may have an incentive to increase prices.

(69)    The Commission notes  that  the  sensitivities based on  the load  factor tend  to
        overestimate excess capacity. As mentioned above and  in Section 8.11.4.2 and
         8.12.4.2 of the Decision, the load factor as used by the Commission can indicate a
        higher level of excess capacity in the market than is in fact available and is therefore in
       any event likely to overestimate spare capacity that is available on the market. First,

                                             17

[PÁGINA PDF 399]
        excess capacity measured as capacity multiplied by the difference between 100% and
         the load factor implies that 100% is the benchmark for cargo airlines to be considered
         fully utilized. However, this is not the case. Cargo airlines are deemed already fully
         utilized when load factors are around 80-90%. Should a benchmark of 90% be used
         instead of 100%,24 then excess capacity would be substantially lower: [40-50]% on the
         route from Europe to South Korea instead of [60 – 70]% and [90-100]% on the route
       from South Korea to Europe instead of [150-160]%.25 Second, as detailed in the
        Appendix, some carriers measured the load factor using actual weights, which can be
        even up  to [10-20] percentage  points lower  than load  factors measured using
        chargeable  weights.  This  implies  that  these  carriers’  excess  capacity  is  also
         significantly overestimated.

3.3.2.  Change in excess capacity compared to the situation pre-Transaction
(70)    This analysis also shows the excess capacity faced by each of the Parties individually
        pre-merger, e.g. how much was competitors’ excess capacity from Korean Air’s point
        of view, where Asiana is also considered a competitor, and vice versa.
(71)    The merged entity will face significantly less rival excess capacity post-merger than
        each of the merging firms is facing pre-merger. A reduction in the excess capacity
        faced by each of the merging parties also reflects to what extent the merger softens the
        competitive  pressure. As a  result,  the  consolidation  of  levels  of  capacities  as
        encountered in the present case through a merger will, in general, increase the market
       power of the merged entity.
(72)   On Europe to South Korea, pre-merger, Korean Air’s competitors including Asiana
       had excess capacity on Europe to South Korea equivalent to [80-90]% of Korean Air’s
        volumes, which implies that competitors’ (including Asiana) excess capacity already
        could not fully accommodate all Korean Air customers on Europe to South Korea,
        while Asiana’s competitors including Korean Air had excess capacity equivalent to
        around [120-130]% of Asiana’s volumes. Post-merger, the Parties will face less than
         half the excess capacity faced pre-merger by Korean Air and less than a quarter that
        faced by Asiana. The sum of all rivals’ excess capacity will not be sufficient to fully
        cover the Merged Entity’s sales volume, and the Transaction also substantially reduces
      how much excess capacity each of the Parties faced pre-merger. The Merged Entity
       would then likely have an incentive to raise prices post-merger.

         Air’s volumes, which implies that competitors’ (including Asiana) excess capacity
        already could more than fully accommodate all Korean Air customers on South Korea
         to Europe, while Asiana’s competitors including Korean Air had excess capacity
         equivalent to around [400-410]% of Asiana’s volumes. Post-merger, the Parties will
         face about half the excess capacity faced pre-merger by Korean Air and less than a

3.3.3.   Differentiated capacity and fragmented supply
(74)    The Phase  II investigation confirms  that customers regard capacity in cargo as
         differentiated (see also sections 8.11.2 and 8.11.3). For example, non-stop connections
        with air cargo carriers like the Notifying Parties, [names of competitors] generally
         represent a higher value […]. Should therefore only [names of competitors] excess
         capacity be considered, that is, only those offers that most resemble the Notifying
         Party’s offer be considered, then the available excess capacities would be much lower.
         In fact, as explained above, the Parties are close (or even closest) competitors of each
         other. This means that, in the event of a price increase post-merger, a large share of the
        Notifying Party’s customers would likely not switch to an alternative supplier capable
        of offering an inferior type of capacity (as compared to that offered by the Parties) at
         the same pre-merger prices. These customers will then be worse-off because they will
         either endure the increased prices or switched to a less favorite types of connection
         (for example, with transhipment or via integrators). Moreover, customers switching
       away from the Parties would present a windfall demand for the Notifying Party’s
         competitors, who themselves will also have then an incentive to raise their prices.
       These post-merger pricing incentives of the Parties and their rivals stemming from the
         close (or even particularly close) competition between the Parties could be present
        even in absence of the rival capacity constraints. The capacity constraints explained
       above and the closeness based arguments are then reinforcing each other.
(75)     In the event of a price increase post-merger, a large share of the Parties’ customers
       would likely not switch to an alternative supplier capable of offering an inferior type
        of capacity (as compared to that offered by the Parties) at the same pre-merger prices.
       These customers will then be worse-off because they will either endure the increased
         prices  or  switched  to a  less  favorite  types  of  connection  (for example,  with
        transhipment or via integrators). Moreover, customers switching away from the Parties
       would present a windfall demand for the Parties’ competitors, who themselves will
         also have then an incentive to raise their prices. These post-merger pricing incentives
        of the Parties and their rivals’ stemming from the close (or even particularly close)
        competition between the Parties could be present even in absence of the rival capacity
         constraints.26

(79)   A closer examination of the results below further clarify how limited excess capacity
         actually is in both relevant markets, well beyond the aggregate results. In fact, about
       [10-20]% of excess capacity on the route from Europe to South Korea and about
       [10-20]% of excess capacity on the route from South Korea to Europe are due to a
         single competitor. Despite the numerous attempts, the Commission could not reach out
         to this competitor, and the excess capacity estimates are therefore exclusively based on
         the parties’ volume and capacity estimates and on the average load factors. On the
         routes between Europe and South Korea, this competitor had market shares between
        [0-5]% and [0-5]% in 2019, between [0-5]% and [0-5]% in 2020, and close to [0-5]%
         in 2021: It is highly unlikely this competitor could suddenly decide to dedicate their
        excess  capacity  to  the  affected markets  considering how  limited  their  current
        involvement is.
3.4.    Conclusion
(80)   As indicated in Section 8.11 and 8.12, the Commission’s analysis suggests that limited
        excess capacity exists on the routes between Europe and South Korea: Competitors are
        unable to expand output sufficiently to counteract an increase in prices post-merger,
        nor to deter it in the first place.
(81)    Capacity constraints are also further exacerbated by the extent to which customers
        perceive capacity to be differentiated. On both routes, the impact of the Transaction is
        such that the merged entity would face rival excess capacity not sufficient to fully
        cover the merged entity’s sales volume, which is also substantially smaller than what
        each of the Parties faced pre-merger. The merged entity would then likely have an
         incentive to raise prices post-merger.
(82)   On the route from Europe to South Korea, the impact of the Transaction is such that
         the merged entity would face rival excess capacity not sufficient to fully cover the
       merged entity’s sales volume, and thus competitors are unable to expand output
         sufficiently to counteract an increase in prices post-merger, nor to deter it in the first
         place.
(83)   On the route from South Korea to Europe, even though excess capacity is higher than
       on the route from Europe to South Korea, competitors are unlikely able to expand
        output sufficiently to counteract an increase in prices post-merger, nor to deter it in the
           first place.
(84)    Capacity constraints are also further exacerbated by the extent to which capacity is
         differentiated and significantly fragmented across a large number of competitors. On
         the route from Europe to South Korea, no competitor’s excess capacity exceeds
       [5-10]% of the Parties’ combined volumes, and a long tail of competitors has excess
         capacity below [0-5]%, while on the route from South Korea to Europe, only six
        competitors have excess  capacity exceeding [5-10]%  of  the  Parties’ combined
        volumes, and a long tail of competitors has excess capacity below [0-5]%.
(85)    The amount of excess capacity faced by the Parties is also substantially smaller than
       what each of the Parties faced pre-merger. This reduction in countervailing capacity
        reduces the competitive pressure on the merged entity relative to the competitive
         pressure on each of the merging firms pre-merger. The merged entity would then
         likely have an incentive to raise prices post-merger.

4.     APPENDIX I - OVERVIEW COMPETITOR BY COMPETITOR
(86)    This section provides an additional overview of the information provided by each
        competitor in order to address the criticisms raised in the Data Room Report to the
         extent not already addressed in the above. The order in which the competitors are
          listed reflects the order followed in the Data Room Report, which was randomised to
        ensure confidentiality. The following list has been made confidential, the Notifying
        Party has had access to all details via the Data Room procedure.
4.1.    Competitor
4.1.1.   The Notifying Party’s view
(87)    The Notifying Party highlighted that (i) the Commission did not to seek clarification
       on the appropriate load factor to use nor to develop an approach to identifying an
         appropriate load factor estimate in the case of transhipment carriers, and therefore
         relied on an average of  all known competitors’ load factors instead; and  (ii) the
        respondent did not provide figures about the amount of volumes that could be
         reallocated from China and Japan to Korea, and the Notifying Party argues “it is
         certain that the respondent has a sizable portion of its capacity taken up by volumes
         destined for China or Japan. The absence of figures in this regard is a significant
        omission, and may have a material effect on the analysis of competitive constraints
        facing the Parties.”27
4.1.2.   The Commission’s view
(88)    With respect to the  first remark, the respondent clarified that the load factor  is
         calculated based on actual weight against the defined aircraft capacity and the load
         factor in the case of transhipment was based on applying the highest load factor
       between the two legs to the whole route. Section 3.2 above shows nonetheless that
         alternative definition for the load factors or to aggregate multiple legs would not result
         in a material change.
(89)    With respect to the second remark, the Commission sought from the respondent the
        removal of a number of confidentiality claims from certain answers to permit to the
        Notifying Party’s external advisors to understand better the absence of competitive
         constraints faced by the Parties as the respondent would not consider transporting
         additional volume on the routes between Europe and South Korea. More specifically,
         as the non-confidential version of the minutes now clearly shows, the respondent did
        not provide figures about the amount of volumes that could be reallocated from China
       and Japan  to Korea because  “Realistically, [CONFIDENTIAL] would not make
         additional cargo capacity available for South Korea, even  if there were additional
        capacity available. [redacted - Given the relative commercial positioning of other
         routes] [CONFIDENTIAL]  is [redacted] unlikely to substitute cargo from those
         origins for South Korea cargo.” Furthermore, the respondent also clarified that: “there
        could be a situation where we may have space on some flights, but we may not be
        using  it on the Europe-Korea traffic route. [redacted  - Given Space Utilisation]
        between [CONFIDENTIAL] and Europe redacted, on average, there may not be much
        spare capacity available for South Korea cargo.”28
4.2.    Competitor
4.2.1.   The Notifying Party’s view
(90)    The Notifying Party highlighted that (i) the respondent provided data for volumes, but
        not for their capacity or their spare capacity; (ii) the unit used for volumes was actual
        weight in tonnes, and since market totals are based on chargeable weight, which for

27    RBB Economics Data Room Report, pages 31-32
28       Non-confidential version of RFI [CONFIDENTIAL].

        each shipment is at least as high as the actual weight, but for shipments with lower
         density, chargeable weight is higher than actual weight, this implies that the size of the
        respondent is understated; and (iii) the respondent only provided information on the
        load factor, but not on spare capacities.29
4.2.2.   The Commission’s view
(91)    With respect to the above remarks, the Commission that (i) in follow up requests the
        respondent provided data on capacity; (ii) the respondent could not provide data in
        chargeable weight, and indicated that the percentage difference between chargeable
        weight and actual weight volumes was likely greater than [5-10]%. A correction based
       on the Notifying Party’s average percentage difference for belly-hold for the two
         routes was applied; (iii) the respondent provided a measure of excess capacity based
       on the load factor, which is exactly the same approach the Notifying Party followed it
           its reply to RFI 21. It is unclear why the Notifying Party could deem reasonable to rely
       on the load factor to quantify the amount of additional capacity currently unused by
         other trades that they could add to the route between Europe and South Korea, while
          this information should be disregarded if provided by other carriers.30
4.3.    Competitor
4.3.1.   The Notifying Party’s view
(92)    The Notifying Party highlighted  that  (i)  the respondent only responded  to  the
       Commission’s market reconstruction questionnaire and not to the Phase II market
         investigation questionnaire about excess capacity; (ii) the data are likely erroneous and
       no sufficient commentary was provided; and (iii) the data provided by the respondent
         are not taken into account.31
4.3.2.   The Commission’s view
(93)    The Commission note that the respondent is not treated as a competitor directly active
       on the affected markets because its capacity is actually offered to other carriers and not
         to cargo customers. Contrary to what submitted by the Notifying Party,  this  is

                     CASE M.10149 – Korean Air / Asiana

             COMMITMENTS TO THE EUROPEAN COMMISSION

Pursuant to Article 8(2) of Council Regulation (EC) No. 139/2004 (the “Merger Regulation”), Korean Air
Co., Ltd (“Korean Air”) hereby enters into the following commitments (the “Passenger Commitments”) vis-
à-vis the European Commission (the “Commission”) with a view to rendering the acquisition of sole control
by Korean Air over Asiana Airlines Inc. (“Asiana”, and, together with Korean Air, the “Parties”), within the
meaning of Article 3(1)(b) of the Merger Regulation (the “Transaction”), compatible with the internal market
and the functioning of the EEA Agreement.

This text shall be interpreted in light of the Commission’s decision pursuant to Article 8(2) of the Merger
Regulation to declare the Transaction compatible with the internal market and the functioning of the EEA
Agreement (the “Decision”), in the general framework of European Union law, in particular in light of the
Merger Regulation, and by reference to the Commission Notice on remedies acceptable under Council
Regulation (EC) No. 139/2004 and under Commission Regulation (EC) No. 802/2004 (the “Remedies
Notice”).

These Passenger Commitments shall take effect upon the date of adoption of the Decision. Korean Air commits
to ensuring that these Passenger Commitments will be binding on any successor company arising from the
Transaction.
